1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Capped Ramp OGF & Degree-Bounded Infinite Product
We want to compute \([x^M] \prod_{i=1}^{N} F_i(x)\) where \(F_i(x) = \sum_{a=1}^{\infty} \min(i, a) x^a\), given \(N \le M \le 2N\).

Closed Form of the Single-Factor Capped Ramp \(F_i(x)\): For a fixed cap \(i \ge 1\), the coefficients of \(F_i(x)\) are \(1, 2, 3, \dots, i, i, i, \dots\). Multiply \(F_i(x)\) by \(1 - x\) to take first differences: \[(1 - x) F_i(x) = x + x^2 + x^3 + \dots + x^i = \frac{x(1 - x^i)}{1 - x}.\] Dividing by \(1 - x\) gives the rational closed form: \[F_i(x) = \frac{x(1 - x^i)}{(1 - x)^2}.\] (Contrast with a truncated ramp \(\sum_{a=1}^{i} a x^a = \frac{x(1 - (i+1)x^i + i x^{i+1})}{(1 - x)^2}\): because \(\min(i, a)\) stays flat at \(i\) for \(a > i\) instead of dropping to \(0\), its numerator is simply the binomial \(x(1 - x^i)\)!)
Assembling the \(N\)-Factor Product & Exploiting \(M \le 2N\): Multiplying \(F_i(x)\) over \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N\) gives: \[\prod_{i=1}^{N} F_i(x) = x^N (1 - x)^{-2N} \prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - x^i).\] Set \(K := M - N\). Since \(N \le M \le 2N\), we have \(0 \le K \le N\), and we need: \[\text{Ans} = [x^M] \prod_{i=1}^{N} F_i(x) = [x^K] \left( (1 - x)^{-2N} \prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - x^i) \right).\] Now look at the missing tail factors \(\prod_{i = N + 1}^{\infty} (1 - x^i) = 1 - x^{N+1} - x^{N+2} + \dots\): every non-constant term in this tail has degree \(\ge N + 1 > K\)! Therefore, in the quotient ring \(K[[x]] / (x^{K+1})\), replacing the finite product \(\prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - x^i)\) by the infinite Euler product \(\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (1 - x^i)\) changes nothing at or below degree \(K\): \[\prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - x^i) \equiv \prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (1 - x^i) = \sum_{k = -\infty}^{\infty} (-1)^k x^{\omega_k} \pmod{x^{K+1}},\] where \(\omega_k = \frac{k(3k - 1)}{2}\) are the generalized pentagonal numbers (Ch 03 §3.3)!



2. \(O(P + \sqrt{M - N} \log_P M)\) Extraction via Euler’s Pentagonal Theorem & Lucas’s Theorem
Expanding \((1 - x)^{-2N} = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} \binom{2N + r - 1}{2N - 1} x^r\) and convolving at degree \(K = M - N\) gives: \[\text{Ans} = \sum_{\substack{k \in \mathbb{Z} \\ \omega_k \le K}} (-1)^k \binom{2N + K - \omega_k - 1}{2N - 1} \pmod{P}.\] Since \(\omega_k = \frac{k(3k - 1)}{2} \le K \le 10^{12}\), there are only \(O(\sqrt{K}) \le 1.6 \times 10^6\) nonzero pentagonal terms! For the prime modulus \(P = 200003\), we precompute factorials up to \(P - 1\) in \(O(P)\) time and evaluate each binomial coefficient \(\binom{2N + K - \omega_k - 1}{2N - 1} \bmod P\) in \(O(\log_P M)\) steps using Lucas’s Theorem (Ch 06): \[\binom{A}{B} \equiv \prod_{j \ge 0} \binom{A_j}{B_j} \pmod{P}.\]
(Connection to the General Upper-Bound Variant \(\prod_{i=1}^{N} \min(B_i, A_i)\) for \(N, M \le 2 \times 10^5 \bmod 998244353\)): When the caps \(B_1, \dots, B_N\) are arbitrary positive integers, the product becomes \([x^{M-N}] (1 - x)^{-2N} \prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - x^{B_i})\). By grouping identical exponents \(c_s = \lvert \{i : B_i = s\} \rvert\) (Ch 03 §3.2), we compute \(\ln \prod_{s=1}^{K} (1 - x^s)^{c_s} = -\sum_{s=1}^{K} c_s \sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor K/s \rfloor} \frac{x^{s j}}{j}\) in \(O(K \log K)\) harmonic time and exponentiate via a single polynomial \(\exp\) in \(O(K \log K)\) time (or multiply the binomial factors \((1 - x^{B_i})\) via a Ch 09 §9.1 divide-and-conquer product tree in \(O(M \log^2 M)\) time).


3. Verification on the Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 2, M = 4\) and \(N = 3, M = 5\))

\(N = 2, M = 4\) (\(K = 2\)): Pentagonal numbers \(\omega_k \le 2\) are \(\omega_0 = 0, \omega_1 = 1, \omega_{-1} = 2\): \[\binom{4 + 2 - 0 - 1}{3} - \binom{4 + 2 - 1 - 1}{3} - \binom{4 + 2 - 2 - 1}{3} = \binom{5}{3} - \binom{4}{3} - \binom{3}{3} = 10 - 4 - 1 = \mathbf{5}.\]
\(N = 3, M = 5\) (\(K = 2\)): \[\binom{6 + 2 - 0 - 1}{5} - \binom{6 + 2 - 1 - 1}{5} - \binom{6 + 2 - 2 - 1}{5} = \binom{7}{5} - \binom{6}{5} - \binom{5}{5} = 21 - 6 - 1 = \mathbf{14}.\] Both match Stage 1!







WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Applying the Infinite Pentagonal Product When \(M > 2N\)




Failure Mode: If \(M > 2N\) (so \(K = M - N > N\)), the infinite product \(\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (1 - x^i)\) includes extraneous factors \((1 - x^{N+1})(1 - x^{N+2})\cdots\) that alter coefficients at degrees \(\ge N + 1\), making the pentagonal formula incorrect for \(K > N\).
Remedy: Always check the degree window \(K = M - N \le N\) before replacing \(\prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - x^i)\) by \(\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (1 - x^i)\)! (If \(N < K \le 2N + 1\), one can expand the first tail correction \(\prod_{i=N+1}^{\infty}(1 - x^i)^{-1} \equiv 1 + \sum_{j=N+1}^{K} p(j - (N+1)) x^j\), whereas here \(M \le 2N\) guarantees \(K \le N\) directly.)









NoteAlgorithm Contract: Pentagonal + Lucas Extraction (ABC 279 Ex)




Input: Integers \(N \in [1, 10^{12}]\) and \(M \in [N, 2N]\).
Preconditions: Prime modulus \(P = 200003\); \(K = M - N \le N\).
Output: \(\sum_{A_1+\dots+A_N=M} \prod_{i=1}^N \min(i, A_i) \bmod 200003\).
Complexity: \(O(P + \sqrt{M - N} \log_P M)\) time and \(O(P)\) space.
Core Invariant: Every \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\) with \(\omega_k = k(3k - 1)/2 \le K\) is visited exactly once (\(k = 0\), followed by \(k = +1, -1, +2, -2, \dots\)), accumulating \((-1)^k \binom{2N + K - \omega_k - 1}{2N - 1} \bmod P\).



long long K = M - N, ans = lucas(2 * N + K - 1, 2 * N - 1);
for (long long k = 1; ; ++k) {
    long long w1 = k * (3 * k - 1) / 2;
    if (w1 > K) break;
    long long term1 = lucas(2 * N + K - w1 - 1, 2 * N - 1);
    ans = (k & 1) ? (ans - term1 + P) % P : (ans + term1) % P;
    long long w2 = k * (3 * k + 1) / 2;
    if (w2 <= K) {
        long long term2 = lucas(2 * N + K - w2 - 1, 2 * N - 1);
        ans = (k & 1) ? (ans - term2 + P) % P : (ans + term2) % P;
    }
}











NoteComplete Solution — CP-III.7 (#205: Luogu P8555 — Small-Characteristic Implicit Tree Power)






1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Bypassing \(\frac{1}{n}\) in Characteristic \(p\)
We are given \(F(x) = x \Phi(F(x))\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with \(\deg \Phi = d \le 5\), \(p \le 10^5\), and \(1 \le k \le n \le 10^{18}\), and we must compute \([x^n] F(x)^k \bmod p\).

Why Classical LIF Crashes & How Formal Residue Calculus Fixes It (Ch 11 §11.4): In Classical Lagrange Inversion (Ch 11 §11.2, Form 1), \([x^n] F(x)^k = \frac{k}{n} [u^{n-k}] \Phi(u)^n\). Whenever \(p \mid n\), \(n \equiv 0 \pmod p\) has no multiplicative inverse in \(\mathbb{F}_p\), and \([u^{n-k}]\Phi(u)^n\) also vanishes in \(\mathbb{F}_p\), creating a \(0 / 0\) division-by-zero failure! Let us go back to the Formal Residue Change-of-Variables Theorem (Ch 11 §11.1) without ever dividing by \(n\): Since \(F(x) = x \Phi(F(x))\) with \(\Phi(0) \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\), the map \(u = F(x)\) is reversible with inverse: \[x = \frac{u}{\Phi(u)}.\] Differentiate \(x = u \Phi(u)^{-1}\) formally with respect to \(u\) (using only the quotient rule, which divides only by \(\Phi(0) \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\), never by \(n\)!): \[dx = \frac{\Phi(u) - u \Phi'(u)}{\Phi(u)^2}\,du.\] Substitute \(F(x) = u\), \(x = \frac{u}{\Phi(u)}\), and \(dx\) directly into the residue extraction of \([x^n] F(x)^k\): \[\begin{aligned}
[x^n] F(x)^k &= \operatorname{res}_x \Big( F(x)^k \, x^{-n-1} \, dx \Big) \\
&= \operatorname{res}_u \left( u^k \left(\frac{\Phi(u)}{u}\right)^{n+1} \frac{\Phi(u) - u \Phi'(u)}{\Phi(u)^2}\,du \right) \\
&= \operatorname{res}_u \Big( u^{-(n - k) - 1} \big(\Phi(u) - u \Phi'(u)\big) \Phi(u)^{n - 1}\,du \Big) \\
&= [u^{n - k}] \Big( \big(\Phi(u) - u \Phi'(u)\big) \, \Phi(u)^{n - 1} \Big).
\end{aligned}\] Look at this Derivative-Free LIF Formula (Ch 11 §11.2, Form 3 / Variant B):

It uses only polynomial addition, multiplication, and the formal derivative \(\Phi'(u) = \sum_{i=1}^{d} i c_i u^{i-1}\).
It has zero divisions! Therefore, it holds universally over \(\mathbb{Z}\) and over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) even when \(p \mid n\)!




2. Base-\(p\) Frobenius Digit Decimation for \(n \le 10^{18}\)
Let \(A(u) := \Phi(u) - u \Phi'(u)\) (which has degree \(\le d\)), \(K := n - k \ge 0\), and \(M := n - 1 \ge 0\). We need to compute: \[[u^K] \big( A(u) \, \Phi(u)^M \big) \pmod{p}.\] Over \(\mathbb{F}_p\), the Frobenius endomorphism \((X + Y)^p \equiv X^p + Y^p \pmod p\) implies that for any polynomial \(\Phi(u) \in \mathbb{F}_p[u]\): \[\Phi(u)^p \equiv \Phi(u^p) \pmod{p}.\] Write \(K\) and \(M\) in base \(p\) by extracting their lowest base-\(p\) digits \(k_0 = K \bmod p\) and \(m_0 = M \bmod p\), so \(K = p K' + k_0\) and \(M = p M' + m_0\) with \(K' = \lfloor K / p \rfloor\) and \(M' = \lfloor M / p \rfloor\). Then: \[A(u) \, \Phi(u)^M = A(u) \, \Phi(u)^{p M' + m_0} \equiv \Big( A(u) \, \Phi(u)^{m_0} \Big) \cdot \Phi(u^p)^{M'} \pmod{p}.\] Notice that \(\Phi(u^p)^{M'}\) is a polynomial in \(u^p\): all of its nonzero terms have exponents congruent to \(0 \pmod p\)! Therefore, when we extract \([u^{p K' + k_0}]\) from the product \(\big(A(u) \Phi(u)^{m_0}\big) \cdot \Phi(u^p)^{M'}\), only the terms in \(B(u) := A(u) \Phi(u)^{m_0}\) whose exponents are congruent to \(k_0 \pmod p\) can contribute! Define the decimated polynomial: \[A_{\text{next}}(u) := \sum_{j \ge 0} \Big( [u^{p j + k_0}] \big( A(u) \, \Phi(u)^{m_0} \big) \Big) u^j.\] What is the degree of \(A_{\text{next}}(u)\)? If \(\deg A \le d\), then \(\deg\big(A(u)\Phi(u)^{m_0}\big) \le d + m_0 d \le p d\), so \(p j + k_0 \le p d \implies j \le d\)! Thus \(\deg A_{\text{next}} \le d\) is preserved at every single digit step! Repeating the update \((A, K, M) \leftarrow (A_{\text{next}}, \lfloor K/p \rfloor, \lfloor M/p \rfloor)\) until \(K = 0\) and \(M = 0\) (about \(\log_p n \le 60\) iterations) returns \(A(0) \bmod p\).


3. Verification on the Hand-Checkable Trace (\(p = 3, \Phi(u) = 1 + u + u^2, n = 3, k = 1\))

Initial state: \(A(u) = (1 + u + u^2) - u(1 + 2u) = 1 - u^2 \equiv 1 + 2u^2 \pmod 3\), \(K = n - k = 2\), \(M = n - 1 = 2\).
Step 1 (\(k_0 = 2, m_0 = 2\)): \[B(u) = A(u) \Phi(u)^2 = (1 - u^2)(1 + 2u + 3u^2 + 2u^3 + u^4) \equiv (1 + 2u^2)(1 + 2u + 2u^3 + u^4) \pmod 3.\] The coefficient of \(u^2\) (\(j = 0, p j + k_0 = 2\)) in \(B(u)\) is \(1 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 1 = \mathbf{2} \pmod 3\).
Next state: \(A_{\text{next}}(u) = 2\), \(K' = 0, M' = 0 \implies\) returns \(A(0) = \mathbf{2}\). Matches Stage 1!







WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Computing \(\Phi(u)^{m_0}\) via \(\exp(m_0 \ln \Phi(u))\) When \(m_0 d \ge p\)




Failure Mode: Even within a single base-\(p\) digit step (\(0 \le m_0 < p\)), \(\Phi(u)^{m_0}\) has degree \(m_0 d \le 5(p - 1)\), which exceeds \(p\) whenever \(m_0 \ge 1\). Attempting to compute \(\Phi(u)^{m_0}\) using polynomial \(\ln\) and \(\exp\) crashes with division by zero at index \(p\)!
Remedy: Because \(\deg \Phi = d \le 5\) is tiny and \(m_0 < p\), compute \(A(u) \Phi(u)^{m_0}\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p[u]\) via binary exponentiation of \(\Phi(u)\) using polynomial multiplication, which requires zero divisions and runs in \(O(d p \log(dp))\) time per digit!









NoteAlgorithm Contract: Characteristic-\(p\) LIF via Frobenius Digit Decimation (Luogu P8555)




Input: \(n, k \in [1, 10^{18}]\) (\(k \le n\)), prime \(p \le 10^5\), polynomial \(\Phi(u)\) of degree \(d \le 5\) with \(\Phi(0) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\).
Preconditions: Prime modulus \(2 \le p \le 10^5\) (where \(p \mid n\) is permitted); \(\Phi(0) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\).
Output: \([x^n] F(x)^k \bmod p\).
Complexity: \(O(d p \log(dp) \log_p n)\) time and \(O(d p)\) space.
Core Invariant: At the start of each loop iteration, \([u^K]\big(A(u)\Phi(u)^M\big) \equiv [x^n]F(x)^k \pmod p\) and \(\deg A \le d\).



Poly A(d + 1, 0); // A(u) = Phi(u) - u * Phi'(u) mod p
for (int i = 0; i <= d; ++i)
    A[i] = (Phi[i] - 1LL * i * Phi[i] % p + p) % p;
long long K = n - k, M = n - 1;
while (K > 0 || M > 0) {
    int k0 = K % p, m0 = M % p;
    Poly B = poly_mul_mod_p(A, poly_pow_mod_p(Phi, m0, p), p); // degree <= d * p
    Poly A_next(d + 1, 0);
    for (int j = 0; j <= d && j * p + k0 < (int)B.size(); ++j)
        A_next[j] = B[j * p + k0];
    A = move(A_next);
    K /= p; M /= p;
}
return A[0];











NoteComplete Solution — CP-III.8 (#163: Luogu P5206 — [WC2019] Counting Trees)






1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Subset Expansion & Generalized Cayley Forest Completion
We must evaluate \(\sum_{T_1, T_2} y^{n - \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert} \pmod{998244353}\) across three modes \(\text{op} \in \{0, 1, 2\}\).

The \(y = 1\) Edge Case & Binomial Subset Linearization (Ch 04 / Ch 08):

First, if \(y = 1\), then \(1^{n - \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert} = 1\) for every pair \((T_1, T_2)\). Since \(\lvert \mathcal{T}_n \rvert = n^{n-2}\) by Cayley’s formula, we immediately output \(1\) (\(\text{op} = 0\)), \(n^{n-2} \bmod p\) (\(\text{op} = 1\)), or \(n^{2n-4} \bmod p\) (\(\text{op} = 2\)).
Now assume \(y \neq 1\). Notice how hard it is to count pairs of trees with an exact edge intersection \(E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) = S\), vs. how easy it is to require that both trees contain a given forest \(S \subseteq E(T_1) \cap E(T_2)\)! Write \(y^{n - \lvert E_1 \cap E_2 \rvert} = y^n (y^{-1})^{\lvert E_1 \cap E_2 \rvert}\) and apply the binomial identity \((y^{-1})^m = \big(1 + (y^{-1} - 1)\big)^m = \sum_{S} (y^{-1} - 1)^{\lvert S \rvert}\): \[y^{n - \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert} = y^n \sum_{S \subseteq E(T_1) \cap E(T_2)} (y^{-1} - 1)^{\lvert S \rvert}.\]

Generalized Cayley Theorem via Symbolic Matrix-Tree (Ch 13 §13.4): Suppose \(S\) is a spanning forest on \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) with \(\lvert S \rvert = n - k\) edges, so \(S\) partitions \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) into \(k\) connected components \(C_1, C_2, \dots, C_k\) of vertex sizes \(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_k\) (\(\sum_{i=1}^{k} s_i = n\)). How many labeled trees \(T \in \mathcal{T}_n\) satisfy \(S \subseteq E(T)\)? By contracting each component \(C_i\) into a super-vertex and applying the weighted Matrix-Tree Theorem (Ch 13 §13.4, where an edge between \(C_i\) and \(C_j\) can be chosen in \(s_i s_j\) ways), the number of spanning trees on \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) containing \(S\) is: \[\#\{ T \in \mathcal{T}_n : S \subseteq E(T) \} = n^{k - 2} \prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i.\]



2. Solving All Three Modes (\(\text{op} = 0, 1, 2\))

Mode \(\text{op} = 0\) (\(T_1, T_2\) both fixed, \(O(n)\) or \(O(n \log n)\)): Insert the \(n - 1\) edges of \(T_1\) into a hash table (or sorted array), count how many edges of \(T_2\) belong to \(E(T_1)\) to get \(c = \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert\), and return \(y^{n - c} \bmod p\).
Mode \(\text{op} = 1\) (\(T_1\) fixed, \(T_2 \in \mathcal{T}_n\) variable, \(O(n)\) Tree DP): Swapping the sum over \(T_2 \in \mathcal{T}_n\) and the sum over \(S \subseteq E(T_1)\) gives: \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Ans}_{\text{op}=1} &= y^n \sum_{S \subseteq E(T_1)} (y^{-1} - 1)^{n - k} \cdot \#\{ T_2 \in \mathcal{T}_n : S \subseteq E(T_2) \} \\
&= y^n \sum_{S \subseteq E(T_1)} \left(\frac{1 - y}{y}\right)^{n - k} n^{k - 2} \prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i \\
&= \frac{(1 - y)^n}{n^2} \sum_{S \subseteq E(T_1)} \prod_{i=1}^{k} \left( \frac{n y}{1 - y} \, s_i \right).
\end{aligned}\] Let \(w := \frac{n y}{1 - y} \bmod p\). What does \(\sum_{S \subseteq E(T_1)} \prod_{i=1}^{k} (w \cdot s_i)\) count combinatorially on the tree \(T_1\)? Choosing \(S \subseteq E(T_1)\) deletes \(k - 1\) edges of \(T_1\) to form \(k\) components \(C_1, \dots, C_k\), and the factor \(w \cdot s_i\) chooses one marked vertex inside each component \(C_i\) and multiplies by \(w\)! This is computed in \(O(n)\) time by a 2-state tree DP on \(T_1\):

dp[u][0]: weight of the subtree at \(u\) when the component containing \(u\) has not yet chosen its marked vertex.
dp[u][1]: weight of the subtree at \(u\) when the component containing \(u\) has already chosen its marked vertex. When merging child \(v\) into \(u\), the edge \((u, v)\) is either deleted (\(\notin S\), so \(v\)’s component is closed and contributes dp[v][1]) or kept (\(\in S\), so \(v\)’s component merges with \(u\)’s component): \[\begin{aligned}
\text{dp}[u][1] &\leftarrow \text{dp}[u][1] \cdot \big(\text{dp}[v][1] + \text{dp}[v][0]\big) + \text{dp}[u][0] \cdot \text{dp}[v][1], \\
\text{dp}[u][0] &\leftarrow \text{dp}[u][0] \cdot \big(\text{dp}[v][1] + \text{dp}[v][0]\big),
\end{aligned}\] initialized with \(\text{dp}[u][0] = 1, \text{dp}[u][1] = w\) for each vertex \(u\). Then \(\text{Ans}_{\text{op}=1} = \frac{(1 - y)^n}{n^2} \, \text{dp}[\text{root}][1] \pmod p\).

Mode \(\text{op} = 2\) (Both \(T_1, T_2 \in \mathcal{T}_n\) variable, \(O(n \log n)\) EGF \(\exp\)): Swapping the sum over \(T_1, T_2 \in \mathcal{T}_n\) with the sum over all spanning forests \(S\) on \(\{1, \dots, n\}\): Every forest \(S\) with \(k = n - \lvert S \rvert\) components of sizes \(s_1, \dots, s_k\) is contained in \(n^{k - 2} \prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i\) trees \(T_1\) and in \(n^{k - 2} \prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i\) trees \(T_2\)! Thus: \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Ans}_{\text{op}=2} &= y^n \sum_{\text{forests } S} \left(\frac{1 - y}{y}\right)^{n - k} \left(n^{k - 2} \prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i\right)^2 \\
&= \frac{(1 - y)^n}{n^4} \sum_{\text{forests } S} \prod_{i=1}^{k} \left( \frac{n^2 y}{1 - y} \, s_i^2 \right).
\end{aligned}\] How many internal spanning trees does a labeled component of size \(s\) have? By Cayley’s formula, \(s^{s - 2}\) (with \(1^{-1} := 1\) for \(s = 1\)). Multiplying by \(\frac{n^2 y}{1 - y} s^2\) gives the single-component weight: \[w_s = \frac{n^2 y}{1 - y} \cdot s^{s - 2} \cdot s^2 = \frac{n^2 y}{1 - y} \, s^s.\] Since a spanning forest \(S\) is an unlabeled SET of labeled connected tree components (Ch 08 §8.2), the Exponential Formula yields: \[\text{Ans}_{\text{op}=2} = \frac{(1 - y)^n}{n^4} \, n! \, [x^n] \exp\!\left( \sum_{s=1}^{n} \frac{n^2 y}{1 - y} \frac{s^s}{s!} x^s \right) \pmod{998244353}.\]



3. Verification on the Hand-Checkable Trace (\(n = 3\))
Let us check \(\text{op} = 2\) for \(n = 3\) using the EGF \(\exp\) formula! Let \(c = \frac{3^2 y}{1 - y} = \frac{9y}{1 - y}\). The component EGF is \(C(x) = c \left(\frac{1^1}{1!} x + \frac{2^2}{2!} x^2 + \frac{3^3}{3!} x^3\right) = c \left(x + 2x^2 + \frac{9}{2} x^3\right)\). Then: \[3! [x^3] \exp\big(C(x)\big) = 6 \left( \frac{9}{2} c + 2 c^2 + \frac{1}{6} c^3 \right) = 27 c + 12 c^2 + c^3.\] Multiplying by \(\frac{(1 - y)^3}{3^4} = \frac{(1 - y)^3}{81}\) and substituting \(c = \frac{9y}{1 - y}\): \[\frac{(1 - y)^3}{81} \left( 27 \frac{9y}{1-y} + 12 \frac{81y^2}{(1-y)^2} + \frac{729y^3}{(1-y)^3} \right) = 3y(1 - y)^2 + 12y^2(1 - y) + 9y^3 = 3y + 6y^2,\] matching Stage 1 identically!






WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Division by Zero at \(y = 1\) in \((1 - y)^{-1}\)




Failure Mode: Both the \(\text{op} = 1\) formula and the \(\text{op} = 2\) EGF formula divide by \(1 - y\) inside the component weights \(\frac{n y}{1 - y}\) and \(\frac{n^2 y}{1 - y}\). If the input has \(y = 1\), computing \((1 - y)^{-1} \bmod 998244353\) divides by zero!
Remedy: Always check if (y == 1) at the very start of the program and return \(1\) (\(\text{op} = 0\)), \(n^{n-2} \bmod p\) (\(\text{op} = 1\)), or \(n^{2n-4} \bmod p\) (\(\text{op} = 2\)) before any division by \(1 - y\).









NoteAlgorithm Contract: Shared-Forest Tree Enumeration (Luogu P5206)




Input: Integer \(n \in [1, 10^5]\), weight \(y \in [0, 998244353)\), mode \(\text{op} \in \{0, 1, 2\}\), and \(2 - \text{op}\) trees on \(\{1, \dots, n\}\).
Preconditions: Modulus \(p = 998244353 > n\); \(y = 1\) handled separately to avoid division by \(1 - y \equiv 0\).
Output: Sum of \(y^{n - \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert} \bmod 998244353\).
Complexity:

\(\text{op} = 0\): \(O(n \log n)\) (or \(O(n)\)) time, \(O(n)\) space.
\(\text{op} = 1\): \(O(n)\) time, \(O(n)\) space via 2-state tree DP.
\(\text{op} = 2\): \(O(n \log n)\) time, \(O(n)\) space via a single degree-\(n\) polynomial \(\exp\).

Core Invariant: In \(\text{op} = 1\), dp[u][0] and dp[u][1] represent the sum of \(\prod (w \cdot s_i)\) over all closed components strictly inside \(u\)’s subtree, with \(0\) or \(1\) marked vertex chosen so far in \(u\)’s open component.



if (y == 1) {
    if (op == 0) return 1;
    if (op == 1) return qpow(n, n - 2);
    return qpow(n, 2 * n - 4);
}
if (op == 2) {
    long long coef = 1LL * n * n % MOD * y % MOD * qpow((1 - y + MOD) % MOD, MOD - 2) % MOD;
    Poly A(n + 1, 0);
    for (int s = 1; s <= n; ++s)
        A[s] = coef * qpow(s, s) % MOD * inv_fact[s] % MOD;
    Poly E = poly_exp(A, n + 1);
    long long pre = qpow((1 - y + MOD) % MOD, n) * qpow(qpow(n, 4), MOD - 2) % MOD;
    return pre * fact[n] % MOD * E[n] % MOD;
}

title: Blind Checkpoint I — Foundations of Formal Power Series & The Symbolic Method
text:
When you solve a practice problem at the end of Chapter 03 (“The Unlabeled Symbolic Method”) or Chapter 04 (“The Labeled Symbolic Method”), half of the battle has already been fought for you: the chapter heading tells you which ring to work in, whether to reach for an Ordinary Generating Function (OGF) or an Exponential Generating Function (EGF), and which algebraic engine (inv, ln, exp, or sparse prefix sums) will unlock the recurrence.
In a live contest, no problem comes with a chapter label. You are handed a raw combinatorial specification, a set of constraints (\(N \le 16\), \(N \le 60\), \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(N \le 10^7\), or \(N \le 10^{13}\)), and a modulus. Your most critical skill is blind diagnostic routing: reading the structural clues in the statement to determine which generating function model applies and how to extract the answer within the time limit.

1. The Part I 3-Axis Diagnostic Rubric






NoteClick to Reveal Part I 3-Axis Diagnostic Rubric (Read AFTER Attempting Stage 1 Blind Diagnosis)





Every generating function problem in Part I (Chapters 01–04) can be routed to its canonical algebraic engine by asking three diagnostic questions in sequence.





flowchart TD
    Start["Raw Combinatorial Problem Statement"] --> Axis1{"Axis 1: Label Symmetry — How do sub-objects combine?"}
    Axis1 -->|"Unlabeled sizes add: k = i + j"| OGF["Ordinary GF: K[[x]] Cauchy Product"]
    Axis1 -->|"Index gap / distance: k = j - i or i - j"| DiffConv["Difference / Reverse Convolution: Q(x) G(x) and Q^R(x) G(x)"]
    Axis1 -->|"Distinguishable labels partitioned via C(n, i)"| EGF["Exponential GF: K[[x]] with x^n / n! or Subset-Indexed Labeled SET"]
    Axis1 -->|"Equivalence classes under symmetry group G <= S_n"| Polya["Burnside's Lemma and Cycle Index Z(G)"]

    OGF --> Axis2{"Axis 2: Composition Structure"}
    EGF --> Axis2
    Axis2 -->|"Fixed k-tuple / 2-Way Split"| Prod["Direct Product A(x) B(x) or Power A(x)^k"]
    Axis2 -->|"Ordered chain / Circular cut SEQ(A)"| SeqInv["Quasi-Inverse (1 - A(x))^{-1} Polynomial Inversion"]
    Axis2 -->|"Unordered multiset MSET(A)"| Euler["Euler Transform / Subset Product"]
    Axis2 -->|"Unordered set of connected labeled components SET(C)"| ExpLn["Exponential Formula: G = exp(C), C = ln(G)"]

    Prod --> Axis3{"Axis 3: Constraint and Sparsity Regime"}
    SeqInv --> Axis3
    Euler --> Axis3
    ExpLn --> Axis3
    Axis3 -->|"N <= 2e5, NTT prime"| NTT["O(N log N) Dense NTT / Newton Engine"]
    Axis3 -->|"N, M <= 1e7, sparse factors"| Sparse["O(N + M) Prefix Sums / O(M log M) Harmonic Series"]
    Axis3 -->|"N <= 16..60 or N <= 1e13 super-increasing"| Special["O(3^N) Min-Label Boxed-Product DP, Partition DFS, or O(log^2 N) Pruning"]







Axis 1: Label Symmetry (OGF vs. EGF vs. Group Orbits)
Before writing a single summation sign, inspect how a composite object of size \(n\) is assembled from a left piece of size \(i\) and a right piece of size \(j = n - i\):

Ordinary Generating Functions (OGFs — Chapters 01 & 03):

Combinatorial Signature: Each choice contributes a weight or count \(i\), and there is no relabeling of internal atoms when two pieces are combined — for each choice of the first piece (counted by \(a_i\)) and each choice of the second piece (counted by \(b_j\)), there is a unique combined configuration of total size \(i + j\).
Algebraic Translation: \(c_n = \sum_{i+j=n} a_i b_j = [x^n]\big(A(x) B(x)\big)\) where \(A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n\).

Difference / Cross-Correlation Sums (Chapter 01):

Combinatorial Signature: The interaction between index \(i\) and index \(j\) depends on their directed displacement \(j - i\) or \(i - j\) rather than \(i + j\), so the sum has the form \(\sum_{i < j} a_i b_{j-i}\) or \(\sum_{i > j} a_i b_{i-j}\).
Algebraic Translation: A sum over \(j - i = k\) is already a standard Cauchy product \([x^j](A(x)B(x))\). A sum over \(i - j = k\) has indices moving in the same direction; reversing one array via \(a^R_k = a_{n-k}\) converts \((n - i) + (i - j) = n - j\) into a Cauchy product \([x^{n-j}](A^R(x)B(x))\).

Exponential Generating Functions & Subset-Indexed Labeled \(\operatorname{SET}\) (EGFs — Chapter 04):

Combinatorial Signature: The object is built on \(n\) distinguishable labeled vertices \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\). Splitting the vertex set into a first part of size \(i\) and a second part of size \(j = n - i\) requires choosing which \(\binom{n}{i}\) labels go to the first part.
Algebraic Translation: \(c_n = \sum_{i+j=n} \binom{n}{i} a_i b_j \iff \frac{c_n}{n!} = \sum_{i+j=n} \frac{a_i}{i!} \frac{b_j}{j!}\), which is ordinary multiplication of \(A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n \frac{x^n}{n!}\) and \(B(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} b_n \frac{x^n}{n!}\).
Non-Symmetric Label Variant (\(N \le 20\)): If the \(N\) labeled elements are not interchangeable (because element \(i\) carries its own individual parameter \(D_i\)), univariate \(x^n/n!\) is too coarse: you apply the Greene–Wilf Boxed Product / Min-Label Component DP (Chapter 04 §4.3) directly over subsets \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) by anchoring the minimum label \(\min(S)\) in \(O(3^N)\) time (a preview of full \(O(N^2 2^N)\) Set Power Series \(\exp\) in Chapter 24 §24.2).

Symmetry Group Orbits (Burnside / Pólya — Chapter 03):

Combinatorial Signature: Two configurations are considered identical if one can be obtained from the other by a permutation \(\sigma \in G\) of the underlying vertices or positions (e.g., unlabeled graphs up to vertex isomorphism \(G = S_n\), or necklaces up to cyclic rotation \(G = C_n\)).
Algebraic Translation: Average the number of configurations fixed by \(\sigma\) over all \(\sigma \in G\): \[|\mathcal{X} / G| = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{\sigma \in G} |\mathcal{X}^\sigma|,\] grouping permutations \(\sigma \in S_n\) by their cycle-type integer partition \(\lambda \vdash n\) whenever \(|\mathcal{X}^\sigma|\) depends only on cycle lengths.




Axis 2: Composition Structure (How Components Assemble)
Once the ring is chosen, identify the structural operator linking atomic pieces into a full configuration:









Combinatorial Assembly
Symbolic Notation
Algebraic Operator
Valuation / Unit Precondition




Fixed \(k\)-tuple of independent parts
\(\mathcal{A}_1 \times \dots \times \mathcal{A}_k\)
\(A_1(x) \cdots A_k(x)\)
None


Ordered sequence of \(\ge 0\) parts
\(\operatorname{SEQ}(\mathcal{A})\)
\(\frac{1}{1 - A(x)}\)
\(\operatorname{val}(A) \ge 1\) (\([x^0]A = 0\))


Circular arrangement of parts
\(\operatorname{CYC}(\mathcal{A})\) or Cut-1-Edge
Cut 1 boundary edge \(\to \operatorname{SEQ}(\mathcal{A})\) or \(\ln\frac{1}{1-A}\)
\(\operatorname{val}(A) \ge 1\)


Unordered multiset of unlabeled parts
\(\operatorname{MSET}(\mathcal{A})\)
\(\prod_{k \ge 1} (1 - x^k)^{-a_k} = \exp\!\left(\sum_{m \ge 1} \frac{A(x^m)}{m}\right)\)
\(\operatorname{val}(A) \ge 1\), \(\mathbb{Q} \subseteq K\)


0-1 subset of distinct unlabeled parts
\(\operatorname{PSET}(\mathcal{A})\)
\(\prod_{k \ge 1} (1 + x^k)^{a_k} = \exp\!\left(\sum_{m \ge 1} \frac{(-1)^{m-1} A(x^m)}{m}\right)\)
\(\operatorname{val}(A) \ge 1\)


Unordered set of labeled components
\(\operatorname{SET}(\mathcal{C})\)
\(G(x) = \exp(C(x)) \iff C(x) = \ln G(x)\)
\([x^0]C = 0 \iff [x^0]G = 1\)





Axis 3: Sparsity & Constraint Regime (How to Extract the Coefficient)
Never call a black-box \(O(N \log N)\) NTT routine before checking the constraint regime:

Regime I (\(N \le 2 \times 10^5\), NTT-friendly prime \(P = 998244353\), dense polynomial): Use FFT/NTT convolution, Newton polynomial inversion inv, or ln/exp in \(O(N \log N)\) time.
Regime II (\(N, M \le 10^7\) or non-NTT prime \(10^9+7\), structured rational OGF): An \(O(M \log M)\) NTT will TLE or fail the modulus! Look for sparse numerator/denominator structure such as \((1 + x)^A (1 - x)^{-B} (1 - x^d)^{-C}\). You can extract coefficients in \(O(N + M)\) time via binomial expansions and linear prefix sums, or in \(O(M \log M)\) via harmonic series summation when summing over \(j \cdot d \le M\).
Regime III (\(N \le 10^{13}\) with lacunary/super-increasing weights, or \(N \le 60\) / \(N \le 16\) combinatorial explosions): Generating functions provide the exact algebraic identity (such as \(\prod (1 + x^{w_k})\), the Pólya cycle index over \(\lambda \vdash N\), or the \(\ln(1+x)\) connected-component sieve), while coefficient extraction uses recursive range-pruning, partition DFS (\(p(60) = 966{,}467\)), or \(O(3^N)\) min-label boxed-product subset DP.

Problem CP-I.1 (#078): RGB Balls 2 (AtCoder Typical90 #065)

Problem Statement
You have \(R\) distinguishable red balls, \(G\) distinguishable green balls, and \(B\) distinguishable blue balls. You want to choose exactly \(K\) balls in total such that:

The number of chosen red balls \(r\) and chosen green balls \(g\) satisfies \(r + g \le X\).
The number of chosen green balls \(g\) and chosen blue balls \(b\) satisfies \(g + b \le Y\).
The number of chosen blue balls \(b\) and chosen red balls \(r\) satisfies \(b + r \le Z\).

Compute the number of valid ways to choose the \(K\) balls, modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le R, G, B \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(1 \le K \le R + G + B\), \(0 \le X, Y, Z \le K\), modulus \(P = 998244353\).
Target Complexity: \(O((R + G) \log(R + G) + B)\) time and \(O(R + G + B)\) space.



Small Hand-Checkable Trace
Suppose \(R = 2, G = 2, B = 2\), \(K = 3\), and \(X = 2, Y = 2, Z = 2\). We must pick \(r \in [0, 2]\) red, \(g \in [0, 2]\) green, and \(b \in [0, 2]\) blue balls with \(r + g + b = 3\) and \(r+g \le 2, g+b \le 2, b+r \le 2\). Since \(r + g + b = 3\), the condition \(g + b \le 2\) is equivalent to \(r = 3 - (g + b) \ge 1\). By symmetry, \(r \ge 1, g \ge 1, b \ge 1\). Because \(r + g + b = 3\), the only valid count tuple is \((r, g, b) = (1, 1, 1)\), which yields \(\binom{2}{1}\binom{2}{1}\binom{2}{1} = 8\) ways.


Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal (What structural clue is hiding in the statement?)

There are three variables \((r, g, b)\) constrained by a fixed total sum \(r + g + b = K\) and three coupled pairwise upper bounds \(r + g \le X\), \(g + b \le Y\), and \(b + r \le Z\). Whenever a fixed sum \(r + g + b = K\) is paired with \((n-1)\)-variable sum bounds like \(g + b \le Y\), you can decouple the inequality by substituting \(g + b = K - r\)!



Hint 2 — Chapter Routing & Initial Generating Function Setup


Routing: Chapter 01 (Section 1.3 — 2-Way Split Convolution & Coefficient Filtering).
Decoupling the Bounds: Using \(r + g + b = K\):

\(g + b \le Y \iff K - r \le Y \iff r \ge K - Y\).
\(b + r \le Z \iff K - g \le Z \iff g \ge K - Z\).
\(r + g \le X \iff K - b \le X \iff b \ge K - X\).

Now the constraints on \(r\), \(g\), and \(b\) are completely independent interval bounds: \[L_R = \max(0, K - Y) \le r \le R, \qquad L_G = \max(0, K - Z) \le g \le G, \qquad L_B = \max(0, K - X) \le b \le B.\]
Form the truncated OGFs for red, green, and blue choices: \[P_R(x) = \sum_{r=L_R}^R \binom{R}{r} x^r, \qquad P_G(x) = \sum_{g=L_G}^G \binom{G}{g} x^g, \qquad P_B(x) = \sum_{b=L_B}^B \binom{B}{b} x^b.\] (Note: Compare this with its dual problem CF 451E — Devu and Flowers, where indistinguishable items with upper bounds \(f_i\) give \(\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1-x^{f_i+1}}{1-x}\); here the balls within each color are distinguishable, giving binomial coefficients \(\binom{R}{r}\) instead of \(1\), and there are only 3 colors with \(R, G, B \le 2 \times 10^5\).)




Hint 3 — Reverse-Engineering the Algebraic Manipulation & Extraction

We want \([x^K]\big(P_R(x) P_G(x) P_B(x)\big)\). Do we need to multiply all three polynomials via NTT? No! Once we compute the 2-way convolution \(C(x) = P_R(x) P_G(x)\) via a single NTT, the coefficient of \(x^K\) in \(C(x) P_B(x)\) is simply a linear dot product over \(s = r + g\): \[[x^K]\big(C(x) P_B(x)\big) = \sum_{s=0}^{\min(K, R+G)} [x^s]C(x) \cdot [x^{K-s}]P_B(x) = \sum_{s = \max(0, K - B)}^{\min(X, R + G)} c_s \binom{B}{K - s}.\] This saves an entire NTT call and avoids allocating a degree-\((R+G+B)\) buffer!







NoteComplete Derivation, Boundary Audit & Solution






1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad & Single-Step Derivation
Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be the set of valid triples \((r, g, b) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^3\) satisfying \(0 \le r \le R\), \(0 \le g \le G\), \(0 \le b \le B\), \(r + g + b = K\), \(r + g \le X\), \(g + b \le Y\), and \(b + r \le Z\). For a fixed triple \((r, g, b)\), there are \(\binom{R}{r}\) ways to choose the red balls, \(\binom{G}{g}\) ways to choose the green balls, and \(\binom{B}{b}\) ways to choose the blue balls. Because choices across colors are independent, the total number of valid \(K\)-subsets is: \[\text{Ans} = \sum_{(r, g, b) \in \mathcal{S}} \binom{R}{r} \binom{G}{g} \binom{B}{b}.\]
Step 1 (Eliminating Pairwise Couplings): Since \(r + g + b = K\) holds for every term in the sum, we substitute \(g + b = K - r\), \(b + r = K - g\), and \(r + g = K - b\) into the three upper-bound inequalities: \[\begin{aligned}
g + b \le Y &\iff K - r \le Y \iff r \ge K - Y, \\
b + r \le Z &\iff K - g \le Z \iff g \ge K - Z, \\
r + g \le X &\iff K - b \le X \iff b \ge K - X.
\end{aligned}\] Defining the lower bounds \(L_R = \max(0, K - Y)\), \(L_G = \max(0, K - Z)\), and \(L_B = \max(0, K - X)\), the coupled constraints reduce to three independent box constraints: \[r \in [L_R, R], \qquad g \in [L_G, G], \qquad b \in [L_B, B], \qquad r + g + b = K.\]
Step 2 (Encoding as an OGF Product): Define the three univariate polynomials in \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}[x]\): \[P_R(x) = \sum_{r = L_R}^R \binom{R}{r} x^r, \qquad P_G(x) = \sum_{g = L_G}^G \binom{G}{g} x^g, \qquad P_B(x) = \sum_{b = L_B}^B \binom{B}{b} x^b.\] By the definition of polynomial multiplication (Cauchy product), the coefficient of \(x^K\) in \(P_R(x) P_G(x) P_B(x)\) sums \(\binom{R}{r}\binom{G}{g}\binom{B}{b}\) over all \(r + g + b = K\) lying in the respective intervals.
Step 3 (2-Way Split & Dot-Product Extraction): Let \(C(x) = P_R(x) P_G(x) = \sum_{s=0}^{R+G} c_s x^s\), where \(c_s = \sum_{r+g=s} [x^r]P_R(x) \cdot [x^g]P_G(x)\) counts the number of valid red-green pairs of combined size \(s = r + g\). Then the condition \(b = K - s \in [L_B, B]\) is equivalent to \(K - B \le s \le K - L_B = \min(K, X)\). Therefore: \[\text{Ans} = [x^K]\big(C(x) P_B(x)\big) = \sum_{s = \max(0, K - B)}^{\min(K, X, R + G)} c_s \binom{B}{K - s} \pmod{998244353}.\]


2. Verification on the Hand-Checkable Trace
For \(R = G = B = 2\), \(K = 3\), \(X = Y = Z = 2\):

\(L_R = \max(0, 3 - 2) = 1\), \(L_G = 1\), \(L_B = 1\).
\(P_R(x) = \binom{2}{1}x + \binom{2}{2}x^2 = 2x + x^2\), and \(P_G(x) = 2x + x^2\).
\(C(x) = P_R(x) P_G(x) = 4x^2 + 4x^3 + x^4\).
Summing over \(s \in [\max(0, 3-2), \min(3, 2, 4)] = [1, 2]\): \[\text{Ans} = c_1 \binom{2}{2} + c_2 \binom{2}{1} = 0 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 2 = 8.\] Matches our hand count of \(8\).







WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Out-of-Range Lower Bounds and Degree Blowup




Empty Interval Pitfall: If \(K - Y > R\) (or \(K - Z > G\), or \(K - X > B\)), the lower bound \(L_R\) exceeds the upper bound \(R\). A naive loop that allocates or indexes \(P_R[L_R \dots R]\) without checking \(L_R \le R\) will either crash or wrap around. Always return \(0\) immediately if \(L_R > R\), \(L_G > G\), or \(L_B > B\).
Unnecessary 3-Way NTT: Computing \(P_R(x) P_G(x) P_B(x)\) via two full NTT convolutions requires padding to the next power of two above \(R + G + B \le 6 \times 10^5\) (\(2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576\)). By shifting \(P_R(x)\) down by \(x^{L_R}\) and \(P_G(x)\) down by \(x^{L_G}\) before the single NTT and dot-producting with \(P_B\), the transform length is at most \(2^{\lceil \log_2((R - L_R) + (G - L_G) + 1) \rceil} \le 2^{19}\), cutting runtime and memory by more than half.









NoteAlgorithm Contract




Input: Integers \(R, G, B, K, X, Y, Z\) (\(0 \le X, Y, Z \le K \le R+G+B\), \(R, G, B \le 2 \times 10^5\)).
Preconditions: Modulus \(P = 998244353\) is NTT-friendly (\(P - 1 = 2^{23} \times 119\)). Factorials \(0!, \dots, \max(R,G,B)!\) are precomputed in \(O(\max(R,G,B))\).
Output: \([x^K]\big(P_R(x) P_G(x) P_B(x)\big) \bmod 998244353\).
Invariant: After the single NTT \(C(x) = P_R(x) P_G(x)\), for every \(s \in [0, R+G]\), \(c_s\) equals the exact number of pairs \((r, g)\) with \(r + g = s\), \(L_R \le r \le R\), and \(L_G \le g \le G\). Pairing each \(s\) with the unique \(b = K - s \in [L_B, B]\) partitions the solution space by \(s = r + g\) with zero omissions or double counts.
Complexity: \(O((R + G) \log(R + G) + B)\) time, \(O(R + G + B)\) auxiliary space.











Problem CP-I.2 (#144): 力 / Force (Luogu P3338 — ZJOI2014)

Problem Statement
In a 1D electrostatic field, \(n\) point charges \(q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n\) (\(q_i \in \mathbb{R}\)) are placed at integer coordinates \(1, 2, \dots, n\). The net electrostatic force on charge \(j\) is \(F_j = q_j E_j\), where the electric field strength \(E_j\) at position \(j \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) is given by: \[E_j = \sum_{i = 1}^{j - 1} \frac{q_i}{(j - i)^2} - \sum_{i = j + 1}^{n} \frac{q_i}{(i - j)^2}.\] Compute \(E_1, E_2, \dots, E_n\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 10^5\), \(0 < q_i < 10^9\). Output answers within relative or absolute error \(10^{-3}\).
Target Complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.



Small Hand-Checkable Trace
For \(n = 3\) and charges \(q = (q_1, q_2, q_3) = (4, 8, 12)\):

\(E_1 = 0 - \left(\frac{q_2}{1^2} + \frac{q_3}{2^2}\right) = -(8 + 3) = -11\).
\(E_2 = \frac{q_1}{1^2} - \frac{q_3}{1^2} = 4 - 12 = -8\).
\(E_3 = \left(\frac{q_1}{2^2} + \frac{q_2}{1^2}\right) - 0 = 1 + 8 = 9\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal (What structural clue is hiding in the statement?)

Look at how the two subscripts vary with \(i\) in the two sums defining \(E_j\):

In the first sum \(\sum_{i < j} q_i \cdot \frac{1}{(j - i)^2}\), as \(i\) increases, \(j - i\) decreases, so the two subscripts sum to a constant: \(i + (j - i) = j\).
In the second sum \(\sum_{i > j} q_i \cdot \frac{1}{(i - j)^2}\), as \(i\) increases, the second subscript \(i - j\) also increases in the same direction, so their difference is constant: \(i - (i - j) = j\). How can you re-index the sequence \(q_1, \dots, q_n\) so that the two subscripts in the second sum also move in opposite directions and add up to a function of \(j\) alone?




Hint 2 — Chapter Routing & Initial Generating Function Setup


Routing: Chapter 01 (Section 1.3 — Index Manipulation & Reverse-Indexing Difference Convolution / Cross-Correlation).

Every remaining child \(j \notin U\) receives at most \(t\) candies (\(0 \le c_j \le t\)).

Otherwise, the distribution is called valid (meaning \(B_M = B_{M+1}\), so there is a tie at the boundary between the \(M\)-th and \((M+1)\)-th largest candy counts).

1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad & Single-Step Derivation
Step 1 (Prefix Reduction to \(\le S\)): Let \(\text{Good}_{\le}(S)\) denote the number of valid candy distributions with total candies \(0 \le \sum_{i=1}^N c_i \le S\). Step 3 (Evaluating the Bounded-Range OGF \(H(S, a, b)\)): For a fixed subset \(U\) of size \(M\), the condition \(\min_{i \in U} c_i = t + 1\) is the set difference between \(\{c_i \ge t + 1 \text{ for all } i \in U\}\) and \(\{c_i \ge t + 2 \text{ for all } i \in U\}\). For any lower bound \(a \ge 1\) on \(U\) and upper bound \(b = t\) on \(\overline{U}\) (of size \(N - M\)), the number of tuples \((c_1, \dots, c_N)\) with \(\sum c_i \le S\), \(c_i \ge a\) (\(i \in U\)), and \(0 \le c_j \le b\) (\(j \notin U\)) is: \[\begin{aligned}
H(S, a, b) &= [x^S] \left( \frac{1}{1 - x} \prod_{i \in U} \frac{x^a}{1 - x} \prod_{j \notin U} \frac{1 - x^{b+1}}{1 - x} \right) \\
&= [x^S] \frac{x^{M a} (1 - x^{b+1})^{N - M}}{(1 - x)^{N + 1}} \\
&= [x^{S - M a}] \left( \sum_{j=0}^{N - M} (-1)^j \binom{N - M}{j} x^{j(b + 1)} \right) \left( \sum_{r \ge 0} \binom{r + N}{N} x^r \right) \\
&= \sum_{j = 0}^{\min\left(N - M, \left\lfloor \frac{S - M a}{b + 1} \right\rfloor\right)} (-1)^j \binom{N - M}{j} \binom{S - M a - j(b + 1) + N}{N},
\end{aligned}\] where \(H(S, a, b) = 0\) whenever \(S < M a\). Summing over all \(\binom{N}{M}\) choices of \(U\) and all \(t = 0, 1, \dots, \lfloor S / M \rfloor - 1\) yields: \[\text{Good}_{\le}(S) = \binom{S + N}{N} - \binom{N}{M} \sum_{t = 0}^{\lfloor S / M \rfloor - 1} \Big( H(S, t + 1, t) - H(S, t + 2, t) \Big).\]

At the very next level \(k - 2\), the saturation threshold is \(F_k - 2 < F_k \le B\)! That means in the left branch \(\text{Solve}(k - 1, B)\), its left child \(\text{Solve}(k - 2, B)\) is guaranteed to saturate immediately (\(B \ge F_k > F_k - 2\)) and return \(2^{k-3}\) in \(O(1)\)!

// Concise non-standard recursion illustrating the O(1) degree-saturation cut:
long long solve(int k, long long B) {
    if (k <= 1) return 1LL;
    if (B >= fib[k + 2] - 2) return 1LL << (k - 1); // P_k(1) = 2^{k-1}
    long long res = solve(k - 1, B);
    if (B >= fib[k]) res += solve(k - 1, B - fib[k]);
    return res;
}

LCM Overflow: When computing \(\operatorname{lcm}(L, D_i) = \frac{L}{\gcd(L, D_i)} \cdot D_i\) for \(M \le 10^{18}\), the product \(\frac{L}{\gcd(L, D_i)} \cdot D_i\) can reach \(10^{36}\) and overflow unsigned long long! Always check if (L / g > M / D[i]) L = M + 1; (or use __int128) to cap any LCM exceeding \(M\) at \(M + 1\) (so \(\lfloor M / L \rfloor = 0\)).
Overcounting Set Partitions by \(k!\): If you write \(dp[mask] = \sum_{\emptyset \neq T \subseteq mask} w(T) dp[mask \setminus T]\) without anchoring pivot = mask & -mask, a partition into \(k\) blocks is counted \(k!\) times (computing \(\operatorname{SEQ}\) instead of \(\operatorname{SET}\)!). Anchoring the lowest set bit of mask inside \(T\) forces a canonical ordering of the blocks — the exact subset-level analog of the Chapter 04 (§4.3) Greene–Wilf boxed product \(G = C^{\square} * G\).









NoteAlgorithm Contract




Input: Integer \(N \le 16\), \(M \le 10^{18}\), and array \(D_1, \dots, D_N \le M\).
Preconditions: Precompute \(\operatorname{lcm}(S)\) capped at \(M + 1\) for all \(2^N\) masks in \(O(2^N \log M)\) time.
Output: Number of valid pairwise-distinct tuples modulo \(998244353\).
Invariant: After processing mask, dp[mask] equals the sum of \(\prod_{r=1}^k w(S_r)\) over all unordered set partitions \(\{S_1, \dots, S_k\}\) of mask, because every set partition has a unique block \(T\) containing \(\min(mask)\).
Complexity: \(O(3^N + 2^N \log M)\) time (\(\frac{1}{2} 3^{16} \approx 2.15 \times 10^7\) operations, \(< 25\text{ ms}\)) and \(O(2^N)\) space.

In classical enumerative combinatorics, the ordinary binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{k}\) counts subsets of size \(k\) chosen from an \(n\)-element set, and the differential operator \(D = \frac{d}{dx}\) probes a generating function by shifting exponents additively (\(x^n \mapsto n x^{n-1}\)). Yet two vast families of competitive programming problems resist additive generating functions:
The unified algebraic language governing both worlds is \(q\)-series (basic hypergeometric series), where the additive step \(+1\) is replaced by the multiplicative scaling \(\times q\).

section: 23.1 \(q\)-Pochhammer Symbols \((a;q)_n\), Gaussian \(q\)-Binomials \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) & The \(q\)-Difference Equation Engine
text:
23.1 \(q\)-Pochhammer Symbols \((a;q)_n\), Gaussian \(q\)-Binomials \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) & The \(q\)-Difference Equation Engine

Concrete Definitions: \(q\)-Brackets, \(q\)-Factorials, and \(q\)-Pochhammer Symbols
Before writing any generating function, let us define the fundamental building blocks in the polynomial ring \(\mathbb{Z}[q]\) (or the formal power series ring \(K[[q]]\) over a commutative ring \(K\)).
For a non-negative integer \(n \ge 0\), the \(q\)-bracket (or \(q\)-integer) \([n]_q\) is the geometric sum of the first \(n\) powers of \(q\): \[[n]_q := 1 + q + q^2 + \dots + q^{n-1} = \frac{1 - q^n}{1 - q} \quad (\text{with } [0]_q = 0).\] When we evaluate at \(q = 1\), every term in the sum equals \(1\), so \(\lim_{q \to 1} [n]_q = n\). Multiplying the first \(n\) non-zero \(q\)-brackets gives the \(q\)-factorial: \[[n]_q! := [1]_q [2]_q \cdots [n]_q = \frac{(1-q)(1-q^2)\cdots(1-q^n)}{(1-q)^n} \quad (\text{with } [0]_q! = 1).\]
In generating function manipulations, carrying around powers of \((1-q)\) in denominators is awkward and unnecessary. We clear them by defining the \(q\)-Pochhammer symbol (or \(q\)-shifted factorial) for any indeterminates \(a, q\) and integer \(n \ge 0\): \[(a; q)_n := \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (1 - a q^i) = (1 - a)(1 - aq)(1 - aq^2)\cdots(1 - a q^{n-1}), \qquad (a; q)_0 := 1.\] When \(n = \infty\), the infinite product \((a; q)_\infty := \prod_{i=0}^\infty (1 - a q^i)\) converges in the \((x, q)\)-adic topology of \(K[[a, q]]\) (or in \(K[[q]]\) whenever \(a \in q K[[q]]\) has positive \(q\)-valuation \(\operatorname{val}_q(a) \ge 1\)). Notice that \([n]_q! = \frac{(q;q)_n}{(1-q)^n}\).
Now we can define the centerpiece of this chapter. For integers \(0 \le k \le n\), the Gaussian \(q\)-binomial coefficient \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) (also written \(\binom{n}{k}_q\)) is the ratio of \(q\)-factorials—or equivalently, the ratio of \(q\)-Pochhammer symbols: \[\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q := \frac{[n]_q!}{[k]_q! [n-k]_q!} = \frac{(q; q)_n}{(q; q)_k (q; q)_{n-k}} = \prod_{i=1}^k \frac{1 - q^{n - k + i}}{1 - q^i}\] (with \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q = 0\) if \(k < 0\) or \(k > n\)).






ImportantLocal Algebraic Hypotheses for \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\)




In the Polynomial Ring \(\mathbb{Z}[q]\): Even though the formula \(\frac{(q;q)_n}{(q;q)_k (q;q)_{n-k}}\) is written as a fraction in the rational function field \(\mathbb{Q}(q)\), every cyclotomic factor \(\Phi_d(q)\) dividing the denominator \((q;q)_k (q;q)_{n-k}\) divides the numerator \((q;q)_n\) to at least as high a power (\(\lfloor n/d \rfloor \ge \lfloor k/d \rfloor + \lfloor (n-k)/d \rfloor\)). Thus \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \in \mathbb{Z}[q]\) is always a genuine polynomial of degree \(k(n-k)\) with non-negative integer coefficients!
In a Prime Field \(\mathbb{F}_p\) (\(q \in \mathbb{F}_p\)): To evaluate \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod p\) via direct modular division \((q;q)_n \cdot ((q;q)_k (q;q)_{n-k})^{-1} \bmod p\), the denominator must be a unit in \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\): we require \(q \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) and \(1 - q^i \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) for all \(1 \le i \le \max(k, n-k)\), i.e., the multiplicative order \(d = \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\) must satisfy \(d > \max(k, n-k)\). When \(d \le \max(k, n-k)\), direct division fails with \(0/0\) and you must use the \(q\)-Lucas Theorem (§23.2).



To verify immediately that \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \in \mathbb{N}[q]\) without factoring cyclotomic polynomials, we split the numerator factor \(1 - q^n\) in two complementary ways: \[(1 - q^n) = (1 - q^{n-k}) + q^{n-k}(1 - q^k) = q^k(1 - q^{n-k}) + (1 - q^k).\] Substituting these two splittings into \(\frac{(q;q)_n}{(q;q)_k (q;q)_{n-k}} = \frac{(q;q)_{n-1}(1-q^n)}{(q;q)_k (q;q)_{n-k}}\) gives the dual \(q\)-Pascal recurrences: \[\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q = \begin{bmatrix} n-1 \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q + q^{n-k} \begin{bmatrix} n-1 \\ k-1 \end{bmatrix}_q = q^k \begin{bmatrix} n-1 \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q + \begin{bmatrix} n-1 \\ k-1 \end{bmatrix}_q.\]



Three Concrete Combinatorial & Linear-Algebraic Models for \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\)
Before touching any generating function identity, you must be able to look at \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) and immediately see the three concrete structures it counts.

Model 1: \(k\)-Dimensional Subspaces of \(\mathbb{F}_q^n\) and RREF Pivot Profiles
Let \(\mathbb{F}_q\) be the finite field with \(q\) elements, and let \(V = \mathbb{F}_q^n\) be the \(n\)-dimensional vector space of row vectors over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). Question: How many distinct \(k\)-dimensional linear subspaces \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n\) exist?
We perform a double count on ordered linearly independent \(k\)-tuples \((v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k) \in V^k\):

Way 1 (Vector by vector): The first vector \(v_1\) can be any non-zero vector in \(\mathbb{F}_q^n\), giving \(q^n - 1\) choices. Once \(v_1, \dots, v_i\) are chosen and span an \(i\)-dimensional subspace of size \(q^i\), the next vector \(v_{i+1}\) can be any vector in \(\mathbb{F}_q^n\) outside that span, giving \(q^n - q^i\) choices. Thus there are \(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(q^n - q^i)\) ordered linearly independent \(k\)-tuples in \(\mathbb{F}_q^n\).
Way 2 (Subspace first, then basis): Choose a \(k\)-dimensional subspace \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n\). Inside this fixed \(W \cong \mathbb{F}_q^k\), by the exact same logic with \(n\) replaced by \(k\), there are \(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(q^k - q^i)\) ordered bases \((v_1, \dots, v_k)\) of \(W\).

Dividing the total number of ordered independent \(k\)-tuples by the number of ordered bases per subspace yields: \[\#\{W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n : \dim W = k\} = \frac{\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(q^n - q^i)}{\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(q^k - q^i)} = \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} \frac{q^i(q^{n-i} - 1)}{q^i(q^{k-i} - 1)} = \prod_{j=1}^k \frac{1 - q^{n-k+j}}{1 - q^j} = \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q.\]
Why is this rational expression a polynomial in \(q\) with \(\binom{n}{k}\) terms at \(q=1\)? Gaussian elimination provides the constructive bijection! Every \(k\)-dimensional subspace \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n\) has a unique \(k \times n\) basis matrix in Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF):

Row \(i\) (\(1 \le i \le k\)) has its leading \(1\) (pivot) in column \(c_i\), with \(1 \le c_1 < c_2 < \dots < c_k \le n\). There are \(\binom{n}{k}\) possible choices for the pivot column set \(C = \{c_1, \dots, c_k\}\).
In row \(i\), all entries to the left of column \(c_i\) are \(0\), and all entries in later pivot columns \(c_{i+1}, \dots, c_k\) are \(0\).
The remaining \((n - c_i) - (k - i)\) non-pivot columns to the right of \(c_i\) can be arbitrary elements of \(\mathbb{F}_q\)!

Thus a fixed pivot profile \(1 \le c_1 < \dots < c_k \le n\) contributes \(q^{\sum_{i=1}^k ((n - c_i) - (k - i))}\) subspaces, and summing over all \(\binom{n}{k}\) pivot profiles gives \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\).


Model 2: Binary Words by Inversion Number
Consider all \(\binom{n}{k}\) binary strings \(w = w_1 w_2 \dots w_n \in \{0, 1\}^n\) containing \(k\) ones and \(n-k\) zeros. An inversion in \(w\) is a pair of indices \(1 \le i < j \le n\) such that \(w_i = 1\) and \(w_j = 0\); denote the number of inversions by \(\operatorname{inv}(w)\). If the \(k\) ones are located at positions \(1 \le c_1 < c_2 < \dots < c_k \le n\) (matching the RREF pivot columns in Model 1!), then the \(i\)-th one at position \(c_i\) has \((n - c_i) - (k - i)\) zeros to its right. Conditioning on the last bit \(w_n \in \{0, 1\}\) reproduces the \(q\)-Pascal recurrence:

If \(w_n = 0\), the last zero forms \(k\) inversions with all \(k\) ones preceding it, contributing \(q^k \begin{bmatrix} n-1 \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\).
If \(w_n = 1\), the last one has no zeros to its right, contributing \(\begin{bmatrix} n-1 \\ k-1 \end{bmatrix}_q\).

Hence: \[\sum_{\substack{w \in \{0,1\}^n \\ |w|_1 = k}} q^{\operatorname{inv}(w)} = \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q.\]


Model 3: Integer Partitions Fitting Inside a \(k \times (n-k)\) Box
Interpret each binary word \(w \in \{0,1\}^n\) with \(k\) ones and \(n-k\) zeros as a monotone lattice path from \((0,0)\) to \((n-k, k)\) on a grid, where 0 is an East step \((+1, 0)\) and 1 is a North step \((0, +1)\). For each North step (1), the number of East steps (0) to its right in \(w\) is the horizontal distance from that North step to the right boundary \(x = n - k\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{inv}(w)\) equals the number of unit squares lying above and to the left of the path inside the \((n-k) \times k\) bounding rectangle! Reading the row lengths from top to bottom gives an integer partition \(\lambda = (\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_k \ge 0)\) with at most \(k\) parts, each at most \(n - k\): \[\sum_{\substack{\lambda : \ell(\lambda) \le k \\ \lambda_1 \le n - k}} q^{|\lambda|} = \sum_{0 \le A_1 \le A_2 \le \dots \le A_k \le n-k} q^{\sum_{i=1}^k A_i} = \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q.\]



Hand-Checkable Concrete Trace (\(n = 4, k = 2\))
Let us trace all \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) objects across Models 1, 2, and 3 for \(n = 4, k = 2\):

The \(q\)-Difference Equation Engine (\(x \mapsto qx\))
In Chapter 18, we extracted coefficients of products and powers by applying \(\frac{d}{dx}\) to create a differential equation. For \(q\)-products such as \((ax; q)_n\) or \(\frac{(ax; q)_\infty}{(x; q)_\infty}\), differentiation produces a useless sum of \(n\) terms. What operator simplifies a \(q\)-product in a single step?






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Multiplicative Shift \(x \mapsto qx\)




Diagnostic Signal: You encounter a generating function \(F(x)\) built from geometric \(q\)-products \(\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1 \pm a q^i x)^{\pm 1}\), or a sum where the \(k\)-th term contains \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) or \((q;q)_k^{-1}\).
Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Instead of differentiating with respect to \(x\), replace \(x\) with \(qx\)! In a geometric product \(P(x) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1 - a q^i x)\), shifting \(x \mapsto qx\) shifts every index \(i \mapsto i+1\): \[P(qx) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1 - a q^{i+1} x) = \frac{1 - a q^n x}{1 - ax} P(x).\] All \(n-1\) interior factors cancel! Clearing the denominator yields a first-order \(q\)-difference equation \((1 - ax)P(qx) = (1 - a q^n x)P(x)\). Because \([x^k] P(qx) = q^k [x^k] P(x)\), extracting \([x^k]\) on both sides immediately gives a two-term recurrence for the coefficients \([x^k]P(x)\)!



Let us apply this engine to derive Cauchy’s Master \(q\)-Binomial Theorem and all of its specializations at once.

Theorem 23.1 (Cauchy’s Master \(q\)-Binomial Theorem)
In the formal power series ring \(\mathbb{Q}(a, q)[[x]]\) (or \(K[[x]]\) whenever \((q;q)_k\) is invertible for \(k \le N\)), \[F(x) := \frac{(ax; q)_\infty}{(x; q)_\infty} = \prod_{i=0}^\infty \frac{1 - a q^i x}{1 - q^i x} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(a; q)_k}{(q; q)_k} x^k.\]
Single-Step Verbalized Derivation:

Apply the multiplicative shift \(x \mapsto qx\): In the infinite product \(F(x) = \frac{(1-ax)(1-aqx)\cdots}{(1-x)(1-qx)\cdots}\), replacing \(x\) by \(qx\) strips the \(i=0\) factor \(\frac{1-ax}{1-x}\) from the front: \[F(qx) = \frac{1 - x}{1 - ax} F(x) \implies (1 - ax) F(qx) = (1 - x) F(x).\]
Extract \([x^k]\) on both sides: Write \(F(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^k\) with \(c_0 = F(0) = 1\). Since \([x^k] F(qx) = q^k c_k\) and \([x^k](x F(qx)) = q^{k-1} c_{k-1}\), comparing coefficients of \(x^k\) for \(k \ge 1\) yields: \[q^k c_k - a q^{k-1} c_{k-1} = c_k - c_{k-1}.\]
Solve the two-term recurrence: Grouping \(c_k\) on the left and \(c_{k-1}\) on the right gives \[(1 - q^k) c_k = (1 - a q^{k-1}) c_{k-1} \implies c_k = \frac{1 - a q^{k-1}}{1 - q^k} c_{k-1}.\] Unrolling from \(c_0 = 1\) yields \(c_k = \frac{(a; q)_k}{(q; q)_k}\). \(\blacksquare\)



Three Essential Specializations of Cauchy’s Theorem

Positive (Finite) \(q\)-Binomial Theorem (Counting subsets by sum/inversions): Set \(a = q^{-n}\) and replace \(x \mapsto -x q^n\) in Theorem 23.1 (or apply \(x \mapsto qx\) directly to \(\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1 + q^i x)\)): \[(-x; q)_n = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (1 + q^i x) = \sum_{k=0}^n q^{\binom{k}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q x^k.\] Combinatorial Check: Choosing \(k\) distinct powers \(q^{i_1} < q^{i_2} < \dots < q^{i_k}\) from \(\{q^0, q^1, \dots, q^{n-1}\}\) is equivalent to subtracting the minimum staircase \(0, 1, \dots, k-1\) (whose sum is \(\binom{k}{2}\)) to leave a partition \(0 \le A_1 \le \dots \le A_k \le n - k\) inside a \(k \times (n-k)\) box (Model 3, GF \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\)).
Negative \(q\)-Binomial Theorem (Multisets / bounded parts): Set \(a = q^n\) in Theorem 23.1 so that \(\frac{(q^n x; q)_\infty}{(x; q)_\infty} = \frac{1}{(x; q)_n}\) and \(\frac{(q^n; q)_k}{(q; q)_k} = \begin{bmatrix} n + k - 1 \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\): \[\frac{1}{(x; q)_n} = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{1}{1 - q^i x} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \begin{bmatrix} n + k - 1 \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q x^k.\]
Euler’s Two Infinite \(q\)-Exponential Series (\(n \to \infty\)): Sending \(n \to \infty\) in the positive and negative \(q\)-binomial theorems (since \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q = \frac{1}{(q; q)_k}\) in \(\mathbb{Z}[[q]]\)) yields: \[(-x; q)_\infty = \prod_{i=0}^\infty (1 + q^i x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{q^{\binom{k}{2}}}{(q; q)_k} x^k, \qquad \frac{1}{(x; q)_\infty} = \prod_{i=0}^\infty \frac{1}{1 - q^i x} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{1}{(q; q)_k} x^k.\]



\(q\)-Vandermonde Convolution and \(q\)-Binomial Inversion






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: \(q\)-Binomial Gaussian Inversion




The Diagnostic Signal: You can easily count configurations on EVERY \(k\)-dimensional subspace \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n\) (summed over subspaces \(U \subseteq W\), giving \(f_k = \sum_{j=0}^k \begin{bmatrix} k \\ j \end{bmatrix}_q g_j\)), and you need to isolate the configurations \(g_n\) that span the FULL space \(\mathbb{F}_q^n\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad:

Look at the \(q\)-binomial identity \(\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(1 + q^i x) = \sum_{r=0}^m q^{\binom{r}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q x^r\). Setting \(x = -1\) makes the \(i = 0\) factor \(1 - 1 = 0\) for every \(m \ge 1\), giving the orthogonality identity \(\sum_{r=0}^m (-1)^r q^{\binom{r}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q = \delta_{m, 0}\).
Therefore, the inverse of the lower-triangular subspace-inclusion matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) weights a subspace of codimension \(r = n - k\) by \((-1)^{n-k} q^{\binom{n-k}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\)!




From the positive \(q\)-binomial theorem, two indispensable algebraic tools follow in one line each:

\(q\)-Vandermonde Identity: Factor the \((m+n)\)-fold product \(\prod_{i=0}^{m+n-1}(1 + q^i x)\) into its first \(m\) factors and its last \(n\) factors: \[\prod_{i=0}^{m+n-1} (1 + q^i x) = \left(\prod_{i=0}^{m-1} (1 + q^i x)\right) \left(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} (1 + q^j (q^m x))\right).\] Extracting \([x^k]\) on both sides and dividing by \(q^{\binom{k}{2}}\) (using \(\binom{j}{2} + \binom{k-j}{2} + m(k-j) - \binom{k}{2} = (m-j)(k-j)\)) yields: \[\begin{bmatrix} m + n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q = \sum_{j=0}^k q^{(m-j)(k-j)} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_q \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k - j \end{bmatrix}_q.\]
\(q\)-Binomial Inversion (Grassmannian Orthogonality): For \(m \ge 0\), evaluating \(\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(1 + q^i x) = \sum_{r=0}^m q^{\binom{r}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q x^r\) at \(x = -1\) gives \(0\) for \(m \ge 1\) (since the \(i=0\) factor is \(1 - 1 = 0\)) and \(1\) for \(m = 0\): \[\sum_{r=0}^m (-1)^r q^{\binom{r}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q = \delta_{m, 0}.\] Since \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ j \end{bmatrix}_q \begin{bmatrix} j \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q = \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \begin{bmatrix} n - k \\ j - k \end{bmatrix}_q\), setting \(m = n - k\) and \(r = n - j\) proves that the lower-triangular matrices \(M_{n,k} = \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) and \(M^{-1}_{n,k} = (-1)^{n-k} q^{\binom{n-k}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) are exact inverses: \[f_n = \sum_{k=0}^n \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q g_k \iff g_n = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^{n-k} q^{\binom{n-k}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q f_k.\]



General First-Order Linear \(q\)-Difference Equations
More generally, suppose a formal power series \(A(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n \in K[[x]]\) satisfies a first-order linear \(q\)-difference equation \[P(x) A(x) = R(x) A(qx) + S(x),\] where \(P(x) = \sum_{j=0}^d p_j x^j\), \(R(x) = \sum_{j=0}^d r_j x^j\), and \(S(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty s_n x^n\). Extracting \([x^n]\) on both sides gives: \[\sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, d)} p_j a_{n-j} = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, d)} r_j q^{n-j} a_{n-j} + s_n \implies (p_0 - r_0 q^n) a_n = s_n + \sum_{j=1}^{\min(n, d)} (r_j q^{n-j} - p_j) a_{n-j}.\] Provided the \(q\)-indicial factor \(p_0 - r_0 q^n\) is a unit in \(K^\times\) for every \(0 \le n \le N\), this recurrence computes \(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_N\) in \(O(N d)\) operations!






NoteAlgorithm Contract: First-Order \(q\)-Difference Equation Solver




Input & Preconditions: Polynomials \(P(x), R(x) \in K[x]\) of degree \(\le d\), truncated series \(S(x) \in K[[x]]/(x^{N+1})\), scalar \(q \in K\), and target degree \(N\). For every integer \(0 \le n \le N\), the \(q\)-indicial coefficient \(\Delta_n := p_0 - r_0 q^n\) must be a unit in \(K^\times\) (\(\Delta_n \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\)).
Postconditions (Output): The unique truncated series \(A(x) = \sum_{n=0}^N a_n x^n \in K[[x]]/(x^{N+1})\) satisfying \(P(x)A(x) \equiv R(x)A(qx) + S(x) \pmod{x^{N+1}}\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N d + N)\) time (using batch Montgomery inversion on \(\Delta_0, \dots, \Delta_N\)) and \(O(N)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After step \(n\), \(a_0, \dots, a_n\) satisfy \([x^m](P(x)A(x) - R(x)A(qx) - S(x)) = 0\) for all \(0 \le m \le n\), because \(A(qx) = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_k q^k x^k\) is strictly causal in degree.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(\Delta_n = p_0 - r_0 q^n \equiv 0 \pmod p\) at any degree \(n \le N\) (which occurs periodically when \(p_0 = r_0\) and \(n\) is a multiple of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(q)\)), the \(q\)-indicial factor is non-invertible (\(0/0\) resonance) and \(a_n\) must be supplied as a free boundary condition or reduced via \(q\)-Lucas.

title: 23 — q-Analogues, Gaussian Binomials, Rothe’s Theorem, q-Lucas & MacWilliams Duality
section: 23.2 Characteristic-\(p\) Hazards: Failure Mode #9 (\(q\)-Lucas Theorem at Roots of Unity) & Chirp-Z \(q\)-Convolution
text:
23.2 Characteristic-\(p\) Hazards: Failure Mode #9 (\(q\)-Lucas Theorem at Roots of Unity) & Chirp-Z \(q\)-Convolution

Failure Mode #9: Division by Zero in \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod p\) when \(\operatorname{ord}_p(q) \le n\)
Suppose a problem asks for \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod p\) where \(p\) is a prime (or asks for \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod (q^P - 1)\) as in ARC 145 F), and \(n\) is larger than the multiplicative order \(d = \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\) of \(q\) modulo \(p\) (the smallest positive integer \(d \ge 1\) such that \(q^d \equiv 1 \pmod p\)).
If you try to precompute \(q\)-factorials \([m]_q! \bmod p\) and multiply by modular inverses, your code will immediately crash or produce garbage: as soon as \(m \ge d\), the factor \(1 - q^d \equiv 0 \pmod p\) makes \([d]_q \equiv 0 \pmod p\), so \([m]_q! \equiv 0 \pmod p\) for all \(m \ge d\)! Even worse, in \(\frac{(q;q)_n}{(q;q)_k (q;q)_{n-k}}\), both the numerator and the denominator contain multiples of \(1 - q^d\), producing an indeterminate \(0/0 \pmod p\).






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: The \(q\)-Lucas Theorem




Diagnostic Signal: You need to evaluate \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) when \(q\) is a primitive \(d\)-th root of unity (\(q^d = 1\) and \(1, q, \dots, q^{d-1}\) are distinct), either over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with \(d = \operatorname{ord}_p(q) \le n\), or modulo a cyclotomic polynomial \(\Phi_d(q)\) dividing \(q^P - 1\).
Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Where did \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) come from? From the positive \(q\)-binomial theorem \(\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1 + q^i x) = \sum_{k=0}^n q^{\binom{k}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q x^k\)! When \(q\) is a primitive \(d\)-th root of unity, the \(d\) elements \(1, q, q^2, \dots, q^{d-1}\) are the exact roots of \(z^d - 1 = 0\). Therefore, a complete period of \(d\) consecutive factors in the product collapses to a binomial in \(x^d\): \[\prod_{j=0}^{d-1} (1 + q^j x) = 1 - (-x)^d = 1 + (-1)^{d-1} x^d.\] Now divide \(n\) and \(k\) by \(d\) with remainder: \(n = n_1 d + n_0\) and \(k = k_1 d + k_0\) (\(0 \le n_0, k_0 < d\)). Grouping the \(n\) factors into \(n_1\) full periods of length \(d\) and \(n_0\) leftover factors decouples the quotient from the remainder!




Theorem 23.2 (The \(q\)-Lucas Theorem)
Let \(q\) be a primitive \(d\)-th root of unity in a field \(K\) (or work in the quotient ring \(\mathbb{Z}[q]/(\Phi_d(q))\)). Write \(n = n_1 d + n_0\) and \(k = k_1 d + k_0\) with integers \(n_1, k_1 \ge 0\) and remainders \(0 \le n_0, k_0 < d\). Then: \[\begin{bmatrix} n_1 d + n_0 \\ k_1 d + k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q = \binom{n_1}{k_1} \begin{bmatrix} n_0 \\ k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q.\] Notice the magic on the right-hand side:

The quotient factor \(\binom{n_1}{k_1}\) is an ordinary integer binomial coefficient (\(q = 1\))! (If \(K = \mathbb{F}_p\) and \(n_1 \ge p\), you reduce \(\binom{n_1}{k_1} \bmod p\) using the classical Lucas theorem base \(p\).)
The remainder factor \(\begin{bmatrix} n_0 \\ k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q\) has \(n_0, k_0 < d\), so every denominator factor \(1 - q^i\) (\(1 \le i \le k_0 < d\)) is strictly non-zero and invertible!

Single-Step Verbalized Derivation:

Period-by-period factorization: Since \(q^d = 1\), the product \(\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1 + q^i x)\) splits into \(n_1\) identical blocks of length \(d\) and one trailing block of length \(n_0\): \[\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (1 + q^i x) = \left(\prod_{j=0}^{d-1} (1 + q^j x)\right)^{n_1} \prod_{i=0}^{n_0-1} (1 + q^i x) = \left(1 + (-1)^{d-1} x^d\right)^{n_1} \sum_{r=0}^{n_0} q^{\binom{r}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n_0 \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q x^r.\]
Extract \([x^k]\) for \(k = k_1 d + k_0\): Because \(0 \le r \le n_0 < d\), a term \(x^{m d} \cdot x^r\) can equal \(x^{k_1 d + k_0}\) if and only if \(m = k_1\) and \(r = k_0\). Extracting \([x^{k_1 d + k_0}]\) on both sides gives: \[q^{\binom{k_1 d + k_0}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n_1 d + n_0 \\ k_1 d + k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q = \binom{n_1}{k_1} (-1)^{(d-1)k_1} q^{\binom{k_0}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n_0 \\ k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q.\]
Cancel the \(q\)-powers: Expand \(\binom{k_1 d + k_0}{2} = d\binom{k_1}{2} + k_1 k_0 d + \binom{k_0}{2} + \binom{d}{2} k_1\). Since \(q^d = 1\), we have \(q^{d\binom{k_1}{2} + k_1 k_0 d} = 1\). Furthermore, \(q^{\binom{d}{2}} = (-1)^{d-1}\) (if \(d\) is odd, \(\binom{d}{2}\) is a multiple of \(d\) so \(q^{\binom{d}{2}} = 1 = (-1)^{d-1}\); if \(d\) is even, \(q^{d/2} = -1\) so \(q^{d(d-1)/2} = (-1)^{d-1} = -1\)). Thus \(q^{\binom{k_1 d + k_0}{2}} = (-1)^{(d-1)k_1} q^{\binom{k_0}{2}}\), and cancelling this non-zero scalar leaves \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q = \binom{n_1}{k_1} \begin{bmatrix} n_0 \\ k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q\). \(\blacksquare\)




Hand-Checkable Concrete Trace: \(\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}_2 \bmod 7\)
Let \(p = 7\) and \(q = 2\). What is \(\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}_2 \bmod 7\)?

Exact polynomial check over \(\mathbb{Z}\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}_q = \frac{(1-q^5)(1-q^4)(1-q^3)}{(1-q)(1-q^2)(1-q^3)} = \frac{(1-q^5)(1-q^4)}{(1-q)(1-q^2)}\). At \(q = 2\), this is \(\frac{31 \times 15}{1 \times 3} = 155\), and \(155 = 22 \times 7 + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod 7\).
Why naive modular division fails: Modulo \(7\), the powers of \(2\) are \(2^1 \equiv 2\), \(2^2 \equiv 4\), \(2^3 \equiv 1 \pmod 7\), so \(d = \operatorname{ord}_7(2) = 3\). Because \(1 - 2^3 \equiv 0 \pmod 7\), both \((2;2)_5 \equiv 0 \pmod 7\) and \((2;2)_3 \equiv 0 \pmod 7\)—naive division hits \(0/0\)!
\(q\)-Lucas Theorem execution: Divide \(n = 5\) and \(k = 3\) by \(d = 3\): \[n = 5 = 1 \cdot 3 + 2 \implies (n_1, n_0) = (1, 2), \qquad k = 3 = 1 \cdot 3 + 0 \implies (k_1, k_0) = (1, 0).\] By Theorem 23.2: \[\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}_2 \equiv \binom{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}_2 = 1 \times 1 = 1 \pmod 7.\]







WarningFailure Mode #9 & Remedy: \(0/0\) Cancellation in \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod p\)




Symptom: Your code precomputes q_fact[i] and q_inv_fact[i] modulo \(p\), and either divides by zero during precomputation or returns \(0\) for every \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) with \(n \ge \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\).
Root Cause: Whenever \(d = \operatorname{ord}_p(q) \le n\) (for instance, when \(q\) is a small element of \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\) or a root of unity in a cyclotomic modulus \(q^P - 1\)), \([d]_q \equiv 0 \pmod p\) is a non-unit in \(\mathbb{F}_p\).
Remedy: First find \(d = \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\) (or stop precomputing q_fact as soon as \(1 - q^d \equiv 0 \pmod p\), which takes at most \(\min(n, p-1)\) steps). Split \(n = n_1 d + n_0\) and \(k = k_1 d + k_0\), evaluate \(\begin{bmatrix} n_0 \\ k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod p\) using the invertible table of size \(< d\), and multiply by \(\binom{n_1}{k_1} \bmod p\) (computed via classical Lucas base \(p\)).



// Non-standard kernel: q-Lucas evaluation when d = ord_p(q) <= n
long long q_binom_mod_p(long long n, long long k, long long q, long long p) {
    if (k < 0 || k > n) return 0;
    q %= p;
    if (q == 0) return 1; // [n choose k]_0 = 1 for all 0 <= k <= n
    if (q == 1) return lucas_binom_mod_p(n, k, p);
    // d = ord_p(q): precompute q_fact[0..d-1] where (1 - q^i) != 0 mod p
    long long n1 = n / d, n0 = n % d, k1 = k / d, k0 = k % d;
    if (k0 > n0) return 0;
    long long rem_q_binom = q_fact[n0] * q_inv_fact[k0] % p * q_inv_fact[n0 - k0] % p;
    return lucas_binom_mod_p(n1, k1, p) * rem_q_binom % p;
}






NoteAlgorithm Contract: \(q\)-Lucas Gaussian Binomial Evaluator




Input & Preconditions: Non-negative integers \(n, k \ge 0\), base \(q \in \mathbb{F}_p\), prime \(p\), and precomputed multiplicative order \(d = \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\) with \(q\)-factorial tables of size \(\min(n+1, d)\).
Postconditions (Output): Exact value of \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(\min(N, d))\) one-time table precomputation, and \(O(\log_p(n/d))\) time per query; \(O(\min(N, d))\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Every factor \(1 - q^i\) in \(\begin{bmatrix} n_0 \\ k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q\) has \(1 \le i \le n_0 < d = \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\), guaranteeing \(1 - q^i \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Degenerate bases \(q \equiv 0 \pmod p\) (where \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_0 = 1\) for all \(0 \le k \le n\)) and \(q \equiv 1 \pmod p\) (where \(d = 1\) and \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_1 \equiv \binom{n}{k} \bmod p\)) must be handled before computing \(\operatorname{ord}_p(q)\), and \(k_0 > n_0\) immediately yields \(0\).






The Dual \(q\)-Exponentials and Chirp-Z \(q\)-Convolution
In Chapter 4, the ordinary exponential generating function (EGF) \(\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{a_n}{n!} x^n\) converted binomial convolutions \(\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} a_k b_{n-k}\) into Cauchy products. How do we multiply sequences weighted by Gaussian \(q\)-binomials \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time?
Because \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q = \frac{(q;q)_n}{(q;q)_k (q;q)_{n-k}}\), any sum of the form \[c_n = \sum_{k=0}^n \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q a_k b_{n-k} \quad \text{or} \quad g_n = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^{n-k} q^{\binom{n-k}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q f_k\] becomes a standard Cauchy convolution after dividing by \((q;q)_n\): \[\frac{c_n}{(q; q)_n} = \sum_{k=0}^n \left(\frac{a_k}{(q; q)_k}\right) \left(\frac{b_{n-k}}{(q; q)_{n-k}}\right), \qquad \frac{g_n}{(q; q)_n} = \sum_{k=0}^n \left(\frac{f_k}{(q; q)_k}\right) \left(\frac{(-1)^{n-k} q^{\binom{n-k}{2}}}{(q; q)_{n-k}}\right).\] Notice the two universal series appearing on the right when \(a_k = 1\) and \(b_k = (-1)^k q^{\binom{k}{2}}\): \[e_q(x) := \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{(q; q)_n} = \frac{1}{(x; q)_\infty}, \qquad E_q(x) := \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{q^{\binom{n}{2}} x^n}{(q; q)_n} = (-x; q)_\infty.\] Because \(\frac{1}{(x; q)_\infty} \cdot (x; q)_\infty = 1\), these two \(q\)-exponentials satisfy the fundamental duality \[e_q(x) E_q(-x) = 1.\] What if the convolution also contains a cross-power \(q^{k(n-k)}\) or \(q^{k n}\), such as in \(q\)-Vandermonde convolution or evaluating a polynomial at \(x = q^0, q^1, \dots, q^N\)? Recall Bluestein’s identity from Chapter 7: \[k(n - k) = \binom{n}{2} - \binom{k}{2} - \binom{n-k}{2}, \qquad k n = \binom{n+k}{2} - \binom{n}{2} - \binom{k}{2}.\] Absorbing \(q^{-\binom{k}{2}}\) into the \(k\)-th term, \(q^{-\binom{n-k}{2}}\) into the \((n-k)\)-th term, and \(q^{\binom{n}{2}}\) into the output \(c_n\) reduces every \(q\)-Vandermonde sum and every \(q\)-power evaluation to a single \(O(N \log N)\) NTT!
