section: 23.3 Euler’s Pentagonal Number Theorem, Jacobi’s Triple Product & Durfee Square Decomposition
text:
23.3 Euler’s Pentagonal Number Theorem, Jacobi’s Triple Product & Durfee Square Decomposition
In Chapter 3, we saw that the partition generating function \(\prod_{k=1}^\infty (1 - q^k)^{-1} = \frac{1}{(q;q)_\infty}\) can be inverted in \(O(N \log N)\) time because its reciprocal \((q; q)_\infty\) is ultra-sparse. Let us now prove why \((q;q)_\infty\) is sparse, embed it inside Jacobi’s Triple Product Identity, and introduce the \(O(N\sqrt{N})\) Durfee Square Engine for problems where NTT is unavailable (arbitrary modulus \(M\)) or where a bivariate \(q\)-product must be unrolled into a sum of rational \(q\)-tails.

Euler’s Pentagonal Number Theorem & Franklin’s Involution

Theorem 23.3 (Euler’s Pentagonal Number Theorem)
In \(\mathbb{Z}[[q]]\), the infinite \(q\)-Pochhammer product \((q; q)_\infty\) expands as a sparse series supported solely on the generalized pentagonal numbers \(\omega_m := \frac{m(3m-1)}{2}\) (\(m \in \mathbb{Z}\)): \[(q; q)_\infty = \prod_{k=1}^\infty (1 - q^k) = \sum_{m=-\infty}^\infty (-1)^m q^{m(3m-1)/2} = 1 - q - q^2 + q^5 + q^7 - q^{12} - q^{15} + \dots\]
Concrete Combinatorial Proof (Franklin’s Involution): Expanding \(\prod_{k=1}^\infty (1 - q^k)\) gives \(\sum_{\lambda \in \mathcal{D}} (-1)^{\ell(\lambda)} q^{|\lambda|}\), where \(\mathcal{D}\) is the set of partitions \(\lambda = (\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 > \dots > \lambda_r > 0)\) into distinct parts. For any non-empty \(\lambda \in \mathcal{D}\), define two parameters on its Ferrers diagram:

The base \(b(\lambda) := \lambda_r\) (the size of the smallest row at the bottom).
The slope \(s(\lambda)\): the length of the longest contiguous \(45^\circ\) diagonal staircase at the right end of the top rows, i.e., the largest integer \(s \ge 1\) such that \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_s\) are consecutive integers (\(\lambda_i = \lambda_1 - i + 1\) for \(1 \le i \le s\)).

Now define a sign-reversing map \(\phi : \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}\) by comparing \(b(\lambda)\) and \(s(\lambda)\):

Case A (\(b(\lambda) \le s(\lambda)\)): Remove the bottom row of length \(b(\lambda)\) and append \(1\) box to the end of each of the first \(b(\lambda)\) rows. The number of rows decreases by \(1\) (flipping the sign \((-1)^{\ell(\lambda)}\)), unless the bottom row itself was part of the slope staircase and \(b(\lambda) = s(\lambda) = r\) (meaning \(\lambda = (2r-1, 2r-2, \dots, r)\) of weight \(r(3r-1)/2\)).
Case B (\(b(\lambda) > s(\lambda)\)): Remove \(1\) box from the end of each of the first \(s(\lambda)\) rows and form a new bottom row of size \(s(\lambda)\). This is the exact inverse of Case A, except when the \(s(\lambda)\)-th row was the bottom row and \(b(\lambda) = s(\lambda) + 1 = r + 1\) (meaning \(\lambda = (2r, 2r-1, \dots, r+1)\) of weight \(r(3r+1)/2\)).

Every partition into distinct parts cancels in pairs \((\lambda, \phi(\lambda))\) of opposite sign except the two exceptional families \(m(3m-1)/2\) (\(m \ge 0\)) and \(m(3m+1)/2\) (\(m \ge 1\)), which each have \(m\) rows and contribute \((-1)^m q^{m(3m \mp 1)/2}\). \(\blacksquare\)



Jacobi’s Triple Product Identity
When we track both a multiplicative weight \(z^{\text{charge}}\) and \(q^{\text{energy}}\), Euler’s pentagonal product generalizes to a symmetric Laurent series in \(z\):

Theorem 23.4 (Jacobi’s Triple Product Identity)
In \(\mathbb{Z}[z, z^{-1}][[q]]\), \[\prod_{k=1}^\infty (1 - q^k)(1 + z q^k)(1 + z^{-1} q^{k-1}) = \sum_{m=-\infty}^\infty z^m q^{\binom{m+1}{2}}.\] (Symmetrical form under \(q \mapsto q^2, z \mapsto z q^{-1}\)): \[\prod_{k=1}^\infty (1 - q^{2k})(1 + z q^{2k-1})(1 + z^{-1} q^{2k-1}) = \sum_{m=-\infty}^\infty z^m q^{m^2}.\]
2-Line Proof of Euler’s Pentagonal Theorem from Jacobi’s Triple Product: In the first form of Theorem 23.4, replace \(q \mapsto q^3\) and set \(z = -q^{-1}\). Then \((1 - q^{3k})(1 - q^{3k-1})(1 - q^{3k-2})\) runs over all factors \((1 - q^n)\) (\(n \ge 1\)), while the right-hand side becomes \(\sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^m q^{3\binom{m+1}{2} - m} = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^m q^{m(3m+1)/2}\). \(\blacksquare\)




The Durfee Square Decomposition (\(O(N\sqrt{N})\) Division-Free Engine)
Suppose you need the partition numbers \(p(0), \dots, p(N)\) modulo an arbitrary composite integer \(M\) (where NTT does not exist), or you need to transform a bivariate infinite product \(\prod_{k=1}^\infty (1 - x q^k)^{-1}\) into a rapidly converging sum where the \(d\)-th term starts at \(q^{d^2}\).






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Durfee Square Decomposition




Diagnostic Signal: You have a partition or distinct-part generating function \(\frac{1}{(xq; q)_\infty}\) or \((-xq; q)_\infty\), and either (a) the modulus \(M\) forbids NTT, or (b) you want to eliminate the infinite product in favor of a finite sum of length \(\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor\) whose denominators \((q;q)_d\) have degree \(d \le \sqrt{N}\).
Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Look at the Ferrers diagram of any integer partition \(\lambda = (\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_\ell > 0)\). Let \(d\) be the side length of its Durfee square—the largest \(d \times d\) square of unit boxes fitting in the top-left corner of the diagram (\(d = \max\{i : \lambda_i \ge i\}\)). Once this \(d \times d\) square (containing \(d^2\) boxes) is removed, the remaining boxes split into two independent pieces:

To the right of the \(d \times d\) square: A partition \(\alpha\) with at most \(d\) rows (whose conjugate \(\alpha'\) is a partition into parts \(\le d\), generated by \(\frac{1}{(q;q)_d}\)).
Below the \(d \times d\) square: A partition \(\beta\) whose parts are all \(\le d\) (generated by \(\frac{1}{(q;q)_d}\), or \(\frac{1}{(xq; q)_d}\) if \(x\) tracks the total number of rows \(d + \ell(\beta)\)).









flowchart LR
    subgraph Ferrers["Ferrers Diagram of Partition λ (Durfee Size d)"]
        direction TB
        D["d × d Durfee Square<br/>Weight: x^d q^(d²)<br/>(Exactly d rows, width d)"]
        R["Right Wing α<br/>At most d rows<br/>GF: 1 / (q; q)_d"]
        B["Bottom Wing β<br/>Parts of size ≤ d<br/>GF: 1 / (xq; q)_d"]
        D --- R
        D --- B
    end







Corollary 23.1 (Durfee Square Identities)
Summing over all possible Durfee square sizes \(d \ge 0\) gives the Durfee Square Identity: \[\frac{1}{(xq; q)_\infty} = \prod_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{1 - x q^k} = \sum_{d=0}^\infty \frac{q^{d^2} x^d}{(q; q)_d (xq; q)_d}, \qquad \frac{1}{(q; q)_\infty} = \sum_{d=0}^\infty \frac{q^{d^2}}{(q; q)_d^2}.\] Notice that for \(d > \lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor\), \(q^{d^2} \equiv 0 \pmod{q^{N+1}}\)! Thus the infinite sum truncates to at most \(\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor + 1\) terms. Because dividing a series by \(1 - q^d\) is a simple \(O(N)\) prefix-sum pass dp[i] += dp[i - d], we can maintain the series \(A_d(q) = \frac{1}{(q;q)_d^2} \bmod q^{N+1}\) incrementally from \(d-1\) to \(d\) using two in-place unbounded knapsack passes of step \(d\) and accumulate \(q^{d^2} A_d(q)\) in \(O(N\sqrt{N})\) time and \(O(N)\) space using only additions!



Hand-Checkable Concrete Trace (\(N = 5\))
Let us verify \(\sum_{d=0}^2 \frac{q^{d^2}}{(q;q)_d^2} \bmod q^6\):

\(d = 0\): \(q^0 / 1 = 1\).
\(d = 1\): \(q^1 / (1-q)^2 = q(1 + 2q + 3q^2 + 4q^3 + 5q^4 + \dots) = q + 2q^2 + 3q^3 + 4q^4 + 5q^5 \pmod{q^6}\).
\(d = 2\): \(q^4 / ((1-q)^2(1-q^2)^2) = q^4(1 + 2q + \dots) = q^4 + 2q^5 \pmod{q^6}\).
Sum: \(1 + q + 2q^2 + 3q^3 + (4+1)q^4 + (5+2)q^5 = 1 + q + 2q^2 + 3q^3 + 5q^4 + 7q^5\), matching \(p(0..5) = (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7)\)!

// Non-standard kernel: Division-free O(N sqrt(N)) Durfee square partition engine mod M
vector<int> partitions_durfee_mod(int N, int M) {
    vector<int> ans(N + 1, 0), ways(N + 1, 0);
    ways[0] = ans[0] = 1; // d = 0: 1 / (q;q)_0^2 = 1
    for (int d = 1; d * d <= N; ++d) {
        // Multiply ways(q) by 1 / (1 - q^d)^2 via two forward knapsack passes
        for (int pass = 0; pass < 2; ++pass)
            for (int i = d; i <= N - d * d; ++i)
                if ((ways[i] += ways[i - d]) >= M) ways[i] -= M;
        for (int i = 0; i <= N - d * d; ++i)
            if ((ans[i + d * d] += ways[i]) >= M) ans[i + d * d] -= M;
    }
    return ans;
}






NoteAlgorithm Contract: Durfee Square \(O(N\sqrt{N})\) Partition Engine




Input & Preconditions: Degree bound \(N \ge 0\) and arbitrary modulus \(M \ge 2\) (need not be prime; uses only addition modulo \(M\)).
Postconditions (Output): Array ans[0..N] where ans[n] \(= [q^n]\frac{1}{(q;q)_\infty} \bmod M\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N\sqrt{N})\) time and \(O(N)\) auxiliary space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At the end of iteration \(d\), ways[i] equals \([q^i]\frac{1}{(q;q)_d^2} \bmod M\) for all \(0 \le i \le N - d^2\), accounting for all partitions whose Durfee square has side length exactly \(d\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Iterating the knapsack pass i downward instead of forward (for (int i = d; i <= N - d * d; ++i)) computes \(0/1\) subset sums \((1 + q^d)^2\) instead of unbounded geometric series \(\frac{1}{(1 - q^d)^2}\); upper-bounding i by N instead of N - d * d wastes \(2\times\) constant factor on coefficients that shift past \(q^N\).

23.4 Vector Spaces over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), Grassmannian Subspace Inversion & Self-Contained 5-Line Krawtchouk / MacWilliams Duality

Counting Linear Maps and Rank-\(r\) Matrices over \(\mathbb{F}_q\)

Proposition 23.1 (Vector Space & Subspace Enumeration over \(\mathbb{F}_q\))
Let us assemble a compact dictionary of linear-algebraic counts over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) that appear repeatedly in competitive programming:








Concrete Linear-Algebraic Object over \(\mathbb{F}_q\)
Exact Formula
Why It Holds (Single-Step Combinatorial / Algebraic Reason)




Full-rank \(r \times m\) matrices (\(r \le m\))
\(\prod_{i=0}^{r-1} (q^m - q^i)\)
Row \(i+1\) must lie outside the \(q^i\)-element span of the first \(i\) rows.


\(r\)-dimensional subspaces \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^m\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} m \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q\)
Divide full-rank \(r \times m\) matrices by the \(\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(q^r - q^i)\) ordered bases of \(W\).


\(n \times m\) matrices over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) of exact rank \(r\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q \begin{bmatrix} m \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q \prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(q^r - q^i)\)
Choose row space \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^m\) (\(\begin{bmatrix} m \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q\) ways) and a surjective \(n \times r\) coordinate matrix (\(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q \prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(q^r - q^i)\) ways).


\(r\)-subspaces \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^m\) avoiding a fixed \(x \neq 0\)
\(q^r \begin{bmatrix} m - 1 \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q\)
By \(GL_m(\mathbb{F}_q)\) symmetry, a fraction \(\frac{q^m - q^r}{q^m - 1}\) of all \(\begin{bmatrix} m \\ r \end{bmatrix}_q\) subspaces avoid \(x\).


\(r\)-subspaces \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^m\) containing a fixed \(x \neq 0\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} m - 1 \\ r - 1 \end{bmatrix}_q\)
Quotient out the \(1\)-dimensional line \(\mathbb{F}_q x\) to get an \((r-1)\)-subspace of \(\mathbb{F}_q^m / \mathbb{F}_q x \cong \mathbb{F}_q^{m-1}\).



When a problem specifies an easy-to-count quantity \(F(V)\) for every subspace \(V \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n\) (such as “all sequences/subsets contained inside \(V\)”), and asks for the quantity \(G(V)\) of objects whose exact linear span is \(V\), we have \(F(V) = \sum_{U \subseteq V} G(U)\). Whenever \(F(V) = f_{\dim V}\) and \(G(V) = g_{\dim V}\) depend only on dimension, grouping by \(k = \dim U\) (since \(V\) contains \(\begin{bmatrix} r \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) subspaces of dimension \(k\)) gives \(f_r = \sum_{k=0}^r \begin{bmatrix} r \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q g_k\), which we invert immediately via \(q\)-Binomial Inversion (§23.1): \[g_r = \sum_{k=0}^r (-1)^{r-k} q^{\binom{r-k}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} r \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q f_k.\]




Self-Contained 5-Line Hypercube Character & Krawtchouk / MacWilliams Duality
Suppose you are given \(n\) integers \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in [0, 2^m)\) (\(m \le 53\)) and asked to count, for every \(0 \le k \le m\), how many subsets of \(\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}\) have an XOR sum with \(\operatorname{popcount} = k\) (CF 1336E2).
First, run Gaussian elimination over \(\mathbb{F}_2^m\) in \(O(nm)\) time to extract a basis of rank \(r \le m\) spanning the subspace (binary linear code) \(\mathcal{C} = \operatorname{span}(a_1, \dots, a_n) \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^m\). Every vector \(v \in \mathcal{C}\) is produced by exactly \(2^{n-r}\) subsets of \(\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}\). Thus the problem reduces to computing the Hamming weight enumerator of \(\mathcal{C}\): \[A_k := \#\{v \in \mathcal{C} : \operatorname{popcount}(v) = k\} \quad (0 \le k \le m).\]
If \(r \le \lfloor m/2 \rfloor\) (\(r \le 26\)), we can simply enumerate all \(2^r\) elements of \(\mathcal{C}\) in \(O(2^r)\) time. What if \(r > m/2\) (say \(r = 45, m = 53\))? Enumerating \(2^{45}\) vectors is impossible!






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Dual Subspace \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\) & MacWilliams Identity




Diagnostic Signal: You need the Hamming weight distribution \(A_0, \dots, A_m\) (or a coordinate-separable polynomial sum) over a linear subspace \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^m\) of high dimension \(r > m/2\).
Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: While \(\mathcal{C}\) has dimension \(r\) and size \(2^r\), its orthogonal complement (dual code) under the \(\mathbb{F}_2\) dot product \(\langle u, v \rangle := \bigoplus_{t=1}^m u_t v_t = \operatorname{popcount}(u \ \& \ v) \bmod 2\), \[\mathcal{C}^\perp := \{u \in \mathbb{F}_2^m : \forall v \in \mathcal{C},\; \langle u, v \rangle = 0\},\] has dimension \(m - r\) and size \(2^{m-r} \le 2^{\lfloor m/2 \rfloor}\)! How do we relate the weight counts \(B_i := \#\{u \in \mathcal{C}^\perp : \operatorname{popcount}(u) = i\}\) of \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\) to the weight counts \(A_j\) of \(\mathcal{C}\)? By writing the indicator function of \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\) as the average of \((-1)^{\langle u, v \rangle}\) over \(v \in \mathcal{C}\)!




Theorem 23.5 (Self-Contained 5-Line Derivation of MacWilliams / Krawtchouk Duality)
Let \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^m\) be an \(r\)-dimensional subspace with weight counts \(A_0, \dots, A_m\), and let \(\mathcal{C}^\perp \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^m\) be its \((m-r)\)-dimensional orthogonal complement with weight counts \(B_0, \dots, B_m\). Then:

Line 1 (Subspace Character Orthogonality): For any vector \(u \in \mathbb{F}_2^m\), the linear form \(v \mapsto \langle u, v \rangle\) on \(\mathcal{C}\) is either identically \(0\) (when \(u \in \mathcal{C}^\perp\), so all \(2^r\) terms \((-1)^{\langle u, v \rangle}\) equal \(+1\)) or surjective onto \(\{0, 1\}\) (when \(u \notin \mathcal{C}^\perp\), so \(2^{r-1}\) terms are \(+1\) and \(2^{r-1}\) terms are \(-1\)): \[\mathbf{1}_{u \in \mathcal{C}^\perp} = \frac{1}{2^r} \sum_{v \in \mathcal{C}} (-1)^{\langle u, v \rangle}.\]
Line 2 (Weight Generating Function of \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\)): Multiply both sides by \(z^{\operatorname{popcount}(u)}\), sum over all \(u \in \mathbb{F}_2^m\), and interchange the finite sums: \[\sum_{i=0}^m B_i z^i = \sum_{u \in \mathbb{F}_2^m} \mathbf{1}_{u \in \mathcal{C}^\perp} z^{\operatorname{popcount}(u)} = \frac{1}{2^r} \sum_{v \in \mathcal{C}} \sum_{u \in \{0,1\}^m} (-1)^{\langle u, v \rangle} z^{\operatorname{popcount}(u)}.\]
Line 3 (Coordinate Factorization): Since \(\langle u, v \rangle = \sum_{t=1}^m u_t v_t\) and \(\operatorname{popcount}(u) = \sum_{t=1}^m u_t\) decompose coordinate-by-coordinate, the inner sum over \(u \in \{0,1\}^m\) factors into a product of \(m\) independent 2-term sums: \[\sum_{u \in \{0,1\}^m} \prod_{t=1}^m (-1)^{u_t v_t} z^{u_t} = \prod_{t=1}^m \left(1 + (-1)^{v_t} z\right).\]
Line 4 (Grouping by Hamming Weight of \(v\)): If \(v \in \mathcal{C}\) has \(\operatorname{popcount}(v) = j\), then \(j\) coordinates have \(v_t = 1\) (contributing \(1 - z\)) and \(m - j\) coordinates have \(v_t = 0\) (contributing \(1 + z\)), yielding the MacWilliams Identity: \[\sum_{i=0}^m B_i z^i = \frac{1}{2^r} \sum_{j=0}^m A_j (1 - z)^j (1 + z)^{m - j}.\]
Line 5 (Dual Recovery via Krawtchouk Polynomials): Because \((\mathcal{C}^\perp)^\perp = \mathcal{C}\) has dimension \(r = m - (m - r)\), swapping the roles of \((\mathcal{C}, r, A)\) and \((\mathcal{C}^\perp, m-r, B)\) and extracting \([z^k]\) expresses \(A_k\) directly as a linear combination of the dual weight counts \(B_j\): \[A_k = \frac{1}{2^{m-r}} \sum_{j=0}^m B_j K_k(j; m), \quad \text{where } K_k(j; m) := [z^k](1 - z)^j (1 + z)^{m - j} = \sum_{t=0}^k (-1)^t \binom{j}{t} \binom{m - j}{k - t}. \quad \blacksquare\]



Constructing the Dual Basis \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\) in 3 Lines of Code
How do we find a basis for \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\) from the RREF basis of \(\mathcal{C}\)? Suppose we permute the \(m\) bit positions (which preserves \(\operatorname{popcount}\)!) so that the \(r\) pivot columns come first. Then the \(r \times m\) RREF generator matrix of \(\mathcal{C}\) has the block form \[G = \begin{bmatrix} I_r \mid P \end{bmatrix},\] where \(I_r\) is the \(r \times r\) identity matrix and \(P\) is an \(r \times (m - r)\) binary matrix. Now consider the \((m - r) \times m\) matrix \[H := \begin{bmatrix} P^T \mid I_{m - r} \end{bmatrix}.\] Its \(m - r\) rows are linearly independent (because of the \(I_{m-r}\) block on the right), and over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), \[G H^T = I_r P + P I_{m-r} = P \oplus P = 0.\] Thus the rows of \(H = [P^T \mid I_{m-r}]\) form an explicit basis for \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\)!



Hand-Checkable Concrete Trace (\(m = 3, r = 2\))
Let \(m = 3\) and let \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^3\) be the \(2\)-dimensional subspace generated by the RREF matrix \[G = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} I_2 \mid P \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{with } P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.\]

Direct enumeration of \(\mathcal{C}\): The \(2^2 = 4\) vectors in \(\mathcal{C}\) are 000 (weight \(0\)), 101, 011, and 110 (all three of weight \(2\)). Thus \((A_0, A_1, A_2, A_3) = (1, 0, 3, 0)\).
Dual basis \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\): By \(H = [P^T \mid I_1] = [1\;\; 1 \mid 1]\), the dual subspace \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\) has dimension \(3 - 2 = 1\) and consists of 000 (weight \(0\)) and 111 (weight \(3\)). Thus \((B_0, B_1, B_2, B_3) = (1, 0, 0, 1)\).
MacWilliams / Krawtchouk recovery: By Line 5 of Theorem 23.5, \[\sum_{k=0}^3 A_k z^k = \frac{1}{2^1} \left( B_0 (1+z)^3 + B_3 (1-z)^3 \right) = \frac{(1 + 3z + 3z^2 + z^3) + (1 - 3z + 3z^2 - z^3)}{2} = 1 + 3z^2,\] recovering \((A_0, A_1, A_2, A_3) = (1, 0, 3, 0)\) from a 2-element dual code!







NoteAlgorithm Contract: RREF Dual-Code Krawtchouk Weight Enumerator




Input & Preconditions: Array of \(n\) bitmasks \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in [0, 2^m)\) (\(m \le 60\)); modulus \(p\) is odd (so \(2\) is invertible mod \(p\)).
Postconditions (Output): Array ans[0..m] where ans[k] is the number of subsequences of \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) whose XOR sum has popcount \(k\), modulo \(p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n m + 2^{\min(r, m-r)} + m^2)\) time and \(O(m^2)\) space, where \(r = \dim\operatorname{span}(a_1, \dots, a_n) \le m\) (at worst \(O(nm + 2^{\lfloor m/2 \rfloor})\)).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Column permutation preserves Hamming weights; \(G H^T = P \oplus P = 0\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) guarantees \(\operatorname{rowspan}(H) = \mathcal{C}^\perp\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Performing only upper-triangular row reduction instead of full Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF) (failing to eliminate 1-bits above each pivot) corrupts the off-pivot block \(P\) and produces vectors \(h \notin \mathcal{C}^\perp\); forgetting to multiply by the nullity factor \(2^{n-r} \bmod p\) undercounts when \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) are linearly dependent.

23.5 Diagnostic Signal Summary Table & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
When you encounter a \(q\)-series, partition product, or \(\mathbb{F}_q\) vector-space counting problem, match its structural bottleneck against the table below to select the right engine immediately:








Diagnostic Signal in Problem / Sum
Underlying Algebraic Identity
Algorithmic Engine & Complexity




Infinite/finite shifted product \(\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1 - a q^k x)\) or ratio \(\frac{(ax;q)_\infty}{(x;q)_\infty}\)
First-order \(q\)-difference equation \(F(qx) = \frac{1 - ax}{1 - x} F(x)\) (Cauchy’s Master Theorem)
Coefficient extraction via linear recurrence \(f_m = \frac{1 - a q^{m-1}}{1 - q^m} f_{m-1}\) in \(O(N)\)


Evaluate \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \pmod p\) when \(n \ge d = \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\), or evaluate \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod (q^P - 1)\)
\(q\)-Lucas Theorem: \(\Phi_d(q)\) cancels in base-\(d\) quotient blocks
Base-\(d\) decomposition \(\binom{n_1}{k_1} \begin{bmatrix} n_0 \\ k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q\) in \(O(d + \log_d n)\) (or cyclotomic CRT over \(d \mid P\))


Sum of the form \(\sum_{k=0}^n c_k q^{\pm \binom{k}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\) or cross-term \(q^{\pm k j}\)
\(q\)-Exponential convolution \(E_q / e_q\) or Bluestein identity \(kj = \binom{k+j}{2} - \binom{k}{2} - \binom{j}{2}\)
Single NTT convolution in \(O(N \log N)\)


Partition GF \(\prod_{k \ge 1}(1-q^k)^{-1}\) or distinct/bounded parts at \(N \le 2\times 10^5\) (or arbitrary mod \(M\))
Euler’s Pentagonal Number Theorem / Durfee Square Decomposition
Division-free \(O(N\sqrt{N})\) sparse recurrence (bypassing \(O(N \log N)\) NTT ln/exp)


Count sequences spanning an exact space \(V\), or \(m \times n\) matrices over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) by rank \(r\)
Grassmannian Subspace Mobius Inversion (\(\mu(U, W) = (-1)^{r-j} q^{\binom{r-j}{2}}\))
Convolve \(f_W\) with \((-1)^t q^{\binom{t}{2}} / (q;q)_t\) via NTT in \(O(N \log N)\)


Count subsequences by XOR popcount for \(m \le 55\) where rank \(r\) and \(m - r\) straddle \(m/2\)
Krawtchouk / MacWilliams Duality on dual code \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\) (\(H = [P^T \mid I_{m-r}]\))
Meet-in-the-middle on \(\min(r, m-r) \le \lfloor m/2 \rfloor\) in \(O(nm + 2^{\lfloor m/2 \rfloor} + m^2)\)

23.6 Practice Ladder
We now apply the engines of Chapter 23 across our 8-problem four-tier practice ladder (2 Stepping Stone, 2 Intermediate, 2 Advanced, 2 Mastery).


Stepping Stone 1 (#123) — October 18, 2017

Source: Codeforces Round 752 (Div. 1) Problem F / 1603F
Prerequisite Tags: \(\mathbb{F}_2\) Vector Spaces, Gaussian \(q\)-Binomials (\(q=2\)), Rank-By-Rank Enumeration


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given three integers \(n, k, x\) (\(1 \le n \le 10^9\), \(1 \le k \le 10^7\), \(0 \le x < 2^k\)), count the number of sequences \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\) of integers in \([0, 2^k)\) such that no non-empty subsequence of \(a\) has bitwise XOR sum equal to \(x\). Output the count modulo \(998244353\) across \(t \le 10^5\) test cases (after \(O(k)\) global precomputation, each test case must run in \(O(\min(n, k))\) or \(O(1)\)).


Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(n = 2, k = 2\))
Here \(a_1, a_2 \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}\). There are \(4^2 = 16\) total pairs \((a_1, a_2)\):

Case \(x = 0\): No non-empty subsequence may XOR to \(0\), which means \(a_1, a_2\) must be linearly independent over \(\mathbb{F}_2\). First element: \(2^2 - 1 = 3\) choices (\(\ne 0\)); second element: \(2^2 - 2 = 2\) choices (\(\notin \{0, a_1\}\)). Total = \(3 \times 2 = 6\).
Case \(x = 1\): Forbidden subsequences are \(\{a_1=1\}\), \(\{a_2=1\}\), or \(\{a_1 \oplus a_2 = 1\}\). Conditioning on \(r = \dim\operatorname{span}(a_1, a_2) \in \{0, 1, 2\}\):

\(r = 0\): Only \((0, 0)\), span is \(\{0\} \not\ni 1\) (\(1\) way).
\(r = 1\): Span is a \(1\)-dimensional subspace \(\{0, v\}\) with \(v \in \{2, 3\}\) (\(2\) choices of \(v \ne 1\)), and \((a_1, a_2) \in \{(v,0), (0,v), (v,v)\}\) (\(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 = 3\) ways). Gives \(2 \times 3 = 6\) ways.
\(r = 2\): Span is a \(2\)-dimensional subspace avoiding \(1\) — impossible in \(\mathbb{F}_2^2\) since every \(2\)-subspace of \(\mathbb{F}_2^2\) is all of \(\mathbb{F}_2^2 \ni 1\) (\(0\) ways).
Total for \(x = 1\): \(1 + 6 + 0 = 7\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Whenever a problem asks about the set of all bitwise XOR sums of subsequences of \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) in \([0, 2^k)\), view each integer as a \(k\)-bit vector in \(\mathbb{F}_2^k\). Notice that there is a sharp structural difference between avoiding \(x = 0\) and avoiding a nonzero target \(x > 0\) because the empty subsequence already has XOR sum \(0\). What linear-algebraic property of the vectors \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{F}_2^k\) determines whether a non-empty subsequence XORs to \(0\), versus whether a non-empty subsequence XORs to \(x > 0\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad


For \(x = 0\), no non-empty subsequence XORs to \(0\) if and only if \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb{F}_2\).
For \(x > 0\), no non-empty subsequence XORs to \(x\) if and only if \(x \notin W := \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_2}(a_1, \dots, a_n)\). Condition on the rank \(r = \dim W \in [0, \min(n, k-1)]\). We can view \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) as a \(k \times n\) matrix \(A\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) of rank \(r\) whose column span \(W\) avoids the nonzero vector \(x\). Equivalently, factor \(A = B \cdot C\), where:


\(C\) is an \(r \times n\) matrix in RREF of full row rank \(r\) (representing the coordinates of \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) relative to a canonical basis of \(W\)). How many such RREF matrices \(C\) exist? Each corresponds uniquely to an \(r\)-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{F}_2^n\), so there are \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2\) choices for \(C\)!
\(B\) is a \(k \times r\) matrix whose \(r\) columns are linearly independent and whose span avoids \(x\), i.e., \(x, b_1, \dots, b_r\) are all linearly independent! How many ways can we choose \(b_1, \dots, b_r\) sequentially so that \(b_i \notin \operatorname{span}(x, b_1, \dots, b_{i-1})\)?




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

In Hint 2, \(\operatorname{span}(x, b_1, \dots, b_{i-1})\) has dimension \(i\) (since \(x \ne 0\)), so \(b_i\) has \(2^k - 2^{i}\) choices for \(i = 1, \dots, r\). Summing over \(r\): \[\text{Ans}(x > 0) = \sum_{r=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 \prod_{i=1}^{r} (2^k - 2^i).\] Furthermore, by the \(q\)-binomial recurrence \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} n \\ r-1 \end{bmatrix}_2 \frac{2^{n-r+1} - 1}{2^r - 1}\), can you simplify or precompute this in \(O(k)\) time? Notice that \((2; 2)_k\) can even be precomputed so each query runs in \(O(\min(n, k))\) or \(O(1)\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Case 1: \(x = 0\). A non-empty subsequence of \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) has XOR sum \(0\) if and only if \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) are linearly dependent over \(\mathbb{F}_2\). Thus \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) is valid if and only if \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{F}_2^k\) are linearly independent.

If \(n > k\), no \(n\) vectors in \(\mathbb{F}_2^k\) can be linearly independent, so the answer is \(0\).
If \(n \le k\), choosing \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) sequentially gives \[\text{Ans}(x = 0) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (2^k - 2^i) = 2^{\binom{n}{2}} (2^k - 1)(2^{k-1} - 1) \cdots (2^{k-n+1} - 1) \pmod{998244353}.\]

Case 2: \(x > 0\). Since \(x \ne 0\), no non-empty subsequence has XOR sum \(x\) if and only if \(x \notin W := \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_2}(a_1, \dots, a_n)\). Let \(r = \dim W \in \{0, 1, \dots, \min(n, k-1)\}\).

Number of \(r\)-dimensional subspaces \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^k\) with \(x \notin W\): To choose an ordered basis \((b_1, \dots, b_r)\) of \(W\) such that \(x \notin W\), we require \(x, b_1, \dots, b_r\) to be linearly independent. Since \(x \ne 0\), \(\dim\operatorname{span}(x, b_1, \dots, b_{i-1}) = i\), so there are \(2^k - 2^i\) choices for \(b_i\) (\(1 \le i \le r\)). Dividing by \(|\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb{F}_2)| = \prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(2^r - 2^i)\) gives the number of valid subspaces \(W\): \[\#\{W : \dim W = r,\; x \notin W\} = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^r (2^k - 2^i)}{\prod_{i=0}^{r-1} (2^r - 2^i)} = 2^r \begin{bmatrix} k - 1 \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2.\]
Number of \(n\)-tuples \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) spanning a fixed \(r\)-dimensional subspace \(W\): Fixing a basis of \(W \cong \mathbb{F}_2^r\), an \(n\)-tuple spanning \(W\) corresponds to a surjective linear map \(\mathbb{F}_2^n \twoheadrightarrow \mathbb{F}_2^r\), i.e., an \(r \times n\) matrix of full row rank \(r\), of which there are \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 \prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(2^r - 2^i)\).
Multiplying the two factors: The \(\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(2^r - 2^i) = |\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb{F}_2)|\) factors cancel directly, yielding \[\text{Ans}(x > 0) = \sum_{r=0}^{\min(n, k-1)} \begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 \prod_{i=1}^r (2^k - 2^i).\]
Even Faster \(O(k)\) Per-Query (or \(O(k)\) Global) Closed Form: Notice that \(\prod_{i=1}^r (2^k - 2^i) = 2^{\binom{r+1}{2}} \prod_{i=1}^r (2^{k-i} - 1) = (-1)^r 2^{\binom{r+1}{2}} (2^{k-1}; 2^{-1})_r\). Even more simply, using Cauchy’s \(q\)-binomial identity \(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(1 + z 2^i) = \sum_{r=0}^k 2^{\binom{r}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} k \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 z^r\), both \(x=0\) and \(x>0\) take \(O(k)\) precomputation of \((2; 2)_k\) and \(2^i\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(n \le 10^9, k \le 10^7, x \in [0, 2^k)\); prime modulus \(p = 998244353\) has \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2) \gg 10^7\), so \((2; 2)_r \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) for all \(r \le 10^7\).
Postconditions (Output): Number of valid sequences modulo \(998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(k)\) global precomputation of \((2; 2)_r\) and inverses; \(O(\min(n, k))\) per testcase (or \(O(1)\) when \(x=0\)).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Every sequence \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) has a unique span \(W\) of dimension \(r \in [0, \min(n, k)]\); \(x \notin W \iff \dim(W + \mathbb{F}_2 x) = r + 1\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: When \(x = 0\) and \(n > k\), the answer is immediately \(0\) (by Pigeonhole Principle on dimension); when \(n \le 10^9\) and \(x > 0\), \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2\) must be accumulated via \(2^n \bmod p\) and the \(O(k)\) prefix product \(\prod_{i=1}^r \frac{2^{n-i+1}-1}{2^i-1}\) rather than indexing an array up to \(n\).









Stepping Stone 2 (#033) — make 1

Source: AtCoder Beginner Contest 278 Problem Ex (abc278_h)
Prerequisite Tags: Grassmannian Subspace Mobius Inversion, \(q\)-Binomials (\(q=2\)), Stirling Numbers of the First Kind, Bluestein Chirp-Z Transform


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given integers \(N\) and \(B\) (\(1 \le N \le 2\times 10^5\), \(1 \le B \le 10^7\), \(N \le 2^B\)), count the number of sequences \(A = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_N)\) of distinct integers in \([0, 2^B)\) such that:

No subset of \(\{a_1, \dots, a_{N-1}\}\) has bitwise XOR sum equal to \(1\), and
Some subset of \(\{a_1, \dots, a_N\}\) has bitwise XOR sum equal to \(1\).

Output the count modulo \(998244353\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time.


Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(N = 2, B = 2\))
We want ordered pairs \((a_1, a_2)\) of distinct integers in \(\{0, 1, 2, 3\}\) such that \(1 \notin \operatorname{span}(a_1)\) and \(1 \in \operatorname{span}(a_1, a_2)\):

\(1 \notin \operatorname{span}(a_1)\) means \(a_1 \ne 1\), so \(a_1 \in \{0, 2, 3\}\).

If \(a_1 = 0\): \(\operatorname{span}(a_1) = \{0\}\). Then \(\operatorname{span}(0, a_2) = \{0, a_2\}\) contains \(1\) iff \(a_2 = 1\) (\(1\) pair: \((0, 1)\)).
If \(a_1 = 2\): \(\operatorname{span}(a_1) = \{0, 2\}\). Then \(\operatorname{span}(2, a_2)\) contains \(1\) iff \(a_2 \in \{1, 3\}\) (\(2\) pairs: \((2, 1), (2, 3)\)).
If \(a_1 = 3\): \(\operatorname{span}(a_1) = \{0, 3\}\). Then \(\operatorname{span}(3, a_2)\) contains \(1\) iff \(a_2 \in \{1, 2\}\) (\(2\) pairs: \((3, 1), (3, 2)\)).

Total valid pairs: \(1 + 2 + 2 = 5\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(m = N - 1\), and let \(W = \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_2}(a_1, \dots, a_m) \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^B\) be the subspace spanned by the first \(m\) elements. Condition 1 requires \(1 \notin W\), while Condition 2 requires \(1 \in \operatorname{span}(W \cup \{a_N\})\). If \(W\) is already fixed and avoids \(1\), which elements \(a_N \in \mathbb{F}_2^B\) cause \(\operatorname{span}(W \cup \{a_N\})\) to contain \(1\), and why are those elements automatically distinct from \(a_1, \dots, a_m\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Since \(\operatorname{span}(W \cup \{a_N\}) = W \cup (a_N \oplus W)\), we have \(1 \in \operatorname{span}(W \cup \{a_N\}) \iff a_N \in 1 \oplus W\). Because \(1 \notin W\), the affine coset \(1 \oplus W\) is disjoint from \(W\), giving \(|1 \oplus W| = 2^r\) valid and automatically distinct choices for \(a_N\), where \(r = \dim W\)! Now, for a fixed \(r\)-dimensional subspace \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^B\) with \(1 \notin W\) (of which there are \(2^r \begin{bmatrix} B-1 \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2\) choices, as shown in SS-1), we need the number \(f_{m, r}\) of \(m\)-tuples \((a_1, \dots, a_m)\) of distinct elements in \(W\) that span all of \(W\).

It is hard to enforce “spans all of \(W\)” directly, but it is trivial to count \(m\)-tuples of distinct elements contained inside a \(j\)-dimensional subspace \(U \subseteq W\): there are simply \((2^j)^{\underline{m}} = 2^j (2^j - 1) \cdots (2^j - m + 1)\) such tuples!
Apply Grassmannian Subspace Mobius Inversion (Section 23.1 / Proposition 23.1): since \((2^r)^{\underline{m}} = \sum_{j=0}^r \begin{bmatrix} r \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 f_{m, j}\), inversion gives \[f_{m, r} = \sum_{j=0}^r (-1)^{r-j} 2^{\binom{r-j}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} r \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 (2^j)^{\underline{m}}.\]




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Summing over \(r = 0, 1, \dots, \min(m, B-1)\), the total answer is \[\text{Ans} = \sum_{r=0}^{\min(m, B-1)} 2^{2r} \begin{bmatrix} B - 1 \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 f_{m, r}.\] We need to evaluate this for \(m = N - 1 \le 2\times 10^5\):

First, expand the falling factorial polynomial \(P(x) = x^{\underline{m}} = \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(x - i) = \sum_{k=0}^m c_k x^k\) in \(O(m \log^2 m)\) or \(O(m \log m)\) using Divide-and-Conquer NTT (or Stirling numbers of the first kind).
Next, evaluate \(P(2^j)\) for all \(j = 0, 1, \dots, m\) simultaneously in \(O(m \log m)\) using the Bluestein Chirp-Z Transform (\(j k = \binom{j+k}{2} - \binom{j}{2} - \binom{k}{2}\)).
Finally, compute \(f_{m, r}\) for all \(0 \le r \le m\) by a single NTT convolution of \(A_j = \frac{(2^j)^{\underline{m}}}{(2; 2)_j}\) and \(B_t = \frac{(-1)^t 2^{\binom{t}{2}}}{(2; 2)_t}\).








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Decoupling the Stopping Element \(a_N\): Let \(m = N - 1\) and \(W = \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_2}(a_1, \dots, a_m)\). Let \(r = \dim W\). Because \(a_1, \dots, a_m\) span \(W\), we must have \(0 \le r \le \min(m, B-1)\).

By the subspace counting formula from SS-1, the number of \(r\)-dimensional subspaces \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^B\) avoiding the nonzero vector \(1\) is \(2^r \begin{bmatrix} B - 1 \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2\).
Once \(W\) and \((a_1, \dots, a_m)\) spanning \(W\) are fixed, Condition 2 (\(1 \in \operatorname{span}(W \cup \{a_N\})\)) holds if and only if \(a_N \in 1 \oplus W\). Since \(1 \notin W\), we have \((1 \oplus W) \cap W = \emptyset\), so every \(a_N \in 1 \oplus W\) is automatically distinct from \(a_1, \dots, a_m \in W\). There are \(|1 \oplus W| = 2^r\) choices for \(a_N\).

Subspace Mobius Inversion for Distinct Spanning Tuples: Let \(f_{m, r}\) be the number of \(m\)-tuples of distinct vectors in an \(r\)-dimensional space \(W \cong \mathbb{F}_2^r\) that span \(W\). Partitioning all \((2^r)^{\underline{m}}\) distinct \(m\)-tuples in \(W\) by their actual span \(U \subseteq W\) (\(\dim U = j\)) gives \[(2^r)^{\underline{m}} = \sum_{j=0}^r \begin{bmatrix} r \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 f_{m, j}.\] By Grassmannian Subspace Mobius Inversion (Section 23.1 / Proposition 23.1), substituting \(\begin{bmatrix} r \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 = \frac{(2; 2)_r}{(2; 2)_{r-j} (2; 2)_j}\) yields \[f_{m, r} = \sum_{j=0}^r (-1)^{r-j} 2^{\binom{r-j}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} r \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 (2^j)^{\underline{m}} = \sum_{j=0}^r (-1)^{r-j} 2^{\binom{r-j}{2}} \frac{(2; 2)_r}{(2; 2)_{r-j} (2; 2)_j} (2^j)^{\underline{m}} = (2; 2)_r \sum_{j=0}^r \frac{(-1)^{r-j} 2^{\binom{r-j}{2}}}{(2; 2)_{r-j}} \cdot \frac{(2^j)^{\underline{m}}}{(2; 2)_j}.\]
Fast Multipoint Evaluation of \((2^j)^{\underline{m}}\) via Bluestein CZT: Let \(P(x) = x^{\underline{m}} = \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(x - i) = \sum_{k=0}^m c_k x^k\). We compute the coefficients \(c_0, \dots, c_m\) via product tree NTT (or \(O(m \log m)\) falling-factorial shift). Then for each \(0 \le j \le m\): \[(2^j)^{\underline{m}} = \sum_{k=0}^m c_k 2^{j k} = 2^{-\binom{j}{2}} \sum_{k=0}^m \left(c_k 2^{-\binom{k}{2}}\right) 2^{\binom{j+k}{2}},\] which is a single correlation convolution in \(O(m \log m)\) time!
Verification on Sample (\(N = 2 \implies m = 1, B = 2\)):

\(r = 0\): \(2^0 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}_2 f_{1, 0} = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot (2^0)^{\underline{1}} = 1\).
\(r = 1\): \(2^2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 f_{1, 1} = 4 \cdot 1 \cdot \left((2^1)^{\underline{1}} - (2^0)^{\underline{1}}\right) = 4 \cdot (2 - 1) = 4\).
Total = \(1 + 4 = 5\), matching the sample trace.




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(N \le 2\times 10^5, B \le 10^7\) (\(N \le 2^B\)); prime modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): Number of valid sequences \(A\) modulo \(998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space (Note: we only need \(\begin{bmatrix} B-1 \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2\) for \(r \le N-1\), computed via the recurrence \(\begin{bmatrix} B-1 \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} B-1 \\ r-1 \end{bmatrix}_2 \frac{2^{B-r}-1}{2^r-1}\) in \(O(N)\) time, independent of \(B\)!).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Disjointness \((1 \oplus W) \cap W = \emptyset\) guarantees \(a_N \notin \{a_1, \dots, a_{N-1}\}\) without extra inclusion-exclusion.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: When \(N = 1\) (\(m = 0\)), the empty prefix has \(W = \{0\}\) (\(r = 0\)) and \(a_1\) must equal \(1\), yielding \(1\); when \(r > B - 1\), \(\begin{bmatrix} B-1 \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 = 0\) because no subspace of \(\mathbb{F}_2^B\) avoiding \(1\) can have dimension \(> B - 1\).









Intermediate 1 (#233) — 布尔立方 (Boolean Cube)

Source: QOJ 5097 / SOJ 703
Prerequisite Tags: Rank Enumeration over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), \(q\)-Binomial Inversion, Bluestein Chirp-Z Transform


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Let \(T \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n \times n \times n}\) (\(1 \le n \le 10^5\)) be a 3D binary cube. Slicing \(T\) along each of the three coordinate axes yields \(n\) matrices of size \(n \times n\), and flattening \(T\) along mode \(\alpha \in \{1, 2, 3\}\) yields an \(n \times n^2\) matrix over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) whose rank \(r_\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}\) is the dimension of the minimal subspace \(U_\alpha \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n\) containing all mode-\(\alpha\) fibers of \(T\). Given the dimension \(n \le 10^5\) and axis rank weights \(w(r_1, r_2)\) with full mode-\(3\) rank \(r_3 = n\) modulo \(998244353\), compute the weighted count of \(n \times n \times n\) binary cubes modulo \(998244353\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time.


Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(n = 2\))
For \(n = 2\), there are \(2^{2 \times 2 \times 2} = 2^8 = 256\) binary \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) cubes \(T \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2 \times 2 \times 2}\). Let \((s_1, s_2, s_3)\) be the dimensions of supporting subspaces \(U_1, U_2, U_3 \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^2\), where \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}_2 = 1\), \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 = 3\), \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}_2 = 1\), and a fixed triple \((U_1, U_2, U_3)\) supports \(2^{s_1 s_2 s_3}\) tensors. By Grassmannian Mobius inversion along each axis, the \(256\) cubes partition by exact mode-rank triple \((r_1, r_2, r_3)\) as follows:

\((r_1, r_2, r_3) = (0, 0, 0)\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}_2^3 \cdot 1 = 1\) cube (the all-zero cube).
\((r_1, r_2, r_3) = (1, 1, 1)\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}_2^3 (2^1 - 1) = 3^3 \cdot 1 = 27\) rank-\(1\) pure tensors \(u \otimes v \otimes w\).
Permutations of \((1, 2, 2)\) (3 permutations: \((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 1)\)): For \((1, 2, 2)\), \(r_1 = 1\) chooses \(1\) of \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 = 3\) lines \(U_1\), and the \(2 \times 2\) slice in \(U_2 \otimes U_3\) must have full rank \(2\) (there are \(6\) invertible \(2 \times 2\) matrices over \(\mathbb{F}_2\)), giving \(3 \times 6 = 18\) cubes per permutation (\(3 \times 18 = 54\) total).
\((r_1, r_2, r_3) = (2, 2, 2)\): Subtracting all lower-rank configurations from \(2^8 = 256\) gives \(256 - (1 + 27 + 18 + 18 + 18) = 174\) full-rank \((2, 2, 2)\) cubes.
Total Check: \(1 + 27 + 18 + 18 + 18 + 174 = 256 = 2^8\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Think of an \(n \times n \times n\) binary cube as a trilinear tensor or as \(n\) matrix slices \(M_1, \dots, M_n \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n \times n}\). Why is it difficult to count cubes by their exact span dimensions \((r_1, r_2, r_3)\) along multiple axes simultaneously? Because requiring the span of the fibers along an axis to have exact dimension \(r\) imposes a non-local linear independence condition. What happens if you instead relax the condition from “the fibers span an \(r\)-dimensional subspace” to “all fibers are contained inside a fixed \(s\)-dimensional subspace \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n\)”?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

When we fix subspaces \(U_1, U_2, U_3 \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n\) of dimensions \(s_1, s_2, s_3\) along the three axes, a cube \(T\) has all its fibers contained in \(U_1, U_2, U_3\) if and only if \(T \in U_1 \otimes U_2 \otimes U_3\), which gives a pure power of \(2\): \(2^{s_1 s_2 s_3}\) choices! Recall the fundamental \(q\)-falling factorial identity connecting subspace-containment moments \(2^{n s}\) to \(q\)-binomials: \[2^{n s} = \sum_{r=0}^s \begin{bmatrix} s \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 \prod_{i=0}^{r-1} (2^n - 2^i) = \sum_{r=0}^s \begin{bmatrix} s \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 2^{\binom{r}{2}} (2^n - 1)(2^{n-1} - 1) \cdots (2^{n-r+1} - 1).\] And when coupling two axes of subspace dimensions \(r\) and \(s\), the number of \(n\)-slice tensors constrained to an \(r\)-subspace along axis 1 and an \(s\)-subspace along axis 2 is \(2^{n r s}\) (or \(2^{r s}\) per slice). How do we sum \(\sum_{r, s} \alpha_r \beta_s 2^{c \cdot r s}\) over \(0 \le r, s \le n\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Use Bluestein’s identity \(r s = \binom{r+s}{2} - \binom{r}{2} - \binom{s}{2}\) with base \(Q = 2^c\)!

Apply Grassmannian Subspace Mobius Inversion along each constrained axis: to go from “contained in an \(s\)-subspace” to “exact span has dimension \(r\)”, convolve with \(\frac{(-1)^{r-s} 2^{\binom{r-s}{2}}}{(2; 2)_{r-s}}\).
Use Bluestein’s Chirp-Z transform to evaluate the cross-axis bilinear form \(\sum_{s=0}^n \beta_s Q^{r s} = Q^{-\binom{r}{2}} \sum_{s=0}^n \left(\beta_s Q^{-\binom{s}{2}}\right) Q^{\binom{r+s}{2}}\) via a single NTT in \(O(n \log n)\) time!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

The Rank-Subspace Duality over \(\mathbb{F}_2\): By the Rank-Nullity Theorem, an \(n \times n\) matrix \(M\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) has rank \(r\) if and only if its row space \(W = \operatorname{rowspan}(M) \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n\) has dimension \(r\).

The number of \(r\)-dimensional subspaces \(W \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n\) is \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2\).
For a fixed \(s\)-dimensional subspace \(U \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n\), the number of matrices \(M \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n \times n}\) with \(\operatorname{rowspan}(M) \subseteq U\) is \((2^s)^n = 2^{n s}\).
Partitioning these \(2^{n s}\) matrices by the exact dimension \(r = \dim\operatorname{rowspan}(M) \le s\) yields the \(q\)-falling factorial identity: \[2^{n s} = \sum_{r=0}^s \begin{bmatrix} s \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 g_r, \qquad g_r = \begin{bmatrix} n \\ r \end{bmatrix}_2 \prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(2^r - 2^i) = \prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(2^n - 2^i).\]

Coupling Across Axes of the \(n \times n \times n\) Cube: View the \(n \times n \times n\) tensor \(T \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n \times n \times n}\) as a trilinear array \(T_{i, j, k}\). Fixing subspaces \(U_1, U_2, U_3 \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n\) of dimensions \(s_1, s_2, s_3\) along the three axes, the number of tensors \(T\) supported inside \(U_1 \times U_2 \times U_3\) is \[\#\{T \in U_1 \otimes U_2 \otimes U_3\} = 2^{s_1 s_2 s_3}.\] Whether \(r_3 = n\) is fixed via Mobius inversion at \(s_3 \le n\) or summed over \(r_3\) when a \(1\)-axis slice-sum constraint weights \((r_1, r_2)\) across all \(n\) slices (e.g., \(\sum_{k=1}^n (2^{s_1 s_2})^k\) or \(2^{n s_1 s_2}\)), reducing along the third axis turns the cross-axis coupling into a bilinear sum of the form \[H_r = \sum_{s=0}^n \beta_s Q^{r s},\] coupled with Grassmannian Mobius inversion on each axis: \[f_r = \sum_{s=0}^r (-1)^{r-s} 2^{\binom{r-s}{2}} \begin{bmatrix} r \\ s \end{bmatrix}_2 H_s.\]

Stage 1 (Subspace Moments): Construct the subspace weights \(\beta_s\) using \((2; 2)_s\) and \(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ s \end{bmatrix}_2\) in \(O(n)\) time.
Stage 2 (Bluestein Cross-Axis Transform): Rewrite \(Q^{r s} = Q^{\binom{r+s}{2} - \binom{r}{2} - \binom{s}{2}}\) and compute \(H_r\) for all \(0 \le r \le n\) via a single length-\(2n\) NTT convolution.
Stage 3 (Grassmannian Mobius Inversion): Convolve \(H_s / (2; 2)_s\) with \((-1)^t 2^{\binom{t}{2}} / (2; 2)_t\) via NTT to extract the exact rank counts \(f_r\).
