section: 19.2 Zeilberger’s Creative Telescoping, WZ Pairs & EI’s Differential-Residue Binomial Sum Engine (Engine 3)
text:
19.2 Zeilberger’s Creative Telescoping, WZ Pairs & EI’s Differential-Residue Binomial Sum Engine (Engine 3)
In Chapter 6, we met two classic engines for evaluating a definite binomial sum \(S_n = \sum_{k} F(n, k)\):

Engine 1 (Snake Oil): Multiply by \(z^n\), swap \(\sum_n\) and \(\sum_k\), and sum the inner series over \(n\).
Engine 2 (Egorychev / Residue Extraction): Write \(F(n, k) = [x^{g(n, k)}] P(x, n, k)\) so the sum over \(k\) becomes a geometric or binomial series inside \([x^m]\).

What happens when neither engine collapses the sum into a closed form? Consider the \(c\)-Delannoy polynomial \[D_n(c) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} \binom{n+k}{k} c^k,\] or Apéry’s sum \(\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}^2 \binom{n+k}{k}^2\). Here \(n\) appears in three places at once, and \(D_n(c)\) has no hypergeometric closed form—yet \(D_0(c), \dots, D_N(c)\) can still be computed in \(O(N)\) time because \(D_n(c)\) is P-recursive! We now develop the two complementary engines that compile such sums directly into \(O(N)\) recurrences.

1. Zeilberger’s Creative Telescoping & WZ Certificate Pairs
Suppose \(F(n, k)\) is a bivariate hypergeometric term, meaning that both shift ratios \(\frac{F(n+1, k)}{F(n, k)}\) and \(\frac{F(n, k+1)}{F(n, k)}\) are rational functions of \((n, k)\) over \(K\). If we try to telescope \(F(n+1, k) - F(n, k) = G(n, k+1) - G(n, k)\) directly, no hypergeometric \(G(n, k)\) may exist.
Zeilberger’s insight (1990) is to take a polynomial linear combination of shifts \(F(n, k), F(n+1, k), \dots, F(n+r, k)\) along \(n\) until their combination becomes an exact first difference \(\Delta_k G(n, k) = G(n, k+1) - G(n, k)\) along \(k\)!






ImportantTheorem 19.1 (Zeilberger’s Creative Telescoping & WZ Certificate)



Let \(F(n, k)\) be a proper hypergeometric term with natural compact support (so \(F(n, k) = 0\) for \(k < 0\) and \(k > n + O(1)\)). Then there exist an order \(r \ge 1\), polynomials \(p_0(n), p_1(n), \dots, p_r(n) \in K[n]\) (independent of \(k\)!), and a rational certificate \(R(n, k) \in K(n, k)\) such that with \(G(n, k) = R(n, k) F(n, k)\), the WZ difference identity holds for all \((n, k)\): \[\sum_{j=0}^{r} p_j(n) \, F(n + j, k) = G(n, k + 1) - G(n, k).\] Summing both sides over all \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\), the right-hand side telescopes to \(0\) on natural support, proving that \(S_n = \sum_{k} F(n, k)\) satisfies the homogeneous P-recursive recurrence: \[\sum_{j=0}^{r} p_j(n) \, S_{n+j} = 0.\]








WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Non-Natural Summation Boundaries (\(\sum_{k=0}^m \binom{n}{k}\) with \(m < n\))



The Trap: Students sometimes apply a homogeneous recurrence derived from creative telescoping to a sum whose upper limit \(m\) cuts off the summand before \(F(n, k)\) naturally vanishes (for example, the partial row sum \(S(n, m) = \sum_{k=0}^m \binom{n}{k}\) for a fixed \(m < n\)). Why It Fails: Pascal’s identity gives the WZ pair \(F(n, k) = \binom{n}{k}\) and \(G(n, k) = -\binom{n}{k-1}\), satisfying: \[F(n + 1, k) - 2 F(n, k) = \binom{n}{k - 1} - \binom{n}{k} = G(n, k + 1) - G(n, k).\] When summed over natural support \(k \in [0, n+1]\), the boundary values \(G(n, n+2) = -\binom{n}{n+1} = 0\) and \(G(n, 0) = -\binom{n}{-1} = 0\) vanish, giving \(S_{n+1} - 2 S_n = 0 \implies S_n = 2^n\). However, if we truncate the sum at \(k = m < n\), summing from \(k = 0\) to \(m\) leaves a non-zero upper boundary term: \[\sum_{k=0}^{m} \big(F(n+1, k) - 2 F(n, k)\big) = G(n, m + 1) - G(n, 0) = -\binom{n}{m}.\] The Remedy: Always evaluate \(G(n, k_{\max} + 1) - G(n, k_{\min})\) explicitly! For truncated limits, creative telescoping produces an inhomogeneous P-recurrence \(S(n+1, m) = 2 S(n, m) - \binom{n}{m}\).




2. EI’s Differential-Residue Binomial Sum Engine (Engine 3)
Finding the rational certificate \(R(n, k)\) by hand can be algebraically tedious. In competitive programming, Elegia (EI, 载谭 Binomial Sums) popularized a far more direct algorithm—Engine 3—that replaces Gosper’s discrete certificate search with formal residue integration by parts in \(K((x))\).






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: EI’s Differential-Residue Method




The Diagnostic Signal: You have a definite binomial sum \(S_n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} \binom{n+k}{k} c^k\) (or any sum where \(n\) enters via binomial factors \(\binom{n}{k}, \binom{n+k}{k}, \binom{2n-k}{n}\)) and you want the P-recursive recurrence for \(S_n\) by hand in 3 lines of algebra.
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad:

Step 1 (Isolate \(n\) into a Power \(B(x)^n\)): Use Egorychev’s residue representation \([x^k](1+x)^m = \binom{m}{k}\) to write \(S_n\) as a constant term (or formal residue) in \(x\) where \(n\) appears only in the exponent of a single rational function \(B(x)\): \[S_n = [x^0]\Big(A(x) B(x)^n\Big) = \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\Big(x^{-1} A(x) B(x)^n\Big).\] For instance, in \(D_n(c) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} \binom{n+k}{k} c^k\), write \(\binom{n+k}{k} = \binom{n+k}{n} = [x^n](1+x)^{n+k}\). Then: \[
\begin{aligned}
D_n(c)
&= [x^n] (1+x)^n \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} c^k (1+x)^k \\[4pt]
&= [x^n] (1+x)^n \big(1 + c(1+x)\big)^n
&& \text{(collapse the sum over } k \text{ by the Binomial Theorem)} \\[4pt]
&= \operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \Bigl[ x^{-n-1} (1+x)^n (1 + c + cx)^n \Bigr]
&& \text{(write } [x^n] G(x) = \operatorname{Res}_{x=0} x^{-n-1} G(x)\text{)} \\[4pt]
&= \operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \left[ x^{-1} \left( \frac{(1+x)(1 + c + cx)}{x} \right)^n \right].
&& \text{(factor } x^{-n-1} = x^{-1} \cdot x^{-n} \text{ into the } n\text{-th power)}
\end{aligned}
\] Here \(A(x) = 1\) and \(B(x) = \frac{(1+x)(1 + c + cx)}{x} = (1+c)x^{-1} + (1 + 2c) + c x\)!
Step 2 (Apply the Formal Residue Derivative Identity \(\operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \frac{d}{dx}(\dots) = 0\)): In the formal Laurent field \(K((x))\), the derivative of any Laurent series has zero coefficient of \(x^{-1}\). Applying \(\operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \frac{d}{dx}\big(\phi(x) B(x)^n\big) = 0\) gives the formal integration-by-parts rule: \[\operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\Big(\phi'(x) B(x)^n\Big) = -n \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\Big(\phi(x) B'(x) B(x)^{n-1}\Big).\]
Step 3 (Eliminate Non-Constant Powers of \(x\) via Linear Algebra): Expand \(B(x)\) and \(x B'(x)\) as Laurent polynomials in \(x\), and express \(S_{n+1}, S_n, S_{n-1}\) in terms of \(\mu_j = \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\big(x^{j-1} B(x)^n\big)\) to eliminate all auxiliary moments \(\mu_j\) (\(j \neq 0\))!





Complete Worked Derivation & Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N \le 4\)): The \(c\)-Delannoy Recurrence
Let us execute Steps 1–3 on \(D_n(c) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}\binom{n+k}{k} c^k\):

Residue Representation: From Step 1 above, let \(B(x) = (1+c)x^{-1} + (1+2c) + cx\). For each integer shift \(j \in \mathbb{Z}\), define the Laurent moment: \[\mu_j(n) = \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\Big(x^{j-1} B(x)^n\Big), \qquad \text{so that } \mu_0(n) = D_n(c).\]
Symmetry Between \(\mu_1(n)\) and \(\mu_{-1}(n)\): Notice that \(x B'(x) = -(1+c)x^{-1} + cx\). First apply \(\operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \frac{d}{dx}\big(B(x)^n\big) = 0\): \[0 = n \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\Big(x^{-1} \big(x B'(x)\big) B(x)^{n-1}\Big) = n \big(-(1+c) \mu_{-1}(n-1) + c \mu_1(n-1)\big),\] which proves \((1+c) \mu_{-1}(m) = c \mu_1(m)\) for all \(m \ge 0\)!
Eliminating \(\mu_{\pm 1}\) via the Quadratic Differential Identity for \(x B'(x)\): Observe that \(B(x) - (1+2c) = (1+c)x^{-1} + cx\) and \(x B'(x) = -(1+c)x^{-1} + cx\) share the same two monomials with opposite signs. Squaring both and subtracting eliminates \(x\) and \(x^{-1}\) completely: \[\big(B(x) - (1+2c)\big)^2 - \big(x B'(x)\big)^2 = 4c(1+c) = (1+2c)^2 - 1 \implies \big(x B'(x)\big)^2 = B(x)^2 - 2(1+2c) B(x) + 1.\] Simultaneously, applying \(\vartheta = x \frac{d}{dx}\) to \(x B'(x) = -(1+c)x^{-1} + cx\) flips the sign back to \(B(x) - (1+2c)\): \[x \frac{d}{dx}\big(x B'(x)\big) = (1+c)x^{-1} + cx = B(x) - (1+2c).\] Now apply the formal residue derivative identity \(0 = \operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \frac{d}{dx}\Big(x B'(x) B(x)^{n-1}\Big)\): \[\begin{aligned}
0 &= \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\left[ x^{-1} \Big( x \frac{d}{dx}\big(x B'(x)\big) B(x)^{n-1} + (n-1) \big(x B'(x)\big)^2 B(x)^{n-2} \Big) \right] \\
&= \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\left[ x^{-1} \Big( \big(B(x) - (1+2c)\big) B(x)^{n-1} + (n-1)\big(B(x)^2 - 2(1+2c)B(x) + 1\big) B(x)^{n-2} \Big) \right] \\
&= \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\left[ x^{-1} \Big( n B(x)^n - (2n - 1)(1 + 2c) B(x)^{n-1} + (n - 1) B(x)^{n-2} \Big) \right],
\end{aligned}\] which immediately extracts the 3-term P-recursive recurrence: \[n D_n(c) = (2n - 1)(1 + 2c) D_{n-1}(c) - (n - 1) D_{n-2}(c) \qquad (n \ge 2).\]


Hand-Checkable Trace for \(c = 2\) (\(1 + 2c = 5\)) up to \(N = 4\):

Algebraic Cross-Check via Diagonal Formula: By Furstenberg’s diagonal formula from Chapter 16, \(D_n(c) = [x^n]\big((1+c) + (1+2c)x + cx^2\big)^n\) has \(p_0 = 1+c, p_1 = 1+2c, p_2 = c\) with \(p_1^2 - 4 p_0 p_2 = (1 + 2c)^2 - 4c(1+c) = 1\), confirming the OGF \(\sum_{n \ge 0} D_n(c) z^n = (1 - 2(1 + 2c)z + z^2)^{-1/2}\) and recurrence \(n D_n(c) = (2n - 1)(1 + 2c) D_{n-1}(c) - (n - 1) D_{n-2}(c)\).
Recurrence vs. Direct Binomial Sum (\(c = 2\)):

\(n = 0\): \(D_0(2) = \binom{0}{0}\binom{0}{0} 2^0 = 1\).
\(n = 1\): \(D_1(2) = \binom{1}{0}\binom{1}{0} 2^0 + \binom{1}{1}\binom{2}{1} 2^1 = 1 + 4 = 5\).
\(n = 2\): \(2 D_2(2) = 5(3) D_1(2) - 1 D_0(2) = 75 - 1 = 74 \implies D_2(2) = 37\), matching \(1 + \binom{2}{1}\binom{3}{1}(2) + \binom{2}{2}\binom{4}{2}(4) = 1 + 12 + 24 = 37\).
\(n = 3\): \(3 D_3(2) = 5(5) D_2(2) - 2 D_1(2) = 25(37) - 10 = 915 \implies D_3(2) = 305\), matching \(1 + 3(4)(2) + 3(10)(4) + 1(20)(8) = 305\).
\(n = 4\): \(4 D_4(2) = 5(7) D_3(2) - 3 D_2(2) = 35(305) - 3(37) = 10564 \implies D_4(2) = 2641\).









NoteAlgorithm Contract: EI’s Differential-Residue Binomial Sum Engine (Engine 3)




Input: A definite hypergeometric binomial sum \(S_n = \sum_{k} F(n, k)\) representable as \(S_n = \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\big(x^{-1} A(x) B(x)^n\big)\) with rational \(A(x), B(x) \in K(x)\), and target index \(N\).
Output: The sequence of values \(S_0, S_1, \dots, S_N \in K\).
Algebraic Preconditions: \(B(x)\) has Laurent degree span \([ -d_1, d_2 ]\) with \(d_1, d_2 \ge 1\); the resulting indicial polynomial \(I(n)\) is invertible in \(K\) for all \(r \le n \le N\) (requiring \(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(p > N\), or \(p\)-adic lifting from Chapter 18.4).
Complexity: \(O((d_1 + d_2)^3)\) offline symbolic work to eliminate the \(d_1 + d_2 - 1\) auxiliary Laurent moments \(\mu_j(n)\), followed by \(O((d_1 + d_2) N)\) time and \(O(d_1 + d_2)\) auxiliary space (or \(O(N)\) space to store all answers) to unroll \(S_0, \dots, S_N\).
Correctness Invariant: In the formal Laurent field \(K((x))\), \(\operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \frac{d}{dx} L(x) = 0\) holds identically for every \(L(x) \in K((x))\) without analytic convergence hypotheses; provided \(k\) ranges over the full natural support of the coefficient extraction, no boundary terms are omitted.

section: 19.3 Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition \(F(P(x))\) & EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODEs (\(F_{<N}'\))
text:
19.3 Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition \(F(P(x))\) & EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODEs (\(F_{<N}'\))

Part A: Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition \(H(x) = F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) in \(O(rNK)\)
In Chapter 2, we learned how to compute \(P(x)^\alpha\), \(\exp(P(x))\), and \(\ln(P(x))\) in \(O(NK)\) time when \(P(x)\) is a \(K\)-sparse polynomial (having at most \(K\) non-zero coefficients) by differentiating once: for example, \(H(x) = \exp(P(x))\) satisfies the first-order ODE \(H'(x) = P'(x) H(x)\).
What if the outer series \(F(y)\) is a general D-finite series of order \(r \ge 2\), satisfying an order-\(r\) linear ODE \[F^{(r)}(y) = \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} a_i(y) \, F^{(i)}(y)\] with polynomial (or rational) coefficients \(a_i(y)\), and we want to compute the composition \(H(x) = F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) for a \(K\)-sparse polynomial \(P(x)\) with \(P(0) = 0\)?






WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: The \(1/P'(x)\) Sparsity-Destruction Trap



The Trap: If you try to form a single order-\(r\) ODE for \(H(x) = F(P(x))\) using the chain-rule operator \(\mathcal{D}_P = \frac{1}{P'(x)} \frac{d}{dx}\) from Chapter 18.3, two disasters occur when \(r \ge 2\):

Valuation Singularity at \(x = 0\): For \(r = 2\), clearing denominators in \(\mathcal{D}_P^2 H + a_1(P)\mathcal{D}_P H + a_0(P) H = 0\) produces: \[P'(x) H''(x) - \big(P''(x) + a_1(P(x)) P'(x)^2\big) H'(x) - a_0(P(x)) P'(x)^3 H(x) = 0.\] Whenever \([x^1]P(x) = 0\) (for example, \(P(x) = x^2 + x^5\), so \(\operatorname{val}(P') = 1\)), the leading coefficient \(P'(x)\) vanishes at \(x = 0\), creating an apparent singularity where the indicial polynomial vanishes!
Sparsity Explosion: Even if \([x^1]P(x) \neq 0\), multiplying by \(P'(x)^r\) expands a \(K\)-sparse polynomial into \(O(K^r)\) terms (or \(O(N)\) terms if you invert \(P'(x)\)), destroying the \(O(NK)\) runtime!

The Remedy (Coupled \(r\)-State First-Order System): Never eliminate \(F'(P(x)), \dots, F^{(r-1)}(P(x))\)! Instead, maintain all \(r\) derivatives evaluated at \(P(x)\) simultaneously as a coupled first-order system.








TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition




The Diagnostic Signal: You need \(H(x) = F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) where \(P(x)\) is \(K\)-sparse (\(K \ll \log^2 N\)) with \(P(0) = 0\), and \(F(y)\) satisfies an order-\(r\) linear ODE \(q_r(y) F^{(r)}(y) = \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} q_i(y) F^{(i)}(y)\) with \(q_r(0) \neq 0\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Define the \(r\) coupled formal power series: \[H_0(x) = F(P(x)), \quad H_1(x) = F'(P(x)), \quad \dots, \quad H_{r-1}(x) = F^{(r-1)}(P(x)).\] Differentiate each \(H_i(x)\) once with respect to \(x\) using the chain rule: \[\begin{aligned}
H_0'(x) &= P'(x) \, H_1(x), \\
H_1'(x) &= P'(x) \, H_2(x), \\
&\;\;\vdots \\
q_r(P(x)) \, H_{r-1}'(x) &= P'(x) \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} q_i(P(x)) \, H_i(x).
\end{aligned}\] Look at what happened:

We never divided by \(P'(x)\)! Even if \(P(x) = x^3 + x^7\), the coefficient of \([x^{n-1}] H_i'(x)\) is simply \(n [x^n] H_i(x)\), which is always nonsingular for every \(n \ge 1\)!
To advance from degree \(n - 1\) to degree \(n\), we first extract \([x^{n-1}]\) from the last equation to get \([x^n] H_{r-1}(x)\) (using only \([x^{\le n-1}] H_0, \dots, H_{r-1}\) since \(\operatorname{val}(P) \ge 1\)), and similarly extract \([x^{n-1}]\) from \(H_i'(x) = P'(x) H_{i+1}(x)\) for \(i = 0, \dots, r-2\). Every equation multiplies by the sparse polynomial \(P'(x)\) in \(O(K)\) time!




// Coupled 2-State Sparse Composition: solves F''(y) = a1*F'(y) + a0*F(y) at y = P(x)
for (int n = 1; n < N; ++n) {
    long long s0 = 0, s1 = 0;
    for (auto [d, c] : sp_P) { // non-zero (deg >= 1, coeff) of K-sparse P(x)
        if (d > n) break;
        long long dc = d * c % MOD;
        s0 = (s0 + dc * H1[n - d]) % MOD;
        s1 = (s1 + dc * ((a0 * H0[n - d] + a1 * H1[n - d]) % MOD)) % MOD;
    }
    H0[n] = s0 * inv[n] % MOD; H1[n] = s1 * inv[n] % MOD;
}

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\)): \(F(y) = \sin y + \cos y\) Composed with \(P(x) = x + x^3\)
Here \(F''(y) = -F(y)\) (\(r = 2, a_0 = -1, a_1 = 0\)) with \(F(0) = 1, F'(0) = 1\). Let \(H_0(x) = F(P(x))\) and \(H_1(x) = F'(P(x)) = \cos P(x) - \sin P(x)\). Since \(P'(x) = 1 + 3x^2\), the coupled system is \(H_0'(x) = (1 + 3x^2) H_1(x)\) and \(H_1'(x) = -(1 + 3x^2) H_0(x)\), giving: \[n h_{0, n} = h_{1, n-1} + 3 h_{1, n-3}, \qquad n h_{1, n} = -h_{0, n-1} - 3 h_{0, n-3}.\]

\(n = 0\): \(h_{0, 0} = 1, \quad h_{1, 0} = 1\).
\(n = 1\): \(h_{0, 1} = \frac{1}{1}(1) = 1, \quad h_{1, 1} = \frac{1}{1}(-1) = -1\).
\(n = 2\): \(h_{0, 2} = \frac{1}{2}(-1) = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad h_{1, 2} = \frac{1}{2}(-1) = -\frac{1}{2}\).
\(n = 3\): \(h_{0, 3} = \frac{1}{3}\left(-\frac{1}{2} + 3(1)\right) = \frac{5}{6}, \quad h_{1, 3} = \frac{1}{3}\left(-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) - 3(1)\right) = -\frac{5}{6}\).
\(n = 4\): \(h_{0, 4} = \frac{1}{4}\left(-\frac{5}{6} + 3(-1)\right) = -\frac{23}{24}\).
Direct Taylor Verification: \(\sin(x + x^3) + \cos(x + x^3) = \left((x + x^3) - \frac{x^3}{6}\right) + \left(1 - \frac{(x+x^3)^2}{2} + \frac{x^4}{24}\right) + O(x^5) = 1 + x - \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{5}{6}x^3 - \frac{23}{24}x^4 + O(x^5)\), matching every coefficient!







NoteAlgorithm Contract: Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition Engine




Input: Order-\(r\) linear ODE \(q_r(y) F^{(r)}(y) = \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} q_i(y) F^{(i)}(y)\) with initial values \(F^{(i)}(0) = f_i\) (\(0 \le i < r\)), a \(K\)-sparse polynomial \(P(x) = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j x^{d_j}\) with \(1 \le d_1 < \dots < d_K < N\), and precision \(N\).
Output: \(H_0(x) = F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) (along with \(H_i(x) = F^{(i)}(P(x)) \bmod x^N\)).
Algebraic Preconditions: \(P(0) = 0\) (\(\operatorname{val}(P) \ge 1\)), \(q_r(0) \in K^\times\), and \(1, 2, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (\(p \ge N\)).
Complexity: \(O(r \cdot D \cdot N \cdot K)\) time and \(O(r N)\) space, where \(D = 1 + \max_i \deg q_i(y)\) (so \(O(rNK)\) when \(q_i\) are constants or degree \(O(1)\)).
Correctness Invariant: Because \(\operatorname{val}(P) \ge 1\), \(\operatorname{val}(P') \ge 0\), so \([x^{n-1}]\big(P'(x) P(x)^m H_i(x)\big)\) depends only on \([x^k] H_i(x)\) for \(0 \le k \le n - 1\); thus at step \(n\), all right-hand side terms are already finalized before dividing by \(n \cdot q_r(0)\).







Part B: EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODEs (\(A(x) F_{<N}' + B(x) F_{<N} = C(x) - R_N(x)\))
Suppose an infinite formal power series \(F(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n x^n\) satisfies a simple first-order linear ODE \[A(x) F'(x) + B(x) F(x) = C(x)\] where \(A(x), B(x), C(x) \in K[x]\) are low-degree polynomials. In many combinatorics problems, however, we do not work with the infinite series \(F(x)\)—we work with its degree-\((N-1)\) truncation: \[F_{<N}(x) = F(x) \bmod x^N = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f_n x^n.\] For example:

We may need the Taylor shift \(F_{<N}(x + c)\) (or \(F_{<N}(x - 1)\)) to convert between binomial moments, falling factorials, or inclusion-exclusion states. Computing \(F_{<N}(x + c)\) via Chapter 6’s reversed convolution costs \(O(N \log N)\) time via NTT.
Or we may need to integrate products of truncated exponentials \(S_{<a}(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{a-1} \frac{x^j}{j!} = e^x \bmod x^a\) in continuous-time Poissonization (UOJ 514).

Elegia’s Breakthrough (EI 科技): If \(F(x)\) satisfies a sparse polynomial ODE, then its truncation \(F_{<N}(x)\) satisfies the exact same left-hand differential operator with a tiny polynomial remainder \(R_N(x)\) on the right-hand side! And because a polynomial ODE is preserved under any affine shift \(x \gets u + c\), we can unroll the shifted polynomial \(G(u) = F_{<N}(u + c)\) directly in \(O(N)\) time with zero NTTs!






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Truncated Taylor ODEs




The Diagnostic Signal: You need to shift, multiply, or integrate a truncated series \(F_{<N}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f_n x^n\) whose parent series \(F(x)\) satisfies a known low-degree ODE \(A(x) F'(x) + B(x) F(x) = C(x)\) (such as \((1+x)^\alpha\), \(e^x\), or \((1-x)^{-\alpha}\)).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Split the infinite series into its head and tail: \[F(x) = F_{<N}(x) + F_{\ge N}(x), \qquad F_{\ge N}(x) = \sum_{n=N}^{\infty} f_n x^n.\] Substitute this split into \(A(x) F'(x) + B(x) F(x) = C(x)\) and move the tail to the right-hand side: \[A(x) F_{<N}'(x) + B(x) F_{<N}(x) = C(x) - \underbrace{\Big( A(x) F_{\ge N}'(x) + B(x) F_{\ge N}(x) \Big)}_{R_N(x)}.\] Now look simultaneously at the maximum degree of the left-hand side and the minimum valuation of the right-hand side:

Since \(\deg F_{<N} \le N - 1\) and \(\deg F_{<N}' \le N - 2\), the left-hand side is a polynomial of degree at most \(N - 1 + d\), where \(d = \max(\deg A - 1, \deg B)\).
On the right-hand side, \(\operatorname{val}(F_{\ge N}) \ge N\) and \(\operatorname{val}(F_{\ge N}') \ge N - 1\), so every term of \(F_{\ge N}\) above \(f_{N+d-1} x^{N+d-1}\) has degree \(\ge N + d\) and cancels identically against \(C(x)\)! Therefore, \(R_N(x)\) is a sparse polynomial localized in degrees \([N - 1, N + d - 1]\) depending on at most \(d + 1\) boundary coefficients \(f_N, f_{N+1}, \dots, f_{N+d}\)!










ImportantTheorem 19.2 (Two Canonical Instances of EI 科技 Truncated ODEs)




Truncated Binomial Series \(F_{<N}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \binom{\alpha}{k} x^k = (1 + x)^\alpha \bmod x^N\): Here \(A(x) = 1 + x, B(x) = -\alpha, C(x) = 0\), so \(d = \max(0, 0) = 0\). The tail \(R_N(x)\) has only a single degree-\((N-1)\) monomial coming from \(1 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}\big(\binom{\alpha}{N} x^N\big)\): \[(1 + x) F_{<N}'(x) - \alpha F_{<N}(x) = -N \binom{\alpha}{N} x^{N-1}.\] To compute the shifted polynomial \(G(u) = F_{<N}(u + c) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_k u^k\), substitute \(x = u + c\): \[(1 + c + u) G'(u) - \alpha G(u) = -N \binom{\alpha}{N} (u + c)^{N-1}.\] Extracting \([u^k]\) from \(k = N - 1\) down to \(0\) (or \(0\) up to \(N - 1\) when \(1 + c \neq 0\)) computes all \(g_0, \dots, g_{N-1}\) in \(O(N)\) time!
The Miracle Derivative of the Truncated Exponential \(S_{<a}(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{a-1} \frac{x^j}{j!} = e^x \bmod x^a\): Since \(e^x\) satisfies \(F'(x) - F(x) = 0\), its truncation \(S_{<a}(x)\) satisfies: \[S_{<a}'(x) - S_{<a}(x) = -\frac{x^{a-1}}{(a-1)!} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{d}{dx}\Big(e^{-x} S_{<a}(x)\Big) = -e^{-x} \frac{x^{a-1}}{(a-1)!}.\] Differentiating \(e^{-x} S_{<a}(x)\) collapses the entire \(a\)-term polynomial into a single monomial!




Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\)): \(O(N)\) Taylor Shift of \(F_{<4}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^3 \binom{5}{k} x^k\) at \(x = u - 1\)
Let \(\alpha = 5, N = 4\), so \(F_{<4}(x) = 1 + 5x + 10x^2 + 10x^3\). Suppose we want \(G(u) = F_{<4}(u - 1) = \sum_{k=0}^3 g_k u^k\) (i.e., \(c = -1\)). Substitute \(x = u - 1\) into \((1 + x) F_{<4}'(x) - 5 F_{<4}(x) = -4 \binom{5}{4} x^3 = -20 x^3\): \[u G'(u) - 5 G(u) = -20 (u - 1)^3 = -20 u^3 + 60 u^2 - 60 u + 20.\] Notice that because \(1 + c = 0\), the left-hand side is simply \((\vartheta_u - 5) G(u) = \sum_{k=0}^3 (k - 5) g_k u^k\)—it is diagonal in \([u^k]\)! Even for general \(c\), extracting \([u^k]\) gives \((k + 1)(1 + c) g_{k+1} + (k - \alpha) g_k = -N \binom{\alpha}{N} \binom{N-1}{k} c^{N-1-k}\), which rearranges into a 2-term backward recurrence from \(k = N-1\) down to \(0\). Here for \(c = -1\):

\(k = 0\): \((0 - 5) g_0 = 20 \implies g_0 = -4\). (Check: \(F_{<4}(-1) = 1 - 5 + 10 - 10 = -4\).)
\(k = 1\): \((1 - 5) g_1 = -60 \implies g_1 = 15\). (Check: \(F_{<4}'(-1) = 5 - 20 + 30 = 15\).)
\(k = 2\): \((2 - 5) g_2 = 60 \implies g_2 = -20\). (Check: \(\frac{1}{2} F_{<4}''(-1) = 10 - 30 = -20\).)
\(k = 3\): \((3 - 5) g_3 = -20 \implies g_3 = 10\). (Check: \(\frac{1}{6} F_{<4}'''(-1) = 10\).)







WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Direction of Unrolling in Shifted Truncated ODEs



The Trap: When shifting \(x = u + c\) in \((1 + x) F_{<N}'(x) - \alpha F_{<N}(x) = -N\binom{\alpha}{N}x^{N-1}\) to get \((1 + c + u) G'(u) - \alpha G(u) = -N\binom{\alpha}{N}(u + c)^{N-1}\), extracting \([u^k]\) yields: \[(k + 1)(1 + c) g_{k+1} + (k - \alpha) g_k = -N \binom{\alpha}{N} \binom{N-1}{k} c^{N-1-k}.\] If you try to unroll forward (\(g_0 \to g_1 \to \dots \to g_{N-1}\)):

You first have to spend \(O(N)\) work to compute the base case \(g_0 = F_{<N}(c)\);
Worse, if \(1 + c \equiv 0 \pmod p\) (i.e., \(c = -1\)), the coefficient of \(g_{k+1}\) is zero and forward unrolling divides by zero! The Remedy: Always unroll backward from \(k = N - 1\) down to \(0\) (using \(g_N = 0\)), solving for \(g_k\) via division by \((k - \alpha)\) whenever \(\alpha \notin \{0, 1, \dots, N-1\} \pmod p\)—or, if \(\alpha = N\) is a small integer, unroll forward using \((k + 1)(1 + c)\)!









NoteAlgorithm Contract: EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODE Engine




Input: A linear ODE \(A(x) F'(x) + B(x) F(x) = C(x)\) of polynomial degree bound \(d = \max(\deg A - 1, \deg B)\), boundary coefficients \(f_N, \dots, f_{N+d-1}\) of \(F(x)\), truncation length \(N\), and shift \(c \in K\).
Output: All coefficients \(g_0, \dots, g_{N-1}\) of the shifted truncated polynomial \(G(u) = F_{<N}(u + c)\).
Algebraic Preconditions: Either \(A(c) \in K^\times\) with \(1, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (for forward unrolling given \(g_0, \dots, g_{d-1}\)) or the highest-degree coefficient of \(A(u+c)G'(u) + B(u+c)G(u)\) has non-vanishing indicial multiplier \((k - \alpha) \in K^\times\) (for backward unrolling from \(g_N = \dots = g_{N+d-1} = 0\)).
Complexity: \(O(d \cdot N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space with zero NTTs.
Correctness Invariant: Because \(\deg F_{<N} \le N - 1\), \(G(u) = F_{<N}(u + c)\) has \(g_m = 0\) identically for all \(m \ge N\), which provides the exact zero boundary values \(g_N = \dots = g_{N+d-1} = 0\) needed to start the backward recurrence without computing any evaluation at \(u = 0\).









TipRevisited Dual-Perspective Callout #5 — Codeforces 840C: On the Bench (#089, Ch 08 [Int-2]): From \(O(N^2)\) Connected-Component DP to \(O(N \log^2 N)\) Laguerre Product Tree & Truncated Taylor Shift



In Chapter 8, Intermediate 2 (#089 CF 840C — On the Bench), we counted permutations of \(N \le 300\) colored balls with zero adjacent equal-color pairs by multiplying the per-color connected-component inclusion-exclusion EGFs \[P_r(x) = \sum_{b=1}^{c_r} (-1)^{c_r - b} \binom{c_r - 1}{b - 1} \frac{x^b}{b!}\] via naive \(O(N^2)\) knapsack DP.
In Advanced 1 (#028 AtCoder ABC 260 Ex — Colorfulness) below, \(N\) jumps to \(2.5 \times 10^5\), and we must compute the \(m\)-th power sum of the number of runs across all permutations for \(m = 1, \dots, M\)! By introducing a second variable \(y\) to track how many adjacent equal-color pairs remain, homogenizing the bivariate polynomial \(P_r(x, y)\) into a 1D polynomial in \(z = \frac{x}{y - 1}\), multiplying across colors via a divide-and-conquer NTT product tree in \(O(N \log^2 N)\), and applying a single Taylor shift \(u = y - 1 \mapsto y\), we upgrade the \(O(N^2)\) Chapter 8 engine to handle \(N = 2.5 \times 10^5\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time!

19.4 Motivating Sub-Section: Singularity Analysis Intuition (\([x^n]F(x) \sim \frac{C}{\Gamma(\alpha)} R^{-n} n^{\alpha - 1}\)) & Holonomic BSGS
Throughout Chapters 18 and 19, we have treated generating functions purely as algebraic objects in \(K[[x]]\). Yet there is a striking correspondence between the leading polynomial \(q_m(x)\) of a D-finite ODE \[q_m(x) F^{(m)}(x) + q_{m-1}(x) F^{(m-1)}(x) + \dots + q_0(x) F(x) = 0\] and the asymptotic growth of the coefficients \(f_n = [x^n] F(x)\) over \(\mathbb{C}\).

1. Why the Dominant Singularity \(x = R\) Controls Both Asymptotics and the ODE Leading Term
Suppose \(F(x) \in \mathbb{C}[[x]]\) has a finite radius of convergence \(R > 0\), and near its dominant singularity \(x = R\) (the singularity closest to the origin in \(\mathbb{C}\)) it behaves algebraically like \[F(x) \sim C \left(1 - \frac{x}{R}\right)^{-\alpha} \qquad (x \to R^-)\] for some exponent \(\alpha \notin \{0, -1, -2, \dots\}\). Expanding \((1 - x/R)^{-\alpha}\) by the generalized binomial theorem and applying Stirling’s approximation \(\binom{n + \alpha - 1}{n} = \frac{\Gamma(n + \alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha) \Gamma(n + 1)} \sim \frac{n^{\alpha - 1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\) yields the Flajolet–Odlyzko Transfer Principle: \[[x^n] F(x) \sim \frac{C}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \, R^{-n} \, n^{\alpha - 1} \qquad (n \to \infty).\]
Now look at what happens when we differentiate \((1 - x/R)^{-\alpha}\): each differentiation multiplies by \((1 - x/R)^{-1}\), increasing the pole order at \(x = R\) by \(1\)! Therefore, in any linear ODE \(\sum_{j=0}^m q_j(x) F^{(j)}(x) = 0\) satisfied by \(F(x)\):

Roots of \(q_m(x)\) Are the Singularities of \(F(x)\): For the highest derivative \(F^{(m)}(x) \sim C' (1 - x/R)^{-\alpha - m}\) to cancel against lower derivatives \(F^{(m-1)}(x) \sim C'' (1 - x/R)^{-\alpha - m + 1}\), the leading polynomial \(q_m(x)\) must vanish at \(x = R\) (i.e., \((1 - x/R) \mid q_m(x)\))! For example, in Catalan/central binomial ODEs where \(R = 1/4\), the leading polynomial always contains the factor \((1 - 4x)\); in Delannoy/Schröder ODEs where \(R = 3 - 2\sqrt{2}\), it always contains \((1 - 6x + x^2)\).
Asymptotic Ratio of the P-Recurrence: Dividing the P-recursive relation \(\sum_{s} P_s(n) f_{n+s} = 0\) by \(n^{\deg P}\) and taking \(n \to \infty\) yields the characteristic polynomial \(q_m(x)\) evaluated at \(x = R\), confirming that \(\frac{f_{n+1}}{f_n} \to R^{-1}\left(1 + \frac{\alpha - 1}{n} + O(n^{-2})\right)\).



2. Outlook: \(O(\sqrt{N} \log N)\) Holonomic Baby-Step Giant-Step (Bostan–Chudnovsky–Chudnovsky)
When a sequence \((f_n)\) satisfies an order-\(r\) P-recursive recurrence \(p_r(n) f_{n+r} + \dots + p_0(n) f_n = 0\) and we need a single term \(f_N \bmod p\) for \(N \le 10^9 < p\), \(O(N)\) linear unrolling is too slow. Rewriting the step-\(n\) transition as a \(r \times r\) companion matrix \(M(n) \in \operatorname{Mat}_r(K[n])\) (after clearing denominators into a scalar factorial product \(\prod_{n=0}^{N-1} p_r(n)\)) reduces \(f_N\) to the matrix product: \[P(0, N) = M(N - 1) M(N - 2) \cdots M(1) M(0).\] By setting \(B = \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor\), constructing the block matrix \(M_B(x) = M(x + B - 1) \cdots M(x + 1) M(x)\) of polynomial degree \(O(B)\) via a binary product tree in \(O(r^3 \sqrt{N} \log^2 N)\) time, and evaluating \(M_B(x)\) at the giant-step points \(x = 0, B, 2B, \dots, (B - 1)B\) using the subproduct-tree multipoint evaluation and sampling-point shift engines that we will build in Chapter 20, we can evaluate any P-recursive sequence (and \(N! \bmod p\)) at \(N \le 10^9\) in \(O(\sqrt{N} \log N)\) time!

19.5 Diagnostic Signals & Reverse-Engineering Summary








Structural Cue in the Problem

Time Complexity




Operator product mixing \(x^s\), \(D_x^k\), and \(\vartheta^m\)
Weyl commutation \(P(\vartheta) x^s = x^s P(\vartheta + s)\) & Fourier–Laplace map \(x^s P(\vartheta) \mapsto P(n-s) E_n^{-s}\) (§19.1)
\(O(1)\) symbolic translation


Definite binomial sum \(\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}^a \binom{n+k}{k}^b c^k\) that resists Snake Oil
Engine 3 (EI Differential-Residue) \(S_n = \operatorname{Res}_{x=0} x^{-1} A(x) B(x)^n\) via \(\operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \frac{d}{dx}(\dots) = 0\) (§19.2)
\(O(N)\)


Composition \(F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) where \(F\) satisfies order-\(r\) ODE and \(P(x)\) is \(K\)-sparse (\(P(0)=0\))
Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition maintaining \(H_i(x) = F^{(i)}(P(x))\) (§19.3A)
\(O(r N K)\) (Zero NTTs)


Shifted evaluation \(F_{<N}(x + c)\) or binomial moment \(\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} x^k (1-x)^{n-k} f(k)\)
EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODE \(A(x)F_{<N}' + B(x)F_{<N} = C(x) - R_N(x)\) (§19.3B)
\(O(N)\) (Zero NTTs)


Integrals of powers of truncated exponentials \(S_{<a}(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{a-1} \frac{x^j}{j!}\)
Miracle Truncated Exponential Derivative \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{-x} S_{<a}(x)) = -e^{-x} \frac{x^{a-1}}{(a-1)!}\) (§19.3B)
Reduces degree-\(n a\) products to \(O(1)\)-step ODE
