NoteAlgorithm Contract: Semi-Online CDQ Divide-and-Conquer NTT (solve(l, r))




Input & Index Boundaries: Integer \(N \ge 1\), known kernel array \(g[1 \dots N-1] \in K^{N-1}\) (with \(g_0 = 0\)), and \(O(1)\) callbacks \(\psi_n(S_n)\) and \(\alpha_n(f_n)\) on the \(0\)-indexed domain \([0, N-1]\).
Preconditions: Strict causality (\(k = j - i \ge 1\), so \(g_0 = 0\)); any \(k = 0\) term must be absorbed into \(\psi_n\) beforehand. \(K = \mathbb{F}_p\) is an NTT-friendly prime field (or \(\mathbb{C}\) for FFT).
Postconditions: Upon termination of solve(0, N - 1), \(S[n] = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \alpha_i(f_i) g_{n-i}\) and \(f[n] = \psi_n(S[n])\) are finalized for all \(0 \le n \le N - 1\).
Complexity: At depth \(d \in [0, \lceil \log_2 N \rceil]\), there are \(2^d\) nodes of length \(L \approx N / 2^d\), each performing one convolution of size \(\le 2L\) in \(O(L \log L)\) time. Summing across all \(\log_2 N\) levels gives \[
T(N) = 2 T(N / 2) + O(N \log N) = O(N \log^2 N) \text{ time}, \qquad O(N) \text{ space}.
\]
1-Sentence Recursion Invariant: Upon entry to solve(l, r), the accumulator \(S[j]\) for every \(j \in [l, r]\) already contains the exact sum of all causal contributions \(\alpha_i(f_i) g_{j-i}\) from indices \(i \in [0, l - 1]\).
Core Loop Snippet:

auto solve = [&](auto& self, int l, int r) -> void {
    if (l == r) { f[l] = psi(l, S[l]); alpha[l] = get_alpha(l, f[l]); return; }
    int m = (l + r) >> 1;
    self(self, l, m);
    Poly A(alpha.begin() + l, alpha.begin() + m + 1), B(g.begin(), g.begin() + (r - l) + 1);
    Poly C = multiply(A, B); // g[0] = 0
    for (int j = m + 1; j <= r; ++j) S[j] = (S[j] + C[j - l]) % MOD;
    self(self, m + 1, r);
};




Extending CDQ NTT to Self-Convolution \(C = F * F\) & Failure Mode #13
What if the recurrence is self-referential, such as \(f_n = \psi_n\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \alpha_i(f_i) \, \beta_{n-i}(f_{n-i})\right)\) where both factors \(\alpha_i\) and \(\beta_{n-i}\) are unknown until step \(i\) and \(n - i\)?
Suppose we pad \(N\) to a power of \(2\) so every CDQ node \([l, r]\) is a dyadic interval \([k \cdot 2^s, (k + 1) 2^s - 1]\) of length \(2^s\) with midpoint \(m = l + 2^{s-1} - 1\). Consider an ordered pair of positive indices \((i, j)\) with \(i \ge 1, j \ge 1\) contributing \(\alpha_i \beta_j\) to target index \(n = i + j \in [m + 1, r]\). Which index is finalized later—\(i\) or \(j\)?

Case 1: The Root Left-Aligned Node (\(l = 0\)). Here \([l, m] = [0, 2^{s-1} - 1]\) and \([m + 1, r] = [2^{s-1}, 2^s - 1]\). For any \(n \in [m + 1, r]\), if both \(i \le m\) and \(j \le m\), then both \(i\) and \(j\) belong to \([0, m]\)! Therefore, convolving \(\alpha[0 \dots m]\) with \(\beta[0 \dots m]\) once at node \([0, r]\) accounts for every pair \((i, j) \in [1, m] \times [1, m]\) summing to \(n \in [m + 1, r]\) (including both \((i, j)\) and \((j, i)\) when \(i \neq j\), and the diagonal \((i, i)\) once).
Case 2: Interior Dyadic Nodes (\(l > 0\)). Since \([l, r] = [k \cdot 2^s, (k + 1) 2^s - 1]\) with \(k \ge 1\), we have \(l = k \cdot 2^s \ge 2^s = r - l + 1\), so \[
r - l < l.
\] Now suppose \(i + j = n \in [m + 1, r]\) where at least one of \(i, j\) lies in \([l, m]\). If \(i \in [l, m]\), then the partner index \(j = n - i\) satisfies \[
1 \le (m + 1) - m \le j = n - i \le r - l < l.
\] Thus \(j \in [1, r - l]\) lies strictly to the left of \(l\)! Because \([l, m]\) and \([1, r - l]\) are disjoint, an unordered pair \(\{i, j\}\) with \(i \in [l, m]\) and \(j \in [1, r - l]\) corresponds to two ordered terms in \(\sum_{a+b=n} \alpha_a \beta_b\):

\((a, b) = (i, j)\) with \(a \in [l, m], b \in [1, r - l]\): contributed by \(\alpha[l \dots m] * \beta[1 \dots r - l]\).
\((a, b) = (j, i)\) with \(a \in [1, r - l], b \in [l, m]\): contributed by \(\beta[l \dots m] * \alpha[1 \dots r - l]\).








WarningFailure Mode #13: The Self-Convolution CDQ Symmetry Bug (l == 0 vs. l > 0 Missing Factor of 2)



The Bug: When solving a symmetric self-convolution \(S_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f_i f_{n-i}\) (\(\alpha = \beta = f\), with \(f_0 = 0\)) via CDQ NTT, a common mistake is to write C = multiply(f[l..m], f[0..r-l]) and add C[j - l] to S[j] at every node \([l, r]\). This produces the correct values at \(l = 0\) (where f[0..m] * f[0..m] naturally includes both \((i, k)\) and \((k, i)\)), but under-counts every \(l > 0\) transfer by a factor of \(2\)!
Why It Happens: For \(l > 0\), f[l..m] contains indices \(a \in [l, m]\), whereas f[0..r-l] contains indices \(b \in [0, r-l]\). Because \(r - l < l\) on a dyadic grid, the two index ranges \([l, m]\) and \([0, r-l]\) are completely disjoint! Convolving f[l..m] with f[0..r-l] only counts ordered pairs \((a, b)\) where the first index is in \([l, m]\) and the second is in \([0, r-l]\), completely omitting the symmetric ordered pair \((b, a)\) where the first index is in \([0, r-l]\) and the second is in \([l, m]\).
The 1-Line Remedy:

Always pad the CDQ domain to \([0, 2^K - 1]\) so \(r - l < l\) holds at every node with \(l > 0\).
For symmetric self-convolution (\(\alpha = \beta = f\), \(f_0 = 0\)), at \(l = 0\) convolve f[0..m] * f[0..m] with weight 1, and at \(l > 0\) convolve f[l..m] * f[0..r-l] with weight 2:

Poly A(f.begin() + l, f.begin() + m + 1);
Poly B(f.begin(), f.begin() + (l == 0 ? m : r - l) + 1);
Poly C = multiply(A, B);
long long sym = (l == 0 ? 1 : 2);
for (int j = m + 1; j <= r; ++j)
    S[j] = (S[j] + sym * C[j - l]) % MOD;

For asymmetric bilinear products (\(\alpha \neq \beta\)), at \(l = 0\) compute \(\alpha[0 \dots m] * \beta[0 \dots m]\), and at \(l > 0\) compute \(\alpha[l \dots m] * \beta[0 \dots r - l] + \beta[l \dots m] * \alpha[0 \dots r - l]\).

section: 9.3 Full-Online 0-Indexed Relaxed Convolution (van der Hoeven / Nyaan)
text:
9.3 Full-Online 0-Indexed Relaxed Convolution (van der Hoeven / Nyaan)

Why Stateless Online Engines Beat Tangled CDQ Trees
While self-convolution CDQ NTT (§9.2) works well for a single quadratic equation like \(F' = \frac{1}{2} A F^2 + 1\), what happens when a problem chains two or more causal products together—such as \(B(x) = W(x) E(x)\) coupled with \(E'(x) = G'(x) E(x)\) in ABC 230 Ex (§9.4), or \(F(x) = 1 + \frac{x}{6}\big(F(x) \cdot (F(x)^2 + 3F(x^2)) + 2F(x^3)\big)\) in LOJ 6538?
With recursive CDQ, chaining two products requires interleaving multiple solve(l, r) functions and manually tracking which cross-terms \(l = 0\) vs. \(l > 0\) have been doubled. In 1997, Joris van der Hoeven discovered Relaxed Convolution (popularized in competitive programming by Nyaan and maspy), which encapsulates the entire dyadic block schedule inside a stateful streaming object:

At each step \(q = 0, 1, 2, \dots\), you push the newly discovered pair \((a_q, b_q)\) into rc.next(a_q, b_q), and it immediately returns the exact \(q\)-th convolution coefficient \[
c_q = \sum_{i=0}^{q} a_i \, b_{q - i}.
\] Because rc.next(a_q, b_q) is called inside a plain for (int q = 0; q <= N; ++q) loop, you can instantiate as many RelaxedConvolution objects as you want (rc1, rc2, rc3) and pipe the output of one directly into the input of the next!



The 2D Grid Block-Tiling Decomposition (d = lowbit(q))
How can rc.next(a_q, b_q) compute \(c_q = \sum_{i+j=q} a_i b_j\) on the fly in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) total time?
Consider the infinite quarter-plane grid \(\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \times \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) of index pairs \((i, j)\). At step \(q = 0\), \(c_0 = a_0 b_0\). For every step \(q \ge 1\), the anti-diagonal \(i + j = q\) splits cleanly into:

Two border cells \((q, 0)\) and \((0, q)\), which contribute \(a_q b_0 + a_0 b_q\) and are added directly in \(O(1)\) time at step \(q\); and
The positive interior grid \((i, j) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1} \times \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), which we partition into dyadic \(d \times d\) blocks triggered at step \(q \ge 1\) according to \(d = \operatorname{lowbit}(q) = q \ \& \ -q = 2^k\) (the largest power of \(2\) dividing \(q\)):


Power-of-Two Steps (\(q = d = 2^k\), i.e., \(q = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, \dots\)): Convolve the single \(d \times d\) square block on the main interior diagonal: \[
A[1 \dots d] \times B[1 \dots d],
\] and accumulate all terms with index sum \(i + j > q\) into \(c[q + 1 \dots 2q]\).
Off-Diagonal Interior Steps (\(d < q\), i.e., \(q = m \cdot d\) with \(m \ge 3\) odd): Convolve the two symmetric \(d \times d\) off-diagonal blocks: \[
\text{Block 1: } A[q - d + 1 \dots q] \times B[d \dots 2d - 1], \qquad \text{Block 2: } A[d \dots 2d - 1] \times B[q - d + 1 \dots q],
\] and accumulate both products into \(c[q + 1 \dots q + 2d - 1]\).







ImportantCrucial Subtlety: Why Separating Border Cells (i = 0, j = 0) + Interior lowbit(q) Beats Pure 0-Indexed lowbit(q + 1)



Why do we separate the border terms \(a_q b_0 + a_0 b_q\) in \(O(1)\) and apply \(d = \operatorname{lowbit}(q)\) to the \(1\)-indexed interior \(\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1} \times \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), rather than applying a single \(d = \operatorname{lowbit}(q + 1)\) block rule directly to the \(0\)-indexed grid \(\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \times \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\)?

No Missing Corner Cells: On an unshifted \(0\)-indexed grid, triggering only a single block size \(d = \operatorname{lowbit}(q + 1)\) at step \(q = 5\) (\(q + 1 = 6, d = 2\)) would convolve \(A[4 \dots 5] \times B[1 \dots 2]\), missing the border cell \((5, 0)\) because \(5 + 1 = 6\) is divisible by \(2^1\) whereas \(0 + 1 = 1\) is only divisible by \(2^0\)! Separating the \(i = 0\) and \(j = 0\) borders in \(O(1)\) shifts the interior to \((i, j) \ge (1, 1)\), so every step \(q \ge 1\) needs only a single block size \(d = \operatorname{lowbit}(q)\) (\(1\) convolution if \(d = q\), or \(2\) convolutions if \(d < q\)).
Built-In Self-Referential Causality: Because the interior blocks at step \(q\) convolve \(A[q - d + 1 \dots q]\) with \(B[d \dots 2d - 1]\), the minimum sum of indices in any interior block triggered at step \(q\) is \[
(q - d + 1) + d = q + 1 > q.
\] Consequently, every interior pair \((i, j) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}^2\) with \(i + j = q\) was ALREADY accumulated into \(c_q\) during steps \(1, 2, \dots, q - 1\)! At step \(q\), the only terms missing from \(c_q = \sum_{i=0}^q a_i b_{q-i}\) are the two border terms \(a_0 b_q + a_q b_0\)!



Let us verify this on the interior grid \((i, j) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1} \times \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), where each cell \((i, j)\) shows the exact step \(q = \text{step}(i, j)\) at which d = lowbit(q) computes \(a_i b_j\) and adds it to \(c_{i+j}\):
Interior Grid (i >= 1, j >= 1) showing step q where a_i * b_j is accumulated (d = lowbit(q)):
      j=1   j=2   j=3   j=4   j=5   j=6   j=7   j=8
i=1 | q=1 | q=2 | q=3 | q=4 | q=5 | q=6 | q=7 | q=8 |
i=2 | q=2 | q=2 | q=4 | q=4 | q=6 | q=6 | q=8 | q=8 |
i=3 | q=3 | q=4 | q=4 | q=4 | q=6 | q=6 | q=8 | q=8 |
i=4 | q=4 | q=4 | q=4 | q=4 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 |
i=5 | q=5 | q=6 | q=6 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 |
i=6 | q=6 | q=6 | q=6 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 |
i=7 | q=7 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 |
i=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 | q=8 |
Let us prove why this interior grid partitions \(\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1} \times \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\) with zero omissions and zero duplicates, and why \(\text{step}(i, j) < i + j\) for every \((i, j) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}^2\):






NoteTheorem 9.3 (Exact Partition & Strict Causality of lowbit(q) Relaxed Convolution)



For every integer \(q \ge 1\) with \(d = \operatorname{lowbit}(q)\):

If \(d = q\), define \(\mathcal{B}_q = [1, d] \times [1, d]\).
If \(d < q\), define \(\mathcal{B}_q = \big([q - d + 1, q] \times [d, 2d - 1]\big) \cup \big([d, 2d - 1] \times [q - d + 1, q]\big)\).

Then:

Exact Partition: The sets \(\{\mathcal{B}_q\}_{q \ge 1}\) are pairwise disjoint and their union is all of \(\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1} \times \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\).
Availability: Every \((i, j) \in \mathcal{B}_q\) satisfies \(\max(i, j) \le q\), so \(a_i\) and \(b_j\) are known at step \(q\).
Strict Interior Causality: Every \((i, j) \in \mathcal{B}_q\) satisfies \(i + j \ge q + 1\). Consequently, for every \(n \ge 1\), the entire interior sum \[
c_n^{\text{int}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} a_i \, b_{n - i}
\] is completely accumulated into \(c_n\) by the end of step \(q = n - 1\)!



Proof:

Given any cell \((i, j) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}^2\), let \(2^k\) be the unique power of \(2\) such that \(\min(i, j) \in [2^k, 2^{k+1} - 1]\), and set \(d = 2^k\). Let \(M = \max(i, j) \ge d\), and let \(q = \lceil M / d \rceil \cdot d\) be the smallest multiple of \(d\) that is \(\ge M\).

If \(\operatorname{lowbit}(q) = d\), then \(M \in [q - d + 1, q]\) and \(\min(i, j) \in [d, 2d - 1]\), so \((i, j)\) belongs to the interior step \(\mathcal{B}_q\).
If \(\operatorname{lowbit}(q) = 2^r > d\) (which happens if and only if \(\lceil M / d \rceil\) is an even multiple of \(2^{r-k}\), meaning \(M \le q \le 2^r\)), then since \(M \ge d\), this can only happen when \(q = 2^r\) itself and \(1 \le i, j \le 2^r\), so \((i, j)\) belongs to the power-of-two square \(\mathcal{B}_{2^r}\) (specifically inside \([1, 2^r]^2 \setminus [1, 2^{r-1}]^2\) because \(\max(i, j) = M > q - d \ge 2^{r-1}\)). Thus every \((i, j) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}^2\) belongs to a unique \(\mathcal{B}_q\).

By definition of \(\mathcal{B}_q\), \(\max(i, j) \le q\).
If \(d = q\), we only accumulate pairs with \(i + j \ge q + 1\) (since any pair in \([1, d]^2\) with \(i + j \le q = d\) has \(i, j \le d - 1\), and because \(d = 2^k \ge 2\) for \(i + j \le d\), both \(i, j \le 2^{k-1} - 1\) or \((i, j)\) was already covered at \(q' = d / 2\)!). And if \(d < q\), every \((i, j) \in \mathcal{B}_q\) has \(i + j \ge (q - d + 1) + d = q + 1\). Thus \(\mathcal{B}_q\) only contributes to indices \(n = i + j \ge q + 1\). \(\blacksquare\)



The 3-Step Self-Referential Protocol & Complete Engine
Because \(c_q^{\text{int}} = \sum_{i=1}^{q-1} a_i b_{q-i}\) is already sitting in c[q] before step \(q\) begins, we obtain the universal 3-Step Self-Referential Protocol at step \(q \ge 1\):

Read Interior Sum: Read rc.c[q], which already equals \(\sum_{i=1}^{q-1} a_i b_{q-i}\).
Resolve Step-\(q\) Equations: Use rc.c[q] (together with \(a_0, b_0\)) to solve for \(f_q\), \(a_q\), and \(b_q\).
Commit Step \(q\) (rc.next(a_q, b_q)): Call rc.next(a_q, b_q), which adds the border terms \(a_q b_0 + a_0 b_q\) to c[q], runs the lowbit(q) block convolution(s) to push contributions into \(c[q + 1 \dots 2q]\), and returns the finalized \(c_q = \sum_{i=0}^q a_i b_{q-i}\)!







NoteAlgorithm Contract & Concise Core: RelaxedConvolution (van der Hoeven / Nyaan)




Input & Index Boundaries: Online stream of coefficient pairs \((a_q, b_q) \in K^2\) arriving sequentially at \(0\)-indexed steps \(q = 0, 1, \dots, N\).
Preconditions: Step \(q\) is invoked only after steps \(0, 1, \dots, q - 1\) have completed; \(K = \mathbb{F}_p\) is an NTT-friendly prime field.
Postconditions: Calling next(a_q, b_q) at step \(q\) appends \(a_q, b_q\), finalizes and returns \(c_q = \sum_{i=0}^q a_i b_{q-i}\), and pre-accumulates \(\mathcal{B}_q\) into c[q + 1 .. q + 2d - 1] so that c[q + 1] holds the exact interior sum \(\sum_{i=1}^{q} a_i b_{q+1-i}\) prior to step \(q + 1\).
Complexity: Across \(N\) calls (\(q = 0 \dots N - 1\)), for each \(d = 2^k \le N\), there are \(\lfloor N / d \rfloor\) steps with \(\operatorname{lowbit}(q) = d\), each doing \(O(d \log d)\) work. Summing over \(k = 0 \dots \lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor\) gives \[
\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor} \frac{N}{2^k} \cdot O(2^k \log(2^k)) = O(N \log^2 N) \text{ time}, \qquad O(N) \text{ space}.
\]
1-Sentence Loop Invariant: Prior to the \(q\)-th call next(a_q, b_q) (\(q \ge 1\)), c[q] already holds the complete interior convolution sum \(c_q^{\text{int}} = \sum_{i=1}^{q-1} a_i b_{q-i}\) from all positive index pairs \((i, j) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}^2\) with \(i + j = q\).

struct RelaxedConvolution {
    vector<long long> a, b, c;
    long long next(long long aq, long long bq) {
        int q = a.size(), d = q & -q; a.push_back(aq); b.push_back(bq);
        if ((int)c.size() <= 2 * q + 2) c.resize(2 * q + 3, 0);
        if (q == 0) return c[0] = aq * bq % MOD;
        c[q] = (c[q] + aq * b[0] + a[0] * bq) % MOD;
        auto add = [&](int la, int lb) {
            Poly P = multiply({a.begin()+la, a.begin()+la+d}, {b.begin()+lb, b.begin()+lb+d});
            for (int i = 0; i < (int)P.size(); ++i) if (la + lb + i > q) c[la + lb + i] = (c[la + lb + i] + P[i]) % MOD;
        };
        if (d == q) add(1, 1); else { add(q - d + 1, d); add(d, q - d + 1); }
        return c[q];
    }
};








TipRevisited Dual-Perspective Cross-Reference: Online Relaxed Convolution vs. Chapter 10 Newton Iteration



Several landmark problems in Part III admit dual solutions—an online \(O(N \log^2 N)\) solution using the tools of this chapter, and an offline \(O(N \log N)\) Newton solution in Chapter 10:

#244 (yukicoder 3029 — Colored Tree / Cactus Weight):

Chapter 09 Perspective (Coupled Online Relaxed Convolution in \(O(N \log^2 N)\)): When two or more tree generating functions \((R(x), G(x))\) satisfy a coupled algebraic system \(R(x) = x \Phi_1(R(x), G(x))\), \(G(x) = x \Phi_2(R(x), G(x))\), the leading factor of \(x\) makes the system strictly causal! Chaining RelaxedConvolution instances resolves \((r_n, g_n)\) step-by-step in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time with zero Jacobian matrices and under 15 lines of loop code.
Chapter 10 Perspective (\(2 \times 2\) Coupled Jacobian Newton Iteration in \(O(N \log N)\), Ch 10.2 & Ch 10 Int-1): Linearizing the coupled system via the \(2 \times 2\) Jacobian matrix \(J_F(x)\) and inverting \(\det J_F(x)\) halves the constant factor to \(O(N \log N)\), which becomes essential when \(N \ge 5 \times 10^5\) or when the equation is non-causal.

#023 (AtCoder ABC 230 Ex — Bullion, Ch 09 Int-2 vs. Ch 10.3):

Solved in Ch 09.4 & Int-2 in \(O(W \log^2 W)\) time via a single RelaxedConvolution instance coupled with a \(4\)-line harmonic divisor loop, and revisited in Chapter 10.3 via \(O(W \log W)\) Pólya–Euler Newton iteration.

#249 (HDU 5322 — Hope):

A non-autonomous DP recurrence with index-dependent multipliers \(w_n = n!\) and \((n - i)^2\) where offline Newton inversion is algebraically impossible; Semi-Online CDQ NTT (solve(l, r), §9.2) decouples the source weight from the lag kernel \((n - i)^2\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time.

title: 09 — Causal Recurrences: Semi-Online CDQ Divide-and-Conquer NTT & Full-Online Relaxed Convolution
section: 9.4 10-Line Online Replacements for inv, ln, exp, and Pólya Euler Transforms
text:
9.4 10-Line Online Replacements for inv, ln, exp, and Pólya Euler Transforms
One of the greatest practical payoffs of RelaxedConvolution is that every major power series primitive from Chapters 01–03—polynomial inversion, logarithm, exponential, square root, arbitrary power, and even coupled Pólya multiset transforms—can be written in 5 to 10 lines of loop code without a single Newton iteration!

The Online Differential-Equation Dictionary
Let us derive the exact 1-line RelaxedConvolution update for each primitive up to degree \(N\):

Online Multiplicative Inverse \(F(x) = A(x)^{-1} \bmod x^{N+1}\) (where \(a_0 \in K^\times\)): Write \(A(x) F(x) = 1\). For \(q = 0\), \(f_0 = a_0^{-1}\). For \(q \ge 1\), \([x^q](A \cdot F) = 0 \implies a_0 f_q + a_q f_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q-1} a_i f_{q-i} = 0\). Equivalently, feed \((a_q, f_{q-1})\) into a shifted product \(B(x) = \frac{A(x) - a_0}{x} \cdot F(x)\) where \([x^{q-1}]B = \sum_{i=1}^q a_i f_{q-i}\): \[
f_0 = a_0^{-1}, \qquad f_q = -a_0^{-1} \cdot \texttt{rc.next}(a_q,\; f_{q-1}) \quad (q \ge 1).
\] (Why does rc.next(a_q, f_{q-1}) need zero lookahead? Because at step \(m = q - 1 \ge 0\), the inputs are \(\tilde{a}_m = a_{m+1} = a_q\) and \(f_m = f_{q-1}\), both of which are already known before \(f_q\) is computed!)
Online Exponential \(E(x) = \exp(G(x)) \bmod x^{N+1}\) (where \(g_0 = 0\) and \(p > N\)): Differentiating gives \(E'(x) = G'(x) E(x)\). Extracting \([x^{q-1}]\) for \(q \ge 1\) yields \[
q \, e_q = \sum_{i=1}^{q} (i g_i) \, e_{q-i} = [x^{q-1}] \big(G'(x) E(x)\big).
\] Notice the index shift! At step \(m = q - 1 \ge 0\), \([x^m] G'(x) = (m + 1) g_{m+1} = q g_q\) and \([x^m] E(x) = e_m = e_{q-1}\) are both already known! Thus: \[
e_0 = 1, \qquad e_q = \frac{1}{q} \cdot \texttt{rc.next}(q \cdot g_q,\; e_{q-1}) \quad (1 \le q \le N).
\]
Online Logarithm \(L(x) = \ln F(x) \bmod x^{N+1}\) (where \(f_0 = 1\) and \(p > N\)): From \(L'(x) F(x) = F'(x)\), write \(L'(x) = F'(x) - L'(x) (F(x) - 1)\). Extracting \([x^{q-1}]\) for \(q \ge 1\) gives \[
q \, \ell_q = q \, f_q - \sum_{i=1}^{q-1} (i \ell_i) \, f_{q-i} \implies \ell_q = f_q - \frac{1}{q} \cdot \texttt{rc.next}((q - 1)\ell_{q-1},\; f_q) \quad (q \ge 1, \text{ with } \ell_0 = 0).
\]
Online Square Root \(S(x) = \sqrt{F(x)} \bmod x^{N+1}\) (where \(f_0 = 1\) and \(\operatorname{char}(K) \neq 2\)): Write \(S(x) = 1 + T(x)\) with \(T(0) = 0\). Then \(F(x) = S(x)^2 = 1 + 2T(x) + T(x)^2 \implies 2 t_q = f_q - [x^q] T(x)^2\). Since \(t_0 = 0\), at step \(q \ge 1\) the interior sum \(\sum_{i=1}^{q-1} t_i t_{q-i}\) is already in rc.c[q], and the border terms \(2 t_0 t_q = 0\) vanish! Thus: \[
s_0 = 1, \qquad s_q = \frac{f_q - \texttt{rc.c}[q]}{2}, \qquad \texttt{rc.next}(s_q,\; s_q) \quad (q \ge 1, \text{ initialized with } \texttt{rc.next}(0, 0)).
\]
Online Power \(H(x) = F(x)^\alpha \bmod x^{N+1}\) (where \(f_0 = 1\) and \(p > N\)): From \(F(x) H'(x) = \alpha F'(x) H(x)\), rewrite as \(H'(x) = \alpha F'(x) H(x) - \frac{F(x) - 1}{x} \cdot x H'(x)\), or chain Online \(\ln\) into Online \(\exp\) in two lines!










Operator
Differential / Algebraic Identity
1-Line Update at Step \(q = 1, 2, \dots, N\) (Index \(m = q - 1\))
Characteristic Requirement




inv (\(F = A^{-1}\), \(a_0 = 1\))
\(F = 1 - \frac{A - 1}{x} \cdot x F\)
f[q] = (MOD - rc.next(a[q], f[q - 1])) % MOD;
Any commutative ring \(K\) (\(a_0 \in K^\times\))


exp (\(E = \exp G\), \(g_0 = 0\))
\(E' = G' E\)
e[q] = rc.next(q * g[q] % MOD, e[q - 1]) * inv[q] % MOD;
\(p > N\) (\(1, \dots, N \in K^\times\))

\(L' = F' - (L') \cdot (F - 1)\)
l[q] = (f[q] + MOD - rc.next((q - 1) * l[q - 1] % MOD, f[q]) * inv[q] % MOD) % MOD;
\(p > N\) (\(1, \dots, N \in K^\times\))

\((S - 1)^2 = F - 1 - 2(S - 1)\)
s[q] = (f[q] + MOD - rc.c[q]) * inv2 % MOD; rc.next(s[q], s[q]);
\(\operatorname{char}(K) \neq 2\) (\(2 \in K^\times\))









WarningCharacteristic-\(p\) Pitfall: Algebraic vs. Differential Online Engines



Look at the rightmost column of the table above:

Differential online engines (exp, ln, pow) integrate \(E'(x), L'(x), H'(x)\) term-by-term by multiplying \([x^{q-1}]\) by \(q^{-1} \bmod p\). They therefore require \(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(p > N\). If \(p \le N\), \(\text{inv}[p]\) does not exist because \(D(x^p) = p x^{p-1} \equiv 0 \pmod p\)!
Algebraic online engines (inv, sqrt, and Catalan-type tree equations \(F = 1 + x F^2\)) never differentiate or integrate: they only divide by \(a_0\) or \(2\). Thus, they remain 100% valid over small-prime fields \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with \(p \le N\) (provided \(p > 2\) for sqrt).





Online Pólya / Euler Transform (MSET on the Fly)
In Chapter 03, when the generator series \(B(x) = \sum_{n=1}^N b_n x^n\) was completely known in advance, we computed the multiset Euler transform \[
E(x) = \operatorname{MSET}(B)(x) = \prod_{n \ge 1} \frac{1}{(1 - x^n)^{b_n}} = \exp\!\left( \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{B(x^k)}{k} \right)
\] offline in \(O(N \log N)\) time by populating \(G(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{B(x^k)}{k}\) via a harmonic loop and calling \(\exp(G(x))\).
What if \(B(x)\) is not known in advance, because \(b_n\) itself depends on \(e_0, e_1, \dots, e_{n-1}\)—for example, in rooted unlabeled trees \(B(x) = x E(x)\) or nested multiset bags \(B(x) = W(x) E(x)\) (ABC 230 Ex — Bullion, Int-2 below)?
Let us trace the exact causal dependencies in \(E(x) = \exp(G(x))\) where \(G(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{B(x^k)}{k}\):

Differentiating \(G(x)\) and multiplying by \(x\) gives \[
x G'(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} x^k B'(x^k) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \sum_{d \ge 1} d \, b_d \, x^{k d} = \sum_{n \ge 1} \left( \sum_{d \mid n} d \, b_d \right) x^n.
\]
Therefore, the coefficient \(n g_n = [x^{n-1}] G'(x)\) needed by the Online Exponential at step \(n\) is simply the divisor sum \[
n g_n = \sum_{d \mid n} d \, b_d.
\]
Notice that \(n g_n\) depends only on \(b_d\) for divisors \(d \mid n\), and every divisor \(d\) of \(n\) satisfies \(d \le n\)!
Consequently, the moment \(b_n\) becomes known at step \(n\), we immediately run a harmonic inner loop over multiples \(m = n, 2n, 3n, \dots \le N\), adding \(n \cdot b_n\) to an accumulator ng[m]:
for (int m = n; m <= N; m += n)
    ng[m] = (ng[m] + 1LL * n * b[n]) % MOD;
Across all \(n = 1 \dots N\), this harmonic inner loop executes \(\sum_{n=1}^N \lfloor N / n \rfloor = O(N \log N)\) additions. And by the time the outer loop reaches step \(n\) and finishes adding \(n \cdot b_n\) to ng[n], every divisor \(d \mid n\) (\(d \le n\)) has already contributed \(d \cdot b_d\) to ng[n], so ng[n] holds the exact value \(n g_n\) ready to be passed into rc_exp.next(ng[n], e[n - 1])!







NoteAlgorithm Contract: Online inv, ln, exp, and Pólya Euler via CDQ / Relaxed Convolution




Input & Index Boundaries: Target truncation degree \(N \ge 1\) and online coefficient stream \(a_q, g_q, f_q\), or \(b_q\) arriving for \(q = 1, 2, \dots, N\).
Preconditions:

Online inv: \(a_0 \in K^\times\) (any commutative ring \(K\)).
Online sqrt: \(f_0 = 1\) and \(2 \in K^\times\) (\(\operatorname{char}(K) \neq 2\)).
Online exp, ln, pow, and Pólya MSET: \(g_0 = 0\) (for exp / MSET) or \(f_0 = 1\) (for ln / pow), and \(1, 2, \dots, N \in K^\times\) (\(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(p > N\)).

Postconditions: At the end of step \(q \in [1, N]\), the exact \(q\)-th coefficient of \(A(x)^{-1}\), \(\exp(G(x))\), \(\ln F(x)\), \(\sqrt{F(x)}\), or \(\operatorname{MSET}(B)(x)\) is finalized and ready for immediate causal consumption at step \(q + 1\).
Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space per RelaxedConvolution engine (plus \(O(N \log N)\) harmonic sieve additions for online Pólya MSET).
1-Sentence Loop Invariant: Prior to computing step \(q \ge 1\) of the online primitive, all coefficients of the output series up to degree \(q - 1\) have been finalized, and for online Pólya MSET, the divisor-sum accumulator ng[q] already holds \(\sum_{d \mid q, d < q} d \cdot b_d\).

9.5 Chapter 09 Practice Ladder (8 Problems: 2 SS / 2 Int / 2 Adv / 2 Mas)
Every problem below is self-contained and ordered by structural complexity. Use the three progressive hints before consulting the complete derivation.


Stepping Stone 1 (#060) — AtCoder ARC 138 E: Decreasing Subsequence

Source: AtCoder Regular Contest 138, Problem E
Prerequisite Tags: [Binomial Convolution, Staircase Rook / RSK Bijection, Semi-Online CDQ NTT]
Problem Statement: Given integers \(N\) and \(K\), consider sequences \(A = (A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N)\) of integers such that \(0 \le A_i \le i\) for all \(1 \le i \le N\). Count the number of such sequences that contain a strictly decreasing subsequence of positive elements of length \(K\)—that is, indices \(1 \le i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_K \le N\) such that \[
A_{i_1} > A_{i_2} > \dots > A_{i_K} > 0.
\] Output the answer modulo \(998244353\).
Constraints: \(2 \le K \le N \le 5000\) in the original contest (\(O(N^2)\) DP), and up to \(N \le 10^5\) when accelerated via semi-online block CDQ NTT in \(O\!\left(\frac{N^2}{K} \log K\right)\) or \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time. Modulus \(p = 998244353\). Time limit: \(3.0\text{ s}\).
Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(N = 2, K = 2\), there are \((2+1)! = 6\) sequences \((A_1, A_2) \in \{0, 1\} \times \{0, 1, 2\}\). A decreasing positive subsequence of length \(2\) requires \(A_1 > A_2 > 0\), which is impossible since \(A_1 \le 1\) and \(A_2 \ge 1\); thus \(\text{Ans} = 0\). For \(N = 3, K = 2\), out of \(4! = 24\) sequences, the sequences with \(A_{i_1} > A_{i_2} > 0\) are \((A_1, 2, 1)\) for \(A_1 \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(2\) ways) giving \(\text{Ans} = 2\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

There are \(\prod_{i=1}^N (i + 1) = (N + 1)!\) sequences in total. Switch to the complement: count sequences \((A_1, \dots, A_N)\) containing no decreasing subsequence of positive elements of length \(K\). How can you convert the choice of \(A_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, i\}\) (where positive values can be repeated across different \(i\)) into a non-attacking rook placement (where each row and column has at most one rook) on a staircase board, or into a sequence of interval transitions?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

At each step \(i = 1, \dots, N\), we first introduce a new positive value \(i\) into our pool, and then \(A_i\) either picks \(0\) or picks a value from \(\{1, \dots, i\}\). If we record these \(2N\) events (insert row \(i\), then query column \(i\)) and resolve ties among equal values \(A_i = A_j\) from right to left, the choices of \(A_1, \dots, A_N\) are in bijection with configurations of \(N\) intervals \([l_r, r_r] \subseteq [1, 2N]\) (or Dyck paths / matchings of size \(N\)) avoiding a \(K\)-chain of nested intervals! Specifically, if we fix the number of active positive elements \(M \in [0, N]\) (chosen in \(\binom{N+1}{M+1}\) ways on the staircase board), by RSK / Greene’s theorem and the reflection principle across the strip \(0 \le x - y < K\), transitioning along the boundary diagonal from \((i, i)\) to \((n, n)\) multiplies by the translation-invariant reflection kernel \(g_{n - i}\), with unit interior weight \(w_{n, i} = 1\) and diagonal boundary transition \(\psi_n(S_n) = S_n\) (plus the staircase step \((n, n) \to (n + 1, n)\)).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Let \(dp[i][j]\) (\(0 \le j \le i \le N\)) be the number of valid partial configurations on the first \(i\) steps with \(j\) unmatched active openings, where the condition “no \(K\)-nesting” restricts active transitions across the boundary \(j = K - 1\). For the \(O(N^2)\) contest bound (\(N \le 5000\)), unroll the binomial recurrence directly in \(O(N^2)\) time. To achieve the semi-online CDQ speedup, notice that advancing across a strip of width \(d \le K\) is a causal binomial convolution in \(i\): unpacking \(\binom{i - i' + c}{i - i'} = \frac{(i - i' + c)!}{(i - i')! \, c!}\) decouples the lag \(k = i - i'\) from the source index \(i'\), allowing CDQ NTT (solve(l, r)) to transfer each block in \(O(L \log L)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1 (Complement & Staircase / Matching Bijection): The total number of sequences \(A = (A_1, \dots, A_N)\) with \(0 \le A_i \le i\) is \((N + 1)!\). We count the complement: sequences where the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of positive values has length \(\le K - 1\). By the official staircase-matching bijection (maroonrk / maspy), at step \(i = 1, \dots, N\), we first add a candidate row \(R_i\) and then column \(L_i\) either remains unmatched (\(A_i = 0\)) or matches to an available row (converting duplicate values \(A_i = A_j > 0\) into disjoint arcs by linking each match to the most recent copy). Choosing which \(m\) columns and \(m\) rows participate in the active staircase strip of width \(< K\) (weighted by the remaining unrestricted choices via \(\binom{N + 1}{n + 1}\)) reduces the problem to counting lattice paths / rook configurations inside a strip of width \(K - 1\) along the main diagonal.
Step 2 (Exact 2D Contest DP & Diagonal Reflection Reduction with Explicit \(\psi_n, w_{n, i}\)):

Direct \(O(N^2)\) Contest DP (\(N \le 5000\)): Let \(f[i][j]\) (\(0 \le i \le N\), \(0 \le j \le \min(i, K - 1)\)) be the number of valid partial matchings after \(i\) steps with \(j\) open (unmatched) chain heads. At step \(i\), we first insert a new potential head (shifting \(j \to j + 1\) or leaving it inactive) and then choose whether \(A_i\) closes one of the open heads, giving the \(O(N^2)\) transition over \(0 \le j < K\).
Diagonal Reflection Reduction (\(O(N \log^2 N)\)): By RSK / Greene’s theorem on the staircase Ferrers diagram, a configuration with no \(K\)-decreasing chain corresponds to a pair of standard / semi-standard tableaux of width \(\le K - 1\), or equivalently a lattice walk from \((0, 0)\) to \((n, n)\) staying within the diagonal strip \(0 \le x - y < K\) with periodic reflections across \(x - y = -1\) and \(x - y = K\). Eliminating the interior of the strip by summing over first-return excursions between touches of the main diagonal \(x = y\) gives the causal boundary recurrence on \(dp[0 \dots N]\) (\(dp[0] = 1\)): \[
dp[n] = \psi_n\!\left( \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} dp[i] \cdot g_{n - i} \cdot w_{n, i} \right) \qquad (1 \le n \le N),
\] where every symbol has a concrete closed form:
Interior Weight \(w_{n, i} = 1\): Because the strip boundaries \(x - y = -1\) and \(x - y = K\) are parallel to the main diagonal \(x = y\), the excursion count between diagonal touch \((i, i)\) and \((n, n)\) is translation-invariant and depends only on the lag \(k = n - i\).
Reflection Kernel \(g_k\) (\(k = n - i \ge 1\)): By the André reflection principle across the two parallel boundaries separated by \(K + 1\), the number of primitive/unconstrained diagonal-to-diagonal transitions of lag \(k\) is \[
g_k = \sum_{r \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^r \left[ \binom{2k - 1}{k - r K} - \binom{2k - 1}{k - 1 - r K} \right].
\]
Boundary Wrapper \(\psi_n(S_n)\): At diagonal coordinate \((n, n)\), \(\psi_n(S_n) = S_n \bmod p\) finalizes the diagonal state before multiplying by the outer binomial completion weight \(\binom{N + 1}{n + 1} (N - n)!\) when summing the complement over \(n = K, \dots, N\).

Step 3 (Decoupling the Binomial Kernel for Semi-Online CDQ NTT):

Semi-Online CDQ NTT Execution: Since the reflection kernel \(g_k\) (\(1 \le k \le N\)) depends only on the lag \(k = n - i\), we precompute \(g_1, \dots, g_N\) in \(O(N)\) total time using precomputed factorials (since for each \(k\), only \(O(k / K)\) values of \(r \in \mathbb{Z}\) have non-zero binomial coefficients, summing to \(\sum_{k=1}^N O(k / K) = O(N^2 / K) \subseteq O(N)\) when \(K \asymp N\), or \(O(N \log N)\) across all \(k\)).
A single call to solve(0, N) (§9.2) then computes all \(dp[0 \dots N]\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time (or \(O(N^2)\) via a direct loop for \(N \le 5000\)). Subtracting the complement count from \((N + 1)! \bmod 998244353\) yields the exact answer.








NoteAlgorithm Contract: ARC 138 E (#060)




Input & Preconditions: Integers \(N, K\) (\(2 \le K \le N \le 10^5\)), \(0\)-indexed diagonal DP array \(dp[0 \dots N]\), and lag kernel \(g[1 \dots N]\) with \(g_0 = 0\); precomputed factorials and inverse factorials up to \(2N\) modulo \(p = 998244353\) (\(p > 2N\)).
Output & Postconditions: solve(0, N) populates \(dp[0 \dots N]\), from which subtracting the complement sum from \((N + 1)! \bmod p\) outputs the exact number of sequences with a decreasing positive subsequence of length \(K\).
Invariants: Upon entering solve(l, r), \(S[n]\) for each \(n \in [l, r]\) stores the exact sum of reflected strip transitions \(\sum_{i=0}^{l-1} dp[i] \, g_{n-i}\) from all finalized diagonal states \(i < l\).
Complexity: \(O(N^2)\) time and \(O(N)\) space for the direct loop (\(N \le 5000\)); \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space via Semi-Online CDQ NTT (solve(0, N)).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: (1) In the reflection sum for \(g_k\), only \(O(k / K)\) shifts \(r \in \mathbb{Z}\) have non-negative lower indices in \(\binom{2k}{k \pm rK}\), so iterating over all \(r \in [-N, N]\) instead of \(|rK| \le k + 1\) causes an \(O(N^2)\) TLE; (2) Forgetting to set \(g_0 = 0\) introduces a self-loop at lag \(0\) in solve(l, r); (3) When subtracting the complement count from \((N + 1)! \bmod p\), add \(p\) before taking modulo to prevent negative residues.









Stepping Stone 2 (#021) — AtCoder ABC 222 H: Beautiful Binary Tree

Source: AtCoder Beginner Contest 222, Problem H
Prerequisite Tags: [Coupled Binary Tree Recurrence, Self-Referential Causal Convolution, Multi-Resolution Landmark]
Problem Statement: For an integer \(N \ge 1\), a rooted binary tree (where each vertex has a left child, a right child, both, or neither, and left vs. right children are distinguished) with vertices labeled 0 or 1 is called a beautiful binary tree of degree \(N\) if:

Every vertex labeled 0 has at least one child, and all of its children are labeled 1.
Every leaf (a vertex with no children) is labeled 1.
The tree contains exactly \(N\) vertices labeled 1 in total (and any number of vertices labeled 0). Compute the number \(H_N\) of beautiful binary trees of degree \(N\) modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints:

Subtask 1 (All-\(n\) Causal Recurrence Regime — Ch 09): Compute \(H_1, H_2, \dots, H_N \bmod 998244353\) for \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\).
Subtask 2 (Original Contest Single-\(N\) Extreme Regime — Preview of Ch 11 & Ch 18): \(1 \le N \le 10^7\), Time limit \(2.0\text{ s}\).

Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(N = 1\), \(H_1 = 1\). For \(N = 2\), \(H_2 = 6\). For \(N = 3\), \(H_3 = 47\) (and for \(N = 4\), \(H_4 = 420\)).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(T_1(x)\) and \(T_0(x)\) be the ordinary generating functions of valid subtrees rooted at a 1-vertex and a 0-vertex, respectively, where the variable \(x\) marks the number of 1-vertices.

A 0-vertex contributes \(0\) to the count of 1s, must have at least one child, and every child must be a 1-vertex (left only, right only, or both): thus \(T_0(x) = 2 T_1(x) + T_1(x)^2\).
A 1-vertex contributes \(1\) to the count of 1s (\(x\)), and each of its two ordered child slots can be empty (\(1\)), a 0-subtree (\(T_0\)), or a 1-subtree (\(T_1\)): thus \(T_1(x) = x(1 + T_0(x) + T_1(x))^2\). Substitute \(T_0(x) = 2 T_1(x) + T_1(x)^2\) into \(T_1(x)\)! What single-variable causal equation does \(U(x) = T_1(x)\) satisfy, and why does the leading factor of \(x\) make it a strictly contractive causal operator?




Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Substituting \(T_0 = 2 T_1 + T_1^2\) into \(1 + T_0 + T_1\) gives \(1 + 3 T_1 + T_1^2\), so \(U(x) = T_1(x)\) satisfies \[
U(x) = x \big(1 + 3 U(x) + U(x)^2\big)^2 = x \, \Phi\big(U(x)\big), \qquad \Phi(y) = (1 + 3y + y^2)^2,
\] and the number of beautiful binary trees with \(N\) ones (via the standard pointed-tree / Lagrange bijection \(H_N = [x^N] U(x) = \frac{1}{N}[y^{N-1}](1 + 3y + y^2)^{2N}\)) equals \(u_N = [x^N] U(x)\)!

Because \(U(0) = 0\) and \(U(x) = x \Phi(U(x))\), for every \(n \ge 1\), \(u_n = [x^{n-1}](1 + 3 U(x) + U(x)^2)^2\) depends only on \(u_1, \dots, u_{n-1}\). How can you compute \(u_1, \dots, u_N\) for Subtask 1 (\(N \le 2 \times 10^5\)) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time using two chained RelaxedConvolution instances?
For Subtask 2 (\(N = 10^7\)), how does differentiating \(Q(y) = (1 + 3y + y^2)^{2N}\) logarithmically (\((1 + 3y + y^2) Q'(y) = 2N(3 + 2y) Q(y)\)) give an \(O(N)\) 2-term recurrence with zero NTTs?




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


All-\(n\) Online Solution (\(O(N \log^2 N)\)): Let \(S(x) = U(x)^2\) and \(P(x) = 1 + 3U(x) + S(x)\), so \(U(x) = x P(x)^2\). Using 2 RelaxedConvolution instances (rc_S for \(U^2\) and rc_P2 for \(P^2\)), at step \(q = n - 1\) we feed \(u_q\) into rc_S.next(u_q, u_q), form \(p_q = [q=0] + 3u_q + s_q\), and read \(u_{q+1} = \texttt{rc\_P2.next}(p_q, p_q)\) in 6 lines of code!
Single-\(N\) \(O(N)\) Sparse Power Solution (\(N = 10^7\)): Using Lagrange Inversion \(H_N = \frac{1}{N}[y^{N-1}] Q(y)\) where \(Q(y) = (1 + 3y + y^2)^{2N}\) (Ch 11) and Chapter 02’s \(O(NK)\) Sparse Power Trick (Ch 02.4): \[
H_N = \frac{1}{N} q_{N-1}, \qquad k \, q_k = 3(2N + 1 - k) \, q_{k-1} + (4N + 2 - k) \, q_{k-2} \quad (1 \le k \le N - 1, \;\; q_0 = 1).
\]








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1 (Combinatorial Grammar & Reduction to a Single Causal Fixed Point): Let \(T_1(x)\) and \(T_0(x)\) be the OGFs of subtrees rooted at 1 and 0, where \(x\) marks vertices labeled 1.

A 0-vertex has no 0-children and must have a non-empty subset of {left, right} children labeled 1: \(T_0(x) = 2 T_1(x) + T_1(x)^2\).
A 1-vertex contributes weight \(x\) and has two ordered child slots, each of which is empty (\(1\)), rooted at 0 (\(T_0\)), or rooted at 1 (\(T_1\)): \[
T_1(x) = x \big(1 + T_0(x) + T_1(x)\big)^2 = x \big(1 + 3 T_1(x) + T_1(x)^2\big)^2.
\] Setting \(U(x) = T_1(x) = \sum_{n \ge 1} u_n x^n\), the count of beautiful binary trees of degree \(N\) is \(H_N = u_N = [x^N] U(x)\) (which by Lagrange Inversion equals \(\frac{1}{N}[y^{N-1}](1 + 3y + y^2)^{2N}\), as we will prove in Chapter 11).

Step 2 (Method 1: All-\(n\) Chained RelaxedConvolution for \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\)): Define the intermediate series: \[
S(x) = U(x)^2, \qquad P(x) = 1 + 3 U(x) + S(x), \qquad U(x) = x \, P(x)^2.
\] Because of the factor of \(x\) in \(U(x) = x \, P(x)^2\), the coefficient \(u_{q+1} = [x^{q+1}] U(x)\) for \(q \ge 0\) equals \([x^q] P(x)^2\), which is completely determined at step \(q\) from \(u_0, u_1, \dots, u_q\)! We instantiate two RelaxedConvolution engines (rc_S and rc_P2) and run a single causal loop for \(q = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1\):

At \(q = 0\): \(u_0 = 0\), \(s_0 = \texttt{rc\_S.next}(0, 0) = 0\), \(p_0 = 1 + 0 + 0 = 1\), and \(u_1 = \texttt{rc\_P2.next}(1, 1) = 1\).
For \(q = 1, 2, \dots, N - 1\): since \(u_q\) was produced at the end of step \(q - 1\), we immediately compute:

\(s_q = \texttt{rc\_S.next}(u_q, u_q)\) (representing \([x^q] U(x)^2\));
\(p_q = (3 u_q + s_q) \bmod p\) (representing \([x^q](1 + 3U(x) + U(x)^2)\));
\(u_{q+1} = \texttt{rc\_P2.next}(p_q, p_q)\) (representing \([x^q] P(x)^2 = [x^{q+1}] U(x)\)). Let us trace \(q = 1, 2\) by hand:

\(q = 1\): \(u_1 = 1 \implies s_1 = 0, \; p_1 = 3(1) + 0 = 3 \implies u_2 = [x^1](1 + 3x + \dots)^2 = 2 p_0 p_1 = 6\).
\(q = 2\): \(u_2 = 6 \implies s_2 = u_1^2 = 1, \; p_2 = 3(6) + 1 = 19 \implies u_3 = 2 p_0 p_2 + p_1^2 = 38 + 9 = 47\). All \(H_n = u_n \bmod p\) for \(1 \le n \le N\) are obtained in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and 8 lines of code!

Step 3 (Method 2: Single-\(N\) Reduction to \(O(N)\) Sparse Power Recurrence for \(N \le 10^7\)): By the Lagrange Inversion Formula (Chapter 11) applied to \(U(x) = x \, \Phi(U(x))\) with \(\Phi(y) = (1 + 3y + y^2)^2\): \[
H_N = [x^N] U(x) = \frac{1}{N} [y^{N-1}] \Phi(y)^N = \frac{1}{N} [y^{N-1}] \big(1 + 3y + y^2\big)^{2N}.
\] Let \(Q(y) = (1 + 3y + y^2)^{2N} = \sum_{k \ge 0} q_k y^k\). Applying Chapter 02’s \(O(NK)\) Sparse Power Recurrence (Section 2.4) to \((1 + 3y + y^2) Q'(y) = 2N(3 + 2y) Q(y)\) and extracting \([y^{k-1}]\) yields the 2-term linear recurrence: \[
k \, q_k = 3(2N + 1 - k) \, q_{k - 1} + (4N + 2 - k) \, q_{k - 2} \qquad (1 \le k \le N - 1),
\] with base cases \(q_0 = 1\) and \(q_{-1} = 0\).

Hand-Check for \(N = 1, 2, 3\):

\(N = 1\): \(H_1 = \frac{1}{1} q_0 = 1\).

Intermediate 1 (#086) — Codeforces 553E: Kyoya and Train

Source: Codeforces Round 309 (Div. 1), Problem E
Prerequisite Tags: [Backward Time-Window DP, Pointwise Min Envelope, Semi-Online CDQ FFT]
Problem Statement: Kyoya is at vertex \(1\) of a directed multigraph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) directed edges, and wants to reach vertex \(n\) within \(T\) time units; if he arrives at vertex \(n\) strictly after time \(T\), he must pay a fine of \(x\). Each directed edge \(e_k = (a_k \to b_k)\) (\(1 \le k \le m\)) costs \(c_k\) dollars to board, and its travel duration \(s \in \{1, 2, \dots, T\}\) is a random variable Taking value \(s\) with given probability \(p_{k, s}\) (where \(\sum_{s=1}^T p_{k, s} = 1\)). Whenever Kyoya arrives at a vertex \(u \neq n\) at time \(t \le T\), he may dynamically choose the next outgoing edge \(e_k \in \delta^+(u)\) to minimize his total expected future cost (boarding costs plus the potential fine \(x\)). Compute the minimum expected total cost starting from vertex \(1\) at time \(t = 0\) with absolute or relative error at most \(10^{-6}\).
Constraints: \(2 \le n \le 50\), \(1 \le m \le 100\), \(1 \le T \le 20000\), \(0 \le c_k, x \le 10^6\). Probabilities are given as \(p_{k, s} = \text{int} / 10^5\). Time limit: \(8.0\text{ s}\). Required complexity: \(O(m T \log^2 T + n^3)\).
Sample Trace (\(T \le 4\)): Let \(n = 2, m = 1, T = 2, x = 10\), with a single edge \(e_1 = (1 \to 2)\) of cost \(c_1 = 1\) and travel-time probabilities \(p_{1, 1} = 0.5, p_{1, 2} = 0.5\). Then \(dp[2][t] = 0\) for \(t \le 2\) and \(dp[2][t] = 10\) for \(t > 2\). At \(t = 2\), taking \(e_1\) arrives at \(t' \in \{3, 4\} > 2\), so \(dp[1][2] = 1 + 1.0 \times 10 = 11\). At \(t = 1\), \(t' = 2\) (prob \(0.5\), cost \(0\)) and \(t' = 3\) (prob \(0.5\), cost \(10\)), so \(dp[1][1] = 1 + 0.5(0) + 0.5(10) = 6\). At \(t = 0\), \(t' \in \{1, 2\} \le 2\), so \(dp[1][0] = 1 + 0.5(0) + 0.5(0) = 1.0\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(dp[u][t]\) (\(0 \le t \le T\)) be the minimum expected cost to reach vertex \(n\) starting from vertex \(u\) at time \(t\). What happens if \(t > T\)? Since the deadline \(T\) has already been missed, the fine \(x\) is unavoidable, so Kyoya should simply take the deterministic shortest path \(d(u, n)\) with respect to edge costs \(c_k\): \[
dp[u][t] = d(u, n) + x \qquad (\forall\, t > T), \qquad dp[n][t] = 0 \quad (\forall\, t \le T).
\] Why must the DP over \(t \in [0, T]\) proceed backward in time from \(t = T\) down to \(t = 0\), and why can’t we solve it offline with polynomial inversion?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

For each edge \(e_k = (u \to v)\) and time \(t \in [0, T]\), the expected cost of taking edge \(e_k\) at time \(t\) is \[
\text{val}[k][t] = c_k + \sum_{s=1}^{T - t} p_{k, s} \, dp[v][t + s] + \underbrace{\left(\sum_{s = T - t + 1}^{T} p_{k, s}\right) \big(d(v, n) + x\big)}_{\text{late-arrival tail }(t + s > T)},
\] and the vertex recurrence is the pointwise minimum envelope \[
dp[u][t] = \min_{e_k \in \delta^+(u)} \text{val}[k][t].
\] Because of the outer \(\min\) over outgoing edges, \(dp[v][t]\) cannot be written as a rational function of a shift operator. However, notice that \(t + s > t\): the values \(dp[v][t']\) for \(t' > t\) are strictly earlier in backward time! How do we adapt solve(l, r) so that the right half \([m + 1, r]\) transfers to the left half \([l, m]\)?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Run Backward Semi-Online CDQ FFT solve(l, r) on \([0, T]\):

First recurse on the right half solve(m + 1, r) (later times \(t' \in [m + 1, r]\)).
Once solve(m + 1, r) returns, \(dp[v][t']\) is finalized for all \(v \in [1, n]\) and \(t' \in [m + 1, r]\). For each edge \(e_k = (u \to v)\), we must accumulate \(\sum_{t' = m + 1}^{r} dp[v][t'] \, p_{k, t' - t}\) into \(\text{val}[k][t]\) for all \(t \in [l, m]\).
This is a difference convolution \((t') - t = s\): reverse the kernel slice \(p_k[1 \dots r - l]\) by setting \(B(x) = \sum_{s=1}^{r-l} p_{k, s} x^{(r - l) - s}\) and \(A(x) = \sum_{t'=m+1}^r dp[v][t'] x^{t' - (m + 1)}\). Then \((t' - (m + 1)) + ((r - l) - (t' - t)) = (r - l) + t - (m + 1)\), so \([x^{(r - l) + t - (m + 1)}](A \cdot B)\) gives the exact transfer to \(\text{val}[k][t]\)!
Finally, recurse on the left half solve(l, m), where the base case \(l = r = t\) sets \(dp[u][t] = \min_{e_k \in \delta^+(u)} \text{val}[k][t]\).








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1 (All-Pairs Shortest Paths & Late-Arrival Initialization): First run Floyd–Warshall (or Dijkstra from \(n\) on the reversed graph) in \(O(n^3)\) time to compute \(d(u, n)\), the minimum sum of edge costs \(c_k\) from \(u\) to \(n\). For every edge \(e_k = (u \to v)\) and time \(t \in [0, T]\), any travel duration \(s > T - t\) causes Kyoya to arrive at \(v\) at time \(t + s > T\), incurring deterministic cost \(d(v, n) + x\). We pre-initialize the edge accumulator \(\text{val}[k][t]\) with the constant boarding cost plus this late-arrival tail: \[
\text{val}[k][t] \gets c_k + \big(d(v, n) + x\big) \sum_{s = T - t + 1}^{T} p_{k, s} \qquad (0 \le t \le T),
\] computed for all \(k, t\) in \(O(m T)\) time via suffix sums of \(p_{k, s}\).
Step 2 (Backward CDQ Divide-and-Conquer FFT solve(l, r)): Now the remaining sum to accumulate into \(\text{val}[k][t]\) is \[
\sum_{t' = t + 1}^{T} dp[v][t'] \cdot p_{k, t' - t}.
\] Define the backward recursive procedure solve(l, r) on \([0, T]\):

Base Case (\(l = r = t\)): All contributions from \(t' \in [t + 1, T]\) have already been added to \(\text{val}[k][t]\). We finalize \(dp[n][t] = 0\), and for every \(u \in \{1, \dots, n - 1\}\): \[
dp[u][t] = \min_{e_k = (u \to v)} \text{val}[k][t].
\]
Recursive Step (\(l < r\), with \(m = \lfloor (l + r) / 2 \rfloor\)):

Recurse Right (Later Times First): Call solve(m + 1, r). Upon return, \(dp[v][t']\) is finalized for all \(v \in [1, n]\) and \(t' \in [m + 1, r]\).
Cross-Boundary Difference Convolution (\([m + 1, r] \to [l, m]\)): For each edge \(e_k = (u \to v)\) (\(1 \le k \le m\)), we need to compute for every \(t \in [l, m]\): \[
\Delta_{k, t} = \sum_{t' = m + 1}^{r} dp[v][t'] \cdot p_{k, t' - t}.
\] Let \(L_A = r - m\) and \(L_B = r - l\). Define the two real polynomials: \[
A(x) = \sum_{i = 0}^{r - m - 1} dp[v][m + 1 + i] \, x^i, \qquad B(x) = \sum_{s = 1}^{r - l} p_{k, s} \, x^{(r - l) - s}.
\] Multiply \(C(x) = A(x) \cdot B(x)\) using a single real/complex FFT of length \(2^{\lceil \log_2(L_A + L_B) \rceil} \le 4(r - l)\). For each \(t \in [l, m]\), setting \(i = t' - (m + 1)\) and \(s = t' - t\) gives exponent \[
i + \big((r - l) - s\big) = \big(t' - m - 1\big) + \big(r - l - t' + t\big) = (r - l - m - 1) + t.
\] Thus \([x^{(r - l - m - 1) + t}] C(x) = \Delta_{k, t}\), which we add to \(\text{val}[k][t]\) for each \(t = l, l + 1, \dots, m\).
Recurse Left (Earlier Times Second): Call solve(l, m).


Step 3 (Final Output & Complexity Verification): After solve(0, T) completes, output \(dp[1][0]\).

Input & Preconditions: Directed multigraph with \(n \le 50\) vertices, \(m \le 100\) edges, time horizon \(T \le 20000\), fine \(x\), edge costs \(c_k\), and duration probabilities \(p_{k, s}\) for \(s \in [1, T]\) with \(\sum_{s=1}^T p_{k, s} = 1\); vertex \(n\) is reachable from all vertices; \(\text{val}[k][t]\) is pre-initialized with \(c_k + (d(v, n) + x)\sum_{s > T-t} p_{k, s}\).
Postconditions: solve(0, T) finalizes \(dp[u][t]\) for all \(u \in [1, n]\) and \(t \in [0, T]\), and \(dp[1][0]\) gives the minimum expected cost within \(10^{-6}\) error.
Index & Truncation Boundaries: Time index \(t\) runs over \([0, T]\), recursion runs in reverse time (solve(mid + 1, r) before solve(l, mid)), and each cross-interval FFT on \([l, r]\) convolves \(dp[v][mid + 1 \dots r]\) with \(p_k[1 \dots r - l]\).
Complexity: \(O(m T \log^2 T + n^3)\) time and \(O(m T)\) space.
1-Sentence Recursion Invariant: Upon entering solve(l, r), \(\text{val}[k][t]\) for every edge \(e_k = (u \to v)\) and every \(t \in [l, r]\) already includes all expected future cost contributions from arrival times \(t' > r\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: At \(u = n\) (the destination), \(dp[n][t] = 0\) for all \(t \in [0, T]\) and must never be overwritten by outgoing edges from \(n\); forgetting to pre-add the late-arrival penalty \((d(v, n) + x)\sum_{s > T-t} p_{k, s}\) before starting CDQ undercounts trajectories that exceed time \(T\).

Source: AtCoder Beginner Contest 230, Problem Ex
Prerequisite Tags: [Pólya Multiset Operator, Online Euler Transform, Dual Relaxed Convolution]
Problem Statement: We have gold bars of \(K\) distinct positive integer weights \(w_1 < w_2 < \dots < w_K \le W\) (with an unlimited supply of bars of each available weight) and an unlimited supply of identical pouches, where each empty pouch itself has weight \(1\). A valid pouch of weight \(n\) consists of an outer pouch (of weight \(1\)) containing an unordered multiset of at least \(2\) items, where each item is either a gold bar of some allowed weight \(w_i\) or another valid pouch, such that the total weight of the outer pouch plus all items inside it equals \(n\). Two pouches are considered identical if one can be obtained by permuting the items inside any pouch. For each \(n = 2, 3, \dots, W\), compute the number of valid pouches of weight \(n\) modulo \(998244353\).
Constraints: \(2 \le W \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(1 \le K \le W\), \(1 \le w_1 < w_2 < \dots < w_K \le W\). Time limit: \(4.0\text{ s}\). Required complexity: \(O(W \log^2 W)\).
Sample Trace (\(W \le 4\)): Suppose \(W = 4\) and the only available gold bar weight is \(\{w_1\} = \{1\}\) (\(A(x) = x\)).

\(n = 2\): No pouch has weight \(1\) (\(b_1 = 0\)), so items of weight \(1\) are just the gold bar (\(f_1 = 1\)). A pouch of weight \(2\) has outer pouch weight \(1\), leaving weight \(1\) for its contents—impossible since it must contain \(\ge 2\) items! Thus \(b_2 = 0\) (and \(f_2 = 0\)).
\(n = 3\): Contents must have total weight \(2\) and size \(\ge 2\), which can only be two gold bars \(\{1, 1\}\) (\(1\) way). Thus \(b_3 = 1\) (and \(f_3 = 1\)).
\(n = 4\): Contents must have total weight \(3\) and size \(\ge 2\), which can only be three gold bars \(\{1, 1, 1\}\) (\(1\) way). Thus \(b_4 = 1\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(F(x) = \sum_{n=1}^W f_n x^n\) be the OGF of valid single items (for each \(n \ge 1\), \(f_n = b_n + a_n\), where \(a_n \in \{0, 1\}\) indicates whether a gold bullion of weight \(n\) exists in the input, and \(b_n\) is the number of valid pouches of weight \(n\), with \(b_1 = 0\)). A pouch of weight \(n\) consists of the pouch bag itself (weight \(1\), factor \(x\)) together with an unordered multiset of size \(\ge 2\) chosen from all valid items (bullions and smaller pouches). How do you express a multiset of size \(\ge 2\) using the Euler transform \(\operatorname{MSET}(F)\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

The Euler transform \(\operatorname{MSET}(F)(x) = \prod_{m \ge 1} (1 - x^m)^{-f_m} = \exp\!\left(\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{F(x^k)}{k}\right)\) counts multisets of any size \(\ge 0\):

Size \(0\) (empty multiset) contributes \(1\).
Size \(1\) (singleton item) contributes \(F(x)\). Therefore, multisets of size \(\ge 2\) have OGF \(\operatorname{MSET}(F)(x) - 1 - F(x)\), and multiplying by \(x\) (for the pouch’s own weight \(1\)) gives the exact functional equation for pouches \(B(x) = \sum_{n=2}^W b_n x^n\): \[
B(x) = x \Big( \exp\big(G(x)\big) - 1 - F(x) \Big), \qquad \text{where } F(x) = A(x) + B(x), \quad G(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{F(x^k)}{k}.
\] Notice the factor of \(x\) on the right-hand side! Why does \(b_n = [x^n] B(x)\) depend only on \(f_1, \dots, f_{n-1}\)?




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Let \(E(x) = \exp(G(x)) = \sum_{m \ge 0} e_m x^m\). Then for every \(n \ge 2\): \[
b_n = [x^{n-1}] \big(E(x) - 1 - F(x)\big) = e_{n-1} - f_{n-1}, \qquad f_n = a_n + b_n = a_n + e_{n-1} - f_{n-1}.
\] And how do we advance \(e_{n-1}\) from \(n - 1\) to \(n\)? By Section 9.4’s Online Exponential \(E'(x) = G'(x) E(x)\):

At step \(q = n - 1 \ge 1\), we already know \(e_{q-1}\), so if we know \(q g_q = \sum_{d \mid q} d f_d\), a single call e[q] = rc.next(q * g_q, e[q - 1]) * inv[q] produces \(e_q = e_{n-1}\)!
Once \(e_q\) is known, we immediately get \(b_{q+1} = e_q - f_q\) and \(f_{q+1} = a_{q+1} + b_{q+1}\), and propagate \((q + 1) f_{q+1}\) to all multiples \(m = j(q + 1) \le W\) in \(O(W / q)\) harmonic time!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1 (Symbolic Formulation of Valid Pouches): Let \(A(x) = \sum_{i=1}^K x^{w_i} = \sum_{n=1}^W a_n x^n\) (\(a_n \in \{0, 1\}\)) be the OGF of available bullion weights, \(B(x) = \sum_{n=2}^W b_n x^n\) be the OGF of valid pouches, and \(F(x) = A(x) + B(x) = \sum_{n=1}^W f_n x^n\) be the OGF of all valid single items (bullions + pouches). A valid pouch has weight \(1\) (from the pouch itself) plus a multiset of \(\ge 2\) valid items. By the Pólya / Euler multiset construction (Chapter 03), the OGF of all multisets of items is \[
E(x) = \operatorname{MSET}(F)(x) = \prod_{m \ge 1} \frac{1}{(1 - x^m)^{f_m}} = \exp\!\left( \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{F(x^k)}{k} \right) = \exp(G(x)),
\] where \(G(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{F(x^k)}{k}\). Subtracting the empty multiset (\(1\)) and the single-item multisets (\(F(x)\)) and multiplying by \(x\) (for the pouch’s weight \(1\)) yields \[
B(x) = x \big( E(x) - 1 - F(x) \big) \implies F(x) = A(x) + x \big( E(x) - 1 - F(x) \big).
\] (Note: If the outer pouch itself can take any weight \(w_i \in \{w_1, \dots, w_K\}\), then \(B(x) = A(x)(E(x) - 1 - F(x))\), and we simply use a second RelaxedConvolution instance rc_B to multiply \(A(x)\) with \(E(x) - 1 - F(x)\), as shown in Section 9.4.)
Step 2 (Causal Differential Reduction of \(E(x) = \exp(G(x))\)): Differentiating \(E(x) = \exp(G(x))\) gives \(E'(x) = G'(x) E(x)\). Recall from Section 9.4 that \[
G(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \sum_{d \ge 1} \frac{f_d}{k} x^{k d} \implies q \, g_q = [x^{q-1}] G'(x) = \sum_{d \mid q} d \, f_d \qquad (q \ge 1).
\] Extracting \([x^{q-1}]\) from \(E'(x) = G'(x) E(x)\) gives \[
q \, e_q = \sum_{i=1}^{q} (i g_i) \, e_{q - i} = [x^{q-1}] \big( G'(x) E(x) \big) \qquad (q \ge 1, \quad e_0 = 1).
\] And extracting \([x^{q+1}]\) from \(B(x) = x(E(x) - 1 - F(x))\) for \(q \ge 1\) gives \[
b_{q+1} = e_q - f_q, \qquad f_{q+1} = a_{q+1} + b_{q+1} = a_{q+1} + e_q - f_q.
\]
Step 3 (Hand-Checkable Trace for \(q = 1, 2\) & Complete Algorithm):

Initialization (\(q = 0\)):

\(e_0 = 1\).
For weight \(1\): no pouch can have weight \(1\) (\(b_1 = 0\)), so \(f_1 = a_1 \in \{0, 1\}\).
Immediately propagate \(1 \cdot f_1\) to all multiples \(m = 1, 2, \dots, W\): set qg[m] = f_1.

Loop for \(q = 1, 2, \dots, W - 1\):

At the start of step \(q\), every divisor \(d \mid q\) satisfies \(1 \le d \le q\), so \(f_d\) has already been finalized and added to qg[q]! Thus \(\text{qg}[q] = q g_q = \sum_{d \mid q} d f_d\) is 100% complete.
Call e[q] = rc.next(qg[q], e[q - 1]) * inv[q] % MOD; (note that in rc, index \(m = q - 1\) pairs \([x^{q-1}]G' = q g_q\) with \([x^{q-1}]E = e_{q-1}\), returning \([x^{q-1}](G' E) = q e_q\)).
Compute \(b_{q+1} = (e_q - f_q) \bmod p\) and \(f_{q+1} = (a_{q+1} + b_{q+1}) \bmod p\).
Propagate \((q + 1) f_{q+1}\) to all multiples of \(q + 1\):
long long val = 1LL * (q + 1) * f[q + 1] % MOD;
for (int m = q + 1; m <= W; m += q + 1)
    qg[m] = (qg[m] + val) % MOD;

Output: Print \(b_2, b_3, \dots, b_W \bmod 998244353\).

Input & Preconditions: Maximum weight \(W \le 2 \times 10^5\) and indicator array \(a[1 \dots W] \in \{0, 1\}^W\) of available gold bar weights; prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > W\); base cases \(e_0 = 1\), \(b_1 = 0\), \(f_1 = a_1\), and qg[m] = f_1 initialized for all \(1 \le m \le W\).

Source: AtCoder Regular Contest 123, Problem F & AtCoder Regular Contest 115, Problem E (LEQ and NEQ)
Prerequisite Tags: [Connected-Component Run-Length IE, Non-Homogeneous Causal Recurrence, CDQ Divide-and-Conquer]

NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1 (Connected-Component Inclusion-Exclusion Setup): In any sequence \(X = (X_1, \dots, X_N)\), let \(E = \{1, 2, \dots, N - 1\}\) be the set of adjacent pairs \((k, k + 1)\). We want no pair in \(E\) to have \(X_k = X_{k+1}\). By Inclusion-Exclusion over subsets \(F \subseteq E\) of violated edges:

Choosing \(F \subseteq E\) partitions \(\{1, \dots, N\}\) into \(c = N - |F|\) connected components (contiguous intervals) \((j_0, j_1], (j_1, j_2], \dots, (j_{c-1}, j_c]\) with \(0 = j_0 < j_1 < \dots < j_c = N\).
The weight \((-1)^{|F|} = \prod_{r=1}^c (-1)^{(j_r - j_{r-1}) - 1}\) factors cleanly across the \(c\) intervals.
On each interval \((j, i]\) of length \(i - j\), all \(X_{j+1} = \dots = X_i\) must take the same integer value in \([1, \min_{k=j+1}^i A_k]\), giving \(\min_{k=j+1}^i A_k\) choices (multiplied by \(w_{i-j}\) in the general weighted recurrence). Summing over the last interval \((j, i]\) gives the causal DP: \[
dp[0] = 1, \qquad dp[i] = \sum_{j=0}^{i-1} (-1)^{i - j - 1} dp[j] \cdot w_{i - j} \cdot \min_{k = j + 1}^{i} A_k \qquad (1 \le i \le N).
\] Multiplying both sides by \((-1)^i\) and setting \(\widetilde{dp}[i] = (-1)^i dp[i]\) removes the alternating sign from \(i - j\): \[
\widetilde{dp}[0] = 1, \qquad \widetilde{dp}[i] = -\sum_{j=0}^{i-1} \widetilde{dp}[j] \cdot w_{i - j} \cdot \min_{k = j + 1}^{i} A_k.
\]

Step 2 (\(O(N)\) Monotonic Stack Solution for \(w_{i-j} = 1\)): When \(w_{i-j} = 1\), at step \(i\) we need the weighted sum \[
S_i = \sum_{j=0}^{i-1} \widetilde{dp}[j] \cdot m(j, i), \qquad \text{where } m(j, i) = \min_{k = j + 1}^{i} A_k.
\] As \(j\) goes from \(0\) to \(i - 1\), the suffix minimum \(m(j, i)\) is a non-decreasing step function of \(j\). We maintain its constant steps on a monotonic stack of pairs \((\text{val}_r, \text{sum\_dp}_r)\) alongside the running total \(S\):

Before processing \(A_i\), push a new singleton segment \((\text{val} = +\infty, \text{sum\_dp} = \widetilde{dp}[i - 1])\).
While the top of the stack has \(\text{val}_r \ge A_i\):

Pop \((\text{val}_r, \text{sum\_dp}_r)\), subtract \(\text{val}_r \cdot \text{sum\_dp}_r\) from \(S\) (if \(\text{val}_r < +\infty\)), and add \(\text{sum\_dp}_r\) to acc_dp.

Push \((A_i, \text{acc\_dp})\) onto the stack and add \(A_i \cdot \text{acc\_dp}\) to \(S\).
Now \(S = S_i \bmod p\), so set \(\widetilde{dp}[i] = (p - S) \bmod p\).
Finally, recover \(dp[N] = (-1)^N \widetilde{dp}[N] \bmod p\).

Step 3 (\(O(N \log^2 N)\) CDQ Divide-and-Conquer NTT for General \(w_{i-j}\)): When \(w_{i-j}\) is an arbitrary sequence, at CDQ node \([l, r]\) with midpoint \(m = \lfloor (l + r) / 2 \rfloor\), define the left suffix-minimum array \(L_j = \min_{k=j+1}^m A_k\) for \(j \in [l, m - 1]\) (with \(L_m = +\infty\)) and the right prefix-minimum array \(R_i = \min_{k=m+1}^i A_k\) for \(i \in [m + 1, r]\). Then for any \(j \in [l, m]\) and \(i \in [m + 1, r]\): \[
\min_{k = j + 1}^{i} A_k = \min(L_j, R_i).
\] Notice that \(L_j\) is non-decreasing as \(j \to m\) and \(R_i\) is non-increasing as \(i \to r\). Splitting the transfer \([l, m] \to [m + 1, r]\) into the regime \(L_j \le R_i\) (where the factor \(L_j\) attaches to \(\widetilde{dp}[j]\) on the left) and \(L_j > R_i\) (where the factor \(R_i\) attaches to the output at \(i\) on the right) via Cartesian-tree / two-pointer block decomposition evaluates all cross-transfers in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time. (And for ARC 123 F — Arithmetic Progression, the Stern–Brocot / Farey tree traversal coupled with priority-queue / causal generation extracts the \(K\)-th lexicographically smallest arithmetic progression in the target window.)

Advanced 2 (#225) — LibreOJ 6503: Magic (魔术)

Source: LibreOJ #6503 (雅礼集训 2018 Day 4)
Prerequisite Tags: [Connected-Component Run-Length IE, EGF Block Assembly, Divide-and-Conquer NTT]
Problem Statement: A magician has \(m\) colors of magic cards, where color \(i\) (\(1 \le i \le m\)) has \(a_i \ge 1\) identical cards, and the total number of cards is \(n = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i\). Two cards of the same color are indistinguishable. Given an integer \(k\) (\(0 \le k < n\), with \(k = 0\) requiring no two adjacent cards to share the same color), compute the number of card sequences of length \(n\) in which exactly \(k\) adjacent indices \(1 \le r \le n - 1\) have card \(r\) and card \(r + 1\) of the same color, modulo \(998244353\). (Note: If cards of the same color are instead treated as distinguishable, simply multiply the final answer by \(\prod_{i=1}^m a_i! \bmod 998244353\).)
Constraints: \(1 \le m \le 10^5\), \(1 \le n = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i \le 4 \times 10^5\), \(0 \le k < n\). Modulus \(p = 998244353\). Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\). Required complexity: \(O(n \log^2 n)\).
Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(m = 2\) colors with counts \(a = (2, 1)\) (\(n = 3\) indistinguishable cards per color: two 1s and one 2), the \(\binom{3}{2,1} = 3\) arrangements are (1, 2, 1) (\(0\) monochromatic adjacent pairs) and (1, 1, 2), (2, 1, 1) (\(1\) monochromatic adjacent pair each). Thus \(f_0 = 1\) for \(k = 0\) and \(f_1 = 2\) for \(k = 1\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

By Chapter 08’s Connected-Component Inclusion-Exclusion (连续段容斥), suppose the \(a_i\) identical cards of color \(i\) are partitioned into \(j\) non-empty contiguous blocks (\(1 \le j \le a_i\)).

Using Stars and Bars, in how many ways can \(a_i\) identical cards be split into an ordered sequence of \(j\) non-empty blocks? \(\binom{a_i - 1}{j - 1}\) ways.
How many adjacent monochromatic pairs are forced inside these \(j\) blocks? Since fusing two blocks of the same color creates \(1\) monochromatic adjacency, splitting \(a_i\) cards into \(j\) blocks forces at least \(a_i - j\) monochromatic adjacencies.




Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

First consider the \(k = 0\) case (zero adjacent monochromatic pairs): If color \(i\) is split into \(j\) blocks (\(a_i - j\) forced violations), its Inclusion-Exclusion sign is \((-1)^{a_i - j}\), and because the \(j\) blocks of color \(i\) are indistinguishable when interleaved with blocks of other colors, its Exponential Generating Function (EGF) is \[
P_i(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{a_i} (-1)^{a_i - j} \binom{a_i - 1}{j - 1} \frac{x^j}{j!}.
\] When we multiply \(P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m P_i(x) = \sum_{B=m}^n p_B x^B\), what does \(B! [x^B] P(x)\) represent? It sums over all ways to interleave \(B = \sum_{i=1}^m j_i\) total blocks across all \(m\) colors. And for general \(k \ge 0\) (exact \(k\) adjacent monochromatic pairs), replace the sign \((-1)^{a_i - j}\) with \((y - 1)^{a_i - j}\) via Binomial Inversion (\(y \mapsto y - 1\)).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Notice that \(\sum_{i=1}^m (a_i - j_i) = n - \sum_{i=1}^m j_i = n - B\) depends only on the total number of blocks \(B = \sum_{i=1}^m j_i\), NOT on the individual \(j_i\)’s. Therefore, even for general \(k \ge 0\), we DO NOT need 2D polynomials. Define the 1D polynomial of degree \(a_i\): \[
Q_i(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{a_i} \binom{a_i - 1}{j - 1} \frac{x^j}{j!}.
\] Multiply \(Q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m Q_i(x) = \sum_{B=m}^n q_B x^B\) using a Divide-and-Conquer Product Tree (Ch 01.4) in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time. Then \(g_{n - B} = B! \, q_B\) is the number of ways to force \(v = n - B\) monochromatic adjacencies:

For \(k = 0\): \(\text{Ans} = \sum_{B=m}^n (-1)^{n - B} B! \, q_B\).
For general \(k\): \(\text{Ans}_k = \sum_{v=k}^{n-m} (-1)^{v - k} \binom{v}{k} g_v\).








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1 (Per-Color Block Decomposition & Binomial Inversion): Consider color \(i \in \{1, \dots, m\}\), which has \(a_i\) indistinguishable cards. In any arrangement of the \(n\) cards, there are \(a_i - 1\) potential internal boundaries between consecutive occurrences of color \(i\) if they are placed adjacent to each other. If we select \(v_i = a_i - j_i\) of these internal boundaries to be forced adjacent pairs (\(1 \le j_i \le a_i\)), the \(a_i\) cards of color \(i\) fuse into \(j_i\) contiguous blocks. There are \(\binom{a_i - 1}{a_i - j_i} = \binom{a_i - 1}{j_i - 1}\) ways to choose which boundaries are fused. Now suppose color \(i\) is fused into \(j_i\) blocks for each \(i = 1, \dots, m\), giving \(B = \sum_{i=1}^m j_i\) total blocks and \(v = \sum_{i=1}^m (a_i - j_i) = n - B\) total forced monochromatic adjacencies. Since cards of the same color are indistinguishable, two interleavings of the \(B\) blocks produce the same sequence of fused blocks if and only if they permute the \(j_i\) blocks of color \(i\) among themselves. Thus there are \[
\frac{B!}{j_1! \, j_2! \cdots j_m!}
\] ways to arrange the \(B\) blocks in a line.
Step 2 (Factoring into 1D EGFs & Divide-and-Conquer NTT): Summing over all tuples \((j_1, \dots, j_m)\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m j_i = B\), the number of relaxed configurations \(g_{n - B}\) with \(v = n - B\) forced monochromatic adjacencies is \[
g_{n - B} = B! \sum_{j_1 + \dots + j_m = B} \prod_{i=1}^{m} \binom{a_i - 1}{j_i - 1} \frac{1}{j_i!} = B! \, [x^B] \prod_{i=1}^{m} Q_i(x),
\] where each \(Q_i(x)\) is a polynomial of degree \(a_i\): \[
Q_i(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{a_i} \binom{a_i - 1}{j - 1} \frac{x^j}{j!}.
\] Since \(\sum_{i=1}^m \deg Q_i = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i = n \le 4 \times 10^5\), we compute \(Q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m Q_i(x)\) in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time using a binary divide-and-conquer product tree (multiply_all(l, r)) or a min-heap (Huffman) NTT merge.
Step 3 (Final Inclusion-Exclusion / Binomial Inversion Extraction): Once \(g_{n - B} = B! [x^B] Q(x)\) is computed for all \(B = m, m + 1, \dots, n\) (so \(v = n - B \in [0, n - m]\)):

By Binomial Inversion (Chapter 08.1), the number of sequences with exactly \(k\) monochromatic adjacent pairs is \[
f_k = \sum_{v = k}^{n - m} (-1)^{v - k} \binom{v}{k} g_v = \sum_{B = m}^{n - k} (-1)^{n - B - k} \binom{n - B}{k} B! \, [x^B] Q(x) \pmod{998244353}.
\]
In particular, for \(k = 0\) (no two adjacent cards of the same color), this simplifies to the single linear pass \[
f_0 = \sum_{B = m}^{n} (-1)^{n - B} B! \, [x^B] Q(x) \pmod{998244353}.
\]
Hand-Check for \(m = 2, a_1 = 2, a_2 = 1\) (\(n = 3, k = 0\)):

\(Q_1(x) = x + \frac{x^2}{2}\), \(Q_2(x) = x \implies Q(x) = x^2 + \frac{x^3}{2}\).
\(B = 2\): \((-1)^{3-2} \cdot 2! \cdot 1 = -2\).
\(B = 3\): \((-1)^{3-3} \cdot 3! \cdot \frac{1}{2} = +3\).
\(f_0 = -2 + 3 = 1\) (corresponding to the unique valid sequence 1 2 1). Matches!

Preconditions: Positive color counts \(a_1, \dots, a_m \ge 1\) with \(n = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i \le 4 \times 10^5\), and target adjacency count \(0 \le k < n\).

Source: Universal Online Judge #50 (UOJ Round #3)
Prerequisite Tags: [Riccati Nonlinear ODE, Self-Convolution CDQ NTT, Failure Mode #13, Relaxed Convolution]
Problem Statement: In a nuclear chain reaction, atoms are labeled \(1, 2, \dots, m\). A valid reaction tree of size \(m\) (\(1 \le m \le n\)) is a rooted labeled structure constructed as follows:

If \(m = 1\), the single atom \(1\) forms a trivial tree on its own (\(1\) way).
If \(m \ge 2\), the root must be atom \(1\) (the minimum label among all atoms in its subtree). When the root fires, it simultaneously produces:

Given \(n\) and the binary string \(a_0 a_1 \dots a_{n-1} \in \{0, 1\}^n\), compute the number of valid reaction trees \(f_m\) for every \(m = 1, 2, \dots, n\) modulo \(998244353\).

By Chapter 04’s Boxed Product (\(C' = A' B\)) (Section 4.2), removing the minimum-labeled root from a labeled structure of size \(m\) corresponds to taking the formal derivative \(F'(x)\).
