6.5 The 8-Problem 4-Tier Practice Ladder
We now apply every tool from Sections 6.1–6.4 across our canonical 8-problem 4-tier ladder (2 Stepping Stone, 2 Intermediate, 2 Advanced, 2 Mastery). Every problem is 100% self-contained.


Stepping Stone 1 (#005) — AtCoder fps_24_h: Jump

Source: AtCoder fps_24_h — Jump
Prerequisite Tags: Ch 01 (Cauchy Convolution), Ch 06 (§6.1 Index Alignment, §6.2 Snake Oil / Egorychev)
Target Complexity: \(O((N + M) \log p)\) or \(O(N + M)\) time, \(O(N + M)\) space


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given positive integers \(N, M \le 2.5 \times 10^5\), compute \[\left(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} 2^k \binom{M}{k} + \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \sum_{j=0}^{M} 2^{i+j} \binom{N}{i} \binom{N-1+j}{j}\right) \bmod 998244353.\]

Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(N = 2, M = 1\): the first sum over \(k \in \{0, 1\}\) is \(2^0 \binom{1}{0} + 2^1 \binom{1}{1} = 1 + 2 = 3\). In the double sum over \(i \in \{0, 1\}, j \in \{0, 1\}\), factoring gives \(\left(2^0\binom{2}{0} + 2^1\binom{2}{1}\right)\left(2^0\binom{1}{0} + 2^1\binom{2}{1}\right) = (1 + 4)(1 + 4) = 25\). Total \(= 3 + 25 = 28\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

The first sum \(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} 2^k \binom{M}{k}\) has only \(N\) terms and can be summed directly in \(O(N)\) time. Look at the double sum: does \(i\) interact with \(j\)? No! The summand \(2^i \binom{N}{i} \cdot 2^j \binom{N-1+j}{j}\) factors into a sum over \(i\) times a sum over \(j\)—or even deeper, represents the total coefficient sum of the bivariate rational generating function \(\frac{1 - y}{1 - 2y - x}\) inside the rectangle \([0, N-1] \times [0, M]\)!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Separate the double sum into the product of two independent 1D sums: \[\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \sum_{j=0}^{M} 2^{i+j} \binom{N}{i} \binom{N-1+j}{j} = \left(\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} 2^i \binom{N}{i}\right) \left(\sum_{j=0}^{M} 2^j \binom{N-1+j}{j}\right).\] Notice that the \(i\)-sum is the full binomial expansion of \((1 + 2)^N = 3^N\) minus the \(i = N\) term \(2^N\): \[\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} 2^i \binom{N}{i} = 3^N - 2^N.\] And every term in the \(j\)-sum is computable directly in \(O(M)\) time! (Bonus: let us also see how the bivariate generating function \(\frac{1 - y}{1 - 2y - x}\) explains why the first sum and the double sum appear together in combinatorial grid-jump problems.)



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to \(N + M\) in \(O(N + M)\) time, evaluate the two linear sums in \(O(N + M)\) additions/multiplications, and combine modulo \(998244353\).







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Direct Algebraic Decoupling (\(O(N + M)\))
Let \(S_1 = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} 2^k \binom{M}{k}\) and \(S_2 = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \sum_{j=0}^{M} 2^{i+j} \binom{N}{i} \binom{N-1+j}{j}\). Because the summand of \(S_2\) factors into an \(i\)-dependent factor \(2^i \binom{N}{i}\) and a \(j\)-dependent factor \(2^j \binom{N-1+j}{j}\), the Golden Rule of Index Alignment decouples \(S_2\) immediately: \[\begin{aligned}
S_2
&= \left(\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \binom{N}{i} 2^i\right) \left(\sum_{j=0}^M \binom{N - 1 + j}{j} 2^j\right) \\
&= \big((1 + 2)^N - 2^N\big) \sum_{j=0}^M \binom{N - 1 + j}{j} 2^j \\
&= (3^N - 2^N) \sum_{j=0}^M \binom{N - 1 + j}{j} 2^j.
\end{aligned}\] Meanwhile, \(S_1 = \sum_{k=0}^{\min(N-1, M)} \binom{M}{k} 2^k\). Both \(S_1\) and the remaining \(j\)-sum have at most \(\max(N, M + 1) \le 2.5 \times 10^5\) terms.


2. Deeper Generating Function Insight (Why These Two Sums Belong Together)
In the AtCoder fps_24 curriculum, this expression arises from summing \([x^a y^b] \frac{1 - y}{1 - 2y - x}\) over the rectangle \(0 \le a < N, 0 \le b \le M\):

Using the 2D geometric boundary identity \(\frac{1}{1 - 2y - x} = \sum_{a, b \ge 0} \binom{a+b}{b} 2^b x^a y^b\), summing over \(0 \le a < N\) and \(0 \le b \le M\) telescopes along the top and right boundaries of the \([0, N-1] \times [0, M]\) grid into a boundary sum along \(a = N\) (producing \(\binom{N-1+j}{j} 2^j\)) and \(b = M\) (producing \(\binom{M}{k} 2^k\)).



3. Hand-Checkable Trace & Algorithm Contract

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 2, M = 1\)):

\(S_1 = \sum_{k=0}^1 2^k \binom{1}{k} = 1 + 2 = 3\).
\(3^N - 2^N = 3^2 - 2^2 = 5\), and \(\sum_{j=0}^1 \binom{1+j}{j} 2^j = \binom{1}{0} \cdot 1 + \binom{2}{1} \cdot 2 = 5\), so \(S_2 = 5 \times 5 = 25\) and \(S_1 + S_2 = 28\).

Input & Preconditions: Positive integers \(N, M \le 2.5 \times 10^5\); prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > N + M\) so factorials up to \(N + M\) are invertible.
Postconditions (Output): Returns \((S_1 + S_2) \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N + M)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space to precompute factorials, inverse factorials, and powers of \(2\) up to \(N + M \le 5 \times 10^5\).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing index \(j \in [0, M]\), the running accumulator holds \(\sum_{r=0}^j \binom{N-1+r}{r} 2^r \bmod p\), which is scaled once by \((3^N - 2^N) \bmod p\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: In \(S_1 = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} 2^k \binom{M}{k}\), when \(k > M\) we must have \(\binom{M}{k} = 0\) (cap the loop at \(\min(N - 1, M)\)); when \(N = 1\), \(S_1 = 1\) and \(3^1 - 2^1 = 1\), yielding \(S_1 + S_2 = 2^{M+1} \bmod p\).









Stepping Stone 2 (#055) — AtCoder ARC 110 D: Binomial Coefficient is Fun

Source: AtCoder ARC 110 D — Binomial Coefficient is Fun
Prerequisite Tags: Ch 06 (§6.1 Parallel / Upper-Index Vandermonde Convolution, Negative-Binomial OGF)
Target Complexity: \(O(N + \sum A_i)\) time, \(O(1)\) space


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(N\) non-negative integers \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N\) (\(1 \le N \le 2000\), \(0 \le A_i \le 2000\)) and an integer \(M\) (\(1 \le M \le 10^9\)). Find the sum \[S = \sum_{\substack{B_1, B_2, \dots, B_N \ge 0 \\ B_1 + B_2 + \dots + B_N \le M}} \prod_{i=1}^N \binom{B_i}{A_i} \bmod (10^9 + 7).\]

Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(N = 2\), \(A = (1, 1)\), \(M = 3\): the valid pairs \((B_1, B_2)\) with \(B_1, B_2 \ge 1\) and \(B_1 + B_2 \le 3\) are \((1, 1)\) giving \(\binom{1}{1}\binom{1}{1} = 1\), \((2, 1)\) giving \(\binom{2}{1}\binom{1}{1} = 2\), and \((1, 2)\) giving \(\binom{1}{1}\binom{2}{1} = 2\). Total \(S = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 = \binom{3 + 2}{2 + 2} = \binom{5}{4}\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

The summation runs over non-negative integer tuples \((B_1, \dots, B_N)\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^N B_i \le M\), and each factor \(\binom{B_i}{A_i}\) has the summation variable \(B_i\) in the upper index and the fixed constant \(A_i\) in the lower index. This is the \(N\)-fold generalization of the Parallel / Upper-Index Convolution from Section 6.1!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

What is the ordinary generating function of \(\binom{B_i}{A_i}\) over \(B_i \ge 0\)? By Kernel K1 (or Section 6.1 Identity 3), \[\sum_{B_i = 0}^\infty \binom{B_i}{A_i} x^{B_i} = \frac{x^{A_i}}{(1 - x)^{A_i + 1}}.\] Multiply these \(N\) generating functions together to get the generating function for fixed \(\sum_{i=1}^N B_i = K\), and then multiply by \(\frac{1}{1 - x}\) to sum over all \(0 \le K \le M\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Let \(S_A = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i\). Then the total generating function is \(\frac{x^{S_A}}{(1 - x)^{S_A + N + 1}}\), whose \([x^M]\) coefficient is \(\binom{M + N}{S_A + N}\). Since \(S_A + N \le 2000 \times 2000 + 2000 \approx 4 \times 10^6\) while \(M \le 10^9\), compute \(\binom{M + N}{S_A + N} = \frac{(M + N)^{\underline{S_A + N}}}{(S_A + N)!} \bmod (10^9 + 7)\) directly in \(O(N + S_A)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Generating Function Derivation
Let \(S_A = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i\). By the definition of the Cauchy product of \(N\) formal power series, for a fixed sum \(K = B_1 + \dots + B_N\): \[\begin{aligned}
\sum_{B_1 + \dots + B_N = K} \prod_{i=1}^N \binom{B_i}{A_i}
&= [x^K] \prod_{i=1}^N \left(\sum_{B_i=0}^\infty \binom{B_i}{A_i} x^{B_i}\right) && \text{(Cauchy product of }N\text{ factors)} \\
&= [x^K] \prod_{i=1}^N \frac{x^{A_i}}{(1 - x)^{A_i + 1}} && \text{(Kernel K1: }\sum_{b \ge 0} \binom{b}{a} x^b = \frac{x^a}{(1-x)^{a+1}}\text{)} \\
&= [x^K] \frac{x^{S_A}}{(1 - x)^{S_A + N}}. && \text{(summing exponents in numerator and denominator)}
\end{aligned}\] Now we must sum this coefficient over all \(0 \le K \le M\). Recall from Chapter 01 that taking the prefix sum \(\sum_{K=0}^M [x^K] F(x)\) of a formal power series \(F(x)\) is equivalent to multiplying \(F(x)\) by \(\frac{1}{1 - x} = 1 + x + x^2 + \dots\) and extracting \([x^M]\): \[\begin{aligned}
S = \sum_{K=0}^M [x^K] \frac{x^{S_A}}{(1 - x)^{S_A + N}}
&= [x^M] \frac{x^{S_A}}{(1 - x)^{S_A + N + 1}} && \text{(prefix-sum operator }(1-x)^{-1}\text{)} \\
&= [x^{M - S_A}] \frac{1}{(1 - x)^{S_A + N + 1}} && \text{(shift rule }[x^M] x^{S_A} G(x) = [x^{M-S_A}] G(x)\text{)} \\
&= \binom{(S_A + N + 1) + (M - S_A) - 1}{M - S_A} = \binom{M + N}{M - S_A} = \binom{M + N}{S_A + N}.
\end{aligned}\]


2. Combinatorial Double-Count Verification
Let us also verify \(\binom{M + N}{S_A + N}\) by a direct Stars-and-Bars double-count: Adding a slack variable \(B_{N+1} = M - \sum_{i=1}^N B_i \ge 0\) converts the inequality \(\sum_{i=1}^N B_i \le M\) into the equality \(B_1 + \dots + B_N + B_{N+1} = M\). Imagine \(M + N\) balls in a row. Choosing \(S_A + N\) balls from these \(M + N\) balls:

Use the \((A_1 + 1)\)-st, \((A_1 + A_2 + 2)\)-nd, \(\dots\), \((S_A + N)\)-th chosen balls as dividers that partition the remaining \((M + N) - N = M\) non-divider balls into \(N + 1\) boxes of sizes \(B_1, B_2, \dots, B_{N+1}\).
Then inside box \(i\) (\(1 \le i \le N\)), exactly \(A_i\) balls were chosen in \(\binom{B_i}{A_i}\) ways!



3. Hand-Checkable Trace & Algorithm Contract

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 2, A = (1, 1), M = 3\)): Here \(S_A = 1 + 1 = 2\) and \(D = S_A + N = 4\). The formula gives \(\binom{M + N}{D} = \binom{3 + 2}{4} = \binom{5}{4} = 5\), matching \((B_1, B_2) \in \{(1, 1), (2, 1), (1, 2)\}\).
Input & Preconditions: Array \(A_1, \dots, A_N \ge 0\) (\(N \le 2000\), \(S_A = \sum A_i \le 4 \times 10^6\)), upper bound \(M \le 10^9\), and prime modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7 > S_A + N\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\binom{M + N}{S_A + N} \bmod (10^9 + 7)\).
Time & Space Complexity: Let \(D = S_A + N \le 4,002,000 < 10^9 + 7\). Computing \(\binom{M + N}{D} = \frac{\prod_{j=0}^{D-1} (M + N - j)}{D!} \bmod (10^9 + 7)\) takes \(O(N + \sum A_i)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After \(r\) iterations (\(0 \le r \le D\)), the numerator accumulator holds \((M + N)^{\underline{r}} \bmod p\) and the denominator accumulator holds \(r! \bmod p\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(M < S_A\), then \(M + N < D\) and the product \((M + N)^{\underline{D}}\) contains the factor \(0\), so the answer is \(0\) (return \(0\) immediately); do not precompute factorials up to \(M + N \approx 10^9\)—use the falling-factorial formula of length \(D = S_A + N \le 4 \times 10^6\).









Intermediate 1 (#193) — Luogu P6620: [省选联考 2020 A 卷] 组合数问题

Source: Luogu P6620 — [省选联考 2020 A 卷] 组合数问题
Prerequisite Tags: Ch 06 (§6.4 Stirling Numbers S2, Falling-Factorial Basis Conversion, Division-Free Absorption Identity)
Target Complexity: \(O(m^2 + m \log n)\) time, \(O(m^2)\) (or \(O(m)\)) space


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given positive integers \(n, x, p\) (\(1 \le n, x, p \le 10^9\)) and the coefficients \(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_m\) (\(0 \le a_i \le 10^9\), \(1 \le m \le 10^3\)) of a degree-\(m\) polynomial \(f(k) = \sum_{i=0}^m a_i k^i\). Note that the modulus \(p\) is an arbitrary positive integer and is NOT necessarily prime. Compute: \[\left(\sum_{k=0}^n f(k) x^k \binom{n}{k}\right) \bmod p.\]

Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(n = 3, x = 2, p = 100, m = 2\) with \(f(k) = k^2\) (\(a = [0, 0, 1]\)): directly, \(\sum_{k=0}^3 k^2 2^k \binom{3}{k} = 0 + 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 + 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 + 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 1 = 6 + 48 + 72 = 126 \equiv 26 \pmod{100}\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Look at the three critical features of the problem statement:

\(n \le 10^9\) is huge, while the polynomial degree \(m \le 1000\) is small.
We are summing \(f(k) \binom{n}{k} x^k\) over \(0 \le k \le n\).
The modulus \(p \le 10^9\) is not necessarily prime, so every division (including dividing by \(j!\) to form \(\binom{n}{j}\)) is strictly forbidden! Which tool in Section 6.4 evaluates polynomial-weighted binomial sums with zero divisions?




Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad


Convert each monomial \(k^i = \sum_{j=0}^i \begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix} k^{\underline{j}}\) into the falling-factorial basis using Stirling numbers of the second kind. Because \(\begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix} = \begin{Bmatrix} i-1 \\ j-1 \end{Bmatrix} + j \begin{Bmatrix} i-1 \\ j \end{Bmatrix}\) uses only additions and multiplications, we can precompute \(\begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix} \bmod p\) for \(0 \le j \le i \le m\) in \(O(m^2)\) time!
Then \(f(k) = \sum_{j=0}^m b_j k^{\underline{j}}\) where \(b_j = \sum_{i=j}^m a_i \begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix} \bmod p\).
Apply the Falling-Factorial Absorption Identity \(k^{\underline{j}} \binom{n}{k} = n^{\underline{j}} \binom{n - j}{k - j}\), which holds in \(\mathbb{Z}\) with zero divisions!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

After absorbing \(k^{\underline{j}} \binom{n}{k} = n^{\underline{j}} \binom{n-j}{k-j}\), swap the sums over \(k\) and \(j\), and collapse the inner sum over \(k\) using \(\sum_{k=j}^n \binom{n-j}{k-j} x^k = x^j (1 + x)^{n - j}\). Notice that \(n^{\underline{j}} = n(n-1)\cdots(n-j+1)\) is a product of \(j\) integers and never divides by \(j!\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Division-Free Basis Conversion via \(\begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix}\)
Because \(p\) is not prime, we cannot use NTT or divide by factorials. Instead, recall from Section 6.4 that for every integer \(i \ge 0\), \[k^i = \sum_{j=0}^i \begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix} k^{\underline{j}} \in \mathbb{Z}[k].\] Substituting this into \(f(k) = \sum_{i=0}^m a_i k^i\) and changing the order of summation gives: \[f(k) = \sum_{i=0}^m a_i \sum_{j=0}^i \begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix} k^{\underline{j}} = \sum_{j=0}^m \left(\sum_{i=j}^m a_i \begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix}\right) k^{\underline{j}} = \sum_{j=0}^m b_j k^{\underline{j}},\] where \(b_j = \sum_{i=j}^m a_i \begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix} \bmod p\).


2. Collapsing the Binomial Sum via Absorption
Now substitute \(f(k) = \sum_{j=0}^m b_j k^{\underline{j}}\) into the target sum \(S = \sum_{k=0}^n f(k) x^k \binom{n}{k}\): \[\begin{aligned}
S
&= \sum_{k=0}^n \left(\sum_{j=0}^m b_j k^{\underline{j}}\right) \binom{n}{k} x^k && \text{(expanding }f(k)\text{ in the falling-factorial basis)} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, m)} b_j \sum_{k=j}^n k^{\underline{j}} \binom{n}{k} x^k && \text{(swapping sums; }k^{\underline{j}} = 0\text{ for }k < j\text{)} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, m)} b_j n^{\underline{j}} x^j \sum_{k=j}^n \binom{n - j}{k - j} x^{k - j} && \text{(Absorption Identity }k^{\underline{j}}\binom{n}{k} = n^{\underline{j}}\binom{n-j}{k-j}\text{)} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, m)} b_j n^{\underline{j}} x^j (1 + x)^{n - j} \pmod p. && \text{(Binomial Theorem on }r = k - j \in [0, n - j]\text{)}
\end{aligned}\]


3. Hand-Checkable Trace & Algorithm Contract

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(n = 3, x = 2, p = 100, f(k) = k^2\)):

Since \(k^2 = 1 \cdot k^{\underline{1}} + 1 \cdot k^{\underline{2}}\), we have \((b_0, b_1, b_2) = (0, 1, 1)\).
For \(j = 1\): \(b_1 \cdot 3^{\underline{1}} \cdot 2^1 \cdot (1+2)^{3-1} = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 9 = 54\).
For \(j = 2\): \(b_2 \cdot 3^{\underline{2}} \cdot 2^2 \cdot (1+2)^{3-2} = 1 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 72\).
Total \(S = 54 + 72 = 126 \equiv 26 \pmod{100}\), with zero divisions!

Input & Preconditions: Integers \(n, x, p \in [1, 10^9]\) (\(p\) is an arbitrary positive integer, not necessarily prime) and polynomial coefficients \(a_0, \dots, a_m\) (\(m \le 10^3\)).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\left(\sum_{k=0}^n f(k) x^k \binom{n}{k}\right) \bmod p\) using zero divisions:

Stirling Precomputation: Initialize \(S_2[0][0] = 1 \bmod p\), and for \(i = 1 \dots m\), \(j = 1 \dots i\), compute \(S_2[i][j] = (S_2[i-1][j-1] + j \cdot S_2[i-1][j]) \bmod p\).
Coefficient Transformation: Compute \(b_j = \sum_{i=j}^m a_i S_2[i][j] \bmod p\) for \(0 \le j \le m\).
Final Evaluation: Maintain \(\text{ff}_j = n^{\underline{j}} \bmod p\), \(x^j \bmod p\), and \((1 + x)^{n - j} \bmod p\) for \(0 \le j \le \min(n, m)\).

Time & Space Complexity: \(O(m^2 + \log n)\) time and \(O(m)\) space (using a 1D rolling array for \(S_2\)).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At index \(j \in [0, \min(n, m)]\), \(\text{ff}_j = n(n-1)\cdots(n-j+1) \bmod p\) is maintained purely by multiplication, and \(b_j = [k^{\underline{j}}] f(k) \bmod p\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Because \(p\) is not necessarily prime, never divide by \(j!\) or \((1 + x) \bmod p\) (Failure Mode #4); precompute \((1+x)^{n - \min(n, m)} \bmod p\) once via binary exponentiation and multiply by \((1 + x)\) from \(j = \min(n, m)\) down to \(0\), capping the outer loop at \(\min(n, m)\) so \(n - j \ge 0\) always holds when \(n < m\).









Intermediate 2 (#080) — AtCoder KUPC 2019 K: One or All

Source: AtCoder KUPC 2019 K — One or All
Prerequisite Tags: Ch 06 (§6.3 Projective Möbius / Krawtchouk Transform via Taylor Shift)
Target Complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) time, \(O(N)\) space


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given \(N\) non-negative integers \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{N-1}\) (\(1 \le N \le 10^5\), \(0 \le A_i < 998244353\)), compute for all \(1 \le j \le N\) the Krawtchouk linear combinations \[S_j = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} A_i [x^i] \big((1 + x)^{N - j} (1 - x)^{j - 1}\big) \bmod 998244353.\]

Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(N = 3\) (\(d = 2\)) and \(A = (1, 2, 3)\):

\(j = 1\) (\(k = 0\)): \((1+x)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2 \implies S_1 = 1(1) + 2(2) + 3(1) = 8\).
\(j = 2\) (\(k = 1\)): \((1+x)(1-x) = 1 - x^2 \implies S_2 = 1(1) + 2(0) + 3(-1) = -2 \equiv 998244351\).
\(j = 3\) (\(k = 2\)): \((1-x)^2 = 1 - 2x + x^2 \implies S_3 = 1(1) + 2(-2) + 3(1) = 0\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Look at the basis polynomials \(K_{j-1}(x) = (1 + x)^{N - 1 - (j - 1)} (1 - x)^{j - 1}\) for \(k = j - 1 \in \{0, 1, \dots, N - 1\}\). We want to dualize the inner product \(S_{k+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} A_i [x^i] \big((1 + x)^{N - 1 - k} (1 - x)^k\big)\) for all \(0 \le k \le N - 1\). Notice that \((1 + x)^{N - 1 - k} (1 - x)^k = (1 + x)^{N - 1} \left(\frac{1 - x}{1 + x}\right)^k\) is the exact Projective Möbius / Krawtchouk Transform of Section 6.3!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Let \(d = N - 1\) and let \(M_{k, i} = [x^i] \big((1 + x)^{d - k} (1 - x)^k\big)\) be the Krawtchouk matrix entry. Why can’t we sum \(\sum_{k=0}^d M_{k, i} y^k\) directly into a single power? Because the Binomial Theorem requires a factor of \(\binom{d}{k}\) in front of \((1 + x)^{d - k} (1 - x)^k\)! Once we multiply \(M_{k, i}\) by \(\binom{d}{k}\), the bivariate generating function over \(x\) and \(y\) becomes completely symmetric in \(x\) and \(y\): \[\sum_{k=0}^d \binom{d}{k} M_{k, i} y^k = [x^i] \sum_{k=0}^d \binom{d}{k} (1 + x)^{d - k} \big(y(1 - x)\big)^k = [x^i] \big((1 + x) + y(1 - x)\big)^d = [x^i] \big((1 + y) + x(1 - y)\big)^d = \binom{d}{i} (1 + y)^{d - i} (1 - y)^i.\] Extracting \([y^k]\) from both sides yields the Krawtchouk Reciprocity Identity: \[\binom{d}{k} [x^i] \big((1 + x)^{d - k} (1 - x)^k\big) = \binom{d}{i} [y^k] \big((1 + y)^{d - i} (1 - y)^i\big).\]



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

By the Krawtchouk reciprocity identity \(\binom{d}{k} M_{k, i} = \binom{d}{i} M_{i, k}\), our target sum \(S_{k+1} = \sum_{i=0}^d A_i M_{k, i}\) becomes \[S_{k+1} = \frac{1}{\binom{d}{k}} \sum_{i=0}^d A_i \binom{d}{i} M_{i, k} = \frac{1}{\binom{d}{k}} [y^k] \sum_{i=0}^d \left(A_i \binom{d}{i}\right) (1 + y)^{d - i} (1 - y)^i = \frac{1}{\binom{d}{k}} [y^k] (1 + y)^d F\!\left(\frac{1 - y}{1 + y}\right),\] where \(F(z) = \sum_{i=0}^d A_i \binom{d}{i} z^i\)! And \((1 + y)^d F\!\left(\frac{1 - y}{1 + y}\right)\) is computed in \(O(N \log N)\) time using just 2 Taylor shifts via the Bruhat decomposition of Section 6.3!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Reverse-Engineering the Krawtchouk Reciprocity Identity
Let \(d = N - 1\) and \(k = j - 1 \in \{0, 1, \dots, d\}\). We need to compute, for every \(0 \le k \le d\), \[S_{k+1} = \sum_{i=0}^d A_i [x^i] \big((1 + x)^{d - k} (1 - x)^k\big).\] In this raw form, \(i\) is the extracted exponent \([x^i]\) while \(k\) is in the power \((1 + x)^{d-k}(1 - x)^k\). To swap the roles of \(i\) and \(k\), consider the bivariate generating function \[\Phi(x, y) = \big((1 + x) + y(1 - x)\big)^d = \big((1 + y) + x(1 - y)\big)^d.\]

Expanding the left-hand side in powers of \(y\) via the Binomial Theorem gives: \[[x^i y^k] \Phi(x, y) = \binom{d}{k} [x^i] \big((1 + x)^{d - k} (1 - x)^k\big).\]
Expanding the right-hand side in powers of \(x\) via the Binomial Theorem gives: \[[x^i y^k] \Phi(x, y) = \binom{d}{i} [y^k] \big((1 + y)^{d - i} (1 - y)^i\big).\] Equating the two expressions proves Krawtchouk Reciprocity: \[[x^i] \big((1 + x)^{d - k} (1 - x)^k\big) = \frac{\binom{d}{i}}{\binom{d}{k}} [y^k] \big((1 + y)^{d - i} (1 - y)^i\big).\]



2. Reducing All \(S_{k+1}\) to a Single Projective Möbius Transform
Define the scaled polynomial \(F(z) = \sum_{i=0}^d f_i z^i\) with \(f_i = A_i \binom{d}{i} \bmod 998244353\). Substituting Krawtchouk Reciprocity into \(S_{k+1}\) pulls \([y^k]\) outside the sum over \(i\): \[\begin{aligned}
S_{k+1}
&= \frac{1}{\binom{d}{k}} [y^k] \sum_{i=0}^d f_i (1 + y)^{d - i} (1 - y)^i \\
&= \frac{1}{\binom{d}{k}} [y^k] \left((1 + y)^d F\!\left(\frac{1 - y}{1 + y}\right)\right).
\end{aligned}\] Now apply the 4-Step Bruhat Decomposition from Section 6.3 to \(\frac{1 - y}{1 + y} = -1 + \frac{2}{1 + y}\):

Taylor Shift by \(c = -1\): Compute \(F_1(u) = F(u - 1)\) using poly_taylor_shift(F, -1) in 1 NTT.
Scale by \(2\) and Reverse: Form \(F_2(v) = v^d F_1(2/v) = \sum_{i=0}^d \big([u^i]F_1(u) \cdot 2^i\big) v^{d - i}\) in \(O(d)\) time.
Taylor Shift by \(c = 1\): Substitute \(v = 1 + y\) by computing \(F_3(y) = F_2(y + 1)\) using poly_taylor_shift(F_2, 1) in 1 NTT.
Extract and Unscale: For each \(0 \le k \le d\), \(S_{k+1} = \binom{d}{k}^{-1} [y^k] F_3(y) \bmod 998244353\).



3. Hand-Checkable Trace & Algorithm Contract

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 3, d = 2, A = (1, 2, 3)\)):

Scale \(f_i = A_i \binom{2}{i}\): \(F(z) = 1\binom{2}{0} + 2\binom{2}{1}z + 3\binom{2}{2}z^2 = 1 + 4z + 3z^2\).
Step 1 (\(F_1(u) = F(u - 1)\)): \(1 + 4(u-1) + 3(u-1)^2 = 0 - 2u + 3u^2\).
Step 2 (\(F_2(v) = v^2 F_1(2/v)\)): \(0\cdot v^2 + (-2 \cdot 2)v + (3 \cdot 4) = 12 - 4v + 0v^2\).
Step 3 (\(F_3(y) = F_2(y + 1)\)): \(12 - 4(y + 1) = 8 - 4y + 0y^2\).
Step 4 (Divide by \(\binom{2}{k}\)): \((S_1, S_2, S_3) = (8/1, -4/2, 0/1) = (8, -2, 0)\). Exact match!

Input & Preconditions: Array \(A_0, \dots, A_{N-1} \in \mathbb{F}_p\) (\(N \le 10^5\), \(p = 998244353 > N\) so \(0!, \dots, (N-1)!\) are invertible).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(S_1, \dots, S_N \bmod 998244353\), where \(S_{k+1} = \binom{d}{k}^{-1} [y^k] (1+y)^d F\!\left(\frac{1-y}{1+y}\right)\) for \(d = N - 1\) and \(0 \le k \le d\).
Time & Space Complexity: Computing \(F_3(y) = (1 + y)^d F\!\left(\frac{1 - y}{1 + y}\right)\) requires 2 NTTs of size \(2N\), running in \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After the 4-step Bruhat decomposition (poly_taylor_shift(F, -1), power-of-2 scaling + coefficient reversal, and poly_taylor_shift(F_2, 1)), \([y^k] F_3(y) = \binom{d}{k} S_{k+1} \bmod p\) for every \(0 \le k \le d\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: When reversing \(F_1(u)\) to form \(F_2(v) = v^d F_1(2/v)\), always pad \(F_1\) to exact length \(d + 1 = N\) before reversing so trailing zero high-degree coefficients are not dropped; for \(N = 1\) (\(d = 0\)), return \(S_1 = A_0 \bmod p\) directly.









Advanced 1 (#094) — Codeforces 923E: Perpetual Subtraction

Source: Codeforces 923E — Perpetual Subtraction
Prerequisite Tags: Ch 06 (§6.3 Polynomial Taylor Shift F(x \pm 1), Eigenbasis Diagonalization of Upper-Triangular Transition Matrices)
Target Complexity: \(O(N \log N + N \log M)\) time, \(O(N)\) space


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given an integer \(N \le 10^5\), a step count \(M \le 10^{18}\), and an initial probability distribution \(p_0, p_1, \dots, p_N\) over \(\{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) (given modulo \(998244353\)). Initially, a random integer \(x\) is chosen with \(\Pr[x = i] = p_i\). Then the following operation is repeated \(M\) times independently:

Replace \(x\) with an integer chosen uniformly at random from \(\{0, 1, \dots, x\}\).

Compute the final probability distribution \(p_0^{(M)}, p_1^{(M)}, \dots, p_N^{(M)}\) modulo \(998244353\) after \(M\) steps.

Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(N = 2, M = 1\), and \(P_0 = (0, 0, 1)\) (starts at \(x = 2\) with probability \(1\)): after \(M = 1\) step, \(x\) is uniform on \(\{0, 1, 2\}\), so \(P_1 = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)\). Via the eigenbasis \(y = x - 1\): \(P_0(x) = x^2 = (y + 1)^2 = 1 + 2y + y^2\), scaling by \((k+1)^{-1}\) gives \(Q_1(y) = 1 + \frac{2}{2}y + \frac{1}{3}y^2 = 1 + y + \frac{1}{3}y^2\), and shifting back \(y = x - 1\) gives \(P_1(x) = 1 + (x - 1) + \frac{1}{3}(x - 1)^2 = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3}x + \frac{1}{3}x^2\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

In a single step, if the current state is \(j \in \{0, \dots, N\}\), it transitions to each \(i \in \{0, \dots, j\}\) with probability \(\frac{1}{j + 1}\): \[p_i^{(t+1)} = \sum_{j=i}^N \frac{p_j^{(t)}}{j + 1}.\] Because \(M \le 10^{18}\) is huge, we cannot apply this transition \(M\) times directly. Instead, form the probability generating function \(P_t(x) = \sum_{i=0}^N p_i^{(t)} x^i\). How does the linear operator \(\mathcal{L}: P_t(x) \mapsto P_{t+1}(x)\) act on a polynomial \(P(x)\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Write out \(\mathcal{L}(x^j) = \frac{1}{j+1} \sum_{i=0}^j x^i = \frac{1}{j+1} \frac{x^{j+1} - 1}{x - 1} = \frac{1}{x - 1} \int_1^x t^j\, dt\). What is the eigenbasis of the operator \(\mathcal{L}\)? Instead of monomials \(x^j\), test the shifted monomials \((x - 1)^k\) around \(x = 1\): \[\mathcal{L}\big((x - 1)^k\big) = \frac{1}{x - 1} \int_1^x (t - 1)^k\, dt = \frac{1}{x - 1} \cdot \frac{(x - 1)^{k+1}}{k + 1} = \frac{1}{k + 1} (x - 1)^k.\] Every shifted monomial \((x - 1)^k\) is an exact eigenvector of \(\mathcal{L}\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda_k = \frac{1}{k + 1}\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

This gives a 3-step algorithm for any \(M \le 10^{18}\):

Change to Eigenbasis (\(x = y + 1\), Taylor Shift by \(+1\)): Compute \(Q_0(y) = P_0(y + 1) = \sum_{k=0}^N q_k^{(0)} y^k\) via poly_taylor_shift(P_0, +1) in 1 NTT.
Apply \(M\) Steps in \(O(N \log M)\): Since \(y^k = (x - 1)^k\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\frac{1}{k + 1}\), after \(M\) steps \(q_k^{(M)} = q_k^{(0)} \cdot (k + 1)^{-M} \bmod 998244353\).
Return to Monomial Basis (\(y = x - 1\), Taylor Shift by \(-1\)): Compute \(P_M(x) = Q_M(x - 1)\) via poly_taylor_shift(Q_M, -1) in 1 NTT!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Reverse-Engineering the Operator \(\mathcal{L}\) on \(K[x]\)
Let \(P_t(x) = \sum_{i=0}^N p_i^{(t)} x^i\). A single step of the Markov chain maps \(P_t(x)\) to: \[\begin{aligned}
(\mathcal{L} P_t)(x)
&= \sum_{i=0}^N x^i \sum_{j=i}^N \frac{p_j^{(t)}}{j + 1} && \text{(definition of single-step transition)} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^N \frac{p_j^{(t)}}{j + 1} \sum_{i=0}^j x^i && \text{(swapping }\sum_i\text{ and }\sum_j\text{)} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^N p_j^{(t)} \frac{x^{j+1} - 1}{(j + 1)(x - 1)} && \text{(summing geometric series }\sum_{i=0}^j x^i\text{)} \\
&= \frac{1}{x - 1} \int_1^x P_t(u)\, du. && \text{(recognizing }\int_1^x u^j du = \frac{x^{j+1}-1}{j+1}\text{)}
\end{aligned}\] Why does \(\int_1^x\) have lower limit \(1\)? Because at \(x = 1\), total probability is conserved. This lower limit \(u = 1\) is our Diagnostic Signal to expand \(P_t(u)\) around \(u = 1\) in powers of \(y = u - 1\)!


2. Diagonalizing \(\mathcal{L}\) via Taylor Shift
Substitute \(u = 1 + y\) (so \(x = 1 + y\) and \(P_t(x) = P_t(1 + y) =: Q_t(y) = \sum_{k=0}^N q_k^{(t)} y^k\)). Then: \[(\mathcal{L} P_t)(1 + y) = \frac{1}{y} \int_0^y Q_t(v)\, dv = \frac{1}{y} \sum_{k=0}^N q_k^{(t)} \frac{y^{k+1}}{k + 1} = \sum_{k=0}^N \left(\frac{q_k^{(t)}}{k + 1}\right) y^k.\] In the \(y\)-basis (\(y = x - 1\)), the entire upper-triangular transition matrix becomes diagonal: \[q_k^{(t+1)} = \frac{q_k^{(t)}}{k + 1} \implies q_k^{(M)} = \frac{q_k^{(0)}}{(k + 1)^M} \qquad (0 \le k \le N).\] Equivalently, in matrix language, let \(B_{i, r} = \binom{r}{i}\) be the Pascal matrix (Taylor shift by \(+1\), mapping \(p \mapsto q = B p\)) and \(B^{-1}_{r, j} = (-1)^{r-j}\binom{r}{j}\) be its inverse (Taylor shift by \(-1\)). For the single-step transition matrix \(M_{r, j} = \frac{1}{j + 1}\) (\(0 \le r \le j\)), the Hockey-Stick identity \(\sum_{r=i}^j \binom{r}{i} = \binom{j+1}{i+1}\) and Absorption identity \(\frac{1}{j+1}\binom{j+1}{i+1} = \frac{1}{i+1}\binom{j}{i}\) immediately verify that every entry \((B M)_{i, j}\) for \(0 \le i \le j\) satisfies: \[(B M)_{i, j} = \sum_{r=i}^j \binom{r}{i} \frac{1}{j + 1} = \frac{1}{j + 1} \binom{j + 1}{i + 1} = \frac{1}{i + 1} \binom{j}{i} = (\Lambda B)_{i, j},\] where \(\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}\!\left(1, \frac{1}{2}, \dots, \frac{1}{N+1}\right)\), confirming \(B M = \Lambda B \iff M = B^{-1} \Lambda B\)!


3. Hand-Checkable Trace & Algorithm Contract

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 2, M = 2, P_0(x) = x^2\)):

\(Q_0(y) = P_0(y + 1) = 1 + 2y + y^2\).
After \(M = 2\) steps, divide \([y^k]\) by \((k+1)^2\): \(Q_2(y) = 1 + \frac{2}{4}y + \frac{1}{9}y^2 = 1 + \frac{1}{2}y + \frac{1}{9}y^2\).
Shift back \(P_2(x) = Q_2(x - 1) = 1 + \frac{1}{2}(x - 1) + \frac{1}{9}(x^2 - 2x + 1) = \frac{11}{18} + \frac{5}{18}x + \frac{2}{18}x^2\).

Input & Preconditions: Initial distribution array \(P_0 = [p_0, \dots, p_N] \in \mathbb{F}_p^{N+1}\) (\(N \le 10^5\)), step count \(M \le 10^{18}\), and prime \(p = 998244353 > N + 1\) so \(1, \dots, N + 1\) are invertible.
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(P_M = [p_0^{(M)}, \dots, p_N^{(M)}] \bmod 998244353\) via 3 steps:

Forward Taylor Shift (\(c = +1\)): Compute \(Q_0 = \text{poly\_taylor\_shift}(P_0, 1)\) in 1 NTT: \[q_k^{(0)} = \frac{1}{k!} \sum_{j=k}^N (j!\, p_j) \frac{1^{j-k}}{(j - k)!}.\]
Diagonal Eigenvalue Scaling (\(M\) steps): For each \(0 \le k \le N\), set \(q_k^{(M)} = q_k^{(0)} \cdot ((k + 1)^{-1})^{M \bmod (p - 1)} \bmod 998244353\).
Inverse Taylor Shift (\(c = -1\)): Compute \(P_M = \text{poly\_taylor\_shift}(Q_M, -1)\) in 1 NTT: \[p_i^{(M)} = \frac{1}{i!} \sum_{k=i}^N \big(k!\, q_k^{(M)}\big) \frac{(-1)^{k-i}}{(k - i)!}.\]

Time & Space Complexity: 2 NTTs of size \(2N\), taking \(O(N \log N + N \log p)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: In the shifted eigenbasis \(y = x - 1\), each mode \(q_k^{(t)} = [y^k] P_t(y + 1)\) evolves independently as \(q_k^{(t)} = q_k^{(0)} (k + 1)^{-t} \bmod p\), preserving total probability \(q_0^{(t)} = P_t(1) = \sum_{i=0}^N p_i^{(t)}\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: When \(M = 0\), \((k + 1)^{-0} = 1\) and the composition of \(+1\) and \(-1\) Taylor shifts returns \(P_0\) unchanged; reduce the exponent \(M \bmod (p - 1)\) by Fermat’s Little Theorem (since \(1 \le k + 1 \le N + 1 < p\) is nonzero modulo \(p\)).









Advanced 2 (#096) — Codeforces 960G: Bandit Blues

Source: Codeforces 960G — Bandit Blues
Prerequisite Tags: Ch 04 (Cycle EGF ln(1/(1-x))), Ch 06 (§6.4 Unsigned Stirling S1, Rényi–Foata Bijection, Doubling + Taylor Shift)
Target Complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) time, \(O(N)\) space


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given three integers \(n, A, B\) (\(1 \le n \le 10^5\), \(0 \le A, B \le n\)), count the number of permutations \(p = (p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n)\) of \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) that have exactly \(A\) prefix maxima (indices \(i\) where \(p_i = \max_{1 \le j \le i} p_j\)) and exactly \(B\) suffix maxima (indices \(i\) where \(p_i = \max_{i \le j \le n} p_j\)). Output the answer modulo \(998244353\).

Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(n = 3, A = 2, B = 2\): the formula gives \(\binom{A+B-2}{A-1}\begin{bmatrix} n-1 \\ A+B-2 \end{bmatrix} = \binom{2}{1}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = 2 \times 1 = 2\). Indeed, among the \(6\) permutations of \(\{1, 2, 3\}\), the \(2\) valid permutations with \(2\) prefix maxima and \(2\) suffix maxima are \((1, 3, 2)\) and \((2, 3, 1)\) (where \(3\) is in the middle).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Where is the global maximum element \(n\) located in the permutation? Wherever \(n\) stands, \(n\) is simultaneously the last prefix maximum (since nothing after \(n\) can exceed \(n\)) and the first suffix maximum (since nothing before \(n\) can exceed \(n\)). Thus the elements to the left of \(n\) must form \(A - 1\) prefix maxima, and the elements to the right of \(n\) must form \(B - 1\) suffix maxima (equivalently, \(B - 1\) prefix maxima when read right-to-left). By the Rényi–Foata Bijection (Section 6.4), which sequence counts permutations of \(m\) elements with \(k\) prefix maxima?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By the Rényi–Foata Bijection, the number of permutations of \(m\) distinct elements with \(k\) prefix maxima is the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind \(\begin{bmatrix} m \\ k \end{bmatrix}\)! If \(i\) elements lie to the left of \(n\) and \(n - 1 - i\) elements lie to the right of \(n\), we get \[\text{Ans} = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \binom{n - 1}{i} \begin{bmatrix} i \\ A - 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} n - 1 - i \\ B - 1 \end{bmatrix}.\] Can we collapse this sum over \(i\) into a single Stirling number without even convolving two columns? Look at what \(\begin{bmatrix} i \\ A - 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\begin{bmatrix} n - 1 - i \\ B - 1 \end{bmatrix}\) count in terms of disjoint cycles (or their EGF \(\frac{1}{k!}\left(\ln\frac{1}{1-x}\right)^k\))!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Partitioning \(n - 1\) elements into \(A - 1\) left cycles and \(B - 1\) right cycles is identical to partitioning all \(n - 1\) elements into \((A - 1) + (B - 1) = A + B - 2\) cycles first (\(\begin{bmatrix} n - 1 \\ A + B - 2 \end{bmatrix}\) ways) and then choosing which \(A - 1\) of those cycles go to the left of \(n\) (\(\binom{A + B - 2}{A - 1}\) ways)! Thus \(\text{Ans} = \binom{A + B - 2}{A - 1} \begin{bmatrix} n - 1 \\ A + B - 2 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(\begin{bmatrix} n - 1 \\ A + B - 2 \end{bmatrix} = [x^{A+B-2}] x^{\overline{n-1}}\) is computed in \(O(n \log n)\) time via stirling_1st_row (Doubling + Taylor Shift)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Decomposition Around the Global Maximum \(n\)
First handle boundary cases: if \(A = 0\) or \(B = 0\) or \(A + B - 2 > n - 1\) or \(A + B - 2 < 0\), the answer is \(0\) (since \(n\) itself contributes \(1\) to both \(A\) and \(B\), and each of the remaining \(n - 1\) elements can contribute to at most one of \(A\) or \(B\)). If \(n = 1\), the answer is \(1\) if \(A = 1, B = 1\) and \(0\) otherwise.
Now assume \(n \ge 2\) and \(A, B \ge 1\). Suppose the global maximum \(n\) stands at position \(i + 1\) (\(0 \le i \le n - 1\)).

Any prefix maximum after position \(i + 1\) would have to exceed \(n\), which is impossible. Thus the \(A\) prefix maxima consist of \(A - 1\) prefix maxima among the \(i\) elements to the left of \(n\), plus \(n\) itself.
Symmetrically, the \(B\) suffix maxima consist of \(n\) itself, plus \(B - 1\) suffix maxima among the \(n - 1 - i\) elements to the right of \(n\).
Choosing which \(i\) elements of \(\{1, \dots, n - 1\}\) go to the left of \(n\) takes \(\binom{n - 1}{i}\) ways. By the Rényi–Foata bijection (Section 6.4), the number of permutations of an \(m\)-element set with \(k\) prefix maxima (or \(k\) suffix maxima, by reversing the sequence) is \(\begin{bmatrix} m \\ k \end{bmatrix}\). Hence: \[\text{Ans} = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \binom{n - 1}{i} \begin{bmatrix} i \\ A - 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} n - 1 - i \\ B - 1 \end{bmatrix}.\]



2. Collapsing the Binomial Convolution of Stirling Columns
We can prove the identity \[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \binom{n - 1}{i} \begin{bmatrix} i \\ A - 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} n - 1 - i \\ B - 1 \end{bmatrix} = \binom{A + B - 2}{A - 1} \begin{bmatrix} n - 1 \\ A + B - 2 \end{bmatrix}\] in two complementary ways:

Combinatorial Proof: By the Rényi–Foata correspondence, each record-block between consecutive prefix maxima (and suffix maxima) is a directed cycle rooted at its maximum element. Partitioning \(\{1, \dots, n - 1\}\) into an ordered pair of a left set with \(A - 1\) cycles and a right set with \(B - 1\) cycles is bijectively equivalent to partitioning \(\{1, \dots, n - 1\}\) into \(A + B - 2\) unordered cycles (\(\begin{bmatrix} n - 1 \\ A + B - 2 \end{bmatrix}\) ways) and then selecting which \(A - 1\) of those cycles belong to the left side (\(\binom{A + B - 2}{A - 1}\) ways).
One-Line EGF Proof: By Regime 4 of Section 6.4, the column EGF of \(\begin{bmatrix} m \\ k \end{bmatrix}\) is \(\sum_{m \ge 0} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ k \end{bmatrix} \frac{x^m}{m!} = \frac{1}{k!}\left(\ln\frac{1}{1-x}\right)^k\). Therefore, the binomial convolution of column \(A - 1\) and column \(B - 1\) is: \[\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \binom{n-1}{i} \begin{bmatrix} i \\ A-1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} n-1-i \\ B-1 \end{bmatrix}
&= (n - 1)! [x^{n-1}] \left( \frac{\left(\ln\frac{1}{1-x}\right)^{A-1}}{(A - 1)!} \cdot \frac{\left(\ln\frac{1}{1-x}\right)^{B-1}}{(B - 1)!} \right) \\
&= \frac{(A + B - 2)!}{(A - 1)!(B - 1)!} \cdot (n - 1)! [x^{n-1}] \frac{\left(\ln\frac{1}{1-x}\right)^{A+B-2}}{(A + B - 2)!} \\
&= \binom{A + B - 2}{A - 1} \begin{bmatrix} n - 1 \\ A + B - 2 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}\]



3. Hand-Checkable Trace & Algorithm Contract

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(n = 4, A = 2, B = 2\)):

We need \(\binom{2}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
Expanding \(x^{\overline{3}} = x(x+1)(x+2) = x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x\) gives \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = [x^2] x^{\overline{3}} = 3\).
Thus \(\text{Ans} = 2 \times 3 = 6\).

Input & Preconditions: Integers \(n \le 10^5\), \(0 \le A, B \le n\), and prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > n\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\binom{A + B - 2}{A - 1} \begin{bmatrix} n - 1 \\ A + B - 2 \end{bmatrix} \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: Compute \(P_{n-1}(x) = x^{\overline{n-1}} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \begin{bmatrix} n - 1 \\ k \end{bmatrix} x^k\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time via the recursive doubling relation \(P_{2m}(x) = P_m(x) P_m(x + m)\) (poly_taylor_shift, Regime 3 of §6.4), or in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time via a D&C product tree \(\prod_{j=0}^{n-2}(x + j)\); space complexity is \(O(n)\).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At each doubling step from degree \(m\) to \(2m\) (plus a linear factor \((x + 2m)\) when odd), \(P_m(x) = x(x+1)\cdots(x+m-1) \bmod p\) holds identically in \(\mathbb{F}_p[x]\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(A = 0\) or \(B = 0\) or \(A + B - 2 > n - 1\) or \(A + B - 2 < 0\), return \(0\) immediately (do not index \([x^{A+B-2}]P_{n-1}(x)\) out of bounds!); when \(n = 1\), return \(1\) if \(A = 1, B = 1\) and \(0\) otherwise.









Mastery 1 (#098) — Codeforces 995F: Cowmpany Cowmpensation

Source: Codeforces 995F — Cowmpany Cowmpensation
Prerequisite Tags: Ch 06 (§6.4 O(d) Consecutive-Grid Lagrange Interpolation, Polynomial Degree Bound of Prefix-Sum Tree DP, Falling-Factorial Decomposition)
Target Complexity: \(O(N^2)\) time, \(O(N^2)\) space


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
A company hierarchy is a rooted tree of \(N\) employees (\(1 \le N \le 3000\)), rooted at employee \(1\). You must assign each employee \(u\) an integer salary \(s_u \in \{1, 2, \dots, D\}\) (\(1 \le D \le 10^9\)) such that for every employee \(u \neq 1\), \(s_u \le s_{\text{parent}(u)}\). Count the number of valid salary assignments modulo \(10^9 + 7\).

Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(N = 3\) where root \(1\) has two leaf children \(2\) and \(3\), and \(D = 2\):

Leaves \(u \in \{2, 3\}\) have \(\text{dp}[u][y] = y\).
Root \(1\) has \(\text{dp}[1][x] = \sum_{y=1}^x y^2 = \frac{x(x+1)(2x+1)}{6}\), a degree-\(3\) polynomial!
At \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3\), \(\text{dp}[1][x] = (0, 1, 5, 14)\); at \(D = 2\), \(\text{dp}[1][2] = 5\) (specifically: \(s_1 = 1 \implies (1,1,1)\); \(s_1 = 2 \implies (2, 1\text{ or }2, 1\text{ or }2)\) giving \(1 + 4 = 5\)).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(\text{dp}[u][x]\) be the number of valid salary assignments in the subtree of \(u\) when all salaries in \(u\)’s subtree are chosen from \(\{1, 2, \dots, x\}\) (i.e., \(s_u \le x\)). If \(u\) is assigned salary \(y \in \{1, \dots, x\}\), each child \(v\) of \(u\) independently has \(\text{dp}[v][y]\) valid subtree assignments. Thus: \[\text{dp}[u][x] = \sum_{y=1}^x \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \text{dp}[v][y], \qquad \text{dp}[u][0] = 0.\] Why can we evaluate \(\text{dp}[1][D]\) when \(D \le 10^9\) is huge and \(N \le 3000\) is small? What kind of function of \(x\) is \(\text{dp}[u][x]\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Prove by structural induction on the tree that for every vertex \(u\) with subtree size \(\text{sz}(u)\), \(\text{dp}[u][x]\) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(\text{sz}(u)\)!

Base case (leaf \(u\), \(\text{sz}(u) = 1\)): \(\text{dp}[u][x] = \sum_{y=1}^x 1 = x\), which is a polynomial of degree \(1 = \text{sz}(u)\).
Inductive step: Multiplying polynomials across children \(v \in \text{child}(u)\) adds their degrees: \(\deg\left(\prod_v \text{dp}[v][y]\right) = \sum_v \text{sz}(v) = \text{sz}(u) - 1\). And by Faulhaber’s theorem / finite calculus (\(\Delta_x \text{dp}[u][x] = \prod_v \text{dp}[v][x]\)), taking the prefix sum \(\sum_{y=1}^x\) increases the polynomial degree by exactly \(1\), to \((\text{sz}(u) - 1) + 1 = \text{sz}(u)\)!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Since \(\text{dp}[1][x]\) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(N\), it is uniquely determined by its \(N + 1\) consecutive values at \(x = 0, 1, 2, \dots, N\)!

Run the tree DP only for \(x \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) in \(O(N^2)\) time.
Call eval_consecutive_lagrange(dp[1][0..N], D) from Section 6.4 to evaluate \(\text{dp}[1][D] \bmod (10^9 + 7)\) in \(O(N)\) time! (Bonus Alternative View: Why is \(\text{dp}[1][x]\) a degree-\(N\) polynomial combinatorially? Because any valid assignment uses \(k \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) distinct salary values, chosen in \(\binom{x}{k}\) ways!)








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Polynomial Degree Proof via Finite Calculus & Falling Factorials
We give two complementary proofs that \(P_u(x) := \text{dp}[u][x]\) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(\text{sz}(u)\):

Proof A (Finite Difference / Faulhaber Induction): In the falling-factorial basis, any polynomial \(Q(y) = \sum_{k=0}^d c_k (y - 1)^{\underline{k}}\) of degree \(d\) satisfies \[\sum_{y=1}^x Q(y) = \sum_{k=0}^d c_k k! \sum_{y=1}^x \binom{y - 1}{k} = \sum_{k=0}^d c_k k! \binom{x}{k + 1} = \sum_{k=0}^d \frac{c_k}{k + 1} x^{\underline{k+1}},\] which is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(d + 1\) with constant term \(0\) at \(x = 0\). By induction on the tree:

For each child \(v\) of \(u\), \(P_v(y)\) is a polynomial of degree \(\text{sz}(v)\).
Their pointwise product \(Q_u(y) = \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} P_v(y)\) is a polynomial in \(y\) of degree \(\sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \text{sz}(v) = \text{sz}(u) - 1\).
Therefore, \(P_u(x) = \sum_{y=1}^x Q_u(y)\) (with \(P_u(0) = 0\)) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \((\text{sz}(u) - 1) + 1 = \text{sz}(u)\).

Proof B (Combinatorial Order-Compression Bijection in the Binomial Basis): In any valid salary assignment to the \(N\) employees of the tree using salaries from \(\{1, 2, \dots, x\}\), let \(k \in \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\) be the number of distinct salary values that actually appear.

Let \(c_k\) be the number of valid relative salary assignments onto all of \(\{1, 2, \dots, k\}\) (surjective onto \(\{1, \dots, k\}\)).
For any \(x \ge 0\), every valid assignment in \(\{1, \dots, x\}\) is uniquely obtained by choosing \(k\) distinct values from \(\{1, \dots, x\}\) in \(\binom{x}{k}\) ways and mapping them in order-preserving fashion to a surjective assignment on \(\{1, \dots, k\}\) in \(c_k\) ways: \[\text{dp}[1][x] = \sum_{k=1}^N c_k \binom{x}{k} = \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{c_k}{k!} x^{\underline{k}},\] which is manifestly a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(N\)!




2. \(O(N^2)\) Tree DP + \(O(N)\) Consecutive Lagrange Interpolation

Traverse the tree in post-order (from \(u = N\) down to \(1\) if parent indices \(< u\), or via DFS):

Initialize \(Q_u[y] = 1\) for \(1 \le y \le N\).
For each child \(v\) of \(u\) and each \(y \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), set \(Q_u[y] \gets Q_u[y] \cdot \text{dp}[v][y] \bmod (10^9 + 7)\).
Set \(\text{dp}[u][0] = 0\), and for \(x = 1 \dots N\), compute the prefix sum \(\text{dp}[u][x] = (\text{dp}[u][x-1] + Q_u[x]) \bmod (10^9 + 7)\).

Once \(\text{dp}[1][0], \text{dp}[1][1], \dots, \text{dp}[1][N]\) are computed, invoke eval_consecutive_lagrange(dp[1][0..N], D) (Section 6.4): \[\text{dp}[1][D] = \sum_{i=0}^N (-1)^{N - i}\, \text{dp}[1][i] \cdot \frac{\prod_{0 \le j \le N, j \neq i} (D - j)}{i!\, (N - i)!} \bmod (10^9 + 7).\]



3. Hand-Checkable Trace & Algorithm Contract

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 3\), root \(1\) with leaves \(2, 3\), \(D = 4\)):

From the tree DP at \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3\), \(Y = [\text{dp}[1][0 \dots 3]] = [0, 1, 5, 14]\).
Lagrange interpolation at \(D = 4\): \[\text{dp}[1][4] = 0 + (-1)^2 \cdot 1 \cdot \frac{4 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}{1! 2!} + (-1)^1 \cdot 5 \cdot \frac{4 \cdot 3 \cdot 1}{2! 1!} + (-1)^0 \cdot 14 \cdot \frac{4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2}{3! 0!} = 4 - 30 + 56 = 30 = 1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2.\]

Input & Preconditions: Rooted tree of \(N \le 3000\) vertices, salary bound \(D \le 10^9\), and prime modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7 > N\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\text{dp}[1][D] \bmod (10^9 + 7)\) via eval_consecutive_lagrange(dp[1][0..N], D).
Time & Space Complexity:

Tree DP: Each tree edge \((u, v)\) performs \(N\) multiplications, and each vertex \(u\) performs \(N\) additions, totaling \(O(N^2)\) time and \(O(N^2)\) space.
Lagrange Evaluation: Prefix and suffix products of \((D - j)\) and inverse factorials up to \(N \le 3000 < 10^9 + 7\) run in \(O(N)\) time. Total complexity: \(O(N^2)\) time and \(O(N^2)\) space.

Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At every vertex \(u\), \(\text{dp}[u][x]\) is the evaluation at \(x \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) of a polynomial \(P_u(x)\) of degree \(\text{sz}(u)\) satisfying \(P_u(0) = 0\) and \(P_u(x) - P_u(x-1) = \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} P_v(x)\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(D \le N\), return \(\text{dp}[1][D]\) directly from the DP table in \(O(1)\) time (or use prefix/suffix products \(\text{pref}[i]\cdot\text{suff}[i]\) rather than dividing a total product by \(D - i\), avoiding division by zero when \(D \in \{0, \dots, N\}\)).









Mastery 2 (#109) — Codeforces 1278F: Cards

Source: Codeforces 1278F — Cards
Prerequisite Tags: Ch 06 (§6.4 Stirling Numbers S2, 1-NTT Row Generation, Falling-Factorial Binomial Moment Collapse)
Target Complexity: \(O(k \log k)\) time (or \(O(k^2)\) for \(k \le 5000\)), \(O(k)\) space


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
A deck of \(m\) cards contains \(1\) Joker and \(m - 1\) ordinary cards. You perform the following experiment \(n\) times independently (\(1 \le n, m < 998244353\)): shuffle the deck uniformly at random and look at the top card. Let \(X\) be the total number of times the top card is the Joker across the \(n\) rounds. Given \(k\) (\(1 \le k \le 5000\) in the original problem, and up to \(k \le 2 \times 10^5\) in the NTT version), compute the expected value \(\mathbb{E}[X^k] \bmod 998244353\).

Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(n = 3, m = 2\) (\(p = 1/2\)), \(k = 2\): \(X \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(3, 1/2)\) has \(\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \operatorname{Var}(X) + (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 = \frac{3}{4} + \frac{9}{4} = 3\). Using Stirling numbers \(\begin{Bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{Bmatrix} = 1, \begin{Bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{Bmatrix} = 1\): \(\sum_{j=1}^2 \begin{Bmatrix} 2 \\ j \end{Bmatrix} 3^{\underline{j}} (1/2)^j = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 1 \cdot 6 \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{2} = 3\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

In each of the \(n\) independent rounds, the top card is the Joker with probability \(p = \frac{1}{m}\) and an ordinary card with probability \(q = 1 - p = \frac{m - 1}{m}\). Thus \(X \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n, p)\), and we want the \(k\)-th raw moment of a Binomial random variable: \[\mathbb{E}[X^k] = \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i} p^i (1 - p)^{n - i} i^k \bmod 998244353.\] Here \(n \le 998244352\) is huge while \(k\) is the degree of the monomial \(i^k\). How do we collapse \(\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i} p^i (1 - p)^{n - i} i^k\) from \(n\) terms down to \(k\) terms?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Never compute raw moments \(\mathbb{E}[X^k]\) of a Binomial distribution directly in the monomial basis \(i^k\)! Instead, compute the falling-factorial moments \(\mathbb{E}[X^{\underline{j}}]\) first, using the Absorption Identity \(i^{\underline{j}}\binom{n}{i} = n^{\underline{j}}\binom{n-j}{i-j}\): \[\mathbb{E}[X^{\underline{j}}] = \sum_{i=j}^n i^{\underline{j}} \binom{n}{i} p^i (1 - p)^{n - i} = n^{\underline{j}} p^j \sum_{i=j}^n \binom{n - j}{i - j} p^{i - j} (1 - p)^{n - i} = n^{\underline{j}} p^j (p + 1 - p)^{n - j} = n^{\underline{j}} p^j.\] Look at that: the \(j\)-th falling-factorial moment of \(\operatorname{Binomial}(n, p)\) is simply \(n^{\underline{j}} p^j\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Convert \(X^k = \sum_{j=0}^k \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} X^{\underline{j}}\) via Stirling numbers of the second kind. By linearity of expectation: \[\mathbb{E}[X^k] = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} \mathbb{E}[X^{\underline{j}}] = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} n^{\underline{j}} m^{-j} \bmod 998244353.\] Use Regime 1 (stirling_2nd_row) from Section 6.4 to compute all \(\begin{Bmatrix} k \\ 0 \end{Bmatrix}, \dots, \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ k \end{Bmatrix}\) in 1 NTT (\(O(k \log k)\) time)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Binomial Falling-Factorial Moment Collapse
Let \(p = m^{-1} \bmod 998244353\) (well-defined since \(1 \le m < 998244353\)) and \(q = 1 - p\). The random variable \(X\) takes value \(i \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}\) with probability \(\binom{n}{i} p^i q^{n - i}\). Expanding \(i^k\) in the falling-factorial basis via Section 6.4: \[i^k = \sum_{j=0}^k \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} i^{\underline{j}}.\] Substituting this into \(\mathbb{E}[X^k]\) and applying the Falling-Factorial Absorption Identity \(i^{\underline{j}}\binom{n}{i} = n^{\underline{j}}\binom{n - j}{i - j}\): \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X^k]
&= \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i} p^i q^{n - i} \sum_{j=0}^k \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} i^{\underline{j}} && \text{(basis conversion }i^k = \sum_{j=0}^k \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} i^{\underline{j}}\text{)} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} \sum_{i=j}^n i^{\underline{j}} \binom{n}{i} p^i q^{n - i} && \text{(swapping }\sum_i, \sum_j\text{; }i^{\underline{j}} = 0\text{ for }i < j\text{)} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} n^{\underline{j}} p^j \sum_{i=j}^n \binom{n - j}{i - j} p^{i - j} q^{(n - j) - (i - j)} && \text{(Absorption Identity)} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} n^{\underline{j}} p^j (p + q)^{n - j} && \text{(Binomial Theorem on }r = i - j\text{)} \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} n^{\underline{j}} \left(\frac{1}{m}\right)^j. && \text{(since }p + q = 1\text{ and }1^{n-j} = 1\text{)}
\end{aligned}\]


2. Indicator-Variable Combinatorial Double-Count (Bonus Verification)
Why does \(\mathbb{E}[X^k] = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} n^{\underline{j}} m^{-j}\) hold combinatorially? Write \(X = I_1 + I_2 + \dots + I_n\), where \(I_r \in \{0, 1\}\) is the indicator that round \(r\) draws the Joker (\(\mathbb{E}[I_r] = 1/m\)). Expanding \(X^k = (I_1 + \dots + I_n)^k\) gives \(n^k\) terms \(I_{r_1} I_{r_2} \cdots I_{r_k}\) corresponding to functions \(f: \{1, \dots, k\} \to \{1, \dots, n\}\).

If the image of \(f\) has size \(|\operatorname{Im}(f)| = j\), then since \(I_r^c = I_r\) for any \(c \ge 1\) and different rounds are independent, \(\mathbb{E}[I_{r_1}\cdots I_{r_k}] = (1/m)^j\)!
How many functions \(f: \{1, \dots, k\} \to \{1, \dots, n\}\) have image size \(j\)? There are \(\begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix}\) ways to partition the domain \(\{1, \dots, k\}\) into \(j\) non-empty blocks, and \(n^{\underline{j}}\) ways to assign distinct rounds in \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) to those \(j\) blocks! Summing over \(j\) gives \(\sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} n^{\underline{j}} m^{-j}\) immediately!



3. Hand-Checkable Trace & Algorithm Contract

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(n = 3, m = 2, k = 3\)):

Using \(\begin{Bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{Bmatrix} = 1, \begin{Bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{Bmatrix} = 3, \begin{Bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \end{Bmatrix} = 1\): \[\mathbb{E}[X^3] = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^1 + 3 \cdot 6 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + 1 \cdot 6 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{3}{2} + \frac{9}{2} + \frac{3}{4} = \frac{27}{4},\] matching \(\frac{1}{8}(0^3 \binom{3}{0} + 1^3 \binom{3}{1} + 2^3 \binom{3}{2} + 3^3 \binom{3}{3}) = \frac{3 + 24 + 27}{8} = \frac{54}{8} = \frac{27}{4}\).

Input & Preconditions: Integers \(1 \le n, m < 998244353\), moment exponent \(k \ge 1\) (\(k \le 5000\) in standard version, \(k \le 2 \times 10^5\) in NTT version), and prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > k\) (with \(m \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\)).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\mathbb{E}[X^k] = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} n^{\underline{j}} (m^{-1})^j \bmod 998244353\):

Compute row \(k\) of the Stirling numbers of the second kind via 1 NTT (stirling_2nd_row, Section 6.4): \[\begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} = [x^j] \left(\sum_{r=0}^k \frac{r^k}{r!} x^r\right) \left(\sum_{s=0}^k \frac{(-1)^s}{s!} x^s\right) \qquad (0 \le j \le k).\]
Accumulate \(\sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} \begin{Bmatrix} k \\ j \end{Bmatrix} n^{\underline{j}} (m^{-1})^j \bmod 998244353\) in \(O(k)\) time.

Time & Space Complexity: \(O(k \log k)\) time and \(O(k)\) space via 1 NTT (or \(O(k^2)\) DP when \(k \le 5000\)).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At index \(j \in [0, \min(n, k)]\), the running term maintains \(\mathbb{E}[X^{\underline{j}}] = n^{\underline{j}} m^{-j} \bmod p\) via \(\text{term}_0 = 1\) and \(\text{term}_{j+1} = \text{term}_j \cdot (n - j) \cdot m^{-1} \bmod p\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Cap the summation at \(\min(n, k)\) (though \(\text{term}_j = 0\) automatically for \(j > n\) since \(n^{\underline{j}}\) hits the factor \(n - n = 0\)); do not precompute factorials up to \(n \le 998244352\)—compute \(n^{\underline{j}}\) incrementally in \(O(k)\) multiplications.

6.6 Chapter Summary, Diagnostic Routing Checklist & Quarantined Library Verification Footnotes

Fast Diagnostic Routing Checklist for Chapter 06
When faced with a binomial sum, polynomial shift, or power-weighted combinatorial expression, run through this 6-question diagnostic checklist in order:

Can the sum be aligned into a 1-NTT Cauchy or Cross-Correlation convolution?

If the summand factors into \(\alpha(n)\beta(k)\gamma(n-k)\), use Cauchy convolution (mul).
If the summand factors into \(\alpha(n)\beta(i)\gamma(i+n)\) (\(j - i = n\)), reverse \(\beta\) into \(\widetilde{B}[r] = \beta(N - r)\) and read \([x^{N+n}](\widetilde{B} \cdot G)\) (§6.1).

Is it a pure binomial product with a standard Vandermonde structure?

Sum of lower indices fixed (\(\binom{R}{k}\binom{S}{n-k}\)) \(\to\) Chu–Vandermonde \(\binom{R+S}{n}\) (§6.1).
Both lower indices carry \(+k\) (\(\binom{R}{a+k}\binom{S}{b+k}\) with \(R \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\)) \(\to\) flip \(\binom{R}{a+k} = \binom{R}{R-a-k}\) (§6.1).
Sum of upper indices fixed (\(\binom{k}{a}\binom{n-k}{b}\)) \(\to\) Parallel summation \(\binom{n+1}{a+b+1}\) via \((1-x)^{-(a+1)}(1-x)^{-(b+1)}\) (§6.1).

Does the free external parameter \(n\) appear in only ONE binomial factor?

Apply Engine 1 (Wilf’s Snake Oil): form \(\sum_{n \ge 0} S_n x^n\), swap \(\sum_n\) inside \(\sum_k\), collapse the \(n\)-sum via Master Kernels K1–K7, sum the \(k\)-series, and extract \([x^n]\) (§6.2).

Do multiple binomial factors depend on both \(n\) and \(k\)?

Apply Engine 2 (Egorychev Extraction): keep one \(\binom{n}{k}\) intact, replace the other binomials via \(\binom{A}{B} = [u^B](1+u)^A\) (Rule E1) or \([u^{A-B}](1-u)^{-B-1}\) (Rule E2), shift \(k\) out of \([u^{\dots}]\) as \(u^{ck}\), and collapse \(\sum_k \binom{n}{k} W(u)^k = (1 + W(u))^n\) (§6.2).

Do you need \(F(x + c)\), \((cx + e)^d F\!\left(\frac{ax+b}{cx+e}\right)\), or \((1 - cx)^{-\alpha} F\!\left(\frac{ax}{1-cx}\right) \bmod x^N\)?

Use poly_taylor_shift in 1 NTT (\(O(d \log d)\) when \(p > d\); Lucas/SOS digit DP when \(p \le d\)) and the 4-step Bruhat decomposition for Möbius transforms (§6.3).
Watch Failure Mode #14: When \(\alpha = -d \in \{-(N-2), \dots, 0\}\) in the \(\alpha\)-Euler Transform, split \(F(y) = F_{\le d}(y) + y^{d+1}F_{>d}(y)\) to shift the tail to \(\alpha' = 1 > 0\) and avoid dividing by \((-d)^{\overline{d+1}} = 0\) (§6.3).

Is a polynomial \(P(k)\) (or monomial \(k^m\)) weighting a huge-\(n\) binomial sum \(\sum_{k=0}^n P(k)\binom{n}{k} a^k b^{n-k}\), or is a DP polynomial in \(x \le 10^9\)?

Convert \(P(k) = \sum_{j=0}^m c_j k^{\underline{j}}\) into the falling-factorial basis (via \(\begin{Bmatrix} i \\ j \end{Bmatrix}\) when given monomials, or via \(\widehat{P}(t)e^{-t}\) in 1 NTT when given point values \(P(0 \dots m)\)) and apply the division-free Absorption Identity \(k^{\underline{j}}\binom{n}{k} = n^{\underline{j}}\binom{n-j}{k-j}\) (§6.4).
If a degree-\(d\) polynomial \(P(x)\) is known at consecutive points \(0, 1, \dots, d\), evaluate \(P(T)\) at \(T \le 10^{18}\) in \(O(d)\) time via eval_consecutive_lagrange (§6.4).

NoteChapter Overview & Algebraic Scope




Ambient Rings & Operators:

The Bivariate Formal Power Series Ring \(K[y][[x]]\) (and \(K[[x, y]]\)) equipped with the Taylor Shift Automorphism \(\mathcal{T}_{-1}: y \mapsto y - 1\), which converts “at least \(j\) designated violations” (\(G(x, y)\)) into “exactly \(k\) violations” (\(F(x, y) = G(x, y - 1)\)).
The Ordinary & Exponential Formal Power Series Rings \(K[[x]]\) and \(K_{\text{exp}}[[x]]\) equipped with the Universal Run-Length Transfer Map (连续段容斥) \(W(x) \mapsto F(x) = \frac{W(x)}{1 + W(x)}\), which replaces global adjacency constraints (“maximal contiguous runs have weight \(W(x)\)”) by free concatenation of signed formal sub-blocks (\(F(x)\)).
The Matrix Ring over Formal Power Series \(M_m(K[[x]])\), where the Goulden–Jackson Cluster Method compresses arbitrary multi-pattern string overlap constraints into an \(m \times m\) correlation matrix \(C(x) = I_m + C^{\text{strict}}(x)\).

Prerequisites: Chapter 01–02 (Truncated polynomial arithmetic, inv, ln, exp, sparse_div), Chapter 03–04 (Unlabeled OGF \(\operatorname{SEQ}\) and Labeled EGF \(\operatorname{SET}/\exp\)), Chapter 05 (Bivariate Marking Generating Functions), and Chapter 06 (Polynomial Taylor Shift \(B(y - 1)\) via Reversal NTT Convolution).
Learning Objectives:

Execute Binomial Inversion as a bivariate substitution \(F(x, y) = G(x, y - 1)\) both outside (via \(O(m \log m)\) reversal NTT Taylor shift) and inside symbolic operators (\(\operatorname{SEQ}\), \(\exp\)), and factorize non-attacking Rook Polynomials across disjoint subboards.
Derive and apply the Universal Run-Length Inclusion–Exclusion Transfer \(F(x) = \frac{W(x)}{1 + W(x)}\) (连续段容斥), master the Colored Multiset Smirnov Rule, and exploit ez_lcw Bounded-Run Sparsity (\(F_{\le k}(x) = \frac{x - x^{k+1}}{1 - x^{k+1}}\)) to solve all run-length bounds \(k = 1, \dots, n\) in \(O(n \log n)\) harmonic time.
Respect the Labeled Order-of-Operations Rule (compute OGF run transfer \(F_{\text{OGF}}(x) = \frac{W_{\text{OGF}}(x)}{1 + W_{\text{OGF}}(x)}\) before dividing by \(c!\) to form \(\widehat{F}_{\text{EGF}}(x)\)) and avoid the Undirected Path Factor-of-\(2\) Trap in forbidden-edge permutation sieves.
Construct the Eulerian Bivariate EGF \(A(x, y) = \frac{1 - y}{e^{(y-1)x} - y}\), extract single Eulerian rows in \(O(n \log n)\) via Worpitzky’s Identity, and count bounded-ascent permutations via the David–Barton Theorem.
Formulate and solve all four regimes of the Goulden–Jackson Cluster Method (single pattern, \(m \times m\) multi-pattern antichain matrix, \((t - 1)\) exact-occurrence bivariate marking, and cyclic necklace trace \(-x Q'(x) / Q(x)\)).

title: Chapter 08: The Sieve & Inclusion–Exclusion Engine: Run-Length Transfer (连续段容斥) & Goulden–Jackson Cluster Method
section: 8.1 Binomial Inversion as Bivariate Taylor Shift \(G(x, y-1)\) & Rook Polynomials
text:
8.1 Binomial Inversion as Bivariate Taylor Shift \(G(x, y-1)\) & Rook Polynomials

Why “At Least \(j\) Designated Violations” Beats “Exactly \(k\) Violations”
In dynamic programming and combinatorial enumeration, constraints that forbid bad events—such as “no two adjacent elements are equal”, “no cell lies in a forbidden set \(B\)”, or “exactly \(k\) colors appear \(S\) times”—destroy independence. If you try to construct a valid object step-by-step while enforcing that zero bad events occur, every choice you make restricts the set of legal choices for all future steps, forcing a high-dimensional DP state.
The core philosophy of the Sieve & Inclusion–Exclusion Engine is to trade a hard avoidance constraint for an easy designation (钦定) relaxation:

Instead of requiring that bad events never happen, we designate a specific subset of \(j\) bad events and force those \(j\) events to occur.
Crucially, on all remaining positions outside those \(j\) designated events, we drop the constraint completely and fill the remaining structure freely!

Because the remaining elements are filled without restriction, they decouple into simple powers, factorials, or independent component generating functions. The price we pay is overcounting: an object that actually commits \(k\) bad events will be counted once for every subset of \(j\) bad events we could have designated among its \(k\) actual violations—that is, \(\binom{k}{j}\) times!



The Bivariate Exact-vs.-At-Least Sieve (\(F(x, y) = G(x, y - 1)\))
Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a combinatorial class of objects weighted by size \(n\) (marked by \(x^n\)) and equipped with a finite set of potential “bad properties” (or target features).

Let \(f_{n, k}\) be the number (or total weight) of objects of size \(n\) that possess exactly \(k\) bad properties. We package \(f_{n, k}\) into the Exact Bivariate Generating Function: \[F(x, y) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{k \ge 0} f_{n, k} x^n y^k\]
Let \(g_{n, j}\) be the number of pairs \((\alpha, S)\) where \(\alpha\) is an object of size \(n\) and \(S\) is a designated subset of \(j\) bad properties that all hold in \(\alpha\) (while any other bad properties outside \(S\) may or may not hold in \(\alpha\)). Since an object \(\alpha\) with exactly \(k\) actual bad properties contains \(\binom{k}{j}\) subsets \(S\) of size \(j\), double counting gives: \[g_{n, j} = \sum_{k \ge j} \binom{k}{j} f_{n, k}\] We package \(g_{n, j}\) into the Relaxed (“At-Least-\(j\) Designated”) Bivariate Generating Function: \[G(x, y) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{j \ge 0} g_{n, j} x^n y^j\]







TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Binomial Inversion as a Taylor Shift




The Diagnostic Signal: You need to find \(f_{n, k}\) (objects with exactly \(k\) occurrences of a property, or \(f_{n, 0}\) with zero occurrences), and you notice that once you fix any \(j\) occurrences of the property, the remaining \(n - j\) pieces of the object can be chosen freely in a clean closed form or via a simple 1D generating function \(g_{n, j}\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: How are the bivariate series \(F(x, y)\) and \(G(x, y)\) related algebraically? Let us substitute the double-counting definition \(g_{n, j} = \sum_{k \ge j} \binom{k}{j} f_{n, k}\) into \(G(x, y)\) and swap the summation order between \(j\) and \(k\): \[\begin{aligned}
G(x, y) &= \sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{j \ge 0} \left( \sum_{k \ge j} \binom{k}{j} f_{n, k} \right) x^n y^j && \text{(definition of } g_{n, j}\text{)} \\
&= \sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{k \ge 0} f_{n, k} x^n \left( \sum_{j=0}^{k} \binom{k}{j} y^j \right) && \text{(swap sums: } 0 \le j \le k\text{)} \\
&= \sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{k \ge 0} f_{n, k} x^n (y + 1)^k = F(x, y + 1) && \text{(Binomial Theorem on } (y+1)^k\text{)}
\end{aligned}\] To solve for \(F(x, y)\), simply shift the formal variable \(y \mapsto y - 1\)!




Theorem 8.1 (The Bivariate Taylor Shift Sieve)
Over any commutative ring \(K\), the Exact Bivariate Generating Function \(F(x, y)\) and the Relaxed Bivariate Generating Function \(G(x, y)\) are related by the Taylor Shift Automorphism \(y \mapsto y - 1\): \[F(x, y) = G(x, y - 1), \qquad G(x, y) = F(x, y + 1)\] Extracting \([x^n y^k]\) from \(F(x, y) = G(x, y - 1)\) by expanding \((y - 1)^j = \sum_{k=0}^j (-1)^{j-k} \binom{j}{k} y^k\) yields the three canonical coefficient formulas of Binomial Inversion:

Exact-\(k\) Extraction: \[f_{n, k} = [x^n y^k] G(x, y - 1) = \sum_{j \ge k} (-1)^{j - k} \binom{j}{k} g_{n, j}\]
Pure Avoidance (\(k = 0\), Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion): \[f_{n, 0} = [x^n] G(x, -1) = \sum_{j \ge 0} (-1)^j g_{n, j}\]
Cumulative At-Least-\(k\) Extraction (\(\sum_{r \ge k} f_{n, r}\)): Suppose a problem asks for the number of objects with at least \(k\) bad properties (i.e., \(\sum_{r \ge k} f_{n, r}\)). Summing the exact-\(r\) formula over \(r = k, \dots, j\) and swapping sums collapses the inner alternating binomial sum via Pascal’s identity \(\binom{j}{r} = \binom{j-1}{r} + \binom{j-1}{r-1}\) into a single telescoping term (\(k \ge 1\)): \[\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r \ge k} f_{n, r}
&= \sum_{j \ge k} g_{n, j} \sum_{r=k}^{j} (-1)^{j - r} \binom{j}{r}
&& \text{(swap the sums over } r \text{ and } j\text{)} \\[4pt]
&= \sum_{j \ge k} g_{n, j} \sum_{r=k}^{j} \left[(-1)^{j - r} \binom{j - 1}{r} - (-1)^{j - (r - 1)} \binom{j - 1}{r - 1}\right]
&& \text{(expand } \binom{j}{r} = \binom{j-1}{r} + \binom{j-1}{r-1} \text{ to telescope)} \\[4pt]
&= \sum_{j \ge k} (-1)^{j - k} \binom{j - 1}{k - 1} g_{n, j}.
&& \text{(telescope from } r = k \text{ to } r = j\text{, since } \binom{j-1}{j} = 0\text{)}
\end{aligned}\]





The Two Computational Pipelines: Outside vs. Inside Symbolic Operators
Theorem 8.1 gives us two distinct algorithmic ways to apply the substitution \(y \mapsto y - 1\):

Pipeline 1: Applying \(y \mapsto y - 1\) After Computing \(g_j\) (\(O(m \log m)\) Reversal Convolution)
Suppose \(n\) is fixed and we have already computed the sequence \(g_0, g_1, \dots, g_m\) of relaxed counts (where \(m\) is the maximum possible number of simultaneous bad events). When \(k! \in K^\times\) for \(0 \le k \le m\) (e.g., over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with prime \(p > m\)), we expand \(\binom{j}{k} = \frac{j!}{k!(j - k)!}\) just as in Chapter 06: \[f_k = \sum_{j=k}^{m} (-1)^{j - k} \binom{j}{k} g_j = \frac{1}{k!} \sum_{j=k}^{m} \bigl(j! g_j\bigr) \frac{(-1)^{j - k}}{(j - k)!}\] This is a reversal Cauchy convolution (polynomial Taylor shift \(G(y - 1)\)), which computes \(f_0, f_1, \dots, f_m\) simultaneously in a single \(O(m \log m)\) NTT!


Pipeline 2: Moving \(y \mapsto y - 1\) Inside Symbolic Operators (\(\operatorname{SEQ}\), \(\exp\), \(\prod\))
What if computing \(g_{n, j}\) for every \((n, j)\) requires a slow 2D dynamic program? Look closely at the map \(\mathcal{T}_{-1}: K[y][[x]] \to K[y][[x]]\) defined by \(H(x, y) \mapsto H(x, y - 1)\). Because \(\mathcal{T}_{-1}\) is an evaluation ring homomorphism that fixes \(x\) and sends \(y \mapsto y - 1\), it commutes with addition, multiplication, quasi-inverses (\(\operatorname{SEQ}\)), and formal exponentials (\(\operatorname{SET}\)): \[\begin{aligned}
\left( \prod_{i=1}^{c} B_i(x, y) \right)\Bigg|_{y \mapsto y - 1} &= \prod_{i=1}^{c} B_i(x, y - 1) \\
\operatorname{SEQ}\bigl(C(x, y)\bigr)\Big|_{y \mapsto y - 1} &= \frac{1}{1 - C(x, y - 1)} \\
\exp\bigl(\widehat{C}(x, y)\bigr)\Big|_{y \mapsto y - 1} &= \exp\bigl(\widehat{C}(x, y - 1)\bigr)
\end{aligned}\] In particular, when we want pure avoidance (\(k = 0\)), we evaluate at \(y = 0\), which sets \(y - 1 = -1\) inside the component series \(C(x, y)\) before we ever apply \(\operatorname{SEQ}\) or \(\exp\)! This collapses a 2D bivariate counting problem into a 1D formal power series operation in \(K[[x]]\).




Rook Polynomials & Disjoint Board Decompositions
A foundational application of Pipeline 1 and Pipeline 2 is counting permutations \(\pi \in S_n\) that avoid a set of forbidden cell positions \(B \subseteq [n] \times [n]\) (or have exactly \(k\) hits \((i, \pi(i)) \in B\)).

Concrete Combinatorial Model
View the permutation \(\pi \in S_n\) as placing \(n\) mutually non-attacking rooks on an \(n \times n\) chessboard at cells \((i, \pi(i))\) for \(1 \le i \le n\) (no two rooks share a row or column). A bad event at row \(i\) is that the rook \((i, \pi(i))\) lands on a forbidden square in \(B\).

Designating \(j\) Forbidden Rooks: To form a relaxed configuration with \(j\) designated bad events, we first choose \(j\) squares in \(B\) that lie in distinct rows and distinct columns—that is, a valid placement of \(j\) non-attacking rooks entirely inside the forbidden board \(B\). Let \(r_j(B)\) be the number of ways to place \(j\) non-attacking rooks on \(B\) (with \(r_0(B) = 1\)).
Completing the Remaining \(n - j\) Rows and Columns Freely: Once those \(j\) rooks are locked into \(j\) rows and \(j\) columns, the remaining \(n - j\) rooks can be placed in the remaining \((n - j) \times (n - j)\) subgrid in any of the \((n - j)!\) ways (ignoring whether they land on \(B\) or not!). Therefore, the relaxed count of permutations with \(j\) designated hits on \(B\) is: \[g_j = r_j(B) \cdot (n - j)! \qquad (0 \le j \le n)\]

Define the Rook Polynomial of the forbidden board \(B\) as the ordinary generating polynomial of \(r_j(B)\): \[R_B(y) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} r_j(B) y^j\] Applying Theorem 8.1 to \(G(y) = \sum_{j=0}^n r_j(B) (n - j)! y^j\) immediately yields the Rook Sieve Formula: \[F_B(y) = G(y - 1) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} r_j(B) (n - j)! (y - 1)^j, \qquad f_0 = \sum_{j=0}^{n} (-1)^j r_j(B) (n - j)!\,\]


Disjoint Subboard Factorization
Suppose the forbidden cells \(B = B_1 \sqcup B_2 \sqcup \dots \sqcup B_c\) partition into \(c\) components that are row- and column-disjoint (no cell in \(B_a\) shares a row or a column with any cell in \(B_b\) for \(a \neq b\); equivalently, in the bipartite conflict graph between rows \([n]\) and columns \([n]\) with edge set \(B\), the \(B_t\) are the connected components). Because rooks placed in \(B_a\) can never attack rooks placed in \(B_b\), a placement of \(j\) non-attacking rooks on \(B\) is simply an independent choice of \(j_t\) non-attacking rooks on each component \(B_t\) with \(j_1 + \dots + j_c = j\): \[R_B(y) = \prod_{t=1}^{c} R_{B_t}(y)\]


Hand-Checkable Trace (\(n = 3\)): Classical Derangements via Rook Polynomials
Consider \(n = 3\) with the diagonal forbidden board \(B = \{(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)\}\) (\(\pi(i) \neq i\)).

The three cells \((1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)\) lie in pairwise distinct rows and columns, so \(B = B_1 \sqcup B_2 \sqcup B_3\) where each \(B_t\) is a \(1\)-cell board with rook polynomial \(R_{B_t}(y) = 1 + y\).
Multiplying across the \(3\) disjoint components gives: \[R_B(y) = (1 + y)^3 = 1 + 3y + 3y^2 + y^3 \implies r_0 = 1,\ r_1 = 3,\ r_2 = 3,\ r_3 = 1\]
Multiplying \(r_j\) by \((3 - j)!\) gives the relaxed polynomial \(G(y)\): \[G(y) = \sum_{j=0}^{3} r_j (3 - j)! y^j = 1 \cdot 3! + 3 \cdot 2! y + 3 \cdot 1! y^2 + 1 \cdot 0! y^3 = 6 + 6y + 3y^2 + y^3\]
Shifting \(y \mapsto y - 1\) gives the exact hit distribution \(F(y) = G(y - 1)\): \[\begin{aligned}
F(y) &= 6 + 6(y - 1) + 3(y - 1)^2 + (y - 1)^3 \\
&= (6 - 6 + 3 - 1) + (6 - 6 + 3)y + (3 - 3)y^2 + y^3 = 2 + 3y + 0y^2 + y^3
\end{aligned}\] Indeed, among the \(3! = 6\) permutations of \(\{1, 2, 3\}\), exactly \(f_0 = 2\) are derangements, \(f_1 = 3\) have \(1\) fixed point, \(f_2 = 0\) have \(2\) fixed points, and \(f_3 = 1\) has \(3\) fixed points!







NoteAlgorithm Contract: Exact-\(k\) Extraction & Rook Sieve (Bivariate Taylor Shift)




Input: Relaxed sequence \(g_0, g_1, \dots, g_m \in K\) where \(g_j = \sum_{k=j}^m \binom{k}{j} f_k\) (or for a rook problem, component rook polynomials \(R_{B_1}(y), \dots, R_{B_c}(y)\) with \(\sum \deg R_{B_t} \le n\), from which \(R_B(y) = \prod_{t=1}^c R_{B_t}(y)\) and \(g_j = r_j(B)(n - j)!\)).
Preconditions:

For a single target \(f_k\) (or \(f_0\)), no division in \(K\) is needed (\(\binom{j}{k} \in \mathbb{Z}\) works over any commutative ring \(K\)).
For simultaneous all-\(k\) extraction via NTT Taylor Shift, \(m! \in K^\times\) (\(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or prime \(p > m\)).

Output: Exact sequence \(f_0, f_1, \dots, f_m \in K\) where \(F(y) = G(y - 1)\).
Complexity:

Single \(f_k\) (or cumulative \(\sum_{r \ge k} f_r\)): \(O(m)\) ring operations.
All \(f_0, \dots, f_m\) via Reversal Convolution: \(O(m \log m)\) time and \(O(m)\) space.
Multiplying \(c\) disjoint rook polynomials of total degree \(n\) via Divide-and-Conquer NTT: \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time.

Core Invariant: Every configuration with \(k\) actual violations contributes \(\binom{k}{j} (-1)^{j-k} \binom{j}{k} = \binom{k}{k}\binom{0}{k-j} = [k = j]\) when summed over \(j\), ensuring configurations with \(k' > k\) cancel to \(0\) and configurations with \(k' = k\) contribute weight \(1\).
