8-Problem 4-Tier Practice Ladder

Stepping Stone 1 (#151) — Spanning Tree Block Sum (Luogu P4002 — [清华集训2017] 生成树计数)

Tier: Stepping Stone 1 | Canonical ID: #151
Source: Luogu P4002 — [清华集训2017] 生成树计数
Prerequisite Tags: Prüfer Sequence EGF, Euler Operator \(\vartheta = x D_x\) (§18.1), Logarithmic Derivative Power Sums (§18.2)


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(N\) vertex-disjoint connected components of sizes \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_N\) and a positive integer exponent \(m\). You wish to add \(N - 1\) edges between the components to connect all \(\sum_{i=1}^N a_i\) vertices into a single spanning tree. Whenever an added edge connects component \(i\) and component \(j\), there are \(a_i a_j\) choices for its endpoints; thus, a contracted spanning tree \(T\) on the \(N\) components in which component \(i\) has degree \(d_i \ge 1\) corresponds to \(\prod_{i=1}^N a_i^{d_i}\) vertex-level spanning trees.
For each vertex-level spanning tree with component degrees \((d_1, \dots, d_N)\), its weight is defined as: \[
\left( \sum_{i=1}^N d_i^m \right) \prod_{i=1}^N d_i^m.
\] Compute the sum of weights over all valid vertex-level spanning trees modulo \(998244353\): \[
\text{Ans} = \sum_{T} \left( \sum_{i=1}^N d_i^m \right) \left( \prod_{i=1}^N d_i^m a_i^{d_i} \right) \pmod{998244353}.
\]

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 30000\), \(1 \le m \le 30000\), \(1 \le a_i < 998244353\), \(\sum_{i=1}^N a_i \not\equiv 0 \pmod{998244353}\).
Required Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Instance 1 (\(N = 2, m = 1, a = (2, 3)\)): There is only \(1\) contracted tree on \(2\) components, with degrees \(d_1 = 1, d_2 = 1\). There are \(a_1^{d_1} a_2^{d_2} = 2^1 \cdot 3^1 = 6\) vertex-level trees, each with degree factor \((1^1 + 1^1)(1^1 \cdot 1^1) = 2\). Total answer: \(6 \times 2 = 12\).
Instance 2 (\(N = 3, m = 1, a = (1, 1, 1)\)): There are \(3^{3-2} = 3\) contracted trees on \(\{1, 2, 3\}\), each of which is a path of \(3\) vertices with degrees \((2, 1, 1)\) in some permutation. For each tree, \(\sum_{i=1}^3 d_i^1 = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4\) and \(\prod_{i=1}^3 d_i^1 a_i^{d_i} = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 2\), contributing \(4 \times 2 = 8\). Across all \(3\) trees, the total weight is \(3 \times 8 = 24\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

By Prüfer’s bijection, a degree sequence \((d_1, \dots, d_N)\) with \(d_i = c_i + 1 \ge 1\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^N c_i = N - 2\) occurs \(\frac{(N-2)!}{c_1! \cdots c_N!}\) times. Notice that the weight \(\left(\sum_{j=1}^N d_j^m\right) \prod_{i=1}^N d_i^m a_i^{d_i}\) is a sum over \(j = 1, \dots, N\) where component \(j\) has degree factor \(d_j^{2m} a_j^{d_j}\) and every other component \(i \neq j\) has degree factor \(d_i^m a_i^{d_i}\). How can we express this using two univariate EGFs \(F(x)\) and \(G(x)\) scaled by \(a_i\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Define the Euler-shifted exponential series: \[
F(x) = (\vartheta + 1)^m e^x = \sum_{c=0}^\infty \frac{(c + 1)^m}{c!} x^c, \qquad G(x) = (\vartheta + 1)^{2m} e^x = \sum_{c=0}^\infty \frac{(c + 1)^{2m}}{c!} x^c.
\] Then the total weight is: \[
\text{Ans} = (N - 2)! \left(\prod_{i=1}^N a_i\right) [x^{N-2}] \left( \prod_{i=1}^N F(a_i x) \cdot \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{G(a_j x)}{F(a_j x)} \right).
\] Take \(\ln\) of the product \(\prod_{i=1}^N F(a_i x) = \exp\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \ln F(a_i x)\right)\) to decouple \(a_i\) from the series coefficients!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Let \(L(x) = \ln F(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{N-2} l_k x^k \bmod x^{N-1}\) and \(H(x) = \frac{G(x)}{F(x)} = \sum_{k=0}^{N-2} h_k x^k \bmod x^{N-1}\). Expanding \(\sum_{i=1}^N L(a_i x)\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^N H(a_i x)\) requires the power sums \(S_k = \sum_{i=1}^N a_i^k\) for \(0 \le k \le N - 2\). By Recipe A (§18.2), the polynomial \(P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^N (1 - a_i x)\) satisfies \(-\vartheta \ln P(x) = -x \frac{P'(x)}{P(x)} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty S_k x^k\), computable in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) via divide-and-conquer NTT!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Prüfer Sequence EGF Factorization: For \(N = 1\), a single component has no edges (\(d_1 = 0\)), so the answer is \(0\). Assume \(N \ge 2\). In the Prüfer sequence of length \(N - 2\), component \(i\) appears \(c_i = d_i - 1 \ge 0\) times, with \(\sum_{i=1}^N c_i = N - 2\). Factoring \(\prod_{i=1}^N a_i^{c_i + 1} = \left(\prod_{i=1}^N a_i\right) \prod_{i=1}^N a_i^{c_i}\), we rewrite the target sum by linearity over the distinguished component \(j \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) in \(\sum_{j=1}^N (c_j + 1)^m\): \[
\text{Ans} = (N - 2)! \left(\prod_{i=1}^N a_i\right) \sum_{j=1}^N \sum_{c_1 + \dots + c_N = N - 2} \frac{(c_j + 1)^{2m} a_j^{c_j}}{c_j!} \prod_{i \neq j} \frac{(c_i + 1)^m a_i^{c_i}}{c_i!}.
\]
Euler Operator Series \(F(x)\) and \(G(x)\): Using the Euler operator \(\vartheta = x D_x\) from §18.1, since \((\vartheta + 1)^k (x^c) = (c + 1)^k x^c\), we define: \[
F(x) = (\vartheta + 1)^m e^x = \sum_{c=0}^{N-2} \frac{(c + 1)^m}{c!} x^c \pmod{x^{N-1}}, \qquad G(x) = (\vartheta + 1)^{2m} e^x = \sum_{c=0}^{N-2} \frac{(c + 1)^{2m}}{c!} x^c \pmod{x^{N-1}}.
\] Then the inner sum over \((c_1, \dots, c_N)\) for a fixed \(j\) is \([x^{N-2}] \left( G(a_j x) \prod_{i \neq j} F(a_i x) \right)\). Summing over \(j = 1, \dots, N\) gives: \[
\text{Ans} = (N - 2)! \left(\prod_{i=1}^N a_i\right) [x^{N-2}] \left( \exp\!\left( \sum_{i=1}^N \ln F(a_i x) \right) \cdot \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{G(a_j x)}{F(a_j x)} \right).
\]
Decoupling \(a_i\) via Power Sums \(S_k = \sum_{i=1}^N a_i^k\): Since \([x^0] F(x) = 1 \in \mathbb{F}_{998244353}^\times\), both \(L(x) = \ln F(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{N-2} l_k x^k \bmod x^{N-1}\) and \(H(x) = G(x) F(x)^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^{N-2} h_k x^k \bmod x^{N-1}\) are well-defined and computable in \(O(N \log N)\) time. Substituting \(a_i x\) into \(L\) and \(H\) yields: \[
\sum_{i=1}^N L(a_i x) \equiv \sum_{k=1}^{N-2} (l_k S_k) x^k \pmod{x^{N-1}}, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^N H(a_j x) \equiv \sum_{k=0}^{N-2} (h_k S_k) x^k \pmod{x^{N-1}},
\] where \(S_k = \sum_{i=1}^N a_i^k\).
Computing \(S_0, S_1, \dots, S_{N-2}\) via Logarithmic Derivative: Form \(P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^N (1 - a_i x)\) by binary-tree divide-and-conquer NTT in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time. By Recipe A: \[
-\vartheta \ln P(x) = -\sum_{i=1}^N \vartheta \ln(1 - a_i x) = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{a_i x}{1 - a_i x} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty S_k x^k,
\] along with \(S_0 = N\). Finally, one polynomial exp on \(\sum_{k=1}^{N-2} (l_k S_k) x^k\) and one Cauchy product with \(\sum_{k=0}^{N-2} (h_k S_k) x^k\) extract \([x^{N-2}]\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time.



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(N, m \le 30000\) and component sizes \(a_1, \dots, a_N \in \mathbb{F}_{998244353}\); requires \(N \ge 2\), \([x^0]F(x) = 1\), and \([x^0]P(x) = 1\) invertible in \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}\).
Postconditions (Output): Total weight of all spanning trees modulo \(998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time for the product tree \(P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^N (1 - a_i x)\) plus \(O(N \log N)\) for ln, inv, exp, and binary exponentiation of \((c+1)^m\); \(O(N)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Each power sum \(S_k = [x^k](-\vartheta \ln P(x))\) aggregates the \(k\)-th powers of all \(N\) component sizes simultaneously, ensuring the scaled series \(\sum_{i=1}^N L(a_i x)\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^N H(a_i x)\) match term-by-term up to \(x^{N-2}\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(N = 1\), the single component is already connected so output \(1\) (or \(0\) if edge weight product requires \(N \ge 2\)); if any \(a_i \equiv 0 \pmod{998244353}\), that component cannot have positive degree in any spanning tree so the answer is \(0\).









Stepping Stone 2 (#064) — Carry-Ordered Digit Recurrence (AtCoder ARC 153 D — Sum of Sum of Digits)

Tier: Stepping Stone 2 | Canonical ID: #064
Source: AtCoder Regular Contest 153, Problem D — Sum of Sum of Digits
Prerequisite Tags: Digit Sum Functional Recurrence, Radix Carry Order, State Space Reduction


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
For a positive integer \(m\), let \(f(m)\) denote the sum of the base-\(10\) digits of \(m\). You are given \(N\) positive integers \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N\). Find the minimum possible value of: \[
S(x) = \sum_{i=1}^N f(x + A_i)
\] over all non-negative integers \(x \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\).

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(1 \le A_i < 10^9\).
Required Complexity: \(O(D \cdot N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space, where \(D = 10\) is the number of decimal digits.



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Instance (\(N = 3, A = (4, 8, 9)\)):

If \(x = 0\): \(f(4) + f(8) + f(9) = 4 + 8 + 9 = 21\).
If \(x = 1\): \(f(5) + f(9) + f(10) = 5 + 9 + 1 = 15\).
If \(x = 2\): \(f(6) + f(10) + f(11) = 6 + 1 + 2 = 9\).
If \(x = 6\): \(f(10) + f(14) + f(15) = 1 + 5 + 6 = 12\).
The minimum possible value is \(9\), achieved at \(x = 2\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Write the digit sum recurrence connecting the \(k\)-th digit decision to the \((k+1)\)-st digit decision: for any integer \(v \ge 0\), \(f(v) = (v \bmod 10) + f(\lfloor v / 10 \rfloor)\). When we choose the \(k\)-th decimal digit \(d_k \in \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\) of \(x\), which elements \(A_i\) generate a carry into position \(k + 1\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

At digit position \(k\) (\(0 \le k \le 9\)), an element \(A_i\) has received a carry into position \(k\) if and only if \((A_i \bmod 10^k) + (x \bmod 10^k) \ge 10^k\). Therefore, if we sort \(A_1, \dots, A_N\) in descending order of \((A_i \bmod 10^k)\), the subset of indices \(A_i\) that have a carry at position \(k\) is always a prefix of length \(c \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) of this sorted order!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Let \(dp[k][c]\) be the minimum total digit sum contributed by positions \(0, 1, \dots, k-1\) such that exactly the first \(c\) elements in the \(\bmod 10^k\) descending order produce a carry into position \(k\). Trying all 10 choices for the \(k\)-th digit \(d \in \{0, \dots, 9\}\) of \(x\) updates both the immediate digit cost and the new carry count \(c' \in \{0, \dots, N\}\) via prefix sums in \(O(1)\) per state!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Telescoping the Digit Sum Operator: Every non-negative integer \(v\) satisfies the exact functional relation: \[
f(v) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left( \left\lfloor \frac{v}{10^k} \right\rfloor - 10 \left\lfloor \frac{v}{10^{k+1}} \right\rfloor \right).
\] Since \(A_i < 10^9\), any optimal \(x\) satisfies \(x < 10^9\) (adding \(10^{10}\) only increases the digit sum), and for \(k = 10\), \(\lfloor (x + A_i) / 10^{10} \rfloor = 0\) unless a carry propagates out of \(k = 9\), in which case each remaining carry contributes \(+1\) to the \(10^{10}\) place.
Monotonicity of Carry Sets (State Space Collapse from \(2^N\) to \(N + 1\)): Fix stage \(k \in \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\). Let \(\pi_k = (i_1, i_2, \dots, i_N)\) be the permutation of \(\{1, \dots, N\}\) sorted in descending order of the remainder \(r_{i, k} = A_i \bmod 10^k\). For any choice of the low \(k\) digits \(x_k = x \bmod 10^k \in [0, 10^k - 1]\), element \(A_i\) carries into stage \(k\) (\(\lfloor (A_i + x_k)/10^k \rfloor = 1\)) if and only if \(r_{i, k} \ge 10^k - x_k\). Because \(\pi_k\) is sorted in descending order of \(r_{i, k}\), the set of carrying elements is a prefix \(\{\pi_k(1), \dots, \pi_k(c)\}\) of size \(c \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\).
Transition from Stage \(k\) to Stage \(k + 1\): Suppose at stage \(k\) the first \(c\) elements of \(\pi_k\) have incoming carry \(1\), and the remaining \(N - c\) elements have incoming carry \(0\). Let \(a_{i, k} = \lfloor A_i / 10^k \rfloor \bmod 10\) be the \(k\)-th digit of \(A_i\). If we choose the \(k\)-th digit of \(x\) to be \(d \in \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\):

An element \(i \in \{\pi_k(1), \dots, \pi_k(c)\}\) (with incoming carry \(1\)) has \(k\)-th digit \((a_{i, k} + d + 1) \bmod 10\), and produces an outgoing carry to stage \(k + 1\) iff \(a_{i, k} + d + 1 \ge 10\).
An element \(i \in \{\pi_k(c+1), \dots, \pi_k(N)\}\) (with incoming carry \(0\)) has \(k\)-th digit \((a_{i, k} + d) \bmod 10\), and produces an outgoing carry to stage \(k + 1\) iff \(a_{i, k} + d \ge 10\). Precomputing prefix counts of each digit \(a_{\pi_k(j), k} \in \{0, \dots, 9\}\) for \(1 \le j \le N\) allows us to evaluate both the total digit sum at stage \(k\) and the exact number of outgoing carries \(c'\) in \(O(1)\) time for each \((c, d)\) pair! At the end of \(D = 10\) stages (\(10^{10} > \max A_i\)), the final answer is \(\min_{0 \le c \le N} (dp[10][c] + c)\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) and \(1 \le A_1, \dots, A_N < 10^9\); \(D = 10\) decimal stages suffice since \(A_i < 10^9 < 10^{10}\).
Postconditions (Output): \(\min_{x \ge 0} \sum_{i=1}^N f(x + A_i)\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(D \cdot N \log N)\) time (or \(O(D \cdot N)\) using radix sort across stages) and \(O(N)\) auxiliary space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After stage \(k\), the permutation \(\pi_{k+1}\) is obtained by stably bucketing \(\pi_k\) by the \(k\)-th digit \(a_{i, k}\) in descending order \(9, 8, \dots, 0\), ensuring that the \(c'\) elements with \(a_{i, k} + d + \text{carry}_i \ge 10\) form the exact prefix of length \(c'\) of \(\pi_{k+1}\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: At \(k = 0\), only \(c = 0\) is reachable (\(dp[0][0] = 0\), \(dp[0][c > 0] = +\infty\)); after stage \(D = 10\), any residual carry \(c \in \{0, \dots, N\}\) into position \(10^{10}\) must be added as \(+c\) to \(dp[10][c]\).









Intermediate 1 (#022) — Piecewise Order-Statistic Integral & Beta Recurrence (AtCoder ABC 226 H — Random K-th Max)

Tier: Intermediate 1 | Canonical ID: #022
Source: AtCoder Beginner Contest 226, Problem H — Random K-th Max
Prerequisite Tags: Tail-Expectation Integral, Bivariate Order-Statistic Generating Polynomial, D-Finite Beta Integral Recurrence (§18.1)


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(N\) independent continuous random variables \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_N\), where each \(X_i\) is drawn uniformly at random from the real interval \([L_i, R_i]\). Let \(Y\) denote the \(K\)-th largest value among \((X_1, X_2, \dots, X_N)\). Compute the expected value \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le K \le N \le 50\), \(0 \le L_i < R_i \le 10^9\), modulus \(998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O(N^4)\) (or \(O(N^3)\) via sliding polynomial division) time and \(O(N^2)\) space.



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Instance (\(N = 2, K = 1, X_1 \sim [0, 2], X_2 \sim [1, 3]\)): The sorted endpoints \(0 < 1 < 2 < 3\) split \([0, 3]\) into three elementary intervals:

On \([0, 1]\): \(\mathbb{P}(X_2 \ge x) = 1\), so at least \(K = 1\) variable is \(\ge x\) with probability \(1\). Integral over \([0, 1]\) is \(1\).
On \([1, 2]\): \(\mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge x) = \frac{2-x}{2}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X_2 \ge x) = \frac{3-x}{2}\). In local coordinate \(t = x - 1 \in [0, 1]\), \(\mathbb{P}(Y \ge 1 + t) = 1 - \frac{1+t}{2}\frac{t}{2} = 1 - \frac{t}{4} - \frac{t^2}{4}\). Integrating over \(t \in [0, 1]\) gives \(1 - \frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{12} = \frac{19}{24}\).
On \([2, 3]\): \(\mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge x) = 0\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X_2 \ge x) = \frac{3-x}{2}\). Integrating over \([2, 3]\) gives \(\frac{1}{4}\). Total expectation: \(\mathbb{E}[Y] = 1 + \frac{19}{24} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{49}{24} \equiv 457528664 \pmod{998244353}\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Because \(Y \ge 0\), use the tail-expectation identity \(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \int_0^\infty \mathbb{P}(Y \ge x)\,dx\). Sort all \(2N\) endpoints \(\{L_i, R_i\}\) into elementary intervals \([x_m, x_{m+1}]\). Inside a single elementary interval \([a, b]\), how does the survival probability \(p_i(x) = \mathbb{P}(X_i \ge x)\) depend on \(x\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Inside \([a, b]\), each variable \(X_i\) has survival probability \(p_i(x) = 1\) (if \(b \le L_i\)), \(p_i(x) = 0\) (if \(a \ge R_i\)), or \(p_i(x) = \frac{R_i - x}{R_i - L_i}\) (if \(L_i \le a < b \le R_i\)). Introducing the local variable \(t = x - a \in [0, b - a]\) and a formal variable \(y\) to mark variables that are \(\ge x\), the probability generating function of the count of variables \(\ge a + t\) is: \[
P(t, y) = \prod_{i=1}^N \Big( (1 - p_i(a + t)) + y \, p_i(a + t) \Big).
\] Notice that if we instead parameterize by \(Y < x\) (meaning at least \(N - K + 1\) variables are \(< x\)), we only need to track the single degree in \(t\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Rather than maintaining a 2D polynomial in \((t, y)\), observe that \(\mathbb{P}(Y \ge x) = \sum_{j=K}^N [y^j] P(t, y)\) can be updated across elementary intervals, or inside each interval \([a, b]\) we can run a 2D knapsack DP over active variables where state \((j, d)\) is the coefficient of \(y^j t^d\). Even better: by conditioning on WHICH variable \(X_i\) equals \(Y = x\) on \([a, b]\) and how many other variables are \(> x\) vs. \(< x\), or by maintaining the active polynomial and dividing out a linear factor when an interval ends, the complexity drops to \(O(N^4)\) or \(O(N^3)\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Piecewise Polynomial Decomposition via Tail Integral: Collect and sort the unique coordinates among \(\{0, L_1, R_1, \dots, L_N, R_N\}\) as \(0 = z_0 < z_1 < \dots < z_M\) (\(M \le 2N\)). By the tail integral identity: \[
\mathbb{E}[Y] = \int_0^{z_M} \mathbb{P}(Y \ge x)\,dx = \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \int_{z_m}^{z_{m+1}} \mathbb{P}(Y \ge x)\,dx.
\]
Bivariate Generating Polynomial on \([a, b] = [z_m, z_{m+1}]\): Fix an elementary interval \([a, b]\) of length \(\Delta = b - a\). Substitute \(x = a + \Delta \cdot u\) with \(u \in [0, 1]\), \(dx = \Delta\,du\). For each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\):

If \(R_i \le a\), \(\mathbb{P}(X_i \ge x) = 0\) (contributes factor \(1\)).
If \(L_i \ge b\), \(\mathbb{P}(X_i \ge x) = 1\) (contributes factor \(y\)).
If \(L_i \le a < b \le R_i\), let \(\ell_i = (R_i - L_i)^{-1} \bmod p\). Then: \[
p_i(u) = \mathbb{P}(X_i \ge a + \Delta u) = (R_i - a)\ell_i - (\Delta \ell_i) u = \alpha_i + \beta_i u,
\] which contributes the linear factor \(\big((1 - \alpha_i) - \beta_i u\big) + y(\alpha_i + \beta_i u)\).

D-Finite Moment Integration and \(O(N^3)\) Sliding Update: Let \(c_{\text{always}}\) be the count of variables with \(L_i \ge b\), and let \(S_{\text{act}}\) be the set of \(A = |S_{\text{act}}|\) active variables with \(L_i \le a < b \le R_i\). On \([a, b]\), at least \(K\) variables are \(\ge x\) if and only if at least \(r = \max(0, K - c_{\text{always}})\) of the active variables in \(S_{\text{act}}\) are \(\ge x\). Expanding \(\prod_{i \in S_{\text{act}}} \big((1 - p_i(u)) + y p_i(u)\big) = \sum_{j=0}^A \sum_{d=0}^A C_{j, d} y^j u^d\) and integrating \(\int_0^1 u^d\,du = \frac{1}{d + 1}\) (the base case of the D-finite Beta recurrence \((d + s + 1)I_{d,s} = s I_{d, s-1}\)) gives the interval contribution: \[
\int_a^b \mathbb{P}(Y \ge x)\,dx = (b - a) \sum_{j=r}^A \sum_{d=0}^A \frac{C_{j, d}}{d + 1}.
\] Furthermore, if we work directly in the unshifted coordinate \(x\) (writing \(p_i(x) = R_i \ell_i - \ell_i x\)), the bivariate polynomial \(Q(x, y) = \prod_{i \in S_{\text{act}}} \big((1 - p_i(x)) + y p_i(x)\big)\) only changes by inserting one factor when \(z_m = L_i\) or synthetic-dividing by one factor when \(z_m = R_i\), reducing the update per endpoint from \(O(N^3)\) to \(O(N^2)\) and total time to \(O(N^3)\)!



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(1 \le K \le N \le 50\) and intervals \([L_i, R_i]\) (\(0 \le L_i < R_i \le 10^9\)); requires \(R_i - L_i \not\equiv 0 \pmod{998244353}\) and \(N + 1 < 998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): \(\mathbb{E}[Y] \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N^3)\) time using sliding bivariate multiplication/division (or \(O(N^4)\) rebuilding per interval) and \(O(N^2)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: On each elementary interval \([z_m, z_{m+1}]\), no endpoint \(L_i\) or \(R_i\) lies in the open interior \((z_m, z_{m+1})\), so every survival probability \(\mathbb{P}(X_i \ge x)\) is an exact polynomial of degree \(\le 1\) on \([z_m, z_{m+1}]\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(c_{\text{always}} + |S_{\text{act}}| < K\) on \([z_m, z_{m+1}]\), then \(\mathbb{P}(Y \ge x) = 0\) on that interval; if \(z_m < \min_i L_i\) and \(N \ge K\), \(\mathbb{P}(Y \ge x) = 1\) contributes \(z_{m+1} - z_m\) directly.









Intermediate 2 (#239) — Algebraic-to-D-Finite ODE Compilation for \(O(N)\) Walk Extraction (yukicoder 1504 — Holonomic Walk)

Tier: Intermediate 2 | Canonical ID: #239
Source: yukicoder No. 1504 — Holonomic Walk
Prerequisite Tags: Recipe A & Recipe B (§18.2), Quadratic Radical Elimination, 3-Term P-Recursive Lattice Walk Unrolling


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Consider weighted lattice paths of length \(n\) starting at \((0, 0)\) in which each step \((1, +1)\) (up-step) has weight \(b\), each step \((1, 0)\) (level-step) has weight \(a\), and each step \((1, -1)\) (down-step) has weight \(c\). Given non-negative integer weights \((a, b, c)\) and a maximum length \(N\):

Let \(b_n\) be the total weight of bridge walks of length \(n\) that end at altitude \(0\) (permitted to visit negative altitudes), whose ordinary generating function is: \[
B(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty b_n x^n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 2ax + (a^2 - 4bc)x^2}}.
\]
Let \(e_n\) be the total weight of excursion (Motzkin) walks of length \(n\) that end at altitude \(0\) and never drop below altitude \(0\), whose ordinary generating function satisfies \(E(x) = 1 + a x E(x) + b c x^2 E(x)^2\): \[
E(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty e_n x^n = \frac{1 - ax - \sqrt{1 - 2ax + (a^2 - 4bc)x^2}}{2bc x^2}.
\]

Compile both \(B(x)\) and \(E(x)\) into D-finite linear ODEs to compute \(b_0, b_1, \dots, b_N\) and \(e_0, e_1, \dots, e_N\) modulo \(998244353\) in \(O(N)\) time with zero NTTs.

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^6\), \(0 \le a, b, c < 998244353\), modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space (or \(O(1)\) streaming space).



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Instance (\(a = 1, b = 1, c = 1, N = 4\)): Here \(\Delta(x) = 1 - 2x - 3x^2\):

Bridges \(B(x) = (1 - 2x - 3x^2)^{-1/2}\):

\(n = 0\): \(b_0 = 1\) (empty walk).
\(n = 1\): \(b_1 = 1\) (step L).
\(n = 2\): \(b_2 = 3\) (LL, UD, DU).
\(n = 3\): \(b_3 = 7\) (LLL and \(6\) permutations of {L, U, D}).
\(n = 4\): \(b_4 = 19\) (\(1\) LLLL \(+ 12\) {L,L,U,D} \(+ 6\) {U,U,D,D}).

Excursions \(E(x) = \frac{1 - x - \sqrt{1 - 2x - 3x^2}}{2x^2}\) (Motzkin numbers):

\(n = 0\): \(e_0 = 1\).
\(n = 1\): \(e_1 = 1\) (L).
\(n = 2\): \(e_2 = 2\) (LL, UD).
\(n = 3\): \(e_3 = 4\) (LLL, LUD, ULD, UDL).
\(n = 4\): \(e_4 = 9\).





Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

With \(N = 2 \times 10^6\), calling an \(O(N \log N)\) polynomial square-root and inverse template requires multiple length-\(2^{22}\) NTTs and risks TLE. Look instead at the algebraic structure of \(B(x) = \Delta(x)^{-1/2}\) and \(E(x) = \frac{1 - ax - \sqrt{\Delta(x)}}{2bc x^2}\) where \(\Delta(x) = 1 - 2ax + (a^2 - 4bc)x^2\): how can you differentiate \(B(x)\) and the pure radical part of \(E(x)\) to turn both algebraic expressions into first-order linear ODEs with low-degree polynomial coefficients?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Let \(\gamma = a^2 - 4bc\) so \(\Delta(x) = 1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2\).

For \(B(x) = \Delta(x)^{-1/2}\), Recipe A gives \(\Delta(x) B'(x) = (a - \gamma x) B(x)\).
For \(E(x)\), isolate the radical \(Y(x) = 2bc x^2 E(x) + ax - 1 = -\sqrt{\Delta(x)}\), which satisfies \(\Delta(x) Y'(x) = -(a - \gamma x) Y(x)\). Alternatively, observe directly that \(Y(x) = -\Delta(x) B(x) = -(1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2) B(x)\), which expresses \(e_n\) as a 3-term linear combination of \(b_n, b_{n+1}, b_{n+2}\)—or unroll \(e_n\) directly from its own 3-term P-recursion!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Extracting \([x^{n-1}]\) from \((1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2) B'(x) = (a - \gamma x) B(x)\) gives: \[
n b_n = a(2n - 1) b_{n-1} - (a^2 - 4bc)(n - 1) b_{n-2} \qquad (n \ge 1).
\] Substituting \(Y(x) = 2bc x^2 E(x) + ax - 1\) into \((1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2) Y'(x) + (a - \gamma x) Y(x) = 0\) and extracting \([x^{n+1}]\) for \(n \ge 2\) gives: \[
(n + 2) e_n = a(2n + 1) e_{n-1} - (a^2 - 4bc)(n - 1) e_{n-2} \qquad (n \ge 2).
\] Precompute modular inverses \(\text{inv}[1 \dots N+2]\) in \(O(N)\) time to unroll both arrays in a single pass!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Compiling \(B(x) = \Delta(x)^{-1/2}\) via Recipe A: Set \(\gamma = (a^2 - 4bc) \bmod p\) and \(\Delta(x) = 1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2\). Taking the logarithmic derivative of \(B(x) = \Delta(x)^{-1/2}\) gives: \[
\frac{B'(x)}{B(x)} = -\frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta'(x)}{\Delta(x)} = \frac{a - \gamma x}{1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2} \implies (1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2) B'(x) - (a - \gamma x) B(x) = 0.
\] Extracting \([x^{n-1}]\) for \(n \ge 1\): \[
n b_n - 2a(n - 1) b_{n-1} + \gamma(n - 2) b_{n-2} - a b_{n-1} + \gamma b_{n-2} = 0 \implies n b_n = a(2n - 1) b_{n-1} - (a^2 - 4bc)(n - 1) b_{n-2},
\] seeded with \(b_0 = 1\) and \(b_1 = a\).
Compiling \(E(x)\) via Recipe B: From \(bc x^2 E(x)^2 + (ax - 1) E(x) + 1 = 0\), define \(Y(x) = 2bc x^2 E(x) + ax - 1 = -\Delta(x)^{1/2}\). By Recipe A with exponent \(+1/2\), \(Y(x)\) satisfies: \[
(1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2) Y'(x) + (a - \gamma x) Y(x) = 0.
\] Substitute \(Y(x) = 2bc x^2 E(x) + ax - 1\) and \(Y'(x) = 2bc x^2 E'(x) + 4bc x E(x) + a\): \[
2bc\Big( x^2(1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2) E'(x) + x(2 - 3ax + \gamma x^2) E(x) \Big) + (1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2)a + (a - \gamma x)(ax - 1) = 0.
\] Notice that the inhomogeneous polynomial on the left simplifies to \(a(1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2) - a(1 - ax) + \gamma x(1 - ax) = (\gamma - a^2)x = -4bc x\). Dividing the entire ODE by \(2bc\) (which is valid symbolically even when \(bc = 0\), as \(bc\) cancels out!) gives the exact linear ODE: \[
x^2(1 - 2ax + \gamma x^2) E'(x) + x(2 - 3ax + \gamma x^2) E(x) = 2x.
\] Extracting \([x^{n+1}]\) for \(n \ge 1\) (where \([x^{n+1}](2x) = 0\)) gives: \[
(n + 2) e_n = a(2n + 1) e_{n-1} - (a^2 - 4bc)(n - 1) e_{n-2} \qquad (n \ge 1, \quad e_0 = 1, \; e_{-1} = 0).
\] Observe that because we divided by \(2bc\) symbolically before setting coefficients to zero, this 3-term recurrence works even in the degenerate case \(bc \equiv 0 \pmod p\) (where \(\gamma = a^2\) and \(e_n = a^n\))!



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(N \le 2 \times 10^6\) and step weights \(a, b, c \in \mathbb{F}_{998244353}\); requires \(N + 2 < 998244353\) so the indicial polynomials \(I_B(n) = n\) and \(I_E(n) = n + 2\) never vanish modulo \(998244353\) for \(1 \le n \le N\).
Postconditions (Output): Arrays \((b_0, \dots, b_N)\) and \((e_0, \dots, e_N)\) modulo \(998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space using linear-time inverse precomputation inv[i] = (MOD - MOD / i) * inv[MOD % i] % MOD.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After symbolic cancellation of \(2bc\), the inhomogeneous forcing term \(2x\) has degree \(1\), so for all \(n \ge 1\) the coefficient \([x^{n+1}]\) of the ODE is strictly homogeneous of shift width \(2\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(bc \equiv 0 \pmod{998244353}\), evaluating \(E(x) = \frac{1-ax-\sqrt{\Delta(x)}}{2bc x^2}\) directly divides by zero, whereas the symbolically simplified recurrence \((n+2)e_n = a(2n+1)e_{n-1} - a^2(n-1)e_{n-2}\) remains valid and outputs \(e_n = b_n = a^n\).









Advanced 1 (#125) — Tree Centroid Differential Recurrence (Codeforces 1667E — Centroid Probabilities)

Tier: Advanced 1 | Canonical ID: #125
Source: Codeforces Round 783 (Div. 1), Problem E — Centroid Probabilities
Prerequisite Tags: Recursive Tree EGF, Truncated Logarithm D-Finite ODE (§18.1), Reversed Convolution vs. Ancestor Suffix Reduction


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given an odd integer \(n \ge 3\). Consider all \((n - 1)!\) labelled recursive trees on \(n\) vertices \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\), formed by attaching each vertex \(i = 2, 3, \dots, n\) to a parent \(p_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, i-1\}\). Because \(n\) is odd, every tree \(T\) has a unique centroid—a vertex \(v\) such that every connected component of \(T \setminus \{v\}\) has at most \(m = \frac{n-1}{2}\) vertices.
For each vertex \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n\), compute the number of trees (among the \((n - 1)!\) recursive trees) in which vertex \(i\) is the unique centroid, modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(3 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\) (\(n\) is odd), modulus \(998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) via D-finite ODE + reversed NTT convolution, or \(O(n)\) via ancestor-probability suffix reduction.



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Instance 1 (\(n = 3, m = 1\)): There are \(2! = 2\) trees on \(\{1, 2, 3\}\):

\(p_2 = 1, p_3 = 1\) (star centered at \(1\)): centroid is \(1\).
\(p_2 = 1, p_3 = 2\) (path \(1 - 2 - 3\)): centroid is \(2\). Output for \(i = 1, 2, 3\): 1 1 0.

Instance 2 (\(n = 5, m = 2\)): Among the \(4! = 24\) trees on \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\):

Vertex \(3\) is the centroid iff \(\{4, 5\}\) both attach inside \(3\)’s subtree (\(1 \times 2 = 2\) ways) while \(2\) attaches to \(1\) (\(1\) way) and \(3\) attaches to \(\{1, 2\}\) (\(2\) ways), giving \(4\) trees.
Vertex \(2\) has subtree size \(\ge 3\) in \(12\) trees, of which \(2\) have centroid \(3\) (when \(3\) attaches to \(2\)), leaving \(12 - 2 = 10\) trees with centroid \(2\).
Vertex \(1\) is the centroid in the remaining \(24 - 10 - 4 = 10\) trees. Output for \(i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\): 10 10 4 0 0.




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Root the recursive tree at vertex \(1\). Then every child of any vertex \(v\) has a label \(> v\). Vertex \(i\) is the unique centroid if and only if:

The subtree rooted at \(i\) has size \(s \ge m + 1 = \frac{n+1}{2}\) (so the component above \(i\) has size \(n - s \le m\)), and
Every child subtree of \(i\) has size \(\le m\). What is the EGF of recursive trees rooted at a minimum-label vertex whose child subtrees all have size \(\le m\)?




Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

We can solve this from two dual perspectives:

D-Finite ODE + Reversed Convolution: The unrestricted EGF of recursive trees is \(T(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} (k-1)! \frac{x^k}{k!} = \ln \frac{1}{1-x}\) since \(T'(x) = \exp(T(x))\). Restricting child subtrees to size \(\le m\) replaces \(T(x)\) on the right-hand side by the truncated logarithm \(T_{\le m}(x) = \sum_{k=1}^m \frac{x^k}{k}\), so \(F'(x) = \exp\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^m \frac{x^k}{k}\right)\). Taking the logarithmic derivative of \(G(x) = F'(x)\) yields a 3-sparse D-finite ODE \((1-x)G'(x) = (1-x^m)G(x)\)!
Ancestor Dominance + Suffix Sum: Alternatively, let \(A_i\) be the number of trees where \(i\)’s subtree has size \(s \ge m + 1\) (without restricting \(i\)’s children). In any such tree, the unique centroid \(j \ge i\) lies inside \(i\)’s subtree, and for any \(j > i\), the probability that \(i\) is an ancestor of \(j\) is \(\frac{1}{i}\)!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


In Perspective 1: From \((1-x)G'(x) = (1-x^m)G(x)\), unroll \(g_k = [x^k]G(x)\) in \(O(n)\) time via \(k g_k = k g_{k-1} - g_{k-1-m}\), set \(f_s = g_{s-1}/s\), and for \(i \ge 2\) evaluate \(\text{ans}_i = (i-1)(n-i)! \sum_{s=m+1}^{n-i+1} f_s \frac{(s-1)! (n-s-1)!}{(n-i-s+1)!}\) via a single reversed NTT convolution in \(O(n \log n)\) time!
In Perspective 2: Summing over \(s \ge m + 1\) via the Hockey-Stick identity gives \(A_i = (n - i)! (i - 1)! \binom{n - m - 1}{i - 1}\) in closed form, and \(\text{ans}_i = A_i - \frac{1}{i} \sum_{j=i+1}^n \text{ans}_j\) unrolls in \(O(n)\) time with zero NTTs!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation
Let \(m = \frac{n-1}{2}\). Notice immediately that for \(i > m + 1\), vertex \(i\) can have at most \(n - i < m\) descendants from \(\{i+1, \dots, n\}\), so its subtree size is at most \(n - i + 1 \le m\), making \(\text{ans}_i = 0\).

Perspective 1 (D-Finite ODE for Constrained Recursive Trees + Reversed Convolution): Let \(F(x) = \sum_{s=1}^n f_s x^s\) be the EGF of recursive trees in which every child subtree of the root has size \(\le m\). Since the root holds the smallest label in its subtree, removing the root leaves a set of recursive trees of sizes \(\le m\), each with EGF \(T_{\le m}(x) = \sum_{k=1}^m (k-1)! \frac{x^k}{k!} = \sum_{k=1}^m \frac{x^k}{k}\). Thus \(G(x) = F'(x) = \exp\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^m \frac{x^k}{k}\right)\). Applying Recipe A to \(G(x)\): \[
\frac{G'(x)}{G(x)} = \sum_{k=1}^m x^{k-1} = \frac{1 - x^m}{1 - x} \implies (1 - x) G'(x) - (1 - x^m) G(x) = 0.
\] Extracting \([x^{k-1}]\) gives the 3-term P-recursive relation: \[
k g_k - (k - 1) g_{k-1} = g_{k-1} - g_{k-1-m} \implies g_k = g_{k-1} - \frac{g_{k-1-m}}{k} \qquad (k \ge 1, \; g_0 = 1).
\] For \(1 \le k \le m\), \(g_k = 1\); for \(m + 1 \le k \le n - 1\), \(k - 1 - m < m\) so \(g_{k-1-m} = 1\) and \(g_k = 1 - \sum_{r=m+1}^k \frac{1}{r}\). Then \(f_s = \frac{g_{s-1}}{s}\). For \(i = 1\), \(\text{ans}_1 = n! f_n = (n-1)! g_{n-1}\). For \(2 \le i \le m + 1\), choosing \(s - 1\) descendants of \(i\) from \(\{i+1, \dots, n\}\) in \(\binom{n-i}{s-1}\) ways, forming a valid centroid subtree on \(i\) in \(s! f_s\) ways, attaching \(i\) to \(\{1, \dots, i-1\}\) in \(i - 1\) ways, and attaching the remaining \(n - s - i + 1\) vertices outside \(i\)’s subtree in \(\frac{(n-s-1)!}{(i-1)!}\) ways gives: \[
\text{ans}_i = (i - 1)(n - i)! \sum_{s=m+1}^{n-i+1} \Big( (s - 1)! g_{s-1} (n - s - 1)! \Big) \cdot \frac{1}{((n - i + 1) - s)!},
\] which is a single reversed convolution evaluated for all \(i\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time via NTT.
Perspective 2 (\(O(n)\) Closed-Form \(A_i\) + Ancestor Suffix Sum): Let \(A_i\) be the number of trees where \(i\)’s subtree has size \(s \ge m + 1\) (with no restriction on \(i\)’s children, replacing \(s! f_s\) by \((s-1)!\)). Using \(\frac{(n-s-1)!}{(n-i-s+1)!} = (i - 2)! \binom{n-s-1}{i-2}\) and the Hockey-Stick identity: \[
A_i = (i - 1)(n - i)! \sum_{s=m+1}^{n-i+1} (i - 2)! \binom{n - s - 1}{i - 2} = (n - i)! (i - 1)! \binom{n - m - 1}{i - 1} \qquad (2 \le i \le m + 1),
\] and \(A_1 = (n - 1)!\). In any tree counted by \(A_i\), the unique centroid is some \(j \ge i\) inside \(i\)’s subtree. Conversely, for any fixed centroid \(j > i\), the attachment of \(\{1, \dots, j\}\) outside \(j\)’s subtree is independent of the internal structure of \(j\)’s subtree, and \(i\) is an ancestor of \(j\) with probability \(\frac{1}{i}\). Therefore: \[
A_i = \text{ans}_i + \frac{1}{i} \sum_{j=i+1}^n \text{ans}_j \implies \text{ans}_i = A_i - \frac{1}{i} \sum_{j=i+1}^n \text{ans}_j,
\] which computes \(\text{ans}_n, \text{ans}_{n-1}, \dots, \text{ans}_1\) in \(O(n)\) time with zero NTTs!



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Odd integer \(3 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\); requires \(n < 998244353\) so all factorials and inverses \(1/i\) exist in \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}\).
Postconditions (Output): Sequence \(\text{ans}_1, \dots, \text{ans}_n \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space via Perspective 2 (or \(O(n \log n)\) via Perspective 1).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Since \(n = 2m + 1\) is odd, the vertices with subtree size \(\ge m + 1\) form a downward chain from vertex \(1\) ending at the unique centroid \(j\), and each \(i < j\) lies on this chain with probability \(1/i\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: For \(i > m + 1\), a vertex \(i\) cannot have \(m = (n-1)/2\) descendants Chosen from \(\{i+1, \dots, n\}\), so \(A_i = 0\) and \(\text{ans}_i = 0\) identically; only indices \(1 \le i \le m + 1\) have non-zero centroid probabilities.









Advanced 2 (#088) — Delannoy Anti-Diagonal P-Recursion (Codeforces 755G — PolandBall and Many Other Balls)

Tier: Advanced 2 | Canonical ID: #088
Source: Codeforces 8VC Venture Cup 2017 — Elimination Round, Problem G — PolandBall and Many Other Balls
Prerequisite Tags: Bivariate Rational Generating Function, Legendre / Delannoy Radical (§18.2), \(O(K)\) P-Recursive Row Unrolling


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
There are \(n\) balls arranged in a single row, numbered \(1, 2, \dots, n\) from left to right. You want to form exactly \(k\) disjoint groups, where each group consists of either a single ball \(\{i\}\) or two adjacent balls \(\{i, i+1\}\). Each ball may belong to at most one group.
Given \(n\) and \(K\), compute the number of ways to form \(k\) groups for every \(k = 1, 2, \dots, K\), modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 10^9\), \(1 \le K < 2^{15} = 32768\), modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O(K)\) time and \(O(K)\) space via D-finite P-recursion (improving over \(O(K \log K \log n)\) polynomial doubling).



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Instance (\(n = 3, K = 3\)):

\(k = 1\): \(3\) singletons \(\{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}\) plus \(2\) adjacent pairs \(\{1, 2\}, \{2, 3\}\), giving \(5\) ways.
\(k = 2\): \(3\) pairs of singletons (\(\{1\}\{2\}\), \(\{1\}\{3\}\), \(\{2\}\{3\}\)) plus \(2\) combinations of one pair and one singleton (\(\{1,2\}\{3\}\), \(\{1\}\{2,3\}\)), giving \(5\) ways.
\(k = 3\): \(1\) way (\(\{1\}\{2\}\{3\}\)). Output for \(k = 1, 2, 3\): 5 5 1.




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(x\) mark the ball count and \(y\) mark the group count. At each step, we can leave a ball unused (weight \(x\)), form a 1-ball group (weight \(xy\)), or form a 2-ball group (weight \(x^2 y\)). Accounting for the boundary at the end of the row (or decomposing into \(k\) groups and \(n - k\) gaps), write the bivariate rational generating function \(G(x, y)\) whose coefficient \([x^n y^k] G(x, y)\) is the answer \(a_k\)!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

The bivariate OGF is: \[
G(x, y) = \frac{1}{1 - (1 + y)x - y x^2}.
\] To extract the row polynomial \(R_n(y) = [x^n] G(x, y) = \sum_{k=0}^K a_k y^k \bmod y^{K+1}\) for a fixed \(n \le 10^9\) in \(O(K)\) time:

Partial Fraction Radical in \(x\): Let \(\Delta(y) = (1 + y)^2 + 4y = 1 + 6y + y^2\). By partial fractions in \(x\), \[
R_n(y) = [x^n] \frac{1}{1 - (1+y)x - yx^2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\Delta(y)}} \left[ \left(\frac{1 + y + \sqrt{\Delta(y)}}{2}\right)^{n+1} - \left(\frac{1 + y - \sqrt{\Delta(y)}}{2}\right)^{n+1} \right].
\] For \(k \le \min(n, K)\), the negative branch \(\left(\frac{1+y-\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}\right)^{n+1} = (-y)^{n+1}\left(\frac{1+y+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}\right)^{-(n+1)}\) has valuation \(y^{n+1}\), so modulo \(y^{\min(n, K)+1}\) we can drop the second branch completely.
Combinatorial Identification with the Delannoy Anti-Diagonal: Choosing \(j\) two-ball groups and \(k - j\) one-ball groups leaves \(n - k - j\) unused balls, giving \(a_k = \sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j} \binom{n - j}{k} = [u^{n-k} v^k] \frac{1}{1 - u - v - uv}\), which is the anti-diagonal entry \(d_{n-k, k}\) of the Delannoy array.




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Apply the partial Euler operators \(\vartheta_u = u \partial_u\) and \(\vartheta_v = v \partial_v\) to the symmetric Delannoy generating function \(D(u, v) = (1 - u - v - uv)^{-1}\) (or eliminate the off-anti-diagonal entries from \(d_{a, b} = d_{a-1, b} + d_{a, b-1} + d_{a-1, b-1}\) along \((a, b) = (n - k, k)\)) to obtain the 3-term P-recursive relation: \[
(k + 1)(n - k)(n + 1 - 2k) a_{k+1} = (n - 2k)\Big( (2n - 1)(n + 1) - 6k(n - k) \Big) a_k - k(n + 1 - k)(n - 1 - 2k) a_{k-1}.
\] This unrolls \(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_K\) in \(O(K)\) time with zero NTTs.







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Bivariate Rational OGF & Partial-Fraction Eigenvalues: A sequence of \(n\) balls partitioned into \(k\) groups of sizes \(\in \{1, 2\}\) and \(n - k - (\text{pairs})\) free balls has OGF: \[
G(x, y) = \frac{1}{1 - (1 + y)x - y x^2} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty R_n(y) x^n.
\] Let \(\Delta(y) = (1 + y)^2 + 4y = 1 + 6y + y^2\), and let \(\lambda_\pm(y) = \frac{1 + y \pm \sqrt{\Delta(y)}}{2}\) be the two characteristic roots, satisfying \(\lambda_+(y) + \lambda_-(y) = 1 + y\), \(\lambda_+(y) \lambda_-(y) = -y\), and \(\lambda_+(y) - \lambda_-(y) = \sqrt{\Delta(y)}\). By partial fractions in \(x\): \[
R_n(y) = \frac{\lambda_+(y)^{n+1} - \lambda_-(y)^{n+1}}{\lambda_+(y) - \lambda_-(y)} = \frac{\lambda_+(y)^{n+1} - \lambda_-(y)^{n+1}}{\sqrt{1 + 6y + y^2}}.
\]
Reduction to the Delannoy Anti-Diagonal \(d_{n-k, k}\): Substituting \(y = t / x\) into \(G(x, y) = \frac{1}{1 - x - xy - x^2 y}\) maps \([x^n y^k] G(x, y)\) to \([x^{n-k} t^k] \frac{1}{1 - x - t - xt}\). Setting \(u = x\) and \(v = t\), \(D(u, v) = \frac{1}{1 - u - v - uv} = \sum_{a, b \ge 0} d_{a, b} u^a v^b\) is the bivariate Delannoy generating function, so: \[
a_k = d_{n-k, k} = [u^{n-k} v^k] \frac{1}{1 - u - v - uv} = \sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j} \binom{n - j}{k}.
\]
The Exact 3-Term P-Recursion for \(a_k = d_{n-k, k}\): Write the binomial sum in terms of Jacobi polynomials as \(a_k = \sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}\binom{n-j}{k} = P_k^{(0, n-2k)}(3)\) (or apply Zeilberger creative telescoping / the bivariate Euler operators \((1-u-v-uv)\vartheta_u D = u(1+v)D\) and \((1-u-v-uv)\vartheta_v D = v(1+u)D\) coupled with the combinatorial step \(d_{a,b} = d_{a-1,b} + d_{a,b-1} + d_{a-1,b-1}\)). Eliminating the off-anti-diagonal shifts along \((a, b) = (n - k, k)\) yields the exact 3-term P-recursive relation: \[
(k + 1)(n - k)(n + 1 - 2k) a_{k+1} = (n - 2k)\Big( (2n - 1)(n + 1) - 6k(n - k) \Big) a_k - k(n + 1 - k)(n - 1 - 2k) a_{k-1}.
\] Let us verify this on our sample trace \(n = 3\):

Base cases: \(a_0 = 1\), \(a_1 = 2n - 1 = 5\).
For \(k = 1\) (\(n = 3\)):

LHS: \((2)(2)(2) a_2 = 8 a_2\).
RHS: \((1)\big(5 \cdot 4 - 6 \cdot 1 \cdot 2\big) a_1 - (1)(3)(0) a_0 = (20 - 12) \cdot 5 - 0 = 40 \implies a_2 = 40 / 8 = 5\).

For \(k = 2\) (\(n = 3\)):

LHS: \((3)(1)(0) a_3 = 0\). Here \(n + 1 - 2k = 0\) is a Case 1 true integer root in \(\mathbb{Z}\) (\(2k = n + 1\)), where the symmetry of the anti-diagonal gives \(a_{k+1} = a_k\) directly! Meanwhile, when \(n \ge p = 998244353\), either \((n - k) \equiv 0 \pmod p\) or \((n + 1 - 2k) \equiv 0 \pmod p\) can occur at most once in \(1 \le k < K < p\) as a Case 2 purely modular root (Failure Mode #8, §18.4); at that single index \(k\) (or using PAdicVal lifting modulo \(p^2\)), we evaluate \(a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}\) in \(O(k)\) time via \(\sum_{j=0}^{k+1} \binom{k+1}{j}\binom{n-j}{k+1}\) and resume the recurrence.



// Unrolling a_k = d_{n-k, k} for k = 0..K in O(K) time
a[0] = 1; if (K >= 1) a[1] = (2LL * n - 1) % MOD;
for (int k = 1; k < K; ++k) {
    if (k + 1 > n) { a[k + 1] = 0; continue; }
    if (2LL * k == n + 1) { a[k + 1] = a[k]; continue; } // True Z-root: symmetry a_{k+1} = a_k
    long long nm = n % MOD, c_next = (k + 1LL) * ((nm - k + MOD) % MOD) % MOD * ((nm + 1 - 2LL * k % MOD + MOD) % MOD) % MOD;
    if (c_next == 0) { // Modular root (when n >= MOD): O(k) direct fallback or PAdicVal lift
        a[k + 1] = eval_single_binom_sum(n, k + 1); continue;
    }
    long long c_cur = (nm - 2LL * k % MOD + MOD) % MOD * (((2 * nm + MOD - 1) % MOD * (nm + 1) - 6LL * k * (nm - k + MOD)) % MOD + MOD) % MOD;
    long long c_prev = 1LL * k * ((nm + 1 - k + MOD) % MOD) % MOD * ((nm - 1 - 2LL * k % MOD + MOD) % MOD) % MOD;
    a[k + 1] = (c_cur * a[k] % MOD - c_prev * a[k - 1] % MOD + MOD) % MOD * inv(c_next) % MOD;
}


Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(1 \le n \le 10^9\) and \(1 \le K < 32768\); requires prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > K\).
Postconditions (Output): Sequence \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_K \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(K)\) time and \(O(K)\) space, with zero NTTs.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: The 3-term P-recursion eliminates the off-anti-diagonal entries of the Delannoy recurrence \(d_{a, b} = d_{a-1, b} + d_{a, b-1} + d_{a-1, b-1}\) across \((a, b) = (n-k, k)\), keeping the computation confined to the 1D slice \(a + b = n\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: For \(k > n\), \(a_k = 0\) identically; at the single possible true integer root \(2k = n + 1\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\), anti-diagonal symmetry gives \(a_{k+1} = a_k\) in \(O(1)\) time; if \(n \ge p\) causes \((n - k) \equiv 0\) or \((n + 1 - 2k) \equiv 0 \pmod p\) (Failure Mode #8), the single singular step is resolved via \(O(K)\) binomial summation or §18.4 PAdicVal lifting modulo \(p^2\).









Mastery 1 (#211) — Bivariate Euler PDE & Roots of Unity Filter (UOJ 450 — [集训队作业2018] 复读机)

Tier: Mastery 1 | Canonical ID: #211
Source: Universal Online Judge (UOJ) #450 — 【集训队作业2018】复读机
Prerequisite Tags: Roots-of-Unity EGF Filter, Cyclotomic Basis Reduction, Bivariate Euler Homogeneous PDE (\(\vartheta_x, \vartheta_y\) from §18.1–18.2)


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
A repeater broadcasts a sequence of length \(n\) over an alphabet of \(k\) distinct machine types \(\{1, 2, \dots, k\}\). A sequence of length \(n\) is valid if and only if the number of occurrences of every machine type \(i \in \{1, \dots, k\}\) is a multiple of \(d\), where \(d \in \{1, 2, 3\}\).
Given \(n, k, d\), compute the number of valid sequences of length \(n\) modulo the prime \(p = 19491001\): \[
\text{Ans} = n! [z^n] \left( \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{z^{d m}}{(d m)!} \right)^k \pmod{19491001}.
\]

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 10^9\), \(d \in \{1, 2, 3\}\), modulus \(p = 19491001\) (prime with \(p - 1 = 19491000\), divisible by \(3\)).

For \(d = 1\): \(k \le 5 \times 10^5\).
For \(d = 2\): \(k \le 5 \times 10^5\).
For \(d = 3\): \(k \le 1000\).

Required Complexity: \(O(\log n)\) for \(d = 1\), \(O(k \log n)\) for \(d = 2\), and \(O(k^2 \log n)\) for \(d = 3\).



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Instance 1 (\(n = 4, k = 2, d = 2\)): Each of the \(k = 2\) machine types must appear an even number of times in a length-\(4\) sequence:

Type 1 appears \(4\) times, Type 2 appears \(0\) times: \(\binom{4}{4} = 1\) way.
Type 1 appears \(2\) times, Type 2 appears \(2\) times: \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) ways.
Type 1 appears \(0\) times, Type 2 appears \(4\) times: \(\binom{4}{0} = 1\) way. Total valid sequences: \(1 + 6 + 1 = 8\). Formula check (\(d = 2\)): \(2^{-2}\big((-2)^4 + 2 \cdot 0^4 + 2^4\big) = \frac{16 + 0 + 16}{4} = 8\).

Instance 2 (\(n = 3, k = 2, d = 3\)): Either all \(3\) characters are Type 1 (\(1\) way) or all \(3\) are Type 2 (\(1\) way). Total: \(2\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Because \(p = 19491001 \equiv 1 \pmod 3\), the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_p\) contains a primitive \(d\)-th root of unity \(\omega = g^{(p-1)/d} \bmod p\) (where \(g = 7\) is a primitive root modulo \(19491001\)). By the roots-of-unity filter, the EGF for a single machine type is: \[
E_d(z) = \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{z^{dm}}{(dm)!} = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{r=0}^{d-1} e^{\omega^r z}.
\] Recall that \(n! [z^n] e^{\alpha z} = \alpha^n\). How can we expand \(E_d(z)^k\) as a linear combination of exponentials \(e^{\alpha z}\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

For \(d = 3\), \(E_3(z)^k = 3^{-k} (e^z + e^{\omega z} + e^{\omega^2 z})^k\). In the cyclotomic ring \(\mathbb{Z}[\omega]\), the minimal polynomial of \(\omega\) is \(1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0\), so \(\omega^2 = -1 - \omega\). Thus if we set \(x = e^z\) and \(y = e^{\omega z}\), then \(e^{\omega^2 z} = x^{-1} y^{-1}\), and we are expanding the bivariate Laurent polynomial: \[
P(x, y) = \left(x + y + x^{-1} y^{-1}\right)^k = \sum_{i=-k}^k \sum_{j=-k}^k c_{i, j} x^i y^j.
\] Once \(c_{i, j}\) are known, substituting \(x^i y^j = e^{(i + j\omega)z}\) and extracting \(n!\,[z^n]\) gives \(3^{-k} \sum_{i, j} c_{i, j} (i + j\omega)^n\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

For \(P(x, y) = A(x, y)^k\) where \(A(x, y)\) is any sparse bivariate Laurent polynomial (such as \(x + y + x^{-1}y^{-1}\), or in \(d = 4, 6\) generalizations where \(A(x, y)\) has \(4+\) terms so trinomial expansion fails), apply the partial Euler operators \(\vartheta_x = x \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\) and \(\vartheta_y = y \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\) from §18.1–18.2 (Recipe A): \[
A(x, y) \vartheta_x P(x, y) = k \big(\vartheta_x A(x, y)\big) P(x, y), \qquad A(x, y) \vartheta_y P(x, y) = k \big(\vartheta_y A(x, y)\big) P(x, y).
\] Extracting \([x^i y^j]\) gives a sparse 2D P-recursive relation that computes every coefficient \(c_{i, j}\) in \(O(1)\) time per state!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Cases \(d = 1\) and \(d = 2\):

If \(d = 1\): \(E_1(z)^k = e^{k z}\), so \(\text{Ans} = n! [z^n] e^{k z} = k^n \bmod p\) in \(O(\log n)\) time.
If \(d = 2\): \(E_2(z)^k = 2^{-k} (e^z + e^{-z})^k = 2^{-k} \sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j} e^{(2j - k)z}\). Extracting \(n!\,[z^n]\) gives: \[
\text{Ans} = 2^{-k} \sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j} (2j - k)^n \pmod p,
\] evaluated in \(O(k \log n)\) time.

Case \(d = 3\) via Cyclotomic Reduction and Bivariate Euler PDE: Since \(p = 19491001\) has primitive root \(g = 7\), \(\omega = 7^{(p-1)/3} \bmod p = 663067\) satisfies \(1 + \omega + \omega^2 \equiv 0 \pmod p\) (when viewed as a formal cube root of unity; or directly in \(\mathbb{F}_p\), \(\omega^2 \equiv -1 - \omega \pmod p\)). Writing \(E_3(z)^k = 3^{-k} (e^z + e^{\omega z} + e^{(-1-\omega)z})^k\), let \(x = e^z\) and \(y = e^{\omega z}\) (or shift by \(e^{k(1+\omega)z}\) to work with non-negative exponents: let \(u = e^{(2+\omega)z}, v = e^{(1+2\omega)z}\) so \(e^z + e^{\omega z} + e^{(-1-\omega)z} = e^{(-1-\omega)z}(1 + u + v)\)). Let us write this in the general Bivariate Euler PDE framework so it applies to any \(m\)-term bivariate base \(A(u, v)^k\):

With the shifted non-negative variables \(u = x^2 y, v = x y^2\), the base polynomial is \(A(u, v) = 1 + u + v\), and for a general \(d\)-periodic filter (e.g., if an idle symbol \(+1\) is also present, \(A(x, y) = 1 + x + y + x^{-1}y^{-1}\)), \(P(x, y) = A(x, y)^k\) satisfies the coupled Euler PDEs: \[
A(x, y) \vartheta_x P(x, y) = k (\vartheta_x A(x, y)) P(x, y), \qquad A(x, y) \vartheta_y P(x, y) = k (\vartheta_y A(x, y)) P(x, y).
\]
Specifically, for \(P(u, v) = (1 + u + v)^k = \sum_{a \ge 0, b \ge 0, a+b \le k} c_{a, b} u^a v^b\), applying \((1 + u + v)\vartheta_u P = k u P\) and \((1 + u + v)\vartheta_v P = k v P\) gives: \[
a \, c_{a, b} = (k - a + 1) c_{a-1, b} - a \, c_{a, b-1},
\] or in explicit trinomial form \(c_{a, b} = \frac{k!}{a! \, b! \, (k - a - b)!}\).
Each monomial \(u^a v^b\) (where \(a\) counts choices of \(e^z\), \(b\) counts choices of \(e^{\omega z}\), and \(k - a - b\) counts choices of \(e^{\omega^2 z}\)) corresponds to the exponential \(\exp\!\Big(\big(a + b\omega + (k - a - b)\omega^2\big)z\Big)\).
Extracting \(n! [z^n]\) gives: \[
\text{Ans} = 3^{-k} \sum_{a=0}^k \sum_{b=0}^{k-a} c_{a, b} \Big( a + b\omega + (k - a - b)\omega^2 \Big)^n \pmod{19491001}.
\]




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Integers \(1 \le n \le 10^9\), \(k \ge 1\), and \(d \in \{1, 2, 3\}\) modulo prime \(p = 19491001\); requires \(3 \mid (p - 1)\) and \(k < p\), so \(d^{-k} \bmod p\), \(\omega = 7^{(p-1)/3} \bmod p\), and all factorials up to \(k\) are invertible in \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\).
Postconditions (Output): Number of valid sequences modulo \(19491001\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(\log n)\) time for \(d = 1\), \(O(k \log n)\) time for \(d = 2\), and \(O(k^2 \log n)\) time with \(O(k)\) space for \(d = 3\).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: The roots-of-unity filter \(\frac{1}{d}\sum_{r=0}^{d-1} \omega^{r m} = [d \mid m]\) projects the exponential generating function onto multiples of \(d\), and the bivariate expansion enumerates all \((d-1)\)-dimensional cyclotomic frequencies without collision.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: When \(a + b\omega + (k - a - b)\omega^2 \equiv 0 \pmod p\), the base of the \(n\)-th power is \(0 \bmod p\), which contributes \(0\) for all \(n \ge 1\) (avoiding \(0^0 = 1\)).









Mastery 2 (#230) — D-Finite P-Recursive Indicial Singularity Lifting (LibreOJ 6728 — U 群把妹王)

Tier: Mastery 2 | Canonical ID: #230
Source: LibreOJ #6728 — U 群把妹王
Prerequisite Tags: Prüfer Degree EGF, Recipe A Power ODE \(A(x)^n\) (§18.2), Failure Mode #8 (\(p\)-Adic Indicial Lifting over \(\mathbb{Z}/p^{V+1}\mathbb{Z}\), §18.4)


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given the number of vertices \(n\) (\(n \ge 2\)) of an unrooted labelled tree \(T\) on \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) and a sequence of degree weights \(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_{n-1}\) (where \(w_d\) is the weight of a vertex of degree \(d\), encoded as the Prüfer EGF \(A(x) = \sum_{c=0}^{n-2} a_c x^c\) with \(a_c = \frac{w_{c+1}}{c!}\)).
Compute the weighted sum over all \(n^{n-2}\) unrooted labelled trees on \(n\) vertices: \[
\text{Ans} = (n - 2)! [x^{n-2}] A(x)^n \pmod p,
\] where \(A(x)\) is a \(K\)-sparse polynomial (or rational power series reduced via Recipe A/B to an order-\(d\) P-recursive sequence \(I(m) p_m = \sum_{i=1}^d P_i(m - i) p_{m-i}\)) and the indicial polynomial \(I(m)\) may vanish modulo \(p\) at up to \(V\) intermediate indices \(1 \le m^* \le n - 2\) (Failure Mode #8).

Constraints: \(2 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\), sparsity \(K \le 50\) (or P-recursion order \(d \le 50\)), prime modulus \(p\) with total indicial valuation loss \(V = \sum_{m=1}^{n-2} v_p(I(m)) \le 3\).
Required Complexity: \(O(n K \cdot \text{poly}(V))\) time and \(O(n)\) space via Recipe A and \(p\)-adic valuation lifting (u, e) modulo \(p^{V+1}\) with zero NTTs (\(O(n K)\) hardware operations when \(V \le 1\) using __int128 modulo \(p^2\)).



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Instance 1 (Combinatorial Check for \(n = 4\), \(w_1 = 1, w_2 = 2, w_3 = 3\)): The \(4^{4-2} = 16\) labelled trees on \(4\) vertices consist of:

\(12\) paths of length \(3\) (two leaves of degree \(1\) and two internal vertices of degree \(2\)): each path has weight \(w_1^2 w_2^2 = 1^2 \cdot 2^2 = 4\), contributing \(12 \times 4 = 48\).
\(4\) stars \(K_{1, 3}\) (three leaves of degree \(1\) and one center of degree \(3\)): each star has weight \(w_1^3 w_3^1 = 1^3 \cdot 3^1 = 3\), contributing \(4 \times 3 = 12\). Total tree weight sum: \(48 + 12 = 60\). Formula check: \(A(x) = 1 + 2x + \frac{3}{2}x^2\). By Recipe A, \(p_m = [x^m] A(x)^4\) satisfies \(m p_m = 2(5 - m) p_{m-1} + \frac{3}{2}(10 - m) p_{m-2}\):
\(m = 0\): \(p_0 = 1\).
\(m = 1\): \(1 \cdot p_1 = 2(4)(1) = 8 \implies p_1 = 8\).
\(m = 2\): \(2 \cdot p_2 = 2(3)(8) + \frac{3}{2}(8)(1) = 48 + 12 = 60 \implies p_2 = 30\), and \((4 - 2)! p_2 = 2 \times 30 = 60\).

Instance 2 (\(p\)-Adic Indicial Singularity Trace at \(p = 3\) for \(P(x) = (1 + x + x^2)^4 = \sum_{m \ge 0} p_m x^m\) up to \(m = 4\)): Here \(m p_m = (5 - m) p_{m-1} + (10 - m) p_{m-2}\). At \(m^* = 3\), the indicial polynomial \(I(3) = 3 \equiv 0 \pmod 3\) vanishes (\(V = 1\)), so we work in \((u, e)\) modulo \(p^{V+1} = 9\):

\(m = 0\): \(p_0 = 1 \mapsto (1, 0)\).
\(m = 1\): \(1 \cdot p_1 = 4 p_0 = 4 \mapsto (4, 0)\).
\(m = 2\): \(2 \cdot p_2 = 3 p_1 + 8 p_0 = 12 + 8 = 20 \implies p_2 = 10 \mapsto (1, 0) \pmod 9\).
\(m = 3\) (Indicial Singularity \(I(3) = 3 \mapsto (1, 1)\)): RHS \(= 2 p_2 + 7 p_1 = 2(1, 0) + 7(4, 0) = (2 + 28, 0) = (30, 0) = 3 \times 10 \mapsto (1, 1) \pmod 9\). Dividing \((1, 1)\) by \(I(3) = (1, 1)\) subtracts the valuations: \(p_3 = (1 \cdot 1^{-1} \bmod 9, \, 1 - 1) = (1, 0)\) (indeed, \(p_3 = 16 \equiv 1 \pmod 3\))!
\(m = 4\): \(4 \cdot p_4 = 1 \cdot p_3 + 6 \cdot p_2 = (1, 0) + (2, 1) = (1 + 6, 0) = (7, 0) \pmod 9\). Dividing by \(4 \equiv 4 \pmod 9\) (\(4^{-1} \equiv 7 \pmod 9\)) gives \(p_4 = (49 \bmod 9, 0) = (4, 0) \implies p_4 \equiv 4 \equiv 1 \pmod 3\) (matching \(p_4 = 19 \equiv 1 \pmod 3\)).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

By Prüfer’s bijection, vertex \(i\) has degree \(d_i = c_i + 1\) iff \(i\) appears \(c_i \ge 0\) times in the Prüfer sequence of length \(n - 2\). Thus: \[
\sum_{T} \prod_{i=1}^n w_{\deg_T(i)} = (n - 2)! [x^{n-2}] A(x)^n, \qquad A(x) = \sum_{c=0}^{n-2} a_c x^c, \quad a_c = \frac{w_{c+1}}{c!}.
\] When \(A(x)\) is \(K\)-sparse (or satisfies a low-order rational ODE), how can you unroll the coefficients of \(P(x) = A(x)^n\) in \(O(n K)\) time without calling NTT, and what happens if the leading coefficient \(I(m)\) of the recurrence is divisible by \(p\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad


Valuation Shift & Recipe A Power ODE: If \(a_0 = w_1 = 0\), then \(\operatorname{val}(A) \ge 1\) so \(\operatorname{val}(A^n) \ge n > n - 2\) and the tree sum is \(0\) (more generally, strip \(v = \operatorname{val}(A)\) via \(A(x) = x^v \widetilde{A}(x)\) so \(\tilde{a}_0 \neq 0\)). Applying Recipe A (§18.2) to \(P(x) = \widetilde{A}(x)^n\) gives \(\widetilde{A}(x) P'(x) = n \widetilde{A}'(x) P(x)\); extracting \([x^{m-1}]\) yields \(\sum_{j \in S} (m - j) \tilde{a}_j p_{m-j} = \sum_{j \in S} n j \tilde{a}_j p_{m-j}\), and isolating \(j = 0\) gives: \[
m \tilde{a}_0 p_m = \sum_{j \in S \setminus \{0\}, \, j \le m} \big(j(n + 1) - m\big) \tilde{a}_j p_{m-j}.
\]
Crossing Modular Indicial Roots (Failure Mode #8): Whenever the indicial polynomial \(I(m)\) (such as \(m \tilde{a}_0\) when \(m \ge p\), or a cleared linear factor \((a m - b)\) in a higher-order D-finite recurrence) is divisible by \(p\) at \(m = m^*\), naive \(\mathbb{F}_p\) arithmetic divides by zero. How many extra base-\(p\) digits must we carry to survive all divisions by \(I(m)\)?




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Compute the total valuation loss \(V = \sum_{m=1}^{n-2} v_p(I(m))\) across the recurrence range. Represent every non-zero recurrence value \(p_m\) in the \(p\)-adic valuation form \((u_m, e_m)\) from §18.4, where \(p_m \equiv u_m \cdot p^{e_m} \pmod{p^{V+1}}\) with \(\gcd(u_m, p) = 1\). Since \(u_m \in (\mathbb{Z}/p^{V+1}\mathbb{Z})^\times\) is always a unit, division by \(I(m) = u_{I} \cdot p^{v_p(I(m))}\) simply multiplies \(u_m\) by \(u_I^{-1} \bmod p^{V+1}\) and subtracts \(v_p(I(m))\) from \(e_m\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Prüfer Degree EGF & Recipe A Compilation: By Prüfer’s bijection on \(n \ge 2\) vertices: \[
\text{Ans} = (n - 2)! [x^{n-2}] A(x)^n, \qquad A(x) = \sum_{c=0}^{n-2} a_c x^c, \quad a_c = \frac{w_{c+1}}{c!}.
\] If \(a_0 = w_1 = 0\), every tree on \(n \ge 2\) vertices has at least two leaves of degree \(1\), so \(\text{Ans} = 0\). Otherwise, let \(S = \{c : a_c \neq 0\}\) (\(|S| = K\)). Taking the logarithmic derivative of \(P(x) = A(x)^n = \sum_{m \ge 0} p_m x^m\) via Recipe A (§18.2) gives \(A(x) P'(x) = n A'(x) P(x)\). Extracting \([x^{m-1}]\) yields \(\sum_{c \in S} (m - c) a_c p_{m-c} = \sum_{c \in S} n c a_c p_{m-c}\); isolating \(c = 0\) on the left and moving \(c \ge 1\) to the right yields the \(K\)-term P-recursive relation: \[
I(m) p_m = \sum_{c \in S \setminus \{0\}, \, c \le m} \big(c(n + 1) - m\big) a_c p_{m-c}, \qquad I(m) = m a_0.
\]
Resolving Indicial Singularities via §18.4 \(p\)-Adic Lifting: In the general P-recursive setting \(I(m) p_m = \sum_{i=1}^d P_i(m - i) p_{m-i}\), let \(V = \sum_{m=1}^{n-2} v_p(I(m))\) be the total \(p\)-adic valuation of the indicial polynomial across the unrolling horizon, and set the working modulus to \(M = p^{V+1}\):

Lift each initial condition and polynomial coefficient into the PAdicVal representation \((u, e)\) with \(u \in (\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z})^\times\) and \(e \in \mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\}\) via PAdicVal::from_int(x, p, M).
At step \(m\), accumulate the right-hand side \(R_m = \sum_{i=1}^d P_i(m - i) p_{m-i}\) using add(a, b, p, M) and unit multiplication (u1 * u2 % M, e1 + e2).
Factor \(I(m) = u_I \cdot p^{e_I}\) with \(\gcd(u_I, p) = 1\). Since \(p \nmid u_I\), \(u_I\) is invertible in \(\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}\); compute \(u_I^{-1} \bmod M\) via the Extended Euclidean Algorithm (or Hensel lifting) and set: \[
p_m = \big((R_m.u \cdot u_I^{-1}) \bmod M, \; R_m.e - e_I\big).
\]
Because the true rational coefficient \(p_{n-2} = [x^{n-2}] A(x)^n\) is \(p\)-integral, its final exponent satisfies \(p_{n-2}.e \ge 0\), and reducing \((p_{n-2}.e > 0 \ ? \ 0 : p_{n-2}.u \bmod p)\) recovers the exact answer modulo \(p\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Integer \(n \ge 2\), sparse degree series \(A(x)\) with \(K\) non-zero terms (or order-\(d\) P-recursion), and prime modulus \(p\) with total indicial valuation loss \(V = \sum_{m=1}^{n-2} v_p(I(m))\); \(I(m) \neq 0\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) for all \(1 \le m \le n - 2\) (all true characteristic-\(0\) roots are seeded as initial conditions), and \(a_0 = w_1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\).
Postconditions (Output): Exact residue \((n - 2)! [x^{n-2}] A(x)^n \bmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n K \cdot \text{poly}(V))\) time and \(O(n \cdot V)\) space using PAdicVal arithmetic modulo \(p^{V+1}\) (\(O(n K)\) hardware operations when \(V \le 1\) using __int128 modulo \(p^2\)).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Each division by \(I(m)\) with \(v_p(I(m)) = e_I\) shifts the \(p\)-adic valuation by \(-e_I\) and consumes at most \(e_I\) base-\(p\) digits of precision when adding terms of different valuations; initializing with \(V + 1\) digits modulo \(p^{V+1}\) guarantees that at least \(1\) exact base-\(p\) digit of \(u_{n-2}\) survives at \(m = n - 2\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(I(m) = 0\) identically in \(\mathbb{Z}\), \(u_m\) is a free parameter (true characteristic-\(0\) indicial root) that must be supplied as an initial condition rather than lifted; for \(p\)-adic roots \(I(m) \equiv 0 \pmod p\) with \(I(m) \neq 0\), track (val, unit) modulo \(p^{V+1}\) and guard the final reconstruction with \(v \ge 0\) (returning \(0 \bmod p\) whenever \(v > 0\)).

Chapter 18 Checklist & Summary
Before moving on to Chapter 19, verify that you have mastered the following core skills:

The Euler Operator Dictionary (§18.1): Rewrite any polynomial-coefficient ODE into canonical \(\vartheta\)-form \(\sum_{i=0}^d x^i P_i(\vartheta) F(x) = 0\) using \(x^j D_x^j = \vartheta^{\underline{j}}\) and extract the P-recursive relation \(P_0(n) f_n = -\sum_{i=1}^d P_i(n-i) f_{n-i}\) without off-by-one shift errors.
Recipes A & B (§18.2): Compile rational powers \(A(x)B(x)^\alpha\), rational exponentials \(A(x)\exp(R(x)/S(x))\), and quadratic radicals \(\frac{-P_1 \pm \sqrt{\Delta}}{2P_2}\) into \(O(N)\) linear recurrences with zero NTTs.
The 7 ODE Archetypes (§18.3): Recognize Bernoulli (\(U = F^{1-m}\)), Riccati (\(F = -\frac{u'}{Cu}\)), autonomous, energy-integral, Liouville, and exponential gauge transformations that linearize or simplify differential equations.
D-Finite Closure & \(p\)-Adic Indicial Lifting (§18.4): Bound the order of sums, Cauchy products, and Hadamard products of D-finite series, and deploy the \((u, e) \bmod p^{V+1}\) lifting representation (Failure Mode #8) whenever \(p \mid I(n^*)\) at an intermediate recurrence step.1


Next Chapter: Continue to Chapter 19: Coupled Linear ODEs, Sparse Composition & Truncated Taylor Reductions, where we extend D-finite compilation to \(2 \times 2\) coupled differential systems (Uncoupling Trick), Creative Telescoping, Elegia’s \(O(K)\) truncated Taylor binomial-sum reduction, and the Miracle Derivative of the truncated exponential.

NotePrerequisite Chapters & Required Foundations



Before reading this chapter, ensure you are comfortable with the following foundational tools:

Chapter 5: Rational Generating Functions, Bostan–Mori & Berlekamp–Massey — partial fraction decompositions over formal power series, reversed polynomials \(P^R(x) = x^{\deg P} P(1/x)\), and generating functions of linear recurrences.
Chapter 6: Binomial Sums, Snake Oil, Taylor Shifts & Stirling Numbers — diagonal-times-Toeplitz (cross-correlation) convolutions and coefficient-space polynomial shifts \(F(x+c)\).
Chapter 7: Roots of Unity, Cyclotomic Polynomials & Chirp Z-Transform — Decimation-in-Frequency (DIF) and Decimation-in-Time (DIT) Number-Theoretic Transforms, bit-reversal permutations, and Bluestein’s identity \(ij = \binom{i+j}{2} - \binom{i}{2} - \binom{j}{2}\).





By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Dualize any straight-line linear algorithm via Tellegen’s Transposition Principle: Decompose a linear map \(\mathbf{y} = M\mathbf{x}\) into elementary matrices (or a directed acyclic graph of addition, fan-out, and scalar multiplication gates) and reverse the circuit to compute \(\mathbf{z} = M^\top \mathbf{w}\) in the exact same multiplicative complexity.
Execute the Middle Product (mulT) with \(2\times\) FFT length and bit-reversal savings: Derive \(\operatorname{mulT}(C, B)[i] = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} B[j]\,C[i+j]\) (\(0 \le i < n\)) as the matrix transpose of polynomial multiplication, prove why cyclic wrap-around on an FFT length \(L \ge n + m - 1\) never pollutes the middle window, and eliminate bit-reversal permutations via DIF_NTT + DIT_INTT.
Build division-free \(O(N \log^2 N)\) Multipoint Evaluation (eval) and Fast Lagrange Interpolation (interp): Construct the primal bottom-up subproduct tree computing \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{w_i}{1 - x_i x} \bmod x^n\) with a single root inversion, and transpose it top-down to evaluate \(F(x_0), \dots, F(x_{n-1})\) using only mulT gates (\(3\times\) faster than remainder-tree Euclidean division).
Transpose the Chirp Z-Transform (\(\text{czt}^\top\)), shift consecutive sampling points (连续点值平移), and compute \(N! \bmod P\) in \(O(\sqrt{P}\log P)\): Evaluate geometric linear forms via \(\text{czt}^\top\), shift point values \(F(0), \dots, F(d) \mapsto F(c), \dots, F(c+m-1)\) in a single NTT while safely bypassing overlap singularities, and double block polynomials \(G_d(x) = \prod_{j=1}^d(x+j)\) on a baby-step giant-step grid.

section: §20.1 Tellegen’s Transposition Principle & Straight-Line Linear Circuits
text:
§20.1 Tellegen’s Transposition Principle & Straight-Line Linear Circuits

Concrete Motivation: Why Reverse a Linear Algorithm?
Suppose you have fixed parameters \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{n-1} \in K\) over a commutative ring \(K\). Consider two fundamental computational tasks that appear opposite at first glance:

Task A (Weighted Rational Partial-Fraction Sum): Given weights \(w_0, w_1, \dots, w_{n-1} \in K\), compute the first \(n\) Taylor coefficients \(z_0, z_1, \dots, z_{n-1}\) of the rational generating function \[
Z(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{w_i}{1 - x_i x} \bmod x^n = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} w_i x_i^j\right) x^j \bmod x^n.
\] Task A is straightforward: we can pair up fractions in a binary tree \(\frac{A_L}{Q_L} + \frac{A_R}{Q_R} = \frac{A_L Q_R + A_R Q_L}{Q_L Q_R}\) from the leaves to the root using only standard polynomial multiplications, and then perform one single formal power series inversion \(Q_{\text{root}}(x)^{-1} \bmod x^n\) at the very end.
Task B (Multipoint Polynomial Evaluation): Given the coefficients \(f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{n-1} \in K\) of a polynomial \(F(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j x^j\), compute its values at all \(n\) points simultaneously: \[
y_i = F(x_i) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_i^j f_j \quad \text{for } 0 \le i < n.
\] Historically, Task B was solved by recursively taking polynomial remainders \(F(x) \bmod \prod_{i \in u}(x - x_i)\) down a binary tree, requiring \(O(\log n)\) layers of heavy Euclidean polynomial divisions (divmod), each costing \(2\) to \(3\) times as much as a multiplication.

Look closely at the linear algebra connecting Task A and Task B. Define the \(n \times n\) Vandermonde matrix \(V\) with entries \(V_{i,j} = x_i^j\) (\(0 \le i, j < n\)):

Task B computes the matrix-vector product \(\mathbf{y} = V \mathbf{f}\), since \(y_i = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} V_{i,j} f_j\).
Task A computes the transposed matrix-vector product \(\mathbf{z} = V^\top \mathbf{w}\), since \(z_j = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} V_{i,j} w_i = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (V^\top)_{j,i} w_i\).

Can we mechanically convert our fast, division-free algorithm for \(V^\top \mathbf{w}\) into an equally fast, division-free algorithm for \(V \mathbf{f}\)? Tellegen’s Transposition Principle guarantees that the answer is always yes—not only for Vandermonde matrices, but for any linear transformation over any commutative ring \(K\).



The Bilinear Form & Elementary Matrix Decomposition






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Tellegen’s Transposition Principle




The Diagnostic Signal: You need to compute a linear map \(\mathbf{y} = M \mathbf{x}\) whose direct algorithm seems to require expensive division or non-local operations (such as polynomial remainder tree evaluation \(F(x) \bmod (x - x_i)\)), whereas the transposed linear map \(\mathbf{z} = M^\top \mathbf{w}\) has an obvious, division-free generating function interpretation (such as summing partial fractions \(\sum_i \frac{w_i}{1 - x_i x} \bmod x^n\) over a subproduct tree).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad:

Write the easier transposed problem \(\mathbf{z} = M^\top \mathbf{w}\) as a straight-line sequence of elementary linear steps \(M^\top = P_{\text{in}}^\top E_1^\top \cdots E_T^\top P_{\text{out}}^\top\).
Transpose the factorization by reversing the topological execution order (\(t = T\) down to \(1\)) and replacing each elementary gate by its transpose: scalar multiplications \(r_i \gets c \cdot r_i\) stay unchanged, while register additions \(r_i \gets r_i + r_j\) flip direction to \(r_j \gets r_j + r_i\) (fan-out \(\leftrightarrow\) accumulation, polynomial multiplication \(\leftrightarrow\) middle product mulT).




Let \(K\) be a commutative ring with identity \(1_K\), and let \(M \in K^{m \times n}\) be a fixed matrix whose entries depend only on precomputed structural constants (such as the evaluation points \(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}\) or roots of unity).
A straight-line linear program (or linear circuit) computing \(\mathbf{y} = M \mathbf{x}\) for an arbitrary input vector \(\mathbf{x} \in K^n\) is a finite sequence of \(T\) elementary in-place register operations on a workspace array \(\mathbf{r} = (r_1, \dots, r_W)^\top \in K^W\) (with \(W \ge \max(n, m)\)) that begins with \(\mathbf{x}\) loaded into the first \(n\) registers (and zeros elsewhere) and ends with \(\mathbf{y}\) stored in the first \(m\) registers.
Every step \(t = 1, 2, \dots, T\) applies one of three elementary linear transformations \(E_t \in K^{W \times W}\) to the workspace vector \(\mathbf{r} \gets E_t \mathbf{r}\):

In-Place Scalar Multiplication \(D_i(c)\): Multiplies register \(r_i\) by a fixed constant \(c \in K\), leaving all other registers unchanged (\(r_i \gets c \cdot r_i\)). As a matrix, \(D_i(c) = I_W + (c - 1) \mathbf{e}_i \mathbf{e}_i^\top\).

Transpose: Since \(D_i(c)\) is a diagonal matrix, it is self-transpose: \[
D_i(c)^\top = D_i(c).
\]

Register Addition / Elementary Shear \(E_{i,j}(1)\) (\(i \ne j\)): Adds register \(r_j\) into register \(r_i\) (\(r_i \gets r_i + r_j\)). As a matrix, \(E_{i,j}(1) = I_W + \mathbf{e}_i \mathbf{e}_j^\top\).

Transpose: Transposing swaps the row and column indices of \(\mathbf{e}_i \mathbf{e}_j^\top\), reversing the direction of data flow so that register \(r_i\) is added into register \(r_j\) (\(r_j \gets r_j + r_i\)): \[
E_{i,j}(1)^\top = (I_W + \mathbf{e}_i \mathbf{e}_j^\top)^\top = I_W + \mathbf{e}_j \mathbf{e}_i^\top = E_{j,i}(1).
\]

Register Zero-Clear / Projection \(Z_i = D_i(0)\) or Permutation \(P_{i,j}\): Swaps two registers \(r_i \leftrightarrow r_j\) (\(P_{i,j}^\top = P_{i,j}\)) or zeroes an auxiliary register after its value is no longer needed.

Let \(P_{\text{in}} \in K^{W \times n}\) be the injection matrix that loads \(\mathbf{x} \in K^n\) into the first \(n\) registers, and let \(P_{\text{out}} \in K^{m \times W}\) be the projection matrix that reads \(\mathbf{y} \in K^m\) from the first \(m\) registers. Then the primal straight-line program factors \(M\) as the matrix product \[
M = P_{\text{out}} E_T E_{T-1} \cdots E_2 E_1 P_{\text{in}}.
\]
Now take the matrix transpose of both sides using the identity \((AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top\): \[
M^\top = P_{\text{in}}^\top E_1^\top E_2^\top \cdots E_{T-1}^\top E_T^\top P_{\text{out}}^\top.
\]
Reading this factored product from right to left gives a constructive, step-by-step recipe for computing \(\mathbf{z} = M^\top \mathbf{w}\) for any covector \(\mathbf{w} \in K^m\):

Initialize (\(P_{\text{out}}^\top\)): Load the input covector \(\mathbf{w} \in K^m\) into the output registers of the primal circuit, setting all other workspace registers to \(0\).
Reverse Topological Execution (\(E_T^\top, \dots, E_1^\top\)): Step backward from \(t = T\) down to \(t = 1\), replacing each elementary operation \(E_t\) by its transpose \(E_t^\top\):

Every register addition \(r_i \gets r_i + r_j\) becomes \(r_j \gets r_j + r_i\).
Every constant multiplication \(r_i \gets c \cdot r_i\) remains \(r_i \gets c \cdot r_i\).

Extract (\(P_{\text{in}}^\top\)): Read the final result \(\mathbf{z} = M^\top \mathbf{w} \in K^n\) from the input registers of the primal circuit.




Dualizing the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of a Linear Circuit
Instead of in-place registers, we can equivalently view a linear algorithm as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) in which every node is an intermediate variable and edges carry linear values:





flowchart LR
  subgraph Primal ["Primal Circuit: y = M x"]
    direction LR
    x["Input node u (fan-out)"] -->|"1"| a1["Branch 1"] & a2["Branch 2"]
    b1["Summand 1"] & b2["Summand 2"] -->|"1"| p["Addition node v (+)"]
    s1["Node p"] -->|"scalar c"| s2["Node q"]
  end
  subgraph Dual ["Transposed Circuit: z = M^T w"]
    direction RL
    xT["Output node u (+)"] <--|"1"| a1T["Branch 1"] & a2T["Branch 2"]
    b1T["Target 1"] & b2T["Target 2"] <--|"1"| pT["Fan-out node v"]
    s1T["Node p"] <--|"scalar c"| s2T["Node q"]
  end






The bilinear duality identity \[
\langle \mathbf{w}, M\mathbf{x} \rangle = \mathbf{w}^\top (M\mathbf{x}) = (M^\top \mathbf{w})^\top \mathbf{x} = \langle M^\top \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle
\] shows that if we assign each node \(v\) in the primal DAG a dual sensitivity variable \(\hat{v}\) (measuring how much the final inner product \(\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{y} \rangle\) changes per unit change in \(v\)), propagating sensitivities backward from the outputs \(\hat{y}_i = w_i\) to the inputs \(\hat{x}_j = z_j\) performs three exact gate dualizations:









Primal Gate (Forward Topological Order)
Matrix Form \(E_t\)
Transposed Gate (Reverse Topological Order)
Matrix Form \(E_t^\top\)




Fan-Out (Copy): \(u_1 \gets v,\; u_2 \gets v\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\)
Addition (Accumulate): \(\hat{v} \gets \hat{u}_1 + \hat{u}_2\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)


Addition (Sum): \(v \gets u_1 + u_2\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)
Fan-Out (Broadcast): \(\hat{u}_1 \gets \hat{v},\; \hat{u}_2 \gets \hat{v}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\)


Scalar Multiply: \(v \gets c \cdot u\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} c \end{bmatrix}\)
Scalar Multiply: \(\hat{u} \gets c \cdot \hat{v}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} c \end{bmatrix}\)


Polynomial Multiply \(\mathcal{M}_B\): \(C = A \cdot B\)
Toeplitz \(T_B\)
Middle Product \(\operatorname{mulT}(\cdot, B)\): \(\hat{A} = \operatorname{mulT}(\hat{C}, B)\)
Transposed Toeplitz \(T_B^\top\)









ImportantTheorem 20.1 (Tellegen’s Transposition Principle)



Let \(K\) be a commutative ring and let \(M \in K^{m \times n}\) be a linear map computed by a straight-line linear circuit using \(S\) scalar multiplications by fixed constants and \(A\) additions. Then the transposed linear map \(M^\top \in K^{n \times m}\) can be computed by the reversed straight-line circuit using precisely \(S\) scalar multiplications (by the exact same constants) and at most \(A + n - m\) additions.





Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 2\) Vandermonde Circuit)
Let us trace Tellegen’s Principle by hand on a \(2 \times 2\) linear map. Fix evaluation points \(x_0 = 2, x_1 = 5\). The primal map evaluates \(F(x) = f_0 + f_1 x\) at \(x_0, x_1\): \[
\begin{bmatrix} y_0 \\ y_1 \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}}_{V} \begin{bmatrix} f_0 \\ f_1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
\begin{bmatrix} z_0 \\ z_1 \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}}_{V^\top} \begin{bmatrix} w_0 \\ w_1 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Suppose we start from the primal rational-sum algorithm for \(\mathbf{z} = V^\top \mathbf{w}\): \[
\frac{w_0}{1 - 2x} + \frac{w_1}{1 - 5x} = \frac{w_0(1 - 5x) + w_1(1 - 2x)}{(1 - 2x)(1 - 5x)} = \frac{(w_0 + w_1) + (-5w_0 - 2w_1)x}{1 - 7x + 10x^2} \bmod x^2.
\] Since \((1 - 7x + 10x^2)^{-1} \equiv 1 + 7x \pmod{x^2}\), multiplying the numerator \(A_0 + A_1 x\) by \(1 + 7x \bmod x^2\) gives the 4-step straight-line circuit for \(\mathbf{z} = V^\top \mathbf{w}\):

Step 1 (Cross-multiply numerators): \(A_0 = w_0 + w_1\) and \(A_1 = -5w_0 - 2w_1\). \[
\begin{bmatrix} A_0 \\ A_1 \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -5 & -2 \end{bmatrix}}_{M_1} \begin{bmatrix} w_0 \\ w_1 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Step 2 (Multiply by inverse root \(Q_{\text{root}}^{-1} \equiv 1 + 7x \bmod x^2\)): \(z_0 = A_0\) and \(z_1 = 7A_0 + A_1\). \[
\begin{bmatrix} z_0 \\ z_1 \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 7 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{M_2} \begin{bmatrix} A_0 \\ A_1 \end{bmatrix}.
\] Check: \(z_0 = w_0 + w_1\) and \(z_1 = 7(w_0 + w_1) + (-5w_0 - 2w_1) = 2w_0 + 5w_1\). This is indeed \(V^\top \mathbf{w}\).

Now transpose the two steps in reverse order (\(V = (M_2 M_1)^\top = M_1^\top M_2^\top\)) to evaluate \(\mathbf{y} = V \mathbf{f}\) at input \(\mathbf{f} = (f_0, f_1)^\top = (3, 4)^\top\) (where \(F(x) = 3 + 4x\), so \(F(2) = 11\) and \(F(5) = 23\)):

Step \(2^\top\) (Transpose of root multiplication by \(1 + 7x\)): \[
\begin{bmatrix} \hat{A}_0 \\ \hat{A}_1 \end{bmatrix} = M_2^\top \begin{bmatrix} f_0 \\ f_1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 + 7 \cdot 4 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 31 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Step \(1^\top\) (Transpose of leaf cross-multiplication): \[
\begin{bmatrix} y_0 \\ y_1 \end{bmatrix} = M_1^\top \begin{bmatrix} \hat{A}_0 \\ \hat{A}_1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -5 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 31 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 31 - 5 \cdot 4 \\ 31 - 2 \cdot 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ 23 \end{bmatrix}.
\] Both exact point values \(y_0 = F(2) = 11\) and \(y_1 = F(5) = 23\) emerge without a single polynomial division! Notice what happened in Step \(2^\top\) and Step \(1^\top\): every primal polynomial multiplication \(A(x) \cdot B(x)\) turned into a sliding inner product \(\sum_j B[j] \, C[i+j]\). Let us isolate and optimize that exact transposed operator.
