NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Generating Function Recurrence and FWT Diagonalization
Root \(T\) at \(1\). In the group ring \(\mathbb{F}_{10007}[\mathbb{Z}_2^k]\) where \(x^a \cdot x^b = x^{a \oplus b}\):
\[F_u(x) = x^{v_u} \prod_{c \in \text{child}(u)} \bigl(F_c(x) + x^0\bigr), \qquad G_u(x) = F_u(x) + \sum_{c \in \text{child}(u)} G_c(x).\]
Applying the length-\(M\) XOR-FWT \(\widehat{P}(r) = \sum_{i=0}^{M-1} (-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(r \ \& \ i)} [x^i] P(x)\) diagonalizes XOR multiplication into \(M\) independent scalar recurrences for \(r = 0, \dots, M-1\), where \(\widehat{x^{v_u}}(r) = (-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(r \ \& \ v_u)} \in \{1, 10006\}\) and \(\widehat{x^0}(r) = 1\).


2. Heavy-Light Separation and the 4-Parameter Matrix Subgroup
For each vertex \(u\) and frequency \(r \in [0, M-1]\), separate \(h_u = \text{heavy}(u)\) from \(\text{light}(u)\):
\[L_u(r) = \widehat{x^{v_u}}(r) \prod_{c \in \text{light}(u)} \bigl(\widehat{F}_c(r) + 1\bigr), \qquad S_u(r) = \sum_{c \in \text{light}(u)} \widehat{G}_c(r).\]
If \(u\) is a leaf (no heavy child, or equivalently feeding \((F_{\text{null}}, G_{\text{null}}, 1)^T = (0, 0, 1)^T\) into the transition), we obtain:
\[\widehat{F}_u(r) = L_u(r) \widehat{F}_{h_u}(r) + L_u(r), \qquad \widehat{G}_u(r) = L_u(r) \widehat{F}_{h_u}(r) + \widehat{G}_{h_u}(r) + \bigl(L_u(r) + S_u(r)\bigr).\]
Representing the transition matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} a & 0 & b \\ c & 1 & d \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) by the 4-tuple \((a, b, c, d) = (L_u, L_u, L_u, L_u + S_u)\), the closure law is:
\[(a_1, b_1, c_1, d_1) \circ (a_2, b_2, c_2, d_2) = (a_1 a_2,\; a_1 b_2 + b_1,\; c_1 a_2 + c_2,\; c_1 b_2 + d_1 + d_2) \pmod{10007}.\]
When applied to the tail \((0, 0, 1)^T\) at the bottom of a heavy chain, a chain product \((a, b, c, d)\) yields \(\widehat{F}_{\text{head}}(r) = b\) and \(\widehat{G}_{\text{head}}(r) = d\).


3. Zero-Divisor Pairs on the Static Top Tree (全局平衡二叉树)
Build the Static Top Tree (全局平衡二叉树) once by recursively picking the weighted midpoint \(m\) on each heavy chain with weight \(w_u = 1 + \sum_{c \in \text{light}(u)} \text{sz}[c]\). At each vertex \(u\) and frequency \(r\), store:

ZeroDivPair light_prod[u][r] maintaining \(\prod_{c \in \text{light}(u)} (\widehat{F}_c(r) + 1)\).
int light_sum[u][r] maintaining \(S_u(r) = \sum_{c \in \text{light}(u)} \widehat{G}_c(r) \pmod{10007}\).

Why are ZeroDivPair instances mandatory here? Because whenever a light child \(c\) has \(\widehat{F}_c(r) \equiv -1 \equiv 10006 \pmod{10007}\), the factor \(\widehat{F}_c(r) + 1\) equals \(0 \pmod{10007}\)! Using light_prod[p][r].div(old_F + 1) and light_prod[p][r].mul(new_F + 1) handles \(0 \pmod{10007}\) factors in \(O(1)\) without information loss.
On Change(u, new_val), update \(v_u \leftarrow \text{new\_val}\) and walk up the Static Top Tree from \(u\) to the root (\(\le 2 \log_2 N\) steps), updating 4-tuples along BST edges and light_prod / light_sum across light pointers. On Query(k), apply the \(O(M \log M)\) inverse XOR-FWT (or dot product of \(\widehat{G}_{\text{root}}\) with frequency basis) to extract \([x^k] G_{\text{root}}(x) \bmod 10007\).


Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Tree \(T\) of \(N \le 3 \times 10^4\) vertices, \(M = 2^k \le 128\), initial values \(v_1, \dots, v_N \in [0, M-1]\), and \(Q \le 3 \times 10^4\) operations; prime modulus \(p = 10007\) with precomputed inv_table[1..10006] in \(O(p)\) time.
Postconditions (Output): Outputs \([x^k] G_1(x) \bmod 10007\) for each Query k.
Time & Space Complexity: \(O((N + Q) M \log N)\) time and \(O(NM)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At every node \(x\) of the Static Top Tree, sum_mat[x][r] = sum_mat[ls[x]][r] * local_mat[x][r] * sum_mat[rs[x]][r], and for every light pointer \(x \to p\), light_prod[p][r] stores the exact ZeroDivPair of \(\prod_{c \in \text{light}(p)} (\widehat{F}_c(r) + 1)\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Whenever \(\widehat{F}_c(r) \equiv 10006 \equiv -1 \pmod{10007}\), the light-child factor \(\widehat{F}_c(r) + 1\) equals \(0 \pmod{10007}\), so naive division without ZeroDivPair permanently zeroes out light_prod[p][r] (Failure Mode #10); also, general \(3 \times 3\) matrix multiplication (\(27\) ops) instead of the 4-parameter subgroup closure (\(4\) ops) causes TLE.









Advanced 2 (#136) — Codeforces 2006E: Iris’s Full Binary Tree

Source: Codeforces Round 969 (Div. 1) — Problem 2006E: Iris’s Full Binary Tree
Prerequisite Tags: Dynamic Tree DP, Heavy-Light / Static Top Tree Maintenance, Full Binary Tree Embedding Height


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given a tree \(T\) with \(N\) vertices numbered \(1, 2, \dots, N\) such that for every \(k = 1, 2, \dots, N\), the induced subgraph \(T_k\) on vertices \(\{1, 2, \dots, k\}\) is a tree (i.e., vertex \(i \ge 2\) is connected to a single parent \(P_i \in \{1, \dots, i-1\}\)).
A rooted tree \(R\) can be embedded into a full binary tree of height \(H\) (having \(2^{H-1}\) leaves at depth \(H\)) by subdividing edges of \(R\) into paths so that every original vertex of \(R\) maps to a distinct node of the binary tree while preserving ancestor-descendant relationships. For each prefix tree \(T_k\) (\(k = 1, 2, \dots, N\)), compute the minimum possible height \(H(T_k)\) over all choices of the root \(r \in \{1, \dots, k\}\).

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5\) per testcase, \(\sum N \le 2 \times 10^5\). Time limit: \(4.0\text{ s}\). Required complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) or \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N = 4\))
Suppose \(T_4\) is a star centered at \(1\) with edges \((1,2), (1,3), (1,4)\):

For a fixed root \(r\), if vertex \(u\) has children \(c_1, \dots, c_d\) with required heights \(h_{c_1} \ge h_{c_2} \ge \dots \ge h_{c_d}\), binary-splitting the \(d\) children into a caterpillar of binary branches beneath \(u\) requires height: \[h_u = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } d = 0, \\ h_{c_1} + 1 & \text{if } d = 1, \\ \max\!\bigl(\max_{1 \le i \le d-1} (h_{c_i} + i),\; h_{c_d} + d - 1\bigr) & \text{if } d \ge 2. \end{cases}\]
Specifically, for \(d = 1\), \(u\) has a single child \(c_1\) at depth \(1\) beneath \(u\), so \(h_u = 1 + h_{c_1}\); for \(d = 3\) with \(h_{c_1} = h_{c_2} = h_{c_3} = 1\), the last two leaves share depth \(d - 1 = 2\), giving height \(1 + 2 = 3\), and yielding for \(k = 1, 2, 3, 4\) on the star: 1, 2, 3, 3.



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

First fix the root \(r\) of \(T_k\). If a vertex \(u\) has \(d\) children \(c_1, \dots, c_d\) whose subtrees already require minimum binary tree heights \(h_{c_1} \ge h_{c_2} \ge \dots \ge h_{c_d}\), notice that at most two children can be attached directly under \(u\) at distance \(1\); if \(d > 2\), we must insert auxiliary binary branching nodes between \(u\) and its children. How does \(h_u\) depend on the sorted sequence \(h_{c_1} \ge h_{c_2} \ge \dots \ge h_{c_d}\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Notice that in the sorted order \(h_{c_1} \ge h_{c_2} \ge \dots \ge h_{c_d}\), the largest child height \(h_{c_1}\) and second-largest child height \(h_{c_2}\) dominate unless there are many children of similar height, and more tightly: because \(\sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \text{sz}[v] < \text{sz}[u]\), how large can the difference \(h_u - \max_{v \in \text{child}(u)} h_v\) be, and how does the optimal root \(r\) relate to the tree’s diameter / heavy centroid path?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

For any vertex \(u\) with child heights sorted as \(h_{c_1} \ge h_{c_2} \ge \dots \ge h_{c_d}\), attaching them along a binary spine beneath \(u\) gives \(h_u = \max\bigl(\max_{1 \le i \le d-1}(h_{c_i} + i),\; h_{c_d} + d - 1\bigr)\) for \(d \ge 2\) (and \(h_{c_1} + 1\) for \(d = 1\)). Along a heavy chain, \(h_u = \max(h_{\text{heavy}(u)} + \Delta_u, B_u)\) is a \((\max, +)\) tropical affine transition! Maintaining these \((\max, +)\) matrices on the Static Top Tree (全局平衡二叉树) or via HLD + binary search along the centroid spine updates \(H(T_k)\) in \(O(\log^2 N)\) per vertex insertion.







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Fixed-Root Height Recurrence as a Tropical \((\max, +)\) Affine Transition
In Problem 2006E, embedding a rooted tree \(R\) into a full binary tree requires that at every vertex \(u\) with children \(c_1, \dots, c_d\) sorted by non-increasing subtree height \(h_{c_1} \ge h_{c_2} \ge \dots \ge h_{c_d}\), we arrange \(c_1, \dots, c_d\) as leaves of a binary caterpillar/tree rooted at \(u\), yielding the exact DP recurrence:
\[h_u = \max\!\left(1,\; \max_{1 \le i \le d} (h_{c_i} + i - [i = d \text{ and } d \ge 2])\right),\]
where if \(d = 0\), \(h_u = 1\); if \(d = 1\), \(h_u = h_{c_1} + 1\); and if \(d \ge 2\), the \(i\)-th largest child (\(1 \le i < d\)) sits at depth \(i\) below \(u\) while the last two children \(c_{d-1}, c_d\) share depth \(d - 1\), so:
\[h_u = \max\!\Bigl(\max_{1 \le i \le d-1} (h_{c_i} + i),\; h_{c_d} + d - 1\Bigr).\]


2. Convexity and Heavy-Light / Centroid Maintenance
Observe that as we move the root \(r\) across an edge \((u, v)\) from \(u\) to \(v\), the height \(h_v(r)\) can only decrease while the complement height \(h_u(r)\) can only increase. Therefore, the function \(r \mapsto H(T_k, r)\) is convex on tree paths, and the optimal root \(r^*\) lies on the heavy-height path from \(1\) (specifically at the point where the downward height \(h_{r^*}\) and upward complement height are balanced, akin to a tree diameter center).
By building the full tree \(T_N\) offline and using Heavy-Light Decomposition (or a Static Top Tree over \(T_N\) where vertices \(k = 1, \dots, N\) are activated one by one):

Each vertex \(u\) maintains a balanced multiset (std::multiset or Fenwick tree over heights) of its active light children’s heights \(\{h_v : v \in \text{light}(u) \cap \{1, \dots, k\}\}\).
Because inserting \(h_{\text{heavy}(u)}\) into the sorted order of light children shifts the rank of light children with \(h_v \le h_{\text{heavy}(u)}\) by \(+1\), the transition from \(h_{\text{heavy}(u)}\) to \(h_u\) is a piecewise \((\max, +)\) step function maintained on the HLD segment tree / Static Top Tree.
Walking down the heavy tree from the current root (or binary-searching along the active diameter path) finds the optimal root \(r^*\) and updates \(\min_{r \in T_k} H(T_k, r)\) in \(O(\log^2 N)\) time per prefix \(k\).



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Integer \(N\) (\(1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5\)) and parent edges forming prefix trees \(T_1, \dots, T_N\) such that every prefix \(\{1, \dots, k\}\) induces a connected subtree of \(T_N\).
Postconditions (Output): Prints \(\min_{r \in \{1,\dots,k\}} H(T_k, r)\) for each \(k = 1, 2, \dots, N\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At step \(k\), every active vertex \(u \le k\) maintains the sorted multiset of its active light-child heights, and the Static Top Tree / HLD segment tree aggregates the exact \((\max, +)\) transition along each heavy chain.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: For \(d \ge 2\) children, the last two children \(c_{d-1}, c_d\) share depth \(d - 1\) beneath \(u\) (giving \(h_{c_d} + d - 1\), not \(h_{c_d} + d\)), whereas for \(d = 1\) the single child \(c_1\) sits at depth \(1\) (\(h_{c_1} + 1\)); forgetting the \([i = d \text{ and } d \ge 2]\) offset off-by-ones all binary branching heights.









Mastery 1 (#166) — Luogu P5281 / LOJ 3044: [ZJOI2019] Minimax 搜索 (Minimax Search)

Source: LibreOJ 3044 / Luogu P5281 — [ZJOI2019] Minimax 搜索
Prerequisite Tags: Static Top Tree (全局平衡二叉树), De Morgan Depth Complementation, Dynamic DP with Zero-Divisor Pairs \((a, c) \equiv a \cdot 0^c\), Amortized Leaf State Flips


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given a rooted tree \(T\) with \(N\) vertices numbered \(1, 2, \dots, N\), rooted at vertex \(1\) (which has depth \(1\)). The value \(w_u\) of each vertex \(u\) is defined recursively:

If \(u\) is a leaf, \(w_u = u\) (its vertex index!).
If \(u\) is an internal vertex at odd depth (\(1, 3, 5, \dots\)), \(w_u = \max_{v \in \text{child}(u)} w_v\).
If \(u\) is an internal vertex at even depth (\(2, 4, 6, \dots\)), \(w_u = \min_{v \in \text{child}(u)} w_v\).

Let \(W = w_1\) be the initial minimax value at the root, and let \(M\) be the total number of leaves in \(T\). For any subset of leaves \(S \subseteq \text{Leaves}(T)\), if we are allowed to replace the value of each leaf \(u \in S\) with an arbitrary integer \(w'_u \in [u - k, u + k]\), define the stability cost \(c(S)\) to be the minimum non-negative integer \(k\) under which it is possible to change the root value \(w_1\) to some \(w'_1 \neq W\) (if \(w_1\) cannot be changed for any \(k\), let \(c(S) = N\)).
Given \(L, R\) (\(1 \le L \le R \le N\)), for each \(k = L, L + 1, \dots, R\), compute the number of leaf subsets \(S \subseteq \text{Leaves}(T)\) such that \(c(S) = k\), modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(2 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(1 \le L \le R \le N\). Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\). Required complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N = 4\))
Suppose \(N = 4\) with root \(1\) (odd depth, \(\max\)) having child \(2\) (even depth, \(\min\)) and leaf \(3\), and vertex \(2\) having leaf child \(4\):

Leaves are \(\{3, 4\}\) (\(M = 2\), \(2^M = 4\) subsets).
Initial values: \(w_4 = 4 \implies w_2 = \min(4) = 4\); \(w_3 = 3\); \(w_1 = \max(w_2, w_3) = \max(4, 3) = 4\), so \(W = 4\).
When can a subset \(S \subseteq \{3, 4\}\) change \(w_1\) from \(W = 4\) using modification radius \(k\)?

\(S = \emptyset\): never changes \(w_1\), so \(c(\emptyset) = 4\).
\(S = \{4\}\): at \(k = 1\), lowering \(w'_4 = 4 - 1 = 3\) gives \(w'_2 = 3\) and \(w'_1 = \max(3, 3) = 3 \neq 4\), so \(c(\{4\}) = 1\).
\(S = \{3\}\): at \(k = 1\), raising \(w'_3 = 3 + 1 = 4\) leaves \(\max(4, 4) = 4\), whereas at \(k = 2\), raising \(w'_3 = 3 + 2 = 5\) gives \(w'_1 = \max(4, 5) = 5 > 4\), so \(c(\{3\}) = 2\).
\(S = \{3, 4\}\): at \(k = 1\), lowering \(w'_4 = 3\) already gives \(w'_1 = 3 \neq 4\), so \(c(\{3, 4\}) = 1\).

Counts for \(k = 1, 2, 3, 4\): 2, 1, 0, 1.



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Instead of computing the number of subsets with \(c(S) = k\) directly, it is much easier to count the number of subsets \(S\) with \(c(S) > k\) (i.e., subsets \(S\) for which every valid modification within radius \(k\) still leaves the root locked at \(w'_1 = W\)). Notice that on the critical path of vertices with \(w_u = W\), the root is a \(\max\) over one child equal to \(W\) and others \(< W\), which in turn is a \(\min\) over one child equal to \(W\) and others \(> W\). Can a single modification simultaneously make \(w'_1 > W\) and \(w'_1 < W\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Because the root \(1\) has \(w_1 = W\), changing \(w'_1 \neq W\) happens if and only if we either make \(w'_1 > W\) or make \(w'_1 < W\)—and these two requirements depend on completely disjoint sets of leaves (leaves in subtrees with \(w_v \le W\) can only help make \(w'_1 > W\), while leaves in subtrees with \(w_v \ge W\) can only help make \(w'_1 < W\))! Thus, if we pick each leaf \(u \in \text{Leaves}(T)\) independently with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\), the probability that \(w'_1 = W\) remains locked is \(P(w'_1 \le W) \cdot P(w'_1 \ge W)\)! Moreover, as \(k\) increases from \(1\) to \(N - 1\), each leaf \(u\) changes its threshold feasibility (\(u + k > W\) or \(u - k < W\)) at most once (specifically at \(k = |u - W| + 1\))!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Let \(p_u\) be the probability that \(w'_u > W\) in the first DP (on subtrees relevant to \(> W\)). At an odd-depth node (\(\max\)), \(w'_u > W\) iff at least one child has \(w'_v > W\): \(p_u = 1 - \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} (1 - p_v)\). At an even-depth node (\(\min\)), \(w'_u > W\) iff all children have \(w'_v > W\): \(p_u = \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} p_v\). By substituting \(\widetilde{p}_u = p_u\) at odd depths and \(\widetilde{p}_u = 1 - p_u\) at even depths (De Morgan Depth Complementation), every internal node at every depth satisfies the identical recurrence: \[\widetilde{p}_u = 1 - \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \widetilde{p}_v = 1 - L_u \cdot \widetilde{p}_{\text{heavy}(u)}.\] Maintain this 1D affine map \(\begin{pmatrix} -L_u & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) on a Static Top Tree (全局平衡二叉树) using ZeroDivPair for \(L_u = \prod_{v \in \text{light}(u)} \widetilde{p}_v\). Since each leaf updates at most once as \(k = 1 \dots N-1\), the entire sweep takes \(O(N \log N)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Decoupling \(w'_1 > W\) and \(w'_1 < W\)
First run a \(O(N)\) DFS to compute the initial minimax value \(w_u\) of every vertex \(u\), setting \(W = w_1\). Notice that all leaf values \(w_u = u\) are distinct. Consequently, at every internal vertex \(u\), at most one child \(v \in \text{child}(u)\) can have \(w_v = w_u\).
Specifically, at the root \(1\) (odd depth, \(\max\)), let \(v^*\) be the unique child of \(1\) with \(w_{v^*} = W\); all other children \(v \neq v^*\) have \(w_v < W\). To keep \(w'_1 = W\) under the adversary’s best choice of leaf modifications:

No child of \(1\) can achieve \(w'_v > W\) (which means \(w'_1 \le W\)). Note that for \(v^*\), since \(v^*\) is at even depth (\(\min\)) and its children all have \(w_c \ge W\), \(v^*\) can never be raised above \(W\) by its children with \(w_c > W\) unless the unique child of \(v^*\) with \(w_c = W\) is raised above \(W\). More generally, a leaf \(u\) with \(u < W\) can never be lowered to make a \(\min\)-ancestor \(< W\) in a way that helps change \(W\) downward; its only possible role is to be raised to \(u + k > W\) to help make \(w'_1 > W\).
Symmetrically, a leaf \(u\) with \(u > W\) can only be lowered to \(u - k < W\) to help make \(w'_1 < W\).
For the unique critical leaf \(u^*\) with \(u^* = W\): if \(u^* \notin S\), then \(w'_{u^*} = W\) is locked, so raising \(w'_1 > W\) depends purely on leaves with \(u < W\) and lowering \(w'_1 < W\) depends purely on leaves with \(u > W\). If \(u^* \in S\) and \(k \ge 1\), the player can move \(w'_{u^*}\) either above \(W\) or below \(W\); by the minimax structure along the critical path of vertices with \(w_v = W\), at least one of these two moves changes the root unless both raising fails (blocked by a \(\min\)-ancestor on the critical path) and lowering fails (blocked by a \(\max\)-ancestor on the critical path).

Therefore, under the uniform probability distribution over \(S \subseteq \text{Leaves}(T)\) (where each leaf belongs to \(S\) independently with probability \(2^{-1} \bmod 998244353\)), let:

\(P_k\): probability that the player can achieve \(w'_1 > W\) using radius \(k\) (where for a leaf \(u\): if \(u > W\), it is already \(> W\) with probability \(1\); if \(u \le W\), it can become \(> W\) iff \(u \in S\) and \(u + k > W\), which has probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) if \(k > W - u\) and \(0\) otherwise).
\(Q_k\): probability that the player can achieve \(w'_1 < W\) using radius \(k\) (where for a leaf \(u\): if \(u < W\), it is already \(< W\) with probability \(1\); if \(u \ge W\), it can become \(< W\) iff \(u \in S\) and \(u - k < W\), which has probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) if \(k > u - W\) and \(0\) otherwise).

Because \(P_k\) only depends on the membership in \(S\) of leaves with \(u < W\) (plus \(u^* = W\)), and \(Q_k\) only depends on the membership in \(S\) of leaves with \(u > W\) (plus \(u^* = W\)), the number of subsets \(S\) with \(c(S) > k\) (for \(1 \le k \le N-1\)) is simply:
\[\text{ways}(c(S) > k) = 2^M \cdot (1 - P_k)(1 - Q_k) \pmod{998244353},\]
with boundary values \(\text{ways}(c(S) > 0) = 2^M\) (since at \(k = 0\) no leaf changes, so \(c(S) \ge 1\) for all \(2^M\) subsets) and \(\text{ways}(c(S) > N - 1) = 1\) (only \(S = \emptyset\) has \(c(\emptyset) = N\)).


2. De Morgan Depth Complementation & Static Top Tree Sweep
In the \(P_k\) tree DP:

At odd depth (\(\max\)), \(p_u = 1 - \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} (1 - p_v)\).
At even depth (\(\min\)), \(p_u = \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} p_v \iff 1 - p_u = 1 - \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} p_v\).

Define \(\widetilde{p}_u = p_u\) if \(\text{depth}(u)\) is odd, and \(\widetilde{p}_u = 1 - p_u\) if \(\text{depth}(u)\) is even. Then at every internal vertex \(u\):
\[\widetilde{p}_u = 1 - \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \widetilde{p}_v = 1 - L_u \cdot \widetilde{p}_{\text{heavy}(u)}, \qquad \text{where } L_u = \prod_{v \in \text{light}(u)} \widetilde{p}_v.\]
Similarly, in the \(Q_k\) tree DP (where odd depth is \(\max\), so \(w'_u < W\) iff all children have \(w'_v < W\), i.e., \(q_u = \prod q_v\) at odd depth and \(q_u = 1 - \prod(1 - q_v)\) at even depth), define \(\widetilde{q}_u = 1 - q_u\) at odd depth and \(\widetilde{q}_u = q_u\) at even depth, which again yields the exact same recurrence:
\[\widetilde{q}_u = 1 - \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \widetilde{q}_v.\]
We can therefore merge both DPs onto the same Static Top Tree (全局平衡二叉树)! As \(k\) increments from \(1\) to \(N - 1\):

At \(k = 1\), leaf \(u^* = W\) activates with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\).
At \(k = d\) (\(d \ge 1\)), the at most two leaves \(u = W - d + 1\) (if \(< W\) and is a leaf) and \(u = W + d - 1\) (if \(> W\) and is a leaf) change their leaf probability from \(0\) (or \(1\)) to \(\frac{1}{2}\).
Each leaf changes at most once during the entire sweep \(k = 1 \dots N-1\), performing at most \(N\) point updates on the Static Top Tree (全局平衡二叉树) using ZeroDivPair for \(L_u\). At \(k\), the number of subsets with \(c(S) = k\) is \(\text{ways}(c(S) > k - 1) - \text{ways}(c(S) > k)\).



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Tree \(T\) of \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) vertices rooted at \(1\), range \([L, R] \subseteq [1, N]\), and prime modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): Outputs \(|\{S \subseteq \text{Leaves}(T) : c(S) = k\}| \bmod 998244353\) for each \(k \in [L, R]\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) total time and \(O(N)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After De Morgan complementation, every internal vertex \(u\) has affine transfer matrix \(M_u = \begin{pmatrix} -L_u & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) where \(L_u = \prod_{v \in \text{light}(u)} \widetilde{p}_v\) is maintained via ZeroDivPair, and each leaf \(u\) triggers at most one root-to-leaf path update at \(k = |u - W| + 1\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Without De Morgan depth complementation (\(\widetilde{p}_u = 1 - p_u\) at even depths), \(\min\) and \(\max\) levels have alternating affine transitions; when a light child \(v\) has \(\widetilde{p}_v \equiv 0 \pmod p\), naive modular division by \(0\) corrupts \(L_u\) permanently unless wrapped in a ZeroDivPair (Failure Mode #10); boundary \(k = N\) must account for \(S = \emptyset\) where \(w_1\) never changes.









Mastery 2 (#145) — Luogu P3348: [ZJOI2016] 大森林 (Great Forest)

Source: Luogu P3348 — [ZJOI2016] 大森林
Prerequisite Tags: Offline Sweep Across Trees, Virtual Auxiliary Nodes, Dynamic Tree / Top Tree Path Distance Queries


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You maintain a sequence of \(N\) rooted trees \(T_1, T_2, \dots, T_N\), each initially consisting of a single vertex \(1\) (with its growth point set to \(1\)). Process \(M\) operations of three types:

0 l r: In every tree \(T_i\) for \(l \le i \le r\), create a new vertex with the next sequential ID \(c + 1\) and attach it as a child of the current growth point of \(T_i\). (Note: this new vertex receives the same ID \(c + 1\) across all trees; even trees outside \([l, r]\) advance the global vertex counter, though the vertex only exists in \(T_l, \dots, T_r\)).
1 l r x: In every tree \(T_i\) for \(l \le i \le r\), change the growth point of \(T_i\) to vertex \(x\) (it is guaranteed that vertex \(x\) exists in \(T_l, \dots, T_r\)).
2 x u v: Query the tree distance (number of edges on the unique simple path) between vertex \(u\) and vertex \(v\) in tree \(T_x\).
Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 10^5\), \(1 \le M \le 2 \times 10^5\). Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\). Required complexity: \(O((N + M) \log M)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N = 2, M = 4\))
Suppose \(N = 2\) trees \(T_1, T_2\) (initially both have node \(1\), growth point \(1\)):

0 1 2: Node \(2\) is added under growth point \(1\) in \(T_1, T_2\).
1 2 2 2: In \(T_2\), growth point changes to \(2\) (in \(T_1\), growth point stays \(1\)).
0 1 2: Node \(3\) is added under current growth point (\(1\) in \(T_1\), \(2\) in \(T_2\)).
Queries 2 1 2 3 and 2 2 2 3:

In \(T_1\), edges are \((1,2)\) and \((1,3)\), so \(\operatorname{dist}_{T_1}(2, 3) = 2\).
In \(T_2\), edges are \((1,2)\) and \((2,3)\), so \(\operatorname{dist}_{T_2}(2, 3) = 1\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Notice that there are no dependencies between different trees \(T_1, \dots, T_N\), and notice that if a 0 l r operation adds a vertex \(u\) to a subrange \([l, r]\), the distance between any two existing vertices in \(T_i\) neither depends on whether \(u\) exists nor changes when \(u\) is added as a leaf! What happens if we pretend that 0 l r adds vertex \(u\) to all trees \(1 \dots N\), and process the trees \(T_1, T_2, \dots, T_N\) offline by sweeping the tree index \(i\) from \(1\) to \(N\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

When we sweep the tree index \(i\) from \(1\) to \(N\), a growth-point change 1 l r x (occurring at chronological time \(t\)) activates at \(i = l\) and deactivates at \(i = r + 1\). How can we avoid moving all the individual leaves created between chronological time \(t\) and the next growth-point change one by one when \(i\) crosses \(l\) or \(r + 1\)?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Create a zero-weight virtual auxiliary node \(V_k\) for each 1 l r x operation (and an initial virtual node \(V_0\) attached to \(1\)). Every real vertex \(u\) (of weight \(1\)) created by a 0 operation after the \(k\)-th 1 operation and before the \((k+1)\)-th 1 operation is permanently attached as a child of the virtual node \(V_k\)! Now, when sweeping \(i\) from \(1 \dots N\):

At \(i = l\), the \(k\)-th 1 l r x operation simply detaches the single virtual node \(V_k\) from \(V_{k-1}\) and attaches \(V_k\) under real node \(x\) (cut + link of the entire subtree \(T_{V_k}\)!).
At \(i = r + 1\), it detaches \(V_k\) from \(x\) and re-attaches \(V_k\) under \(V_{k-1}\)! Measuring weighted distance \(\operatorname{dist}(u, v) = \operatorname{depth}_w(u) + \operatorname{depth}_w(v) - 2\operatorname{depth}_w(\operatorname{LCA}(u, v))\) (where real nodes have weight \(1\) and virtual nodes \(V_k\) have weight \(0\)) answers every query in \(O(\log M)\) time!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Offline Sweep and Virtual Growth-Point Nodes
Observe two fundamental invariants:

Universal Creation: A query 2 x u v guarantees that \(u\) and \(v\) exist in \(T_x\). Attaching a leaf \(w\) during 0 l r to trees outside \([l, r]\) never alters the path between any two vertices that actually exist in \(T_x\), provided that any 1 l' r' w operation only sets the growth point to \(w\) within \([l', r'] \subseteq [l, r]\). Thus we can treat every 0 operation as active across all \(i \in [1, N]\).
Virtual Batching Nodes: Let the 1 l r x operations be numbered \(k = 1, 2, \dots, K\) in chronological order, and create a virtual node \(V_k\) of edge weight \(0\) for each \(k \in [0, K]\):

Initially (for a tree where no 1 operations are active), \(V_0\) is attached to real node \(1\), and for each \(k \ge 1\), \(V_k\) is attached as a weight-\(0\) child of \(V_{k-1}\). Because the chain \(V_0 - V_1 - \dots - V_K\) has total weight \(0\), any real node attached to \(V_k\) is effectively attached directly to the active growth point of the most recent active 1 operation \(\le k\)!
Whenever a 0 operation creates a new real vertex \(u\) (when the most recent 1 operation so far is \(k\)), we permanently link \(u\) to \(V_k\) with vertex/edge weight \(1\).
For the \(k\)-th 1 l r x operation, we schedule two sweep events at tree index \(i = l\) (cut \(V_k\) from its current parent \(V_{k-1}\) and link \(V_k\) to \(x\)) and at tree index \(i = r + 1\) (cut \(V_k\) from \(x\) and link \(V_k\) back to \(V_{k-1}\)).




2. Weighted LCA Distance Query on Dynamic Tree
Why can’t we simply compute \(\operatorname{dist}(u, v)\) by exposing the path \(u \leftrightarrow v\) via make_root(u)? Because computing the LCA in a rooted tree via access(u) followed by access(v) (where the last splay-tree jump node \(w\) during access(v) is \(\operatorname{LCA}(u, v)\)) keeps the root fixed at \(1\), preserving parent-child orientation for cut(V_k, parent(V_k))!
Specifically, assign weight \(\text{val}[u] = 1\) to every real vertex \(u\) and \(\text{val}[V_k] = 0\) to every virtual vertex \(V_k\), maintaining the path sum sum[x] on each auxiliary splay tree. Then the distance between real vertices \(u\) and \(v\) in \(T_i\) is:
\[\operatorname{dist}_{T_i}(u, v) = \operatorname{depth}_w(u) + \operatorname{depth}_w(v) - 2 \operatorname{depth}_w(\operatorname{LCA}(u, v))\]
(counting edges between real vertices, so \(\operatorname{depth}_w(u)\) is the sum of real vertices on the root-to-\(u\) path, and subtracting \(2 \operatorname{depth}_w(\operatorname{LCA}(u, v)) - 2 \cdot 1\) or equivalently assigning weight \(1\) to the parent edge of each real vertex \(u \ge 2\) and weight \(0\) to the parent edge of \(1\) and all \(V_k\) makes \(\operatorname{dist}(u, v) = \operatorname{depth}_w(u) + \operatorname{depth}_w(v) - 2\operatorname{depth}_w(\operatorname{LCA}(u, v))\) exact without any \(+1/-1\) adjustment!).


Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Integers \(N \le 10^5, M \le 2 \times 10^5\) and \(M\) operations of types 0 l r, 1 l r x, 2 x u v; every 1 l r x and 2 x u v references vertices that exist in the specified trees.
Postconditions (Output): Outputs the exact path length between \(u\) and \(v\) in \(T_x\) for each type-2 query in chronological order.
Time & Space Complexity: \(O((N + M) \log M)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At sweep index \(i \in [1, N]\), virtual node \(V_k\) (\(k \ge 1\)) has parent \(x_k\) if \(i \in [l_k, r_k]\) and parent \(V_{k-1}\) otherwise; because real vertices \(u \ge 2\) carry edge-weight \(1\) and virtual nodes \(V_k\) carry edge-weight \(0\), contracting all weight-\(0\) edges produces a tree isomorphic to \(T_i\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Calling make_root(u) to query path distances destroys the fixed parent-child orientation rooted at \(1\) required by cut(V_k, parent(V_k)) during the sweep; always query \(\operatorname{dist}(u, v) = \operatorname{depth}_w(u) + \operatorname{depth}_w(v) - 2\operatorname{depth}_w(\operatorname{LCA}(u, v))\) via access(u) and access(v) while keeping vertex \(1\) as the permanent LCT root, and clamp \([l, r]\) of type-1 operations to the creation interval of \(x\).

22.7 Self-Assessment Checklist & Chapter Summary
Before moving to Chapter 23, verify that you can answer and execute every item on this checklist from first principles:

\(\binom{N}{2}\) Subtree Knapsack vs. \(\Theta(N^2 \log N)\) Unbalanced NTT: Can you prove by LCA double counting why the naive nested loop takes \(\binom{N}{2}\) operations (\(O(NK)\) when truncated to degree \(K\)), and explain why bottom-up NTT without HLD still takes \(\Theta(N^2 \log N)\) on a path or caterpillar?
Heavy-Light Rake & 3-Way Weighted-Midpoint Compress: Can you implement the Rake phase (merging light children via a degree-ordered min-heap) and the Compress phase (splitting heavy chains \([l, r]\) into \([l, m-1]\), \(\{m\}\), and \([m+1, r]\) at the first index \(m\) with \(\sum_{i=l}^m w_i \ge \frac{1}{2} W_{[l,r]}\)), and explain why naive index-midpoint halving (\(m = \lfloor(l+r)/2\rfloor\)) degrades to \(O(N \log^3 N)\)?
Fourier-Domain \(3c^2\) Matrix Product: When multiplying two \(c \times c\) polynomial matrices of total degree \(D\), do you transform the \(2c^2\) input entries once, perform \(O(c^3 \cdot 2^k)\) pointwise scalar multiplications in \(\mathbb{F}_p\), and inverse-transform the \(c^2\) output entries (\(3c^2\) NTTs instead of \(3c^3\))?
Failure Mode #10 (ZeroDivPair \((a, c) \equiv a \cdot 0^c\)): In Dynamic DP on a Weight-Balanced Static Top Tree (全局平衡二叉树) with FWT or point evaluations, do you wrap every light-child product accumulator in a ZeroDivPair so that multiplying and dividing by \(0 \pmod p\) increments/decrements \(c\) without destroying the non-zero residue product \(a \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\)?
Subtree Frequency mulT: When computing \(\sum_{|S|=k} f(S)\) across all \(k = 1 \dots N\), can you decompose \(f(S)\) into vertex/edge indicators, build the directed subtree size histogram \(\text{cnt}[1 \dots N-1]\), and evaluate \(\sum_{s=k}^{N-1} \text{cnt}[s] \binom{s}{k}\) in a single \(O(N \log N)\) reverse-indexed NTT convolution?







NoteImplementation Verification Footnote (Quarantined Research Template R-67)





During the curriculum verification pass (fps_research/CURRICULUM_ARCHITECTURE.md §5), reference template R-67 in cohort3_wave_5b_tree_fps_transposition_compose_q.md (HLD Tree DP divide-and-conquer) was flagged for splitting heavy chains at the unweighted index midpoint \(m = \lfloor(l + r)/2\rfloor\), which degrades to \(\Theta(N \log^3 N)\) when a single vertex on a heavy chain carries a large light-subtree polynomial degree. Section 22.2 replaces R-67 with the verified 3-way weighted-midpoint compress_solve kernel (Theorem 22.3), guaranteeing strict \(\le \lfloor W/2 \rfloor\) subtree weight halving and global \(O(c^2 N \log^2 N)\) complexity.





Where Next?
Having mastered polynomial divide-and-conquer and dynamic algebraic structures on trees, we turn in the next chapter to the \(q\)-analogue world—where powers of \(q\) track inversions, subspace dimensions over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and Ferrers diagram areas:

Next Chapter: Chapter 23: q-Series, Gaussian Binomials, Pentagonal/Durfee Decompositions & q-Difference Equations

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Diagonalize Bitwise Semigroup and Group Algebras (\(K[(S, \oplus)]\)): Derive the \(2 \times 2\) coordinate transform matrices for bitwise OR, AND, and XOR convolutions via characters, execute Fast Zeta/Möbius and Walsh–Hadamard Transforms in \(O(n 2^n)\), and compress products of \(m\) sparse 2-term XOR factors into a single FWT pass in \(O(m + n 2^n)\) via the Small-Support XOR Trick.
Construct the Set Power Series Ring \(\mathcal{R}_n = K[x_1, \dots, x_n]/(x_1^2, \dots, x_n^2)\): Prove that disjoint-union subset convolution is exact multiplication in the square-free multivariate quotient ring \(\mathcal{R}_n\), lift set masks to ranked polynomials in \(K[t]/(t^{n+1})\) via \(\operatorname{popcount}\) grading, and lay out the [1<<n][n+1] buffer in L1-cache-contiguous memory.
Execute \(O(n^2 2^n)\) Transcendental Operations & General Composition on \(\mathcal{R}_n\): Apply pointwise \(O(n^2)\) truncated polynomial ODEs (\(\operatorname{inv}, \ln, \exp, P^\alpha\)) in Ranked Zeta space, implement the Division-Free MSB Derivative Split (\(\exp(F_0 + x_v F_1) = \exp(F_0)(1 + x_v F_1)\)) that halves constant factors and bypasses characteristic-\(p\) non-invertibility, and execute Elegia’s \(O(n^2 2^n)\) Taylor Shift Pyramid for general SPS composition \(G(F(\mathbf{x}))\).
Filter Articulation Points via Pointed Vertex-by-Vertex SPS \(\ln\): Extract biconnected subgraphs on a fixed \(n\)-vertex graph in \(O(n^3 2^n)\) by sequentially rooting at each vertex \(v \in V\) and taking the \((n-1)\)-variable subset logarithm \(\ln C^{(v)}(\mathbf{x})\) to strip components glued at \(v\).
Compute Transcendental Functions in the Dirichlet Ring \(\mathcal{D}_f\) via the \(\Omega(n)\)-Derivation: Construct the prime-multiplicity derivation \((\vartheta f)(n) = \Omega(n) f(n)\) satisfying the Leibniz rule on Dirichlet convolution, and evaluate \(\exp_D(f)\), \(\ln_D(f)\), and \(f^\alpha\) up to \(N\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time or via prime-by-prime Bell series recurrences.

section: 24.1 Bitwise Group Algebras (OR, AND, XOR Fast Walsh–Hadamard / Möbius Transforms)
text:
24.1 Bitwise Group Algebras (OR, AND, XOR Fast Walsh–Hadamard / Möbius Transforms)
Every polynomial engine we have built in Chapters 1–23 operated inside the Cauchy convolution algebra \(K[[x]]\), where multiplying two monomials adds their integer exponents: \(x^i \cdot x^j = x^{i+j}\). Yet many combinatorial problems combine indices not by integer addition, but by bitwise boolean operations on \(n\)-bit masks \(S, T \in \{0, 1\}^n\) (identified with subsets of \(\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}\) or integers in \([0, 2^n - 1]\)):
\[
(A *_{\oplus} B)_S = \sum_{\substack{T, R \in \{0, 1\}^n \\ T \oplus R = S}} A_T B_R, \qquad \oplus \in \{\mathbin{|}, \mathbin{\&}, \oplus_{\text{XOR}}\}.
\]
Before writing down transform matrices, let us name the concrete combinatorial objects being counted and the exact algebraic structure behind them.

From Monoid Algebras to Coordinate-Wise \(2 \times 2\) Kronecker Products
Fix a commutative ring \(K\) and a finite commutative monoid \((M, \oplus)\) of size \(2^n\), where \(M = \{0, 1\}^n\) and \(\oplus\) acts independently on each of the \(n\) bit positions. The monoid algebra \(K[M]\) consists of formal linear combinations \(A = \sum_{S \in M} A_S \mathbf{e}_S\) with multiplication defined on basis elements by \(\mathbf{e}_T \cdot \mathbf{e}_R = \mathbf{e}_{T \oplus R}\).
Because the \(n\) bit coordinates do not carry into one another under \(\mathbin{|}\), \(\mathbin{\&}\), or \(\oplus_{\text{XOR}}\), the \(n\)-bit monoid decomposes as a direct product of \(n\) copies of the 1-bit monoid \((\{0, 1\}, \oplus_1)\). Consequently, the \(2^n\)-dimensional algebra \(K[\{0, 1\}^n]\) factors as the \(n\)-fold tensor product of the 2-dimensional 1-bit algebra:
\[
K[\{0, 1\}^n] \cong \underbrace{K[\{0, 1\}] \otimes_K K[\{0, 1\}] \otimes_K \cdots \otimes_K K[\{0, 1\}]}_{n \text{ times}}.
\]
This tensor factorization means we only ever need to diagonalize a single bit (\(n = 1\), a \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(\mathcal{T}_1\)) and apply that \(2 \times 2\) butterfly across each of the \(n\) bit dimensions sequentially in \(n \cdot 2^{n-1}\) operations!


Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering the \(2 \times 2\) Transform Matrices






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: 1-Bit Characters




The Diagnostic Signal: You are asked to compute \(C_S = \sum_{T \oplus R = S} A_T B_R\) for all \(S \in [0, 2^n-1]\) where \(\oplus\) is a bitwise boolean operation without arithmetic carries between bits.
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Suppose \(n = 1\), so our sequence has two entries \((a_0, a_1)\) and we want a linear map \((a_0, a_1) \mapsto (\hat{a}_0, \hat{a}_1)\) that turns 1-bit convolution into pointwise multiplication \(\hat{c}_0 = \hat{a}_0 \hat{b}_0\) and \(\hat{c}_1 = \hat{a}_1 \hat{b}_1\).

Bitwise OR (\(\mathbin{|}\)): The convolution rules are \(c_0 = a_0 b_0\) and \(c_1 = a_0 b_1 + a_1 b_0 + a_1 b_1\). Notice that \(c_0 = a_0 b_0\) is already a pointwise product! And if we add the two equations together, we get: \[
c_0 + c_1 = a_0 b_0 + a_0 b_1 + a_1 b_0 + a_1 b_1 = (a_0 + a_1)(b_0 + b_1).
\] Thus \((\hat{a}_0, \hat{a}_1) = (a_0, a_0 + a_1)\) diagonalizes 1-bit OR! Over \(n\) bits, iterating this over all coordinates sums over all subsets: \(\widehat{A}_S = \sum_{T \subseteq S} A_T\) (the Subset Fast Zeta Transform / SOS DP). Its inverse subtracts the 0-coordinate from the 1-coordinate: \((a_0, a_1) = (\hat{a}_0, \hat{a}_1 - \hat{a}_0)\) (the Subset Fast Möbius Transform).
Bitwise AND (\(\mathbin{\&}\)): Symmetrically, \(c_1 = a_1 b_1\) is already pointwise, and \(c_0 + c_1 = (a_0 + a_1)(b_0 + b_1)\). Thus \((\hat{a}_0, \hat{a}_1) = (a_0 + a_1, a_1)\) diagonalizes 1-bit AND. Over \(n\) bits, this sums over all supersets: \(\widehat{A}_S = \sum_{T \supseteq S} A_T\) (the Superset Fast Zeta Transform).
Bitwise XOR (\(\oplus\)): Here \(c_0 = a_0 b_0 + a_1 b_1\) and \(c_1 = a_0 b_1 + a_1 b_0\). Adding and subtracting the two equations yields: \[
c_0 + c_1 = (a_0 + a_1)(b_0 + b_1), \qquad c_0 - c_1 = (a_0 - a_1)(b_0 - b_1).
\] Thus \((\hat{a}_0, \hat{a}_1) = (a_0 + a_1, a_0 - a_1)\) is the Walsh–Hadamard butterfly. Over \(n\) bits, every mask \(S\) picks up a \(-1\) factor whenever both \(S\) and \(T\) have bit \(i\) set, giving \(\widehat{A}_S = \sum_{T} (-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(S \mathbin{\&} T)} A_T\).

// Unified in-place O(n 2^n) FWT / Fast Zeta & Mobius loop skeleton
for (int len = 1; len < (1 << n); len <<= 1)
    for (int i = 0; i < (1 << n); i += (len << 1))
        for (int j = 0; j < len; ++j) {
            mint u = A[i + j], v = A[i + len + j];
            // OR:  A[i+len+j] = u + sgn * v;
            // AND: A[i+j]     = u + sgn * v;
            // XOR: A[i+j] = u + v; A[i+len+j] = u - v; (divide by 2^n at end if inverse)
        }


Hand-Checkable Trace (\(n = 2\) XOR Convolution)
Let \(n = 2\), and suppose \(A = [1, 2, 0, 3]\) and \(B = [0, 1, 2, 1]\) indexed by masks \(00_2, 01_2, 10_2, 11_2\). Let us trace \(C = A *_{\text{xor}} B\):

Bit 0 butterfly (\(\text{len} = 1\), pairs \((0,1)\) and \((2,3)\)):

\(A^{(1)} = [1+2, 1-2, 0+3, 0-3] = [3, -1, 3, -3]\).
\(B^{(1)} = [0+1, 0-1, 2+1, 2-1] = [1, -1, 3, 1]\).

Bit 1 butterfly (\(\text{len} = 2\), pairs \((0,2)\) and \((1,3)\)):

\(\widehat{A} = [3+3, -1+(-3), 3-3, -1-(-3)] = [6, -4, 0, 2]\).
\(\widehat{B} = [1+3, -1+1, 1-3, -1-1] = [4, 0, -2, -2]\).

Pointwise product: \(\widehat{C} = \widehat{A} \odot \widehat{B} = [24, 0, 0, -4]\).
Inverse FWT (apply the two butterflies, then divide by \(2^2 = 4\)):

After bit 0: \([24+0, 24-0, 0+(-4), 0-(-4)] = [24, 24, -4, 4]\).
After bit 1: \([24+(-4), 24+4, 24-(-4), 24-4] = [20, 28, 28, 20]\).
Divide by \(4\): \(C = [5, 7, 7, 5]\).
Direct check for \(C_{00_2}\): \(A_0 B_0 + A_1 B_1 + A_2 B_2 + A_3 B_3 = 1(0) + 2(1) + 0(2) + 3(1) = 5\). Exact match!




The Small-Support XOR Trick (\(O(m + n 2^n)\) Sparse Product Compression)
Suppose we must compute the XOR product of \(m\) sparse polynomials, each supported on at most two masks (for example, choosing whether to include or exclude each of \(m\) items with XOR weight \(u_i \in [0, 2^n - 1]\)):
\[
F(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m \left(a + b x^{u_i}\right) \quad \text{in } K[\mathbb{Z}_2^n],
\]
where \(m \le 10^6\) and \(n \le 20\). Transforming \(m\) separate arrays of size \(2^n\) would take \(O(m n 2^n)\) time—an immediate TLE.
How do we collapse all \(m\) transforms into one FWT? Look at what the XOR transform does to a single factor \(P_i(x) = a + b x^{u_i}\) at frequency mask \(M\):
\[
\widehat{P_i}(M) = a (-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(M \mathbin{\&} 0)} + b (-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(M \mathbin{\&} u_i)} = \begin{cases} a + b & \text{if } \operatorname{popcount}(M \mathbin{\&} u_i) \equiv 0 \pmod 2, \\ a - b & \text{if } \operatorname{popcount}(M \mathbin{\&} u_i) \equiv 1 \pmod 2. \end{cases}
\]
Notice that \(\widehat{P_i}(M)\) can only take two possible values: \(a+b\) or \(a-b\)! Therefore, for a fixed frequency mask \(M\), if \(c_{+1}(M)\) counts how many indices \(i \in \{1, \dots, m\}\) have \(\operatorname{popcount}(M \mathbin{\&} u_i)\) even, and \(c_{-1}(M)\) counts how many have \(\operatorname{popcount}(M \mathbin{\&} u_i)\) odd, then the product in frequency space is simply:
\[
\widehat{F}(M) = (a + b)^{c_{+1}(M)} (a - b)^{c_{-1}(M)}.
\]
How do we find \(c_{+1}(M)\) and \(c_{-1}(M)\) for all \(M\) simultaneously? Build a single frequency array \(C\) of length \(2^n\) where \(C_u = \#\{i : u_i = u\}\), and apply a single forward XOR-FWT to \(C\)! By linearity of FWT:
\[
\widehat{C}_M = \sum_{i=1}^m (-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(M \mathbin{\&} u_i)} = c_{+1}(M) - c_{-1}(M).
\]
Combining this with the total count \(c_{+1}(M) + c_{-1}(M) = m\), we solve the \(2 \times 2\) linear system at each mask \(M\):
\[
c_{+1}(M) = \frac{m + \widehat{C}_M}{2}, \qquad c_{-1}(M) = \frac{m - \widehat{C}_M}{2}.
\]
One forward FWT on \(C\), \(2^n\) modular exponentiations, and one inverse FWT on \(\widehat{F}\) solves the entire \(m\)-factor product in \(O(m + n 2^n)\) time! (This generalizes to \(k\)-sparse factors for \(k \le 3\) via \(2^{k-1}\) linear equations.)






WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Characteristic-2 Collapse & Zero Factors in Pointwise FWT Products




Characteristic-2 Collapse in XOR-FWT: The inverse XOR butterfly requires dividing by \(2\) at each of the \(n\) bit layers (or by \(2^n\) at the end). If you work over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) or \(\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z}\), \(2\) is not a unit! Remedy: Lift the coefficients to \(\mathbb{Z}\) (using 64-bit integers int64_t) or a prime field \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with \(p > 2\), execute the XOR-FWT and division by \(2^n\) in the lifted ring, and reduce modulo \(2\) or \(2^k\) only after the inverse transform completes.
Vanishing Pointwise Values in Frequency Space (\(\widehat{P}_M = 0\)): When maintaining dynamic products \(\widehat{F}_M = \prod_i \widehat{P_i}(M) \bmod p\), a factor might evaluate to \(\widehat{P_i}(M) \equiv 0 \pmod p\) (for instance, when \(a \equiv b \pmod p\) and \(c_{-1}(M) > 0\)). You cannot later “remove” that factor by multiplying by \(\widehat{P_i}(M)^{-1} \bmod p\). Remedy: Either count the multiplicity of zero factors per mask \(M\) as a pair (nonzero_part, zero_count), or compute exponents \(c_{+1}(M), c_{-1}(M)\) directly over \(\mathbb{Z}\) before taking modular powers.









NoteAlgorithm Contract: Bitwise FWT / FZT & Small-Support XOR Eigenvalue Trick




Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Bit-width \(n \ge 0\) (\(N = 2^n\) masks indexed \(0 \dots 2^n - 1\)); arrays \(A, B\) of length \(2^n\) over commutative ring \(K\) (or \(m\) sparse tuples for the eigenvalue trick).
Preconditions: For OR/AND FZT and IFMT, any commutative ring \(K\) suffices; for IFWT-XOR, \(2 \in K^\times\) must be invertible (\(\operatorname{char}(K) \neq 2\)). For the small-support XOR eigenvalue trick, the forward frequency FWT must be computed over exact 64-bit integers (int64_t), not modulo \(p\).
Postconditions (Output): Exact bitwise OR, AND, or XOR convolution \(C_S = \sum_{T \oplus R = S} A_T B_R\) for all \(S \in [0, 2^n - 1]\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n 2^n)\) time and \(O(2^n)\) in-place space (or \(O(m + k 2^k + n 2^n)\) for \(k\)-sparse factors).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing bit stages \(0, 1, \dots, b - 1\), each block of size \(2^b\) holds the \(b\)-dimensional character evaluation along the lowest \(b\) bits while higher bits \(b \dots n - 1\) remain in the time domain.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases:

Characteristic-2 Collapse: Dividing by \(2^n\) in IFWT-XOR fails when \(2\) is not a unit in \(K\) (e.g., \(\mathbb{F}_2\) or \(\mathbb{Z}/2^{64}\mathbb{Z}\) without extra precision bits).
Modular Reduction of Frequency Counts: Reducing \(\widehat{C}_M\) modulo \(p\) before solving the linear system for multiplicity counts \(c_r(M)\) corrupts the integer exponents used in \(\prod_r \lambda_r^{c_r(M)} \bmod p\).
Zero Point-Value Factors: When evaluating ratios or dynamic updates in the FWT domain, frequencies with \(\widehat{A}_M \equiv 0 \pmod p\) cannot be divided out naively and require \((a, c)\) zero-divisor tracking (Ch 22 §22.3).

section: 24.2 The Set Power Series Ring \(\mathcal{R}_n = K[x_1, \dots, x_n]/(x_1^2, \dots, x_n^2)\) & Ranked Fast Zeta Transform
text:
24.2 The Set Power Series Ring \(\mathcal{R}_n = K[x_1, \dots, x_n]/(x_1^2, \dots, x_n^2)\) & Ranked Fast Zeta Transform
Bitwise OR convolution combines two subsets \(T, R \subseteq \{0, \dots, n-1\}\) into \(T \cup R\) even when \(T\) and \(R\) overlap. However, in almost all exact partition and graph component problems—such as building a disconnected graph out of vertex-disjoint connected components, or partitioning \(V\) into \(k\) independent sets—we need the disjoint-union subset convolution:
\[
(A *_{\text{sub}} B)_S = \sum_{\substack{T \cup R = S \\ T \cap R = \varnothing}} A_T B_R = \sum_{T \subseteq S} A_T B_{S \setminus T}.
\]
Computing this naively by iterating over submasks for (int T = S; ; T = (T - 1) & S) takes \(\sum_{S} 2^{|S|} = 3^n\) operations. To accelerate this to \(O(n^2 2^n)\) and unlock \(\ln\), \(\exp\), and composition, we first formulate subset convolution as exact multiplication in a commutative quotient ring.

Algebraic Definition of the Set Power Series Ring \(\mathcal{R}_n\)
Fix an \(n\)-element ground set \(V = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}\) and a commutative ring \(K\). Introduce \(n\) formal commuting variables \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}\), one for each vertex in \(V\), and quotient out the square of every variable:
\[
\mathcal{R}_n = K[x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}] / (x_0^2, x_1^2, \dots, x_{n-1}^2).
\]
For each subset \(S \subseteq V\), define the square-free monomial \(\mathbf{x}^S = \prod_{i \in S} x_i\). What happens when we multiply two monomials \(\mathbf{x}^T\) and \(\mathbf{x}^R\) inside \(\mathcal{R}_n\)?

If \(T \cap R = \varnothing\), no variable appears twice, so \(\mathbf{x}^T \cdot \mathbf{x}^R = \mathbf{x}^{T \cup R}\).
If \(T \cap R \neq \varnothing\), there is at least one element \(v \in T \cap R\), which produces a factor \(x_v^2 = 0\) in the quotient ring:

\[
\mathbf{x}^T \cdot \mathbf{x}^R = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x}^{T \cup R} & \text{if } T \cap R = \varnothing, \\ 0 & \text{if } T \cap R \neq \varnothing. \end{cases}
\]
Therefore, formal multiplication of two Set Power Series (SPS) \(A(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{S \subseteq V} A_S \mathbf{x}^S\) and \(B(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{S \subseteq V} B_S \mathbf{x}^S\) in \(\mathcal{R}_n\) is identically their disjoint-union subset convolution!


Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering the Ranked Lift






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: The Popcount Grading Trick




The Diagnostic Signal: You need \(C_S = \sum_{T \subseteq S} A_T B_{S \setminus T}\) for \(n \le 20\) (\(3^n \approx 3.5 \times 10^9\) is TLE, while \(n^2 2^n \approx 4 \times 10^8\) simple additions passes in \(< 0.3\text{ s}\)).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Why couldn’t we just use the \(O(n 2^n)\) OR-FWT (Fast Zeta Transform) from §24.1? Because OR-FWT computes \(\sum_{T \cup R = S} A_T B_R\), which includes overlapping pairs with \(T \cap R \neq \varnothing\). How can we detect whether \(T\) and \(R\) overlap using only a simple scalar statistic? By inclusion-exclusion on set sizes: \[
|T \cup R| = |T| + |R| - |T \cap R| \implies |T| + |R| \ge |T \cup R|,
\] with equality \(|T| + |R| = |T \cup R|\) if and only if \(T \cap R = \varnothing\)! Therefore, if we attach a formal grading variable \(t^{|S|}\) to record the cardinality (rank) of each set \(S\), lifting \(A_S\) to a polynomial \(A_S(t) = A_S t^{|S|} \in K[t]/(t^{n+1})\), and then run the Subset Fast Zeta Transform on the polynomial coefficients: \[
\widehat{A}_M(t) = \sum_{T \subseteq M} A_T t^{|T|} \in K[t]/(t^{n+1}),
\] then multiplying \(\widehat{A}_M(t) \cdot \widehat{B}_M(t)\) in \(K[t]/(t^{n+1})\) and applying the Inverse Fast Zeta Transform at mask \(S\) gives the polynomial: \[
\sum_{T \cup R = S} A_T B_R t^{|T| + |R|}.
\] In this sum, overlapping pairs \(T \cap R \neq \varnothing\) have \(|T| + |R| > |S|\), so they land exclusivamente in degrees \(> |S|\)! The coefficient of \(t^{|S|}\) contains only the disjoint pairs \(|T| + |R| = |S|\)!








flowchart LR
    A["SPS A_S, B_S in R_n"] -->|"Lift by rank k = |S| + Ranked FZT O(n^2 2^n)"| B["Ranked Zeta Space: A_hat_M(t), B_hat_M(t) in K[t]/(t^{n+1})"]
    B -->|"Pointwise Cauchy Product or ODE in K[t]/(t^{n+1}) O(n^2 2^n)"| C["Ranked Zeta Result C_hat_M(t)"]
    C -->|"Ranked IFZT + Extract [t^{|S|}] O(n^2 2^n)"| D["Disjoint Subset Result C_S in R_n"]








L1 Cache-Contiguous Memory Layout: [1<<n][n+1] vs. [n+1][1<<n]
Because \(O(n^2 2^n)\) at \(n = 20\) performs \(\approx 2.2 \times 10^8\) multiply-adds, memory layout determines whether your code runs in \(0.18\text{ s}\) or \(1.8\text{ s}\) (TLE).






ImportantHardware Reality Check: Why [1<<n][n+1] Beats [n+1][1<<n]




If you store the ranked array as P[n + 1][1 << n] (rank outer, mask inner), then during the pointwise \(O(n^2)\) polynomial product or ODE at a fixed mask \(M\), accessing P[0][M], P[1][M], ..., P[n][M] jumps by a stride of \(2^n \times 4\text{ bytes} = 4\text{ MB}\) per step! Every single rank access is an L1/L2 cache miss and TLB thrash.
Instead, flatten the buffer as P[(1 << n) * (n + 1)] indexed via P[M * (n + 1) + d] (equivalent to P[1 << n][n + 1], mask outer, rank inner). For \(n = 20\), all \(21\) ranks of mask \(M\) occupy \(21 \times 4 = 84\text{ bytes}\)—fitting inside two adjacent 64-byte L1 cache lines! Both the FZT butterfly (which vectorizes across \(d \in [0, n]\)) and the pointwise \(O(n^2)\) polynomial loop run entirely inside L1 registers.



// Ranked Fast Zeta / Mobius Transform on L1-contiguous layout P[mask * (n + 1) + d]
void ranked_fzt(vector<mint>& P, int n, bool inv) {
    int S = n + 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); ++mask)
            if (mask & (1 << i)) {
                int u = (mask ^ (1 << i)) * S, v = mask * S;
                for (int d = 0; d <= n; ++d)
                    P[v + d] += inv ? -P[u + d] : P[u + d];
            }
}


Hand-Checkable Trace (\(n = 2\) Subset Convolution)
Let \(V = \{0, 1\}\), and consider \(A(\mathbf{x}) = 1 + 2 x_0 + 3 x_1\) and \(B(\mathbf{x}) = 1 + 4 x_0 + 5 x_1 + 6 x_0 x_1\).

Ranked Lift:

\(M = 00_2\): \(A_{00}(t) = 1\), \(B_{00}(t) = 1\).
\(M = 01_2\): \(A_{01}(t) = 2t\), \(B_{01}(t) = 4t\).
\(M = 10_2\): \(A_{10}(t) = 3t\), \(B_{10}(t) = 5t\).
\(M = 11_2\): \(A_{11}(t) = 0\), \(B_{11}(t) = 6t^2\).

Ranked FZT (\(\widehat{P}_M(t) = \sum_{T \subseteq M} P_T(t)\)):

\(\widehat{A}_{11}(t) = 1 + 2t + 3t + 0 = 1 + 5t\), \(\widehat{B}_{11}(t) = 1 + 4t + 5t + 6t^2 = 1 + 9t + 6t^2\).
\(\widehat{A}_{01}(t) = 1 + 2t\), \(\widehat{B}_{01}(t) = 1 + 4t\); \(\widehat{A}_{10}(t) = 1 + 3t\), \(\widehat{B}_{10}(t) = 1 + 5t\); \(\widehat{A}_{00}(t) = 1\), \(\widehat{B}_{00}(t) = 1\).

Pointwise Product in \(K[t]/(t^3)\):

\(\widehat{C}_{11}(t) = (1 + 5t)(1 + 9t + 6t^2) \bmod t^3 = 1 + 14t + 51t^2\).
\(\widehat{C}_{01}(t) = (1+2t)(1+4t) = 1 + 6t + 8t^2\); \(\widehat{C}_{10}(t) = (1+3t)(1+5t) = 1 + 8t + 15t^2\); \(\widehat{C}_{00}(t) = 1\).

Ranked IFZT & Degree Extraction:

At \(M = 11_2\), IFZT gives \(C_{11}(t) = \widehat{C}_{11}(t) - \widehat{C}_{01}(t) - \widehat{C}_{10}(t) + \widehat{C}_{00}(t) = (1 + 14t + 51t^2) - (1 + 6t + 8t^2) - (1 + 8t + 15t^2) + 1 = 28t^2\).
Notice how the overlapping products \(2x_0 \cdot 4x_0 = 8t^2\) and \(3x_1 \cdot 5x_1 = 15t^2\) were subtracted away by IFZT! Extracting \([t^2] C_{11}(t) = 28\) matches \(1 \cdot 6 + 2 \cdot 5 + 3 \cdot 4 = 28\).








NoteAlgorithm Contract: Ranked Fast Zeta Transform (Disjoint Subset Convolution)




Input: Two set power series \(A, B \in \mathcal{R}_n = K[x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}]/(x_0^2, \dots, x_{n-1}^2)\) of size \(2^n\).
Output: The disjoint subset convolution \(C = A *_{\text{sub}} B\) where \(C_S = \sum_{T \subseteq S} A_T B_{S \setminus T}\).
Algebraic Hypothesis: None — valid over any commutative ring \(K\) regardless of characteristic (division-free).
Complexity: \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time (\(O(n 2^n)\) for ranked FZT/IFZT and \(O(n^2 2^n)\) for pointwise polynomial multiplication in \(K[t]/(t^{n+1})\)), \(O(n 2^n)\) space.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases:

Rank Contamination Across Chained Convolutions: Pointwise multiplication in \(K[t]/(t^{n+1})\) produces valid coefficients at \(t^{|S|}\) after IFZT, but leaves non-zero garbage at higher ranks \(k > |S|\). When chaining multiple subset convolutions, you must zero out \(C_S(k)\) for \(k \neq |S|\) in the primal domain before re-transforming (or perform the entire algebraic expression inside \(K[t]/(t^{n+1})\) before a single final IFZT and rank extraction).
Cache Locality ([mask][rank] vs. [rank][mask]): Laying out the ranked array as A[mask][n + 1] (or flat A[(n + 1) * mask + k]) keeps the \(O(n^2)\) inner polynomial convolution contiguous in L1 cache, whereas A[n + 1][1 << n] can suffer TLB thrashing at \(n = 20\).

section: 24.3 Transcendental Operations on \(\mathcal{R}_n\) (\(\operatorname{inv}, \ln, \exp, P^\alpha\)), MSB Split & SPS Composition
text:
24.3 Transcendental Operations on \(\mathcal{R}_n\) (\(\operatorname{inv}, \ln, \exp, P^\alpha\)), MSB Split & SPS Composition
Because the Ranked Fast Zeta Transform is an algebra homomorphism from \(\mathcal{R}_n\) into \((K[t]/(t^{n+1}))^{2^n}\) (up to discarding higher-degree contamination via clean round-trips, or exact when every operation commutes with the projection modulo \(t^{|S|+1}\)), any formal power series operation on \(\mathcal{R}_n\) reduces to applying \(O(n^2)\) truncated 1D polynomial ODEs from Chapter 2 at each of the \(2^n\) masks!

Pointwise \(O(n^2)\) Truncated Polynomial ODEs in Ranked Zeta Space
A natural question arises: does a single Ranked FZT \(\to\) Pointwise \(\exp\)/\(\ln\) in \(K[t]/(t^{n+1})\) \(\to\) Ranked IFZT work without cleaning intermediate ranks? Yes! Why? Because for any formal power series \(G(y) = \sum_{d \ge 0} g_d y^d\) and any \(F(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{S \neq \varnothing} F_S \mathbf{x}^S \in \mathcal{R}_n\), if we replace each variable \(x_i\) with \(t x_i\) (which multiplies \(\mathbf{x}^S\) by \(t^{|S|}\)), then \(\mathbf{x}^T \cdot \mathbf{x}^R = 0\) for overlapping \(T \cap R \neq \varnothing\) still occurs strictly in powers of \(t\) with exponent \(|T| + |R| > |T \cup R|\). Thus, in the lifted ring \(K[t][x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}]\), for every mask \(S\), the lowest possible power of \(t\) that can produce the OR-union \(\bigcup_j T_j = S\) is \(t^{|S|}\), achieved if and only if the sets \(T_j\) are pairwise disjoint!
Therefore, at each mask \(M \in [0, 2^n - 1]\) independently, let \(p(t) = \widehat{F}_M(t) = \sum_{k=0}^n p_k t^k \in K[t]/(t^{n+1})\). We compute \(q(t) = \sum_{k=0}^n q_k t^k\) using the exact \(O(n^2)\) recurrences from Chapter 2:









Operation
Algebraic Hypothesis on \(F_\varnothing = p_0\)
Pointwise \(O(n^2)\) Recurrence for \(q_k\) (\(k = 1, \dots, n\))
Base Case \(q_0\)




\(Q = F^{-1}\)
\(p_0 \in K^\times\)
\(q_k = -p_0^{-1} \sum_{j=1}^k p_j q_{k-j}\)
\(q_0 = p_0^{-1}\)


\(Q = \ln F\)
\(p_0 = 1\), \(1, \dots, n \in K^\times\)
\(q_k = p_k - \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} j q_j p_{k-j}\)
\(q_0 = 0\)


\(Q = \exp F\)
\(p_0 = 0\), \(1, \dots, n \in K^\times\)
\(q_k = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^k j p_j q_{k-j}\)
\(q_0 = 1\)


\(Q = F^\alpha\)
\(p_0 = 1\), \(1, \dots, n \in K^\times\)
\(q_k = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^k \big((\alpha + 1)j - k\big) p_j q_{k-j}\)
\(q_0 = 1\)



After running the recurrence at all \(2^n\) masks, run ranked_fzt(Q, n, true) and extract \(Q_S = [t^{|S|}] Q_S(t)\)!


The Division-Free MSB Derivative Split (\(\exp\) and \(\ln\) in Any Characteristic)
Look closely at the table above: \(\ln F\) and \(\exp F\) via \(K[t]/(t^{n+1})\) ODEs appear to require \(1, 2, \dots, n \in K^\times\). Yet inside \(\mathcal{R}_n\), for any \(F\) with \(F_\varnothing = 0\), how can \(\exp(F) = \sum_{d=0}^n \frac{F^d}{d!}\) possibly require dividing by \(d!\) when multiplying \(d\) non-empty disjoint subsets \(T_1, \dots, T_d\) already counts each unordered partition \(\{T_1, \dots, T_d\}\) exactly \(d!\) times, canceling the \(d!\) in the denominator over \(\mathbb{Z}\)?!
Indeed, \(\exp(F)\) and \(\ln(1 + F)\) on \(\mathcal{R}_n\) are completely division-free! To see why—and to obtain an algorithm that is simultaneously \(2\times\) faster than full \(n\)-bit \(\exp/\ln\) and works over arbitrary commutative rings \(K\) (including \(\mathbb{F}_2\), \(\mathbb{Z}/2^{64}\mathbb{Z}\), and composite moduli)—isolate the highest-indexed variable \(x_v\).
Every \(F(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathcal{R}_{v+1}\) splits uniquely into terms not containing \(x_v\) and terms containing \(x_v\):
\[
F(\mathbf{x}) = F_0(\mathbf{x}) + x_v F_1(\mathbf{x}), \qquad F_0, F_1 \in \mathcal{R}_v.
\]
Because \(x_v^2 = 0\) in \(\mathcal{R}_{v+1}\), the Taylor series for \(\exp(x_v F_1)\) truncates linearly at \(1 + x_v F_1\)! Therefore:
\[
\exp(F_0 + x_v F_1) = \exp(F_0) \cdot \exp(x_v F_1) = \exp(F_0) + x_v \big(\exp(F_0) *_{\text{sub}} F_1\big).
\]
Let \(E_0 = \exp(F_0) \in \mathcal{R}_v\). Then transitioning from \(v\) variables to \(v+1\) variables requires only a single \(v\)-variable subset convolution \(E_0 *_{\text{sub}} F_1\)! Iterating \(v = 0, 1, \dots, n-1\) gives \(\exp(F)\) using only additions, subtractions, and multiplications in \(K\), with total work:
\[
\sum_{v=0}^{n-1} O(v^2 2^v) = O(n^2 2^n) \quad \text{(with half the constant factor of full $n$-bit $\exp$!)}.
\]
Inverting this relation for \(E = E_0 + x_v E_1 = \exp(F_0 + x_v F_1)\) with \(E_\varnothing = 1\) gives \(F_0 = \ln(E_0)\) and \(E_1 = E_0 *_{\text{sub}} F_1 \implies F_1 = E_0^{-1} *_{\text{sub}} E_1\), where \(E_0^{-1}\) needs only \(E_\varnothing = 1 \in K^\times\)!
// Division-free SPS exp via MSB split: works in ANY commutative ring K!
vector<mint> sps_exp_msb(const vector<mint>& F, int n) {
    vector<mint> E(1 << n); E[0] = 1;
    for (int v = 0; v < n; ++v) { // E[0..2^v-1] already holds exp(F_0)
        vector<mint> F1(F.begin() + (1 << v), F.begin() + (2 << v));
        vector<mint> E1 = subset_conv(vector<mint>(E.begin(), E.begin() + (1 << v)), F1, v);
        copy(E1.begin(), E1.end(), E.begin() + (1 << v));
    }
    return E;
}


Elegia’s \(O(n^2 2^n)\) SPS Composition \(G(F(\mathbf{x}))\) via Taylor Shift Pyramid
What if we need a general composition \(G(F(\mathbf{x})) = \sum_{d=0}^n g_d \frac{F(\mathbf{x})^d}{d!}\) where \(F_\varnothing = 0\) and the input array g[0..n] stores the exponential generating function (EGF) derivatives \(g_d = G^{(d)}(0) \in K\) (if \(G(y) = \sum_{d=0}^n c_d y^d\) is given in ordinary generating function (OGF) form, simply pass \(g_d = c_d \cdot d!\); for example, \(g_d = [d = c]\) extracts the single divided power \(\frac{F(\mathbf{x})^c}{c!}\) without dividing by \(c!\), and \(g_d = d!\) evaluates the geometric series \((1 - F(\mathbf{x}))^{-1} = \sum_{d=0}^n F(\mathbf{x})^d\) for ordered sequences of components)?






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Elegia’s Taylor Shift Pyramid




The Diagnostic Signal: You want to evaluate \(G(F(\mathbf{x})) = \sum_{d=0}^n g_d \frac{F(\mathbf{x})^d}{d!} \in \mathcal{R}_n\) for an arbitrary sequence \(g_0, \dots, g_n \in K\) and \(F_\varnothing = 0\), and either \(d!\) is non-invertible or you cannot express \(G(y)\) via \(\exp/\ln\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Write \(F(\mathbf{x}) = F^{(0)} + x_0 D_0 + x_1 D_1 + \dots + x_{n-1} D_{n-1}\), where \(D_k \in \mathcal{R}_k\) consists of the subsets in \(F\) whose maximum element (MSB) is \(k\): \(D_k(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{S \subseteq \{0, \dots, k-1\}} F_{S \cup \{k\}} \mathbf{x}^S\). Because \(x_k^2 = 0\), adding \(x_k D_k\) to the partial sum \(F_{\le k-1}\) shifts the argument of \(G\) by an infinitesimal \(x_k D_k\) whose square vanishes! By Taylor’s formula for \(G(y + \epsilon)\) with \(\epsilon^2 = 0\): \[
G^{(d)}\!\big(F_{\le k-1} + x_k D_k\big) = G^{(d)}\!\big(F_{\le k-1}\big) + x_k \, G^{(d+1)}\!\big(F_{\le k-1}\big) *_{\text{sub}} D_k.
\] Observe the index bounds: at step \(k\), each \(D_j\) for \(j \ge k\) contributes at least one new vertex, so if we still plan to differentiate \(d\) more times using variables \(\{k, \dots, n-1\}\), we only need \(0 \le d \le n - k\)! Moreover, at step \(k\), \(G^{(d)}(F_{\le k-1})\) only depends on variables \(\{0, \dots, k-1\}\), so it lives in \(\mathcal{R}_k\) (size \(2^k\))! Summing the cost of \(n - k\) subset convolutions of size \(2^k\) across \(k = 0, \dots, n-1\): \[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (n - k) \cdot k^2 2^k = O(n^2 2^n).
\]



// Elegia's O(n^2 2^n) SPS composition: g[d]=G^(d)(0) (EGF; pass c[d]*d! for OGF)
vector<mint> sps_compose(const vector<mint>& F, const vector<mint>& g, int n) {
    vector<vector<mint>> H(n + 1, vector<mint>(1));
    for (int d = 0; d <= n; ++d) H[d][0] = g[d];
    for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k) {
        vector<mint> Dk(F.begin() + (1 << k), F.begin() + (2 << k)); // MSB = k
        vector<vector<mint>> nxt(n - k, vector<mint>(2 << k));
        for (int d = 0; d < n - k; ++d) {
            auto prod = subset_conv(H[d + 1], Dk, k); // reuse Ranked FZT of Dk
            copy(H[d].begin(), H[d].end(), nxt[d].begin());
            copy(prod.begin(), prod.end(), nxt[d].begin() + (1 << k));
        } H.swap(nxt);
    }
    return H[0];
}


Pointed Vertex-by-Vertex Biconnected SPS \(\ln\) (#207 UOJ 94)
Taking \(C(\mathbf{x}) = \ln F(\mathbf{x})\) turns disconnected subgraphs \(F(\mathbf{x})\) into connected subgraphs \(C(\mathbf{x})\). How do we go one connectivity level deeper and strip away articulation points (cut vertices) to extract biconnected (2-vertex-connected) subgraphs on a fixed input graph \(G = (V, E)\)?
Suppose we fix a single vertex \(v \in V\) and look at all connected graphs on \(T \cup \{v\}\) (where \(T \subseteq V \setminus \{v\}\)). When is \(v\) an articulation point of a connected graph \(H\) on \(T \cup \{v\}\)? Precisely when deleting \(v\) splits \(H \setminus \{v\}\) into \(k \ge 2\) non-empty connected components on disjoint subsets \(T_1 \sqcup T_2 \sqcup \dots \sqcup T_k = T\), with each component independently attached to \(v\)!
Therefore, if we form the \((n-1)\)-variable pointed SPS at \(v\):
\[
C^{(v)}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{T \subseteq V \setminus \{v\}} C_{T \cup \{v\}} \mathbf{x}^T \in \mathcal{R}_{V \setminus \{v\}},
\]
then a graph on \(T \cup \{v\}\) is simply a disjoint union of \(v\)-blocks (connected graphs on \(T_i \cup \{v\}\) where \(v\) is not an articulation point)! Because the subsets \(T_i \subseteq V \setminus \{v\}\) are pairwise disjoint, taking the \((n-1)\)-variable subset logarithm
\[
\widetilde{C}^{(v)}(\mathbf{x}) = \ln C^{(v)}(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{in } \mathcal{R}_{V \setminus \{v\}}
\]
and writing its coefficients back into \(C_{T \cup \{v\}}\) exactingly strips away all graphs in which \(v\) is an articulation point, while leaving graphs where \(v \notin S\) untouched! Repeating this \((n-1)\)-variable SPS \(\ln\) sequentially for \(v = 0, 1, \dots, n-1\) eliminates every possible articulation point in \(O(n \cdot n^2 2^{n-1}) = O(n^3 2^n)\) time!






NoteRevisited — Two Faces of One Idea (#9): Species Composition vs. Vertex-by-Vertex SPS \(\ln\) for Biconnected Graphs



Compare our two journeys to biconnected graph enumeration across this textbook:

Chapter 12 ([Mas-1] #183 Luogu P5827 — 点双连通图计数): In Chapter 12, the ground set \(V = \{1, \dots, n\}\) was symmetric (we counted labeled biconnected graphs on \(K_n\)). Because all vertices were interchangeable, rooting at a vertex and decomposing into a set of blocks translated into a 1D compositional equation \(C'(x) = \exp\!\big(B'(x C'(x))\big)\), solved in \(O(n \log n)\) via Lagrange Inversion / Newton Iteration.
Chapter 24 ([Adv-2] #207 UOJ 94 — 胡策的统计): Here, the input is an arbitrary fixed graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(n \le 15\). Vertex symmetry is completely broken: each subset \(S \subseteq V\) has its own edge count \(E(S)\), so a 1D EGF in \(|S|\) cannot distinguish which vertices belong to \(S\). By lifting the EGF variable \(x\) to \(n\) square-free variables \(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \in \mathcal{R}_n\), the global species substitution \(B'(x C'(x))\) splits into \(n\) sequential pointed \((n-1)\)-variable logarithms \(\ln_{\mathcal{R}_{V \setminus \{v\}}} C^{(v)}(\mathbf{x})\), stripping articulation points one vertex at a time!




Hand-Checkable Trace: Stripping Cut-Vertex \(v = 1\) on Path Graph \(0 - 1 - 2\) (\(n = 3\))
Let \(V = \{0, 1, 2\}\) and suppose \(G\) is the path graph with edges \(\{0, 1\}\) and \(\{1, 2\}\).

Connected Subgraph SPS \(C(\mathbf{x})\): After the initial global subset logarithm \(C(\mathbf{x}) = \ln F(\mathbf{x})\), the non-empty connected induced subgraphs containing vertex \(v = 1\) are:

\(\{1\}\) (\(T = \varnothing \subseteq \{0, 2\}\)): \(1\) connected graph (\(C_{\{1\}} = 1\)).
\(\{0, 1\}\) (\(T = \{0\}\)): \(1\) connected graph (\(C_{\{0,1\}} = 1\)).
\(\{1, 2\}\) (\(T = \{2\}\)): \(1\) connected graph (\(C_{\{1,2\}} = 1\)).
\(\{0, 1, 2\}\) (\(T = \{0, 2\}\)): \(1\) connected graph, the path \(0 - 1 - 2\) (\(C_{\{0,1,2\}} = 1\)), in which \(v = 1\) is an articulation point!

Pointed SPS at \(v = 1\): In the \(2\)-variable ring \(\mathcal{R}_{\{0, 2\}} = K[x_0, x_2]/(x_0^2, x_2^2)\), the pointed series is: \[C^{(1)}(x_0, x_2) = C_{\{1\}} + C_{\{0,1\}} x_0 + C_{\{1,2\}} x_2 + C_{\{0,1,2\}} x_0 x_2 = 1 + x_0 + x_2 + x_0 x_2.\]
2-Variable Subset Logarithm: Let \(U = x_0 + x_2 + x_0 x_2\). Since \(x_0^2 = x_2^2 = 0\), we have \(U^2 = (x_0 + x_2)^2 = 2 x_0 x_2\) and \(U^3 = 0\). Therefore: \[\widetilde{C}^{(1)}(x_0, x_2) = \ln(1 + U) = U - \frac{1}{2}U^2 = (x_0 + x_2 + x_0 x_2) - \frac{1}{2}(2 x_0 x_2) = x_0 + x_2 + 0 \cdot x_0 x_2.\]
Verification: Writing \(\widetilde{C}^{(1)}\) back into \(C_{T \cup \{1\}}\) sets \(C_{\{0,1,2\}} = 0\) while preserving the single-edge blocks \(C_{\{0,1\}} = 1\) and \(C_{\{1,2\}} = 1\). The path \(0 - 1 - 2\) (whose cut-vertex is \(1\)) has been cleanly annihilated!







NoteAlgorithm Contract: Set Power Series Transcendental Engine (\(\ln, \exp, \Phi(F)\) & Pointed Biconnected \(\ln\))




Input: Set power series \(F \in \mathcal{R}_n\) of size \(2^n\) (and for general composition, EGF derivative coefficients \(g_0, \dots, g_n \in K\) representing \(\Phi(y) = \sum_{d=0}^n g_d \frac{y^d}{d!}\)).
Output: \(\ln F\), \(\exp F\), \(\Phi(F) \in \mathcal{R}_n\), or the biconnected subgraph SPS after \(n\) pointed \((n-1)\)-variable logarithms.
Algebraic Hypothesis:

MSB Derivative Split (\(\exp F, \ln F\)) & Elegia Composition \(\Phi(F)\): Requires \(F_\varnothing = 0\) for \(\exp F\) and \(\Phi(F)\), or \(F_\varnothing = 1\) for \(\ln F\). Completely division-free — valid over any commutative ring \(K\) regardless of characteristic!
Pointwise ODE in \(K[t]/(t^{n+1})\): Requires \(1, 2, \dots, n \in K^\times\) (\(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(p > n\)).

Complexity: \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time and \(O(n 2^n)\) space for \(\ln, \exp, \Phi(F)\) (with the MSB split achieving a \(\frac{1}{2}\times\) constant-factor speedup by avoiding the top-bit FZT); \(O(n^3 2^n)\) time for \(n\)-step pointed biconnected \(\ln\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases:

Non-Zero Constant Term (\(F_\varnothing \neq 0\)): \(\exp F\) and \(\Phi(F)\) require \(F_\varnothing = 0\) so that \(F\) is nilpotent (\(F^{n+1} = 0\) in \(\mathcal{R}_n\)). If \(F_\varnothing = c \neq 0\), shift the outer function by \(c\) or factor out \(\exp(c)\) before calling the engine.
EGF vs. OGF Coefficient Convention in sps_compose: Elegia’s Taylor shift pyramid evaluates \(\sum_{d=0}^n g_d \frac{F(\mathbf{x})^d}{d!}\). If your outer polynomial is given in OGF form \(\sum_{d=0}^n c_d y^d\), you must pass \(g_d = c_d \cdot d!\).
Single-Edge Graphs (\(|S| = 2\)) in Pointed Biconnected \(\ln\): A single edge \(K_2\) has no articulation point and remains non-zero after pointed vertex-by-vertex \(\ln\); if a problem defines biconnected subgraphs or cycles only on \(|S| \ge 3\), filter out \(|S| \le 2\) explicitly as dictated by the problem statement.
